title: Immune · Immunodeficiency disorders
meta: Mechanisms, genetics, infection patterns and laboratory findings of humoral, cellular, complement, phagocyte and NK-cell defects.

sections.heading: Antibody deficiencies: B-cell development, class switching and plasma-cell output
sections.html:
Antibody deficiencies are the most frequent primary immunodeficiencies seen in practice. They share one infection pattern: recurrent sinopulmonary infection with encapsulated, extracellular bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable and type b Haemophilus influenzae), plus a few organisms that antibody normally neutralises at mucosal or bloodstream stages: enteroviruses and Giardia. Viral infections in general, fungi and intracellular bacteria are handled normally because T-cell immunity is intact, unless the defect also removes T-cell help (hyper-IgM due to CD40L loss).

Why onset follows a timetable

Maternal IgG crosses the placenta through the neonatal Fc receptor, mostly in the third trimester, and decays with a half-life of about 3–4 weeks. The infant's own IgG production rises slowly, so total IgG reaches a physiological nadir at about 3–6 months. A complete B-cell defect is therefore silent at birth and declares itself in the second half of the first year. Premature infants start with less maternal IgG and have a deeper nadir.

[[figure:s23a-fig10]]

X-linked agammaglobulinemia (BTK)

Bruton tyrosine kinase transmits signals from the pre-B-cell receptor (μ heavy chain plus surrogate light chain). Without that signal, precursors stall at the pro-B/pre-B stage in the marrow, so circulating CD19+ B cells are below about 2% and every isotype is very low. Lymphoid tissue that is mostly B-cell follicles (tonsils, adenoids, lymph nodes) is tiny or absent. Boys present after 6 months with otitis, sinusitis, pneumonia, bacteremia and septic arthritis. Two infections are characteristic: chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis (echovirus, coxsackievirus), a slowly progressive encephalitis that reflects the central role of neutralising antibody in enterovirus clearance, and vaccine-associated paralytic polio after live oral polio vaccine. Neutrophils may be low during acute infection. T-cell numbers and function are normal.

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID)

CVID is a diagnosis of exclusion: low IgG together with low IgA and/or IgM, a poor specific antibody response to vaccines, and no secondary cause (drugs such as rituximab or anticonvulsants, protein loss, lymphoid malignancy). B cells are present in most patients, often with reduced class-switched memory B cells, so the lesion is a failure of terminal differentiation into antibody-secreting plasma cells rather than absent B cells. Most cases are polygenic or of unknown cause; monogenic contributors include TACI (TNFRSF13B) variants, ICOS, CD19 complex genes, NFKB1/NFKB2 and CTLA4 haploinsufficiency. Onset peaks in young adulthood, though it can appear in childhood after age 4.

CVID is as much a disorder of immune dysregulation as of deficiency. Beyond infections and bronchiectasis, patients develop autoimmune cytopenias (ITP and autoimmune hemolytic anemia), noncaseating granulomas in lung, liver and spleen, granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease, enteropathy that resembles celiac disease with absent plasma cells on biopsy, and a raised risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma and gastric adenocarcinoma.

Selective IgA deficiency

Serum IgA below 7 mg/dL with normal IgG and IgM in a person older than 4 years. It is the most common primary antibody defect, and most people with it are healthy, partly because pentameric IgM, which also carries a J chain, is transported across mucosa by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor and compensates as secretory IgM. A minority have recurrent sinopulmonary or gastrointestinal infection (including giardiasis), atopy, and autoimmunity such as celiac disease, thyroiditis and SLE. Some form IgG anti-IgA antibodies and can react to IgA in transfused plasma. Some families contain both IgA deficiency and CVID, and IgA deficiency can evolve into CVID.

Hyper-IgM syndromes: class-switch failures

Switching from IgM to IgG, IgA or IgE needs two things: a CD40 signal from CD40 ligand on activated CD4 T cells engaging CD40 on B cells, and the B-cell enzyme activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), which deaminates cytidine in switch-region and variable-region DNA to start class-switch recombination and somatic hypermutation. The phenotype depends on which piece is missing.

DefectInheritanceLymphoid tissueOpportunistic infectionDistinguishing points
CD40L (CD40LG)X-linked, most frequentSmall; no germinal centresYes: Pneumocystis, Cryptosporidium, histoplasmosisMacrophages also lack CD40 activation; neutropenia; cryptosporidial sclerosing cholangitis and liver or biliary cancer
CD40Autosomal recessiveSmallYesSame clinical picture as CD40L deficiency in either sex
AID (AICDA), UNGAutosomal recessiveEnlarged: giant germinal centres, lymphadenopathyNoPyogenic sinopulmonary and gut infections only; autoimmunity; no somatic hypermutation

In all forms IgM is normal or raised and IgG, IgA and IgE are very low. Expression of CD40L on activated T cells by flow cytometry separates the T-cell form from the B-intrinsic forms.

Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy and specific antibody deficiency

Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy is an exaggerated, prolonged physiological nadir: IgG (sometimes IgA) stays below the age-specific range beyond 6 months, but B-cell numbers are normal and responses to protein vaccines such as tetanus are usually adequate. Infections are mild, and levels normalise, typically by age 2–4 years. The diagnosis is confirmed in retrospect, once levels recover.

Specific antibody deficiency means normal IgG, IgA, IgM (and IgG subclasses) with a failure to make protective antibody to polysaccharide antigens. Pure polysaccharide antigens are T-cell independent type 2 antigens: they cross-link B-cell receptors and rely on marginal-zone and B1 B cells, without T-cell help. Children under about 2 years respond poorly to them even when healthy, so the diagnosis is only made after that age. Conjugate vaccines link the polysaccharide to a protein carrier, recruit T-cell help and work in infants and in many people with specific antibody deficiency.

Low immunoglobulins with normal B-cell numbers point away from X-linked agammaglobulinemia. A boy with near-absent CD19+ cells has a block in B-cell development; an adult with present B cells and poor plasma-cell output has CVID.

The infection list is the clue to the arm that is missing: encapsulated bacteria, enteroviruses and Giardia mean antibody; add Pneumocystis or Cryptosporidium and missing T-cell help (CD40L) must be considered.

Step 2 CK asks the next step: quantitative IgG, IgA and IgM with age-specific ranges first, then vaccine responses and B-cell enumeration, then IgG replacement for proven antibody failure.

sections.heading: Severe combined immunodeficiency and 22q11.2 deletion: failures of T-cell development
sections.html:
T cells coordinate almost all adaptive immunity: they kill virus-infected cells, activate macrophages against intracellular organisms and give B cells the help they need for class-switched, high-affinity antibody. A T-cell defect therefore produces a broader infection pattern than an antibody defect: severe or persistent viral infection (CMV, adenovirus, RSV, parainfluenza), mucocutaneous candidiasis, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, chronic diarrhea with failure to thrive, and disseminated infection from live vaccines (BCG, rotavirus, varicella). Because B cells also lose help, most severe T-cell defects behave as combined immunodeficiencies.

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)

SCID is defined by absent or very low autologous naive T cells. It is classified by which other lineages are present, which points to the mechanism.

GeneInheritancePhenotypeMechanism
IL2RG (common γ chain)X-linked; most frequent cause in boysT−B+NK−γc is shared by the receptors for IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15 and IL-21. Loss of IL-7 signalling stops thymocyte development; loss of IL-15 signalling stops NK development. B cells form but cannot make useful antibody without T help and IL-21.
JAK3Autosomal recessiveT−B+NK−JAK3 is the kinase bound to γc, so the phenotype copies X-linked SCID in either sex.
IL7R α chainAutosomal recessiveT−B+NK+T-cell development alone fails; IL-15 signalling and NK cells are spared.
RAG1, RAG2, DCLRE1C (Artemis)Autosomal recessiveT−B−NK+V(D)J recombination fails, so neither T-cell nor B-cell receptors form; NK cells need no rearranged receptor. Artemis loss also causes radiosensitivity.
ADAAutosomal recessiveT−B−NK−Adenosine deaminase loss lets deoxyadenosine build up and be phosphorylated to dATP, which inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and kills dividing lymphocytes. A systemic metabolic disease: costochondral cupping, sensorineural hearing loss, neurologic and hepatic involvement.

Infants look well at birth, then from a few weeks to months develop thrush, intractable diarrhea, failure to thrive and pneumonitis. The thymic shadow is absent and lymph nodes and tonsils are not palpable. Lymphopenia is a clue in most forms, but transplacental maternal T cells may engraft and cause a rash, hepatitis and eosinophilia that resemble graft-versus-host disease, and can make the T-cell count look misleadingly normal; these cells are memory phenotype and do not respond to mitogens.

Omenn syndrome results from hypomorphic (leaky) mutations, most often in RAG1/RAG2. A few oligoclonal T cells escape, expand and infiltrate tissues: generalized erythroderma, alopecia, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, eosinophilia and high IgE, with absent B cells. The skin is inflamed rather than infected, which explains why this is sometimes misread as severe eczema.

Newborn screening. T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) are episomal DNA circles cut out during TCR α-chain rearrangement. They do not replicate, so their number in a dried blood spot reflects recent thymic output. Low or absent TRECs flag SCID and other causes of T-cell lymphopenia (22q11.2 deletion, trisomy 21, prematurity, congenital heart surgery with thymectomy, chylothorax).

22q11.2 deletion syndrome: the thymic side

Hemizygous deletion of about 3 Mb including TBX1 disturbs development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches and the outflow tract. The immune effect ranges from normal to profoundly absent T cells. Most children have partial T-cell lymphopenia that improves over the first years, with normal B cells and immunoglobulin; some develop autoimmune cytopenias, thyroid disease and juvenile arthritis later. Under 1% have complete athymia, a SCID-like state treated with allogeneic cultured thymus tissue implantation. In a lymph node, the T-cell zone (paracortex) is depleted while follicles are preserved.

SCID with an apparently normal T-cell count: check the phenotype and function. Engrafted maternal T cells or Omenn clones are activated memory cells with poor mitogen responses, and TRECs remain low.

Read the lineage pattern as a mechanism: NK cells missing as well as T cells means γc/JAK3 or ADA; B cells missing with NK cells spared means a recombination defect.

On Step 2 CK, an infant with an abnormal TREC screen goes next to lymphocyte flow cytometry; confirmed SCID means no live vaccines, irradiated CMV-safe blood, Pneumocystis prophylaxis, IgG replacement and early hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

sections.heading: Syndromic and pathway-specific T-cell defects: WAS, A-T, IL-12/IFN-γ, Th17 and hyper-IgE
sections.html:
Some inborn errors of immunity affect a defined T-cell pathway or arrive within a recognisable syndrome. Each produces a narrower infection profile than SCID, and each is best remembered by the molecule that fails and the job that molecule does.

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)

X-linked loss of WAS protein, a hematopoietic regulator of actin polymerisation downstream of receptor signalling. Leukocytes cannot reorganise the cytoskeleton to form an immune synapse, migrate or kill; platelets are produced small and are cleared early. The clinical triad is microthrombocytopenia (low count and low mean platelet volume, with petechiae, bloody diarrhea or bleeding after circumcision), eczema and recurrent infection with encapsulated bacteria and herpesviruses. Antibody responses to polysaccharides are poor; IgM tends to be low and IgA and IgE high, while IgG is often normal. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, vasculitis and nephropathy are common, and EBV-associated B-cell lymphoma risk rises with age. Milder mutations cause X-linked thrombocytopenia with little immune disease, and gain-of-function mutations cause X-linked neutropenia.

Ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T)

Autosomal recessive loss of ATM, a kinase that senses DNA double-strand breaks and activates p53, checkpoint kinase 2 and repair. Lymphocytes are affected because V(D)J recombination and class switching generate double-strand breaks deliberately; the cerebellum is affected for reasons that are less clear. Gait ataxia appears when a child starts walking and progresses, followed by oculomotor apraxia, dysarthria and, at a few years of age, telangiectasias of the bulbar conjunctiva and ears. Serum α-fetoprotein is raised after infancy, a useful diagnostic clue. IgA, IgG2 and IgE are low and T-cell lymphopenia is common, with sinopulmonary infection and bronchiectasis. Cells are hypersensitive to ionizing radiation, and patients have a high risk of lymphoma and leukemia; carriers have a higher risk of breast cancer.

IL-12/IFN-γ axis defects (Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease)

Macrophages that ingest mycobacteria release IL-12, which acts through the IL-12 receptor on T and NK cells to drive IFN-γ; IFN-γ then signals back through the IFN-γ receptor and STAT1 to activate macrophage killing. Defects anywhere in this loop cause disseminated BCG, nontuberculous mycobacterial disease and nontyphoidal Salmonella, with normal resistance to most other organisms. The position of the defect changes therapy:

DefectSerum IFN-γResponse to recombinant IFN-γUsual course
IL-12 receptor β1 or IL-12 p40 (upstream)LowYes: the missing signal is suppliedMilder; often controlled with antimycobacterials and IFN-γ
Complete IFN-γ receptor 1 or 2 deficiencyHigh (unused ligand accumulates)No: no receptor to act onSevere early disease; hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
Partial IFN-γR1 or STAT1 loss of functionVariablePartialIntermediate

Th17 failures: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and hyper-IgE

IL-17A, IL-17F and IL-22 from Th17 cells recruit neutrophils to skin and mucosa and induce antimicrobial peptides from epithelium. Their loss causes persistent Candida infection of skin, nails and mucous membranes without invasive candidiasis.

  • Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC): most often due to STAT1 gain-of-function mutations, which tilt signalling away from Th17 development; also IL-17RA, IL-17F and RORC defects. STAT1 gain-of-function adds autoimmunity, aneurysms and bacterial and viral infections.
  • APECED (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy–candidiasis–ectodermal dystrophy): loss of AIRE stops thymic medullary epithelium from presenting tissue-restricted antigens, so autoreactive T cells escape negative selection. Patients make neutralising autoantibodies against IL-17 and IL-22, which explains the candidiasis, and develop hypoparathyroidism and adrenal insufficiency, plus enamel and nail dystrophy.
  • Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome: dominant-negative STAT3 mutations block IL-6 and IL-23 signalling and so Th17 differentiation. Recurrent staphylococcal skin abscesses with little heat or redness, staphylococcal pneumonias that heal with pneumatoceles, newborn-onset eczema, mucocutaneous candidiasis, very high IgE with eosinophilia, and connective-tissue features: retained primary teeth, a broad nose and coarse face, scoliosis, joint hyperextensibility and fractures after minor trauma.
  • DOCK8 deficiency (autosomal recessive hyper-IgE): DOCK8 regulates the actin cytoskeleton of lymphocytes, which die as they squeeze through tissue. Severe, extensive cutaneous viral infection (HSV, HPV, molluscum), severe food allergy and eczema, high IgE and early malignancy. It is a combined immunodeficiency, treated by transplantation.

A very high IgE is not specific. Severe atopic dermatitis alone can raise IgE into the thousands; the hyper-IgE syndromes are recognised by the abscess, pneumatocele and skeletal pattern (STAT3) or by the viral skin and allergy pattern (DOCK8).

A raised serum IFN-γ in a child with disseminated mycobacterial infection points to the receptor rather than to IL-12 signalling, and predicts that recombinant IFN-γ will not help.

Step 2 CK: in APECED, chronic candidiasis is often the first sign; screen periodically for hypocalcemia and adrenal insufficiency, which can be life-threatening if missed.

sections.heading: Complement deficiencies: pathway, regulator and drug-induced
sections.html:
Complement is a set of plasma proteins and membrane regulators that tag microbes for phagocytosis (C3b), recruit leukocytes (C3a, C5a), lyse some bacteria (the membrane attack complex) and clear immune complexes and apoptotic cells. Deficiencies are uncommon, but the clinical consequences follow directly from which function is lost, and the screening assays are designed around the pathway map.

[[figure:s23a-fig11]]

Early classical components (C1q, C1r/s, C4, C2): autoimmunity and pyogenic infection

C1q binds immune complexes and the surfaces of apoptotic cells. Classical-pathway activation then coats the debris with C4b and C3b so that it is carried on erythrocyte CR1 to the liver and spleen and removed quietly. When this fails, apoptotic nuclear material lingers, is taken up by dendritic cells and drives anti-nuclear autoimmunity. The risk of an SLE-like illness is graded by how early the block is: almost all people with complete C1q deficiency develop it, most with C4 deficiency, and a smaller fraction with C2 deficiency. The disease tends to start in childhood, with prominent photosensitive skin disease, and anti-dsDNA may be absent. The same patients have recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria, because classical-pathway C3b deposition on antibody-coated bacteria is impaired. C2 deficiency is the most frequent of these in people of European ancestry and may be detected only after invasive pneumococcal disease.

C3 deficiency: the hub

All three pathways converge on C3. Without it there is no opsonisation by C3b, no C5 convertase and no membrane attack complex. Infants have severe, recurrent pyogenic infections (pneumococcus, H. influenzae, Neisseria), and immune-complex glomerulonephritis (often membranoproliferative) is frequent. A functional C3 deficiency also results from losing a regulator: factor H or factor I deficiency lets the alternative pathway run unchecked in plasma, consuming C3 to very low levels.

Terminal components (C5–C9) and properdin: Neisseria

Gram-negative Neisseria have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane that the membrane attack complex can breach; for these organisms, lysis matters more than opsonisation. People missing any of C5 to C9 (C9 deficiency is mildest) have recurrent meningococcal infection, often first in adolescence, frequently with uncommon serogroups (Y, W, X), and disseminated gonococcal infection. Mortality per episode is paradoxically lower than in complement-sufficient hosts. Properdin, which stabilises the alternative-pathway C3 convertase, is X-linked; boys with properdin deficiency present with fulminant meningococcal disease, often fatal, and survivors have a low AH50 with a normal CH50.

Regulator defects

RegulatorNormal jobConsequence of loss
C1 inhibitor (SERPING1)Inactivates C1r, C1s, MASPs, plasma kallikrein and factor XIIaHereditary angioedema: kallikrein runs free and cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen to bradykinin; C4 is consumed by uncontrolled C1s
Factor HCofactor for factor I; displaces Bb from C3 convertase in plasma and on host surfacesComplete loss: C3 consumption, infection, C3 glomerulopathy. Mutations affecting surface binding: atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome
Factor ICleaves C3b and C4bSecondary C3 depletion and pyogenic infection; aHUS
CD55 (DAF), CD59 on cell membranesAccelerate convertase decay; block MAC insertionAcquired loss of GPI anchors (PIGA) in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria: intravascular hemolysis and thrombosis

Hereditary angioedema: mechanism and laboratory pattern

Autosomal dominant mutation of SERPING1 leaves half the normal C1 inhibitor; attacks follow when demand outstrips supply (trauma, dental work, infection, estrogen, ACE inhibitors). Bradykinin acting on endothelial B2 receptors widens interendothelial gaps, producing deep, non-pitting, non-pruritic swelling of skin, gut wall and larynx lasting 2–5 days, without urticaria, and resistant to antihistamines, glucocorticoids and epinephrine.

  • Type I (most cases): low C1-INH protein and low function.
  • Type II: normal or raised protein that is nonfunctional; function is low.
  • In both, C4 is low, even between attacks in most patients, while C1q is normal.
  • Acquired C1-INH deficiency (older adults, B-cell lymphoproliferative disease or autoantibodies to C1-INH) also lowers C1q.
  • HAE with normal C1-INH (factor XII, plasminogen and other variants) has normal C4 and C1-INH and is often estrogen-sensitive.

ACE-inhibitor angioedema is also bradykinin-mediated, because ACE (kininase II) degrades bradykinin, but complement tests are normal.

Drug-induced complement deficiency

Eculizumab and ravulizumab are humanised monoclonal antibodies that bind C5 and prevent its cleavage, blocking C5a and the membrane attack complex (used for PNH, aHUS, generalized myasthenia gravis and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder). They reproduce terminal complement deficiency, with a markedly raised risk of meningococcal disease, including from nongroupable strains, which vaccination does not fully remove.

Low C3 with normal C4 in a child with recurrent infection does not always mean primary C3 deficiency: consumption through factor H or factor I loss, or C3 nephritic factor, gives the same serum level.

C4 is the screening test for angioedema without hives; C1q separates hereditary (normal) from acquired (low) C1-INH deficiency.

sections.heading: Phagocyte and NK-cell defects: production, adhesion, granules, killing and cytotoxicity
sections.html:
Phagocytes (neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages) form the first line against bacteria and fungi in tissue. Their defects produce a recognisable picture: deep-seated bacterial and fungal infection of skin, lymph nodes, lung, liver and bone, often by Staphylococcus aureus, gram-negative rods and Aspergillus; gingivitis and periodontitis; and, in some disorders, poor pus formation or poor wound healing. Each step of neutrophil function (production, adhesion and migration, granule biology, oxidative killing) has its own disease.

Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD): oxidative killing

NADPH oxidase transfers electrons from NADPH to molecular oxygen inside the phagosome, generating superoxide; superoxide dismutase turns this into hydrogen peroxide, and myeloperoxidase uses H2O2 and chloride to make hypochlorous acid. The burst also drives ion fluxes that activate granule proteases. In CGD any of the oxidase subunits is absent: gp91phox (CYBB, X-linked, about two-thirds of cases, most severe), p47phox (NCF1, autosomal recessive, milder), p22phox, p67phox, p40phox, or EROS.

The classic teaching is that catalase-negative bacteria leak their own H2O2 into the phagosome and are killed with the host's myeloperoxidase, whereas catalase-producing organisms degrade it and survive. Whatever the full mechanism, the organisms are distinctive: S. aureus (liver abscess, lymphadenitis), Burkholderia cepacia complex (pneumonia, sepsis), Serratia marcescens (osteomyelitis), Nocardia and, the leading cause of death, invasive Aspergillus. Because microbes and debris persist, macrophages wall them off in granulomas, which also form without infection: gastric outlet and urinary tract obstruction and a Crohn-like colitis. Female carriers of X-linked CGD have a mosaic of normal and oxidase-negative neutrophils; those with skewed lyonisation and a small normal fraction can have infections, and many have photosensitive discoid-lupus-like lesions and aphthous ulcers.

Leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD): getting out of the vessel

TypeGene and proteinStep lostDistinctive features
LAD-1ITGB2: CD18, the β2 integrin chain of LFA-1 and Mac-1Firm adhesion to endothelial ICAM-1 and transmigrationDelayed umbilical cord separation and omphalitis; marked neutrophilia even without infection; necrotic, pus-poor ulcers; severe periodontitis; poor wound healing
LAD-2SLC35C1: Golgi GDP-fucose transporterSelectin-mediated rolling (sialyl Lewis X is fucosylated)Milder infections, neutrophilia, growth and intellectual disability; red cells lack H antigen (Bombay phenotype); some respond to oral fucose
LAD-3FERMT3: kindlin-3Inside-out activation of β1, β2 and β3 integrinsLAD-1 picture plus a Glanzmann-like platelet bleeding disorder

Chédiak-Higashi syndrome and other granule disorders

Autosomal recessive LYST mutations disturb the size and trafficking of lysosome-related organelles. Neutrophils, lymphocytes and other cells contain giant fused granules visible on the smear; phagosome–lysosome fusion and chemotaxis are poor, and neutropenia is frequent. Melanosome defects cause partial oculocutaneous albinism with silvery hair; platelet dense-granule defects cause easy bruising; and a progressive peripheral and central neuropathy appears in adolescence. Most patients without transplantation enter an accelerated phase, which is hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Myeloperoxidase deficiency is the most frequent inherited phagocyte defect; it is usually asymptomatic because the oxidative burst still kills, but some patients, especially those with diabetes, develop invasive candidiasis. Specific granule deficiency (C/EBPε) gives bilobed neutrophils lacking secondary granules.

Neutropenias of marrow origin

Severe congenital neutropenia gives an absolute neutrophil count below 500/mm3 from birth, with omphalitis, skin and deep abscesses, pneumonia, oral ulcers and gingivitis. The marrow shows maturation arrest at the promyelocyte–myelocyte stage. The commonest cause is a dominant ELANE mutation: misfolded neutrophil elastase triggers the unfolded protein response and apoptosis of myeloid precursors. HAX1 loss (autosomal recessive, the original Kostmann kindred) causes mitochondrial apoptosis and neurodevelopmental disease. The long-term risk is myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukemia. Cyclic neutropenia, also from ELANE mutations, oscillates with a period of about 21 days; nadirs of a few days bring fever, aphthous ulcers, pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy, with little leukemic risk.

NK-cell deficiency and familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis

NK cells kill virus-infected and stressed cells without prior sensitisation. Isolated NK-cell deficiency (for example, GATA2 haploinsufficiency or MCM4 mutation) causes severe or disseminated herpesvirus infection (varicella, CMV, HSV) and extensive HPV disease. GATA2 deficiency also removes monocytes, dendritic cells and B cells, adding nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, lymphedema and a high risk of myelodysplasia.

In familial HLH, cytotoxic T and NK cells recognise their target but cannot kill it, so the target cell (often an infected antigen-presenting cell) persists and keeps stimulating them. The result is unrelenting activation with massive IFN-γ release, macrophage activation and cytokine storm. Genes encode perforin (PRF1), which forms pores for granzyme entry, or the machinery that docks and fuses cytotoxic granules with the membrane (UNC13D, STX11, STXBP2); related syndromes include Chédiak-Higashi, Griscelli type 2 (RAB27A) and X-linked lymphoproliferative disease (SH2D1A, XIAP), the latter triggered by EBV. Infants present with prolonged fever, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, very high ferritin, hypertriglyceridemia, hypofibrinogenemia, raised soluble CD25 and reduced NK-cell cytotoxicity.

Neutrophilia does not exclude a neutrophil disorder. In LAD-1 the count is high precisely because cells cannot leave the vessels, yet tissue infections lack pus.

Group phagocyte disorders by step: production (congenital and cyclic neutropenia), exit (LAD), granules (Chédiak-Higashi, MPO), killing (CGD). The step predicts the test: count, CD18/CD15s flow, smear, DHR.

Step 2 CK management: CGD gets lifelong TMP-SMX and itraconazole with optional IFN-γ; congenital neutropenia gets G-CSF and marrow surveillance; familial HLH gets dexamethasone and etoposide, then transplantation.

title: Immune · Immunodeficiency: diagnosis and management
meta: When to suspect an inborn error of immunity, stepwise testing, IgG replacement, transplantation, prophylaxis, vaccines and blood-product safety, with paediatric emphasis.

sections.heading: Recurrent infections and antibody deficiency: workup and IgG replacement
sections.html:
Most children with frequent infections are immunologically normal: young children in group childcare can have 6–8 viral respiratory infections a year. The task is to recognise the pattern that is not normal and to test in a sensible order, starting with cheap screening tests that match the infections seen.

When to suspect a primary immunodeficiency

  • Infections that are severe (meningitis, bacteremia, osteomyelitis, deep abscess), persistent (chronic otitis or sinusitis despite adequate courses), recurrent (two or more pneumonias in a year, or pneumonias in different lobes), unusual (opportunistic or low-virulence organisms) or needing IV antibiotics to clear.
  • Complications of live vaccines, failure to thrive with chronic diarrhea, or a family history of immunodeficiency or of unexplained early deaths.
  • Infection plus autoimmunity, granulomas or lymphoproliferation (CVID, APDS, CTLA4 and similar dysregulation disorders).
  • Bronchiectasis without cystic fibrosis.

Before testing, exclude common secondary causes: HIV, protein loss (nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy, burns), lymphoid malignancy, drugs (rituximab and other B-cell–depleting agents, glucocorticoids, antiseizure drugs such as phenytoin and carbamazepine), and anatomical problems (cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, foreign body, allergic rhinitis with sinus obstruction).

[[figure:s23a-fig12]]

Stepwise workup of the antibody pattern

  1. CBC with differential and quantitative IgG, IgA and IgM, interpreted against age-specific ranges (values in infants are far below adult values). IgE is added when atopy or hyper-IgE is considered.
  2. Specific antibody function: titers to protein antigens (tetanus, diphtheria) and to pneumococcal polysaccharide serotypes, measured before and 4–8 weeks after a pure polysaccharide (PPSV23) challenge in patients older than 2 years. Specific antibody testing is essential when IgG is only modestly low or normal; it must be done before IgG replacement, because infused IgG contains these antibodies and makes results uninterpretable.
  3. B-cell enumeration (CD19 or CD20) by flow cytometry, plus T-cell and NK-cell subsets if the history is broader. Absent B cells in a boy: test BTK. Present B cells: assess class-switched memory B cells, and consider CVID or hyper-IgM.
  4. Genetic testing by an immunodeficiency gene panel or exome, which now identifies a monogenic cause in a sizeable minority of CVID-like patients and directs targeted treatment (for example, abatacept for CTLA4 or LRBA defects, leniolisib for activated PI3Kδ syndrome).

Interpreting the main patterns

PatternIg levelsVaccine responseB cellsManagement
X-linked agammaglobulinemiaAll very lowAbsentBelow 2%Lifelong IgG replacement; no live oral polio vaccine; treat chronic sinus disease and bronchiectasis
CVID (age 4 years or older)Low IgG plus low IgA and/or IgMPoorUsually presentIgG replacement; screen for autoimmune cytopenias, lung disease (CT, spirometry), liver disease and lymphoma
Selective IgA deficiencyIgA below 7 mg/dL, others normalNormalNormalTreat infections; IgG replacement not indicated unless a proven additional antibody defect; blood-product precautions if anti-IgA reactions
Specific antibody deficiency (over 2 years)NormalPoor to polysaccharide; normal to proteinNormalConjugate pneumococcal vaccination, prompt or prophylactic antibiotics; IgG replacement if infections persist
Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancyLow IgG for ageUsually normal to proteinNormalObservation, treat infections, continue routine vaccines, repeat levels in 6–12 months

Immunoglobulin replacement

Pooled human IgG is given intravenously (IVIG, typically every 3–4 weeks) or subcutaneously (SCIG, weekly or every other week, often at home, or as facilitated SCIG with hyaluronidase every 3–4 weeks). The starting dose for primary antibody deficiency is about 400–600 mg/kg per 4 weeks, adjusted to clinical response rather than to a single trough target; patients with bronchiectasis usually need higher troughs. Indications are proven failure of antibody production (XLA, CVID, hyper-IgM, SCID, severe specific antibody deficiency with infections despite prophylaxis).

Adverse effectRoute and timingResponse
Headache, chills, myalgia, flushingIV, during or soon after infusion, especially first infusions or during active infectionSlow the rate, premedicate, hydrate; switch to SCIG if persistent
Aseptic meningitisIV, high doses, within 24–48 hoursAnalgesia, hydration; SCIG
Thrombosis (stroke, MI, VTE)Mostly IV high doses; older age, immobilityHydrate, infuse slowly, consider SCIG
Acute kidney injuryIV, sucrose-stabilised productsUse non-sucrose products, monitor creatinine
HemolysisIV, high doses, non-O blood groups (anti-A/B in product)Monitor hemoglobin
Local swelling and rednessSubcutaneousExpected; lessens with continued use

Vaccines, transfusion and other measures

  • Patients with severe antibody deficiency do not receive live oral polio vaccine, and other live vaccines are generally withheld; most patients on IgG replacement receive passive protection, and response to vaccines is unreliable. Inactivated vaccines, including yearly inactivated influenza vaccine, are safe. Household contacts should be fully vaccinated.
  • In selective IgA deficiency with a history of anaphylaxis to blood products and anti-IgA antibodies, give washed red cells or platelets and plasma from IgA-deficient donors; for future elective needs, consider autologous donation.
  • In IgA deficiency, IgA-based celiac serology is falsely negative: use IgG-based tests (tissue transglutaminase IgG or deamidated gliadin peptide IgG).
  • CD40L deficiency: Pneumocystis prophylaxis, boiled or filtered drinking water to limit Cryptosporidium, liver surveillance, and early hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which offers the best long-term outcome.

Checking vaccine titers in a patient already on IVIG measures the donors' antibodies, not the patient's. Specific antibody testing must precede replacement, or wait several months after it stops.

Selective IgA deficiency is not a reason to give IVIG: products contain little IgA and cannot replace secretory IgA, and the IgA they contain can provoke reactions in sensitised patients.

sections.heading: Cellular and combined immunodeficiency: newborn screening, protection and definitive therapy
sections.html:
Cellular and combined defects are the immunodeficiencies most likely to kill an infant before diagnosis, and the ones in which ordinary interventions (a live vaccine, an unirradiated transfusion) can cause fatal harm. Early recognition, protection from iatrogenic injury and timely definitive therapy are the priorities.

Newborn screening and the infant with low TRECs

Every US state screens newborn dried blood spots for T-cell receptor excision circles. An absent or low TREC result is followed by lymphocyte flow cytometry on peripheral blood: CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19 or CD20, CD16/56, and the naive T-cell marker CD45RA, with T-cell proliferation to mitogens when T cells are present. Typical SCID has fewer than 300 autologous T cells/mm3 with absent proliferation. Other causes of low TRECs are 22q11.2 deletion, trisomy 21, CHARGE syndrome, prematurity, and T-cell loss into chylous effusions or after cardiac surgery.

Protecting the infant with SCID

  • No live vaccines: rotavirus vaccine, which is due at 2 months, is contraindicated, and BCG is contraindicated where it is given at birth. Inactivated vaccines are of little use and are deferred.
  • Blood products: irradiated (to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease), leukoreduced and CMV-safe (CMV-seronegative or leukoreduced) cellular products.
  • Infection prophylaxis: Pneumocystis prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole from about 4 weeks of age, IgG replacement, antifungal prophylaxis per centre protocol, and protective isolation.
  • Breastfeeding: withheld until the mother's CMV status is known, because breast milk transmits CMV.

Definitive therapy

Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is curative for most forms of SCID. Survival is highest when it is done in the first 3.5 months of life and before infection, which is why newborn screening has improved outcomes so much. A matched sibling donor gives the best results, but haploidentical parental and matched unrelated donors are used. For ADA-SCID, PEG-conjugated ADA enzyme replacement (elapegademase) stabilises the infant until transplantation, and autologous gene therapy is an established alternative at specialist centres. Gene therapy for X-linked SCID is used in trials.

22q11.2 deletion syndrome

Suspect it in an infant with a conotruncal heart defect (interrupted aortic arch type B, truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot), hypocalcemia, cleft palate or velopharyngeal insufficiency, or a low TREC. Confirm with chromosomal microarray or targeted FISH/MLPA. Immunologic evaluation by flow cytometry decides immune precautions:

  • Until T-cell counts are known, transfuse only irradiated, CMV-safe cellular products, which matters because many infants go to cardiac surgery early, and hold live vaccines.
  • Partial deletion phenotype with adequate CD4 and CD8 counts and normal mitogen response: routine vaccines, including MMR and varicella at the usual age.
  • Complete athymia: managed like SCID; cultured thymus tissue implantation is the treatment of choice.
  • Lifelong: calcium monitoring (especially during illness, surgery and puberty), hearing, speech and feeding support, and screening for autoimmune disease and psychiatric illness (including schizophrenia) in adolescence and adulthood.

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome

Consider it in a boy with petechiae or bloody stools in the newborn period plus eczema, and confirm small platelets (low mean platelet volume) on the smear and analyser, then flow cytometry for WAS protein and WAS sequencing. Management bridges to transplantation: IgG replacement, antibiotic prophylaxis, platelet transfusions for bleeding (irradiated), eczema care. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is curative and is best done early. Splenectomy raises the platelet count but greatly increases overwhelming sepsis and is avoided where transplantation is possible; thrombopoietin receptor agonists are a bridge in some patients.

Ataxia-telangiectasia

The diagnosis is usually suspected in a toddler with progressive gait ataxia before telangiectasias are visible. A raised serum α-fetoprotein after the first year of life is the most useful first test; genetic testing of ATM confirms it. Management is supportive and preventive: IgG replacement if antibody production fails, airway clearance for bronchiectasis, pulmonary and nutritional care, and malignancy vigilance. Because cells are hypersensitive to ionizing radiation, minimise diagnostic radiation (prefer ultrasound and MRI) and adjust chemotherapy and radiotherapy if a lymphoma develops. Carriers should be told of their raised breast-cancer risk.

CMC, APECED and the hyper-IgE syndromes

  • Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis: treat with azoles (fluconazole, then others if resistance develops). STAT1 gain-of-function disease may respond to JAK inhibitors; transplantation is reserved for severe disease.
  • APECED: candidiasis is usually the first sign, followed by hypoparathyroidism and adrenal insufficiency, often in that order. Check calcium, phosphate, PTH, morning cortisol and ACTH at diagnosis and at intervals, and look for autoimmune hepatitis, pneumonitis and other organ involvement; anti-interferon autoantibodies are a diagnostic clue.
  • STAT3 hyper-IgE: daily anti-staphylococcal prophylaxis (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is standard), skin care with emollients and dilute bleach baths, prompt drainage of abscesses, and aggressive treatment of pneumonia to prevent pneumatoceles, which become infected with Pseudomonas and Aspergillus. Surgery on pneumatoceles has a high complication rate. Some patients need IgG replacement.
  • DOCK8 deficiency: hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, given the high risk of death from infection and malignancy.

A household with an infant who has SCID still vaccinates its other members, including MMR and varicella; the infant is protected by immunity around it, while the infant receives no live vaccine.

Directed blood donation from relatives raises, not lowers, the risk of transfusion-associated GVHD because of shared HLA haplotypes. Irradiate every cellular product given to an infant with known or suspected T-cell deficiency.

sections.heading: Complement deficiency, hereditary angioedema and C5 inhibitors: testing and treatment
sections.html:
Complement disorders reach clinicians in four ways: recurrent or unusual Neisseria infection, a lupus-like illness in a child, recurrent angioedema without hives, and planned treatment with a C5 inhibitor. Each has its own first test and its own preventive plan.

Screening for a complement deficiency

  • Test with CH50 (classical pathway lytic function) and AH50 (alternative pathway), plus C3 and C4. Test when well, at least a few weeks after infection, because acute illness consumes complement.
  • A CH50 near zero suggests a missing component; then measure single components according to the pattern (both low: C3, C5–C9; CH50 low only: C1q, C2, C4; AH50 low only: factor B, factor D, properdin).
  • Complement is heat-labile: a low result from a sample that waited at room temperature should be repeated on a correctly handled specimen before further testing.

Indications include a single episode of meningococcal disease due to an uncommon serogroup, recurrent neisserial disease or a family history; invasive pneumococcal or H. influenzae infection with normal immunoglobulins and spleen; and SLE beginning in childhood or with a strong family history.

Prevention and management of complement deficiency

  • Terminal component, properdin, C3, factor H or factor I deficiency: quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate (MenACWY) and serogroup B (MenB) vaccines with booster doses while risk persists, plus pneumococcal and H. influenzae type b vaccination. Vaccination does not fully protect; give written instructions to seek care for fever, and consider antibiotic prophylaxis in selected patients.
  • Test siblings: autosomal recessive (most components) or X-linked (properdin) inheritance.
  • Early classical deficiency with SLE: standard lupus therapy (hydroxychloroquine, immunosuppressants). C1q deficiency can be corrected by hematopoietic stem cell transplantation because C1q is made by monocyte-derived cells; plasma infusions have been used for severe disease.
  • Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome from complement dysregulation: C5 inhibition with eculizumab or ravulizumab is the treatment of choice; plasma exchange may be started while ADAMTS13 and STEC results are awaited.
[[figure:s23a-fig11]]

Angioedema without urticaria: the workup

First separate mast-cell (histaminergic) angioedema, which comes with hives or pruritus, responds to antihistamines and glucocorticoids, and in anaphylaxis needs epinephrine, from bradykinin-mediated angioedema, which has no hives, evolves over hours, lasts 2–5 days, and causes abdominal attacks that mimic an acute abdomen.

ConditionC4C1-INH levelC1-INH functionC1qContext
HAE type ILowLowLowNormalFamily history, onset in childhood or adolescence
HAE type IILowNormal or highLowNormalAs type I
Acquired C1-INH deficiencyLowLowLowLowOnset after about 40 years; B-cell lymphoproliferative disease, MGUS, autoantibodies
HAE with normal C1-INHNormalNormalNormalNormalMostly women, estrogen-triggered; genetic testing (F12, PLG and others)
ACE-inhibitor angioedemaNormalNormalNormalNormalFace, lips and tongue; any time during therapy; higher risk in Black patients

The best initial test is C4; if low (or clinical suspicion is high), measure C1-INH antigen and function. A low C1q in an older adult prompts a search for lymphoma or monoclonal gammopathy (serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, free light chains, CT and hematology review).

Treating hereditary angioedema

Every attack involving the face or throat is treated early, and the airway takes priority: a patient with voice change, stridor or dysphagia needs a team ready for intubation or surgical airway. Antihistamines, glucocorticoids and epinephrine are not effective.

  • On-demand therapy (each patient should carry enough for two attacks): IV plasma-derived C1-INH concentrate, IV recombinant C1-INH (not for those allergic to rabbits), subcutaneous icatibant (bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist; self-administered), or subcutaneous ecallantide (plasma kallikrein inhibitor; given by a clinician because of anaphylaxis risk). Fresh frozen plasma is a fallback only when none is available, because it also supplies substrate (kininogen).
  • Short-term prophylaxis before dental work, endoscopy, intubation or surgery: plasma-derived C1-INH concentrate 1–6 hours before the procedure, with on-demand therapy at hand.
  • Long-term prophylaxis (frequent or severe attacks, by shared decision): subcutaneous plasma-derived C1-INH, lanadelumab (monoclonal antibody against plasma kallikrein), or oral berotralstat (kallikrein inhibitor). Attenuated androgens (danazol) are older second-line options with hepatic, lipid, virilising and growth effects and are avoided in children and pregnancy; tranexamic acid is less effective.
  • Avoid estrogen-containing contraceptives and hormone therapy and ACE inhibitors; progestin-only methods are acceptable.
  • Pregnancy and children: plasma-derived C1-INH is the preferred agent for treatment and prophylaxis. Test at-risk children of affected parents; C4 and C1-INH values are unreliable in the first year, so repeat or use genetic testing.

ACE-inhibitor angioedema

Stop the ACE inhibitor permanently and protect the airway; monitor in a setting that allows intubation. HAE-specific drugs have not proven reliably effective. Do not switch to another ACE inhibitor or to sacubitril-valsartan (neprilysin inhibition also raises bradykinin). An angiotensin receptor blocker carries a small risk and can be used with caution if strongly indicated; otherwise choose another class (calcium-channel blocker, thiazide). Swelling can recur for weeks after the drug is stopped.

Patients starting a C5 inhibitor

Eculizumab, ravulizumab and related terminal complement inhibitors carry a boxed warning for life-threatening meningococcal infection. Give MenACWY and MenB vaccines at least 2 weeks before the first dose; if treatment cannot wait, start the drug with antibacterial prophylaxis until 2 weeks after vaccination. Revaccinate per schedule while on therapy, and teach patients to seek emergency care for fever, as vaccination lowers but does not remove the risk.

Swelling of the tongue in a patient on lisinopril for years is still ACE-inhibitor angioedema: the reaction can start at any time, not only in the first weeks.

Normal C4 during an attack virtually excludes HAE types I and II; a low C4 between attacks is typical.

sections.heading: Phagocyte, neutropenia, NK and HLH disorders: diagnosis and management
sections.html:
A child with skin and deep abscesses, unusual organisms, gingivitis or poor wound healing needs evaluation of neutrophil number and function. A CBC with differential is the first test in all of these; the pattern of infection and the neutrophil count then steer the next test.

Chronic granulomatous disease

Suspect CGD with staphylococcal liver abscess, suppurative lymphadenitis, Serratia osteomyelitis, Burkholderia pneumonia, invasive aspergillosis or Nocardia infection, and with granulomatous obstruction or colitis in a child. Diagnose with the dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometric oxidative burst test, then genetic testing to identify the subunit (X-linked CYBB versus autosomal recessive forms, which differ in severity and family counselling). Female relatives of an X-linked patient should have DHR testing to identify carriers.

Long-term management:

  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole daily as antibacterial prophylaxis.
  • Itraconazole daily as antifungal prophylaxis (posaconazole as an alternative); this has cut deaths from Aspergillus.
  • Interferon-γ subcutaneously three times weekly lowers serious infections in many centres; side effects are fever and flu-like symptoms.
  • Avoid exposure to decaying organic matter (mulch, compost, hay, construction dust).
  • Vaccines: live bacterial vaccines (BCG, oral typhoid) are contraindicated; live viral vaccines and all inactivated vaccines are given routinely.
  • Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is curative and is increasingly offered early, especially in X-linked disease; gene therapy is under study.

Infections need prolonged, often surgical treatment (liver abscesses commonly need drainage plus glucocorticoids). Granulomatous complications are inflammatory and respond to glucocorticoids; CGD colitis may need further immunomodulation, with caution about anti-TNF agents because of severe infections.

Myeloperoxidase deficiency can give a reduced DHR signal because the dye depends partly on peroxidase activity. A low DHR with a normal NBT or a normal oxidase assay, and absent peroxidase staining, means MPO deficiency rather than CGD.

Leukocyte adhesion deficiency

Suspect LAD-1 in an infant with delayed separation of the umbilical cord (beyond about 3 weeks), omphalitis, a persistently high neutrophil count, and infections or ulcers that do not form pus; older children have severe periodontitis and early tooth loss. Confirm by flow cytometry for CD18 and CD11 expression on leukocytes (CD15s, sialyl Lewis X, for LAD-2). Severe LAD-1 is fatal in childhood without hematopoietic stem cell transplantation; milder forms are managed with meticulous dental care and prompt, prolonged antibiotics.

Chédiak-Higashi syndrome

A peripheral smear showing giant granules in neutrophils, with partial albinism, confirms the suspicion; LYST testing follows. Treat infections promptly, and plan early hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which prevents the accelerated (HLH) phase and corrects the immune and bleeding defects but does not halt the neurologic decline.

Severe congenital and cyclic neutropenia

  • Persistent ANC below 500/mm3 in an infant with omphalitis, abscesses or oral ulcers: repeat counts, test for maternal alloantibodies in the neonate (alloimmune neonatal neutropenia resolves by a few months), then bone marrow aspirate (promyelocyte–myelocyte arrest) and genetic testing (ELANE, HAX1, others). Screen for Shwachman-Diamond syndrome when there is steatorrhea or skeletal disease.
  • Treatment: daily subcutaneous G-CSF (filgrastim), titrated to an ANC that prevents infection; most patients respond. Yearly marrow examination with cytogenetics and testing for acquired CSF3R mutations or monosomy 7 detects transformation to MDS or AML. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for G-CSF nonresponders, very high G-CSF requirements, or malignant transformation.
  • Cyclic neutropenia: periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy recurring about every 3 weeks. A single normal count does not exclude it; obtain serial CBCs two or three times a week for about 6 weeks to document cycles. G-CSF shortens nadirs and reduces symptoms; malignant transformation is uncommon. Other periodic-fever syndromes (PFAPA) have normal neutrophil counts.

NK-cell deficiency and GATA2 deficiency

Suspect NK deficiency in a patient with severe varicella, disseminated CMV or HSV, or extensive warts. Flow cytometry (CD16/CD56 subsets) and NK cytotoxicity assays guide diagnosis. GATA2 deficiency (monocytopenia, B and NK lymphopenia, disseminated nontuberculous mycobacteria, HPV, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis) carries a high lifetime risk of myelodysplasia and AML; marrow surveillance and early transplantation are standard. HPV vaccination and prompt treatment of mycobacterial infection are part of care before transplant.

Familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis

An infant with prolonged fever, hepatosplenomegaly and cytopenias must be evaluated quickly, because untreated familial HLH is fatal. The HLH-2004 criteria require a molecular diagnosis or at least 5 of: fever; splenomegaly; cytopenias of at least two lineages; hypertriglyceridemia and/or hypofibrinogenemia; hemophagocytosis in marrow, spleen or nodes; low or absent NK-cell activity; ferritin of 500 ng/mL or more; and raised soluble CD25 (soluble IL-2 receptor). Very high ferritin in a child is especially suggestive. Look for triggers (EBV, CMV, other infections, malignancy) and perform flow cytometric screening (perforin expression, CD107a degranulation, SAP and XIAP) while genetic testing proceeds.

  • Induction: dexamethasone plus etoposide (HLH-94 based), with intrathecal methotrexate and hydrocortisone for CNS disease; treat the trigger (for EBV, rituximab is often added).
  • Refractory or recurrent primary HLH: emapalumab (anti–IFN-γ monoclonal antibody) or other salvage, by specialist teams.
  • Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only cure for familial HLH and is performed once the disease is controlled; affected siblings should be tested and transplanted before HLH develops.
  • Supportive care: transfusions, infection prophylaxis (including Pneumocystis and antifungal), and close monitoring for bleeding with low fibrinogen.

Transplantation is the definitive option for severe phagocyte and cytotoxicity disorders (CGD, severe LAD-1, Chédiak-Higashi, G-CSF-refractory congenital neutropenia, GATA2 deficiency, familial HLH). Cyclic neutropenia and myeloperoxidase deficiency are managed without it.
