sections.heading: HIV-1 and HIV-2: virology, life cycle and immunopathogenesis
sections.html:
HIV is an enveloped lentivirus in the retrovirus family. Each virion carries two copies of positive-sense single-stranded RNA plus three enzymes packaged from the pol gene: reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease. The genome has three structural genes and several accessory genes, and almost every one of them maps to a drug target or a diagnostic test.

GeneProductWhy it matters
gagp24 capsid, p17 matrix, nucleocapsidp24 is the antigen detected by 4th-generation screening tests; capsid is the target of lenacapavir
polReverse transcriptase, integrase, proteaseTargets of NRTIs/NNRTIs, INSTIs and PIs
envgp160, cleaved by a host Golgi protease into gp120 and gp41gp120 binds CD4 and the coreceptor; gp41 drives fusion (enfuvirtide target)
tat, revTranscriptional transactivator; nuclear export of unspliced RNANeeded for high-level viral gene expression
nefDown-regulates MHC class I and CD4Helps infected cells escape CD8 T cells
vifTargets host APOBEC3G for degradationWithout Vif, APOBEC3G hypermutates viral DNA

Life cycle

[[figure:s23a-fig20]]
  1. Attachment. gp120 binds CD4 on helper T cells, macrophages and dendritic cells.
  2. Coreceptor binding. A conformational change exposes a site for a chemokine receptor: CCR5 (R5 virus, predominant early in infection and transmitted between people) or CXCR4 (X4 virus, which emerges later in some patients and is linked to faster CD4 loss). People homozygous for the CCR5-Δ32 deletion lack surface CCR5 and are highly resistant to R5 virus.
  3. Fusion. gp41 folds into a hairpin that pulls the viral and cell membranes together.
  4. Reverse transcription. Reverse transcriptase (an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase with RNase H activity) makes double-stranded DNA. It has no proofreading, so mutations accumulate rapidly; this is the basis of drug resistance and of the need for combination therapy.
  5. Integration. Integrase cuts the viral DNA ends and performs strand transfer into host chromosomal DNA. The integrated provirus is permanent.
  6. Transcription and translation by host enzymes, boosted by Tat and Rev.
  7. Assembly and budding at the plasma membrane.
  8. Maturation. Viral protease cleaves the Gag and Gag-Pol polyproteins after budding; without it, virions are immature and noninfectious.

HIV-1 versus HIV-2

HIV-2 is concentrated in West Africa. It has lower viral loads, slower CD4 decline and lower transmission rates. It is intrinsically resistant to NNRTIs and to enfuvirtide, and some protease inhibitors are less active; INSTIs and NRTIs work. The HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay in the screening algorithm is what identifies it, and standard HIV-1 RNA assays do not quantify HIV-2.

Immunopathogenesis

Within the first weeks, HIV replicates explosively and destroys a large share of CCR5-expressing memory CD4 T cells in gut-associated lymphoid tissue, long before blood CD4 counts fall much. Plasma RNA peaks (often millions of copies/mL), and the patient may have the acute retroviral syndrome. CD8 cytotoxic T cells and, later, antibodies bring the viral load down to a set point; a higher set point predicts faster progression.

During clinical latency, the virus is not latent: billions of virions are produced and cleared daily, follicular dendritic cells in lymph nodes trap virus, and CD4 cells are lost through direct cytopathic effect, pyroptosis of abortively infected cells, CD8 killing and chronic immune activation (microbial translocation across the damaged gut wall). Untreated, CD4 counts decline over years. AIDS is defined by a CD4 count below 200/mm3, a CD4 percentage below 14%, or an AIDS-defining illness.

A small pool of resting memory CD4 T cells carries integrated, transcriptionally silent provirus. Antiretroviral drugs act only on replicating virus, so this reservoir survives years of suppression and reseeds viremia within weeks if therapy stops. That is why ART is lifelong.

Immune features of advanced HIV: CD4 lymphopenia with an inverted CD4:CD8 ratio, polyclonal B-cell activation with hypergammaglobulinemia yet poor specific antibody responses, cutaneous anergy (false-negative tuberculin test) and loss of granuloma formation.

Infants born to people with HIV carry maternal IgG anti-HIV antibody for up to about 18 months. Antibody tests cannot diagnose infant infection; nucleic acid tests are required.

Step 2 CK turns each life-cycle step into a management question: which assay detects which stage of infection, and why a coreceptor tropism assay is needed before maraviroc.

sections.heading: Antiretroviral pharmacology and HIV-associated organ disease
sections.html:
Modern ART combines drugs that hit different steps of the life cycle so that no single mutation confers resistance. Learn each class by mechanism, then by the toxicities that follow from it.

ClassExamplesMechanismKey toxicities and interactions
NRTIsTenofovir (TDF, TAF), emtricitabine, lamivudine, abacavir, zidovudineNucleoside/nucleotide analogs, phosphorylated in the cell; lack a 3'-OH, so they terminate the DNA chainClass: mitochondrial toxicity from polymerase-γ inhibition (lactic acidosis, steatosis; worst with older drugs). TDF: proximal tubulopathy, bone loss. Abacavir: HLA-B*57:01 hypersensitivity. Zidovudine: macrocytic anemia, neutropenia, myopathy. Tenofovir, emtricitabine and lamivudine also suppress HBV
NNRTIsEfavirenz, rilpivirine, doravirine, nevirapineBind an allosteric pocket of reverse transcriptase; need no phosphorylationRash; efavirenz: vivid dreams, dizziness, depression; rilpivirine: needs food and gastric acid (no proton-pump inhibitors); nevirapine: hepatotoxicity. Inactive against HIV-2; low genetic barrier to resistance
INSTIsBictegravir, dolutegravir, cabotegravir, raltegravirBlock strand transfer of viral DNA into host DNAWeight gain; insomnia; chelated by antacids, calcium and iron (separate dosing); dolutegravir and bictegravir block tubular creatinine secretion, raising serum creatinine slightly without lowering GFR
Protease inhibitorsDarunavir, atazanavir (boosted with ritonavir or cobicistat)Block cleavage of Gag-Pol polyproteins, leaving immature virionsDyslipidemia, insulin resistance, GI upset; boosters strongly inhibit CYP3A4. Atazanavir: indirect hyperbilirubinemia (UGT1A1 inhibition), stones
Entry/attachment inhibitorsMaraviroc, enfuvirtide, fostemsavir, ibalizumabCCR5 antagonist; gp41 binder; gp120 attachment inhibitor; anti-CD4 antibodyMaraviroc needs a tropism assay showing R5-only virus; enfuvirtide injection-site nodules
Capsid inhibitorLenacapavirDisrupts capsid assembly and disassemblyLong-acting injection; injection-site reactions

Ritonavir and cobicistat raise levels of CYP3A4 substrates. Inhaled or intranasal fluticasone can cause iatrogenic Cushing syndrome and adrenal suppression; simvastatin and lovastatin are contraindicated. Rifampin, an inducer, lowers PI and most INSTI levels.

HIV-associated organ disease

Kaposi sarcoma is an endothelial-derived tumor driven by human herpesvirus 8 (KSHV). Viral proteins such as LANA and a viral G-protein-coupled receptor promote proliferation, survival and angiogenesis. Lesions are violaceous macules, plaques or nodules on the skin, oral palate, gastrointestinal tract or lungs. Histology shows spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces with extravasated red cells and hemosiderin; HHV-8 LANA immunostaining confirms it. Effective ART alone often shrinks limited disease. Bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella) can look similar but has neutrophils and organisms on silver stain and responds to doxycycline or a macrolide.

HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN) occurs mainly in people of African ancestry, strongly linked to APOL1 risk variants, usually with high viral load. It presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria, rapidly progressive kidney failure and, characteristically, large echogenic kidneys despite reduced function. Biopsy shows collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with hypertrophied podocytes and microcystic tubular dilation. Treatment is ART plus renin-angiotensin blockade.

HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder is a subcortical process: slowed thinking, poor attention and memory, apathy and motor slowing, with diffuse atrophy and white-matter change on MRI. Pathology shows microglial nodules and multinucleated giant cells (fused infected macrophages), because neurons themselves are not infected. Contrast with PML (JC virus; asymmetric non-enhancing white-matter lesions), toxoplasmosis (multiple ring-enhancing lesions) and primary CNS lymphoma (often a single enhancing periventricular lesion; EBV DNA in CSF).

Distal symmetric polyneuropathy is the most common HIV neurologic complication: painful burning feet, reduced ankle reflexes, stocking distribution. It is caused by HIV itself and, historically, by the "d-drugs" (stavudine, didanosine) through mitochondrial toxicity.

Other HIV-linked malignancies: EBV-associated lymphomas (primary CNS lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell, Burkitt, primary effusion lymphoma, which is HHV-8 related) and HPV-driven cervical and anal cancer.

sections.heading: Hypersensitivity types I–IV: mechanisms and prototypes
sections.html:
Hypersensitivity is an adaptive immune response that damages the host. The four Gell-Coombs types differ in the effector (IgE, IgG/IgM against fixed antigen, circulating immune complexes, or T cells), and that effector predicts timing, histology and laboratory findings.

TypeEffectorTimingPrototypes
I (immediate)IgE on mast cells and basophilsMinutes; late phase at 2–12 hAnaphylaxis, allergic rhinitis, allergic asthma, urticaria, food allergy
II (cytotoxic, antibody to fixed antigen)IgG or IgM against cell-surface or matrix antigenHours to daysABO transfusion reaction, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, immune thrombocytopenia, Goodpasture syndrome, pemphigus vulgaris, bullous pemphigoid, Graves disease, myasthenia gravis, hyperacute rejection
III (immune complex)Soluble antigen-antibody complexes, complement, neutrophilsArthus: 4–12 h; serum sickness: 1–2 weeksSerum sickness, Arthus reaction, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa with hepatitis B
IV (delayed, cell-mediated)CD4 Th1/Th17 cells and macrophages, or CD8 cytotoxic T cells48–72 h (drug reactions: days to weeks)Tuberculin reaction, granulomas, allergic contact dermatitis, SJS/TEN, DRESS, acute cellular rejection

Type I

Sensitization: dendritic cells present allergen to naive CD4 T cells, which become Th2 cells. IL-4 and IL-13 drive B-cell class switching to IgE; IgE binds the high-affinity receptor FcεRI on mast cells and basophils. Re-exposure: a multivalent allergen cross-links adjacent IgE molecules, triggering degranulation. Preformed mediators (histamine, tryptase, heparin) cause vasodilation, vascular leak, bronchospasm and itch within minutes; newly synthesized lipid mediators (leukotrienes C4/D4/E4, prostaglandin D2) and cytokines follow. The late phase, hours later, is driven by recruited eosinophils (IL-5), Th2 cells and basophils and explains recurrent wheeze after allergen exposure.

Tryptase is stored almost exclusively in mast cells, so a rise above the patient's baseline supports mast-cell activation. Some drugs (vancomycin, opioids, fluoroquinolones, some neuromuscular blockers, iodinated contrast) activate mast cells directly, for example through MRGPRX2, without IgE; these reactions can occur on first exposure.

Type II

Antibody binds an antigen fixed to a cell or tissue. Damage follows from complement-mediated lysis (intravascular hemolysis in ABO incompatibility), opsonization and splenic phagocytosis (warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, immune thrombocytopenia), antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity by NK cells, or receptor stimulation or blockade without cell death (TSH-receptor antibodies in Graves disease; acetylcholine-receptor antibodies in myasthenia gravis). Drugs can act as haptens on the red cell membrane (high-dose penicillin) and produce a positive direct antiglobulin test. Immunofluorescence shows linear deposition along a target, such as the glomerular basement membrane in anti-GBM disease.

Type III

When soluble antigen and antibody form complexes in slight antigen excess, the complexes are small enough to stay in the circulation and deposit in vessel walls, glomeruli and synovium. They fix complement; C5a recruits neutrophils, which release enzymes and cause fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls. Serum C3 and C4 fall during active disease, and immunofluorescence is granular ("lumpy-bumpy"). The Arthus reaction is the local form: in a person with high levels of preformed IgG, injected antigen (classically a too-frequent tetanus-diphtheria booster) forms complexes in the dermis, producing a painful, swollen, sometimes necrotic area 4–12 hours later. Serum sickness is the systemic form, appearing 1–2 weeks after a foreign protein (antivenom, antithymocyte globulin, chimeric antibodies) with fever, urticarial or purpuric rash, arthralgia and sometimes proteinuria.

Type IV

Previously sensitized T cells respond to antigen without antibody. In the tuberculin reaction, memory Th1 cells recognize mycobacterial peptides on dermal antigen-presenting cells and secrete IFN-γ, which activates macrophages; the result is induration peaking at 48–72 hours. Persistent antigen leads to granulomas (epithelioid macrophages and giant cells, sustained by TNF-α). In allergic contact dermatitis, small reactive chemicals (nickel, urushiol from poison ivy, fragrances, topical neomycin) act as haptens, binding skin proteins that are presented to T cells; CD8 T cells kill keratinocytes, producing spongiotic, vesicular dermatitis confined to the contact site. Severe cutaneous drug reactions (SJS/TEN) are driven by drug-specific CD8 T cells that release granulysin, Fas ligand and perforin/granzyme, causing widespread keratinocyte apoptosis.

Pharmacogenomic HLA alleles restrict drug presentation to T cells: HLA-B*15:02 with carbamazepine SJS/TEN (people of Southeast and South Asian ancestry), HLA-B*58:01 with allopurinol, and HLA-B*57:01 with abacavir hypersensitivity.

Contact dermatitis from a nickel belt buckle is type IV, not type I: it appears a day or more after exposure and never causes anaphylaxis. Irritant contact dermatitis (soap, solvents) is not immune-mediated at all.

sections.heading: Transplant immunology: HLA, rejection and graft-versus-host disease
sections.html:
The main barrier to transplantation is the major histocompatibility complex, called HLA in humans and encoded on the short arm of chromosome 6. HLA genes are the most polymorphic in the genome, so almost every unrelated donor differs from the recipient.

FeatureClass I (HLA-A, -B, -C)Class II (HLA-DP, -DQ, -DR)
Expressed onAll nucleated cells and plateletsProfessional antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells); induced on endothelium by IFN-γ
StructureHeavy chain plus β2-microglobulinα and β chains
Presents toCD8 T cells (cytosolic peptides)CD4 T cells (endocytosed peptides)

HLA genes are inherited together as a haplotype from each parent and are expressed codominantly. Two siblings therefore have a 25% chance of sharing both haplotypes (HLA-identical), 50% of sharing one and 25% of sharing none. Each parent and child share exactly one haplotype. For kidney allocation, matching at HLA-A, -B and -DR matters most; for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, close matching (including HLA-C and -DQ) is essential.

How recipients see the graft

  • Direct allorecognition: recipient T cells recognize intact donor MHC molecules on donor ("passenger") dendritic cells. A very high frequency of T cells cross-react this way, which drives early acute rejection.
  • Indirect allorecognition: recipient antigen-presenting cells process donor HLA and present it as peptides on self-MHC. This pathway supports antibody production and chronic rejection.

Rejection types

[[figure:s23a-fig21]]
TypeTimingMechanismPathologyReversible?
HyperacuteMinutes to hoursPreformed antibodies (ABO, anti-HLA) bind graft endothelium; complement and thrombosisThrombosis, neutrophils, ischemic necrosis; graft is cyanotic and mottledNo; remove graft. Prevented by ABO compatibility and crossmatch
Acute T-cell-mediated (cellular)Days to months, most often in the first 6 months; any time if immunosuppression lapsesCD8 and CD4 T cells against donor HLA (type IV)Kidney: interstitial lymphocytes, tubulitis, and in severe cases intimal arteritis (endarteritis)Usually; pulse corticosteroids, antithymocyte globulin if resistant
Antibody-mediatedWeeks to yearsDonor-specific anti-HLA antibodies (preformed or de novo) activate complement on endotheliumMicrovascular inflammation (glomerulitis, peritubular capillaritis); C4d in peritubular capillariesPartly; plasmapheresis, IVIG, sometimes rituximab
ChronicMonths to yearsRepeated antibody and T-cell injury plus nonimmune factorsConcentric fibrointimal hyperplasia of arteries, interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophyNo

Chronic rejection has organ-specific names: cardiac allograft vasculopathy (diffuse concentric narrowing of epicardial and intramyocardial arteries; denervated hearts may present with dyspnea, arrhythmia or sudden death rather than angina), bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome in lung grafts, and vanishing bile duct syndrome in liver grafts. C4d marks the footprint of complement activation by antibody: C4 is cleaved by the classical pathway and its C4d fragment binds covalently to the capillary wall, where it persists after antibody has gone.

Graft-versus-host disease

GVHD occurs when immunocompetent donor T cells enter a host who cannot reject them and who expresses foreign HLA. Settings: allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (most often), lymphocyte-rich solid organs (small bowel, liver), and transfusion of non-irradiated cellular blood products to susceptible people.

  • Acute GVHD targets skin (maculopapular rash, often starting on palms, soles and ears), liver (cholestatic jaundice) and gut (voluminous diarrhea, cramping). Conditioning damage releases cytokines that amplify donor T-cell activation.
  • Chronic GVHD resembles autoimmune disease: lichenoid or sclerotic skin, oral lichen planus-like lesions, dry eyes and mouth, esophageal strictures, fasciitis and bronchiolitis obliterans.
  • Graft-versus-leukemia effect: the same donor T cells attack residual leukemia, which is why allogeneic transplantation can cure relapsed disease and why donor lymphocyte infusions work.

Transfusion-associated GVHD appears 1–2 weeks after transfusion with fever, rash, diarrhea, liver injury and, unlike stem cell GVHD, marrow aplasia with pancytopenia, because the host marrow itself is the target. Mortality exceeds 90%. It is prevented by irradiating cellular blood products for recipients at risk: congenital cellular immunodeficiency (SCID, DiGeorge), stem cell transplant recipients, those treated with purine analogs such as fludarabine, people with Hodgkin lymphoma, fetuses and neonates receiving intrauterine or exchange transfusion, and anyone receiving directed donations from blood relatives or HLA-matched platelets (a donor homozygous for a shared haplotype is invisible to the host).

Leukoreduction lowers CMV transmission, febrile reactions and HLA alloimmunization, but it does not reliably prevent transfusion-associated GVHD. Only irradiation (or pathogen-reduction technology) inactivates donor lymphocytes.

Sensitization to HLA comes from three exposures: pregnancy, blood transfusion and a prior transplant. Highly sensitized candidates wait longer because few donors are crossmatch-compatible.

sections.heading: Immunosuppressive drugs: mechanisms and toxicities
sections.html:
T-cell activation needs three signals: antigen on MHC binding the T-cell receptor (signal 1), costimulation through CD28 binding B7 (CD80/CD86) (signal 2), and IL-2 acting through its receptor to drive proliferation (signal 3). Each immunosuppressant interrupts one of these steps or the DNA synthesis that follows.

DrugMechanismDistinctive toxicities
CyclosporineBinds cyclophilin; complex inhibits calcineurin, so NFAT stays phosphorylated and IL-2 transcription fallsNephrotoxicity, hypertension, hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia, hyperuricemia, tremor; gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, hyperlipidemia
TacrolimusBinds FKBP12; complex inhibits calcineurinSame renal and electrolyte effects; more post-transplant diabetes and neurotoxicity (tremor, headache, posterior reversible encephalopathy); alopecia
Sirolimus, everolimusBind FKBP12; complex inhibits mTORC1, blocking IL-2-receptor signaling and the G1-to-S transitionHyperlipidemia, cytopenias, impaired wound healing and lymphoceles, mouth ulcers, pneumonitis, proteinuria; little nephrotoxicity; antiproliferative (used on drug-eluting stents, lower skin-cancer rates)
BasiliximabMonoclonal antibody against CD25 (IL-2 receptor α chain)Induction agent; few adverse effects
Antithymocyte globulinPolyclonal antibodies that deplete T cellsCytokine-release fever and rigors, cytopenias, serum sickness; raises infection and PTLD risk
BelataceptCTLA-4-Ig fusion protein; binds CD80/CD86 and blocks costimulationPost-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (especially CNS); contraindicated in EBV-seronegative recipients
AzathioprineConverted to 6-mercaptopurine and then thioguanine nucleotides that block purine synthesis and are incorporated into DNAMyelosuppression (TPMT or NUDT15 deficiency; xanthine oxidase inhibitors), hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, lymphoma and skin cancer
MycophenolateReversibly inhibits IMP dehydrogenase, the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo guanine nucleotide synthesisDiarrhea and GI upset, leukopenia, CMV disease, PML; teratogenic (pregnancy loss, ear and facial malformations)
MethotrexateInhibits dihydrofolate reductase; at low weekly doses also raises extracellular adenosine (anti-inflammatory)Mucositis, myelosuppression, hepatic fibrosis, pneumonitis, teratogenicity; reduced by folic acid, reversed by leucovorin
GlucocorticoidsCytosolic receptor translocates to the nucleus; represses NF-κB and AP-1, induces annexin A1 (inhibits phospholipase A2)See below

Why the antimetabolites spare most tissues

Lymphocytes depend heavily on the de novo purine pathway because their salvage pathway capacity is limited, whereas most other cells recycle purines through HGPRT. Blocking IMP dehydrogenase therefore stops lymphocyte proliferation with relatively little effect on other dividing cells. Azathioprine is cleared by three routes: TPMT methylation, xanthine oxidase oxidation, and conversion to active thioguanine nucleotides (which NUDT15 helps deactivate). Low TPMT or NUDT15 activity, or a xanthine oxidase inhibitor (allopurinol, febuxostat), shunts drug toward the active nucleotides and causes severe marrow suppression. Testing TPMT and, where available, NUDT15 before starting is standard.

Calcineurin inhibitors in practice

Both cyclosporine and tacrolimus are narrow-therapeutic-index CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein substrates. Inhibitors (azole antifungals, clarithromycin and erythromycin, diltiazem and verapamil, ritonavir and cobicistat, grapefruit juice) raise levels and cause toxicity; inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, St John's wort) lower levels and risk rejection. Acute nephrotoxicity is hemodynamic, from afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, and is dose-related and reversible; chronic use causes striped interstitial fibrosis and arteriolar hyalinosis. They can also cause thrombotic microangiopathy.

Glucocorticoids

Glucocorticoids reduce transcription of IL-1, IL-2, IL-6, TNF-α and other cytokines, induce lymphocyte and eosinophil apoptosis, and block prostaglandin and leukotriene synthesis upstream. The blood count shows neutrophilia (demargination as endothelial and neutrophil adhesion molecules are down-regulated, plus marrow release), with lymphopenia, eosinopenia and monocytopenia. Long-term adverse effects include Cushingoid habitus, hyperglycemia, hypertension, osteoporosis and avascular necrosis of the femoral head, cataracts and glaucoma, proximal myopathy, mood change and psychosis, thin skin and poor wound healing, growth suppression in children, and suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, so stopping abruptly after prolonged use can precipitate adrenal crisis.

Typical kidney transplant regimen: induction with basiliximab or antithymocyte globulin, then maintenance with tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisone. Step 2 CK tests drug-level interactions, prophylaxis and toxicity recognition.

Sirolimus is avoided immediately after transplant surgery because it impairs wound healing; it is often chosen later to spare the kidneys or after skin cancers.

sections.heading: Biologics, checkpoint inhibitors and other immune drug reactions
sections.html:
Monoclonal antibodies and fusion proteins act on one molecule, so their adverse effects follow directly from what that molecule normally does. Name suffixes help: -ximab chimeric, -zumab humanized, -umab human, -cept receptor-Fc fusion.

AgentTargetAdverse effects explained by the target
Infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept and other TNF inhibitorsTNF-αTNF maintains granulomas: reactivation of latent TB (often extrapulmonary or disseminated) and endemic fungi; hepatitis B reactivation; worsening of heart failure; demyelination; drug-induced lupus; paradoxical psoriasis; lymphoma
RituximabCD20 on B cells (not plasma cells)Hepatitis B reactivation, including in HBsAg-negative anti-HBc-positive patients; PML (JC virus); first-infusion reactions; hypogammaglobulinemia; poor vaccine responses for months
Natalizumabα4 integrinBlocks lymphocyte entry into the CNS, so JC virus escapes surveillance: PML
OmalizumabFree IgE (the Cε3 domain that binds FcεRI)Lowers free IgE and FcεRI density; rare anaphylaxis, which can be delayed, so early doses are given under observation
AbciximabPlatelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIaBleeding; acute severe thrombocytopenia within hours
BevacizumabVEGF-AHypertension, proteinuria, impaired wound healing, bleeding, GI perforation, arterial thrombosis
CetuximabEGFRAcneiform rash, hypomagnesemia; first-dose anaphylaxis in people with IgE to galactose-α-1,3-galactose
EculizumabC5Meningococcal infection (terminal complement needed against Neisseria)
Secukinumab and other IL-17 blockersIL-17AMucocutaneous candidiasis; flares of inflammatory bowel disease

Immune checkpoint inhibitors

CTLA-4 is up-regulated on activated T cells and on regulatory T cells; it binds B7 (CD80/CD86) with higher affinity than CD28 and removes B7 from antigen-presenting cells, so it acts early, in lymph nodes, to limit priming. PD-1 on chronically stimulated T cells binds PD-L1 on tumor and peripheral tissue cells and dampens T-cell receptor signaling at the effector site. Ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4), nivolumab and pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1), and atezolizumab and durvalumab (anti-PD-L1) release these brakes, restoring antitumor immunity at the cost of loss of peripheral tolerance.

Immune-related adverse events can affect any organ, usually within the first months but sometimes after treatment stops. Skin (rash, pruritus, vitiligo) is earliest and most common; colitis and hypophysitis are more typical of anti-CTLA-4; thyroiditis (transient thyrotoxicosis then hypothyroidism), pneumonitis and abrupt autoimmune type 1 diabetes are more typical of anti-PD-1. Hepatitis, nephritis, primary adrenal insufficiency, inflammatory arthritis, myositis, myasthenia-like syndromes and myocarditis (rare but often fatal, more frequent with combination therapy) also occur. Combination anti-CTLA-4 plus anti-PD-1 therapy has the highest rate of severe events.

Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction

Within hours of the first dose of an effective antibiotic for a spirochetal infection (syphilis, especially secondary; Lyme disease; leptospirosis; relapsing fever), lysed organisms release lipoproteins that stimulate a burst of TNF-α, IL-6 and IL-8. The patient has fever, rigors, myalgia, headache, tachycardia, transient hypotension and a brighter rash. It is self-limited within about a day and is treated with antipyretics and fluids; it is not an allergy, and the antibiotic is continued. In pregnancy it may provoke contractions or fetal heart rate changes.

Vaccine reactions and why they happen

  • Local reactions (pain, swelling) and fever reflect the intended innate response.
  • Arthus-type reactions after tetanus- or diphtheria-toxoid boosters given too frequently are type III reactions to high preformed antibody.
  • Live attenuated vaccines replicate: MMR causes fever and rash about 1–2 weeks after vaccination (with a small rise in febrile seizures in that window) and, rarely, transient thrombocytopenia; varicella vaccine can cause a mild rash. In people with severe T-cell deficiency, live vaccine strains can cause disseminated disease.
  • True anaphylaxis to a vaccine component is rare and is a contraindication to further doses of that vaccine.

Pattern to remember: blocking a cytokine that holds granulomas together (TNF) unmasks intracellular pathogens; depleting B cells unmasks hepatitis B and JC virus; blocking integrin trafficking to the brain unmasks JC virus.

Abrupt fever and rigors a few hours after penicillin for secondary syphilis is not penicillin allergy. Labelling it as allergy deprives the patient of the drug of choice.

title: Immune · HIV, allergy, transplant medicine and immune drug safety: management
meta: Diagnosis and management: HIV testing and ART, anaphylaxis and drug allergy, transplant care, biologic safety.

sections.heading: HIV: diagnosis, initial evaluation and starting ART
sections.html:
Who to test

Offer HIV screening at least once to everyone aged 15–65 (younger and older if at risk), at every pregnancy, and repeatedly (at least yearly, more often with ongoing risk) to people with new sexual partners, sex partners with HIV, men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, and anyone diagnosed with another sexually transmitted infection, tuberculosis or hepatitis B or C. Test on an opt-out basis without separate written consent.

Recognizing acute HIV

Two to four weeks after exposure, many people develop an acute retroviral syndrome: fever, sore throat, generalized lymphadenopathy, a maculopapular rash on the trunk, painful mucocutaneous ulcers, myalgia, diarrhea, and sometimes aseptic meningitis. Labs may show lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia and mildly raised aminotransferases. A negative heterophile test in a "mononucleosis" picture, especially with oral or genital ulcers, should prompt HIV testing. The viral load is very high, so the patient is highly infectious.

The laboratory algorithm

[[figure:s23a-fig23]]
  1. Screen with an HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody combination immunoassay (4th generation). It detects p24 antigen before antibodies appear, narrowing the window to a few weeks.
  2. If reactive, run an HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay. A positive result confirms infection and tells HIV-1 from HIV-2.
  3. If the differentiation assay is negative or indeterminate, run an HIV-1 RNA nucleic acid test. A positive RNA test with negative differentiation antibodies means acute HIV-1 infection (antigen present, antibody not yet). A negative RNA test means the screening result was false positive.

If acute infection is suspected clinically, send HIV RNA together with the Ag/Ab test; RNA becomes detectable about 10 days after infection, before p24 antigen. Western blot is no longer part of the algorithm. Rapid point-of-care antibody-only tests miss acute infection.

A low-level HIV RNA result (for example a few hundred copies/mL) in a person with a negative antibody test and no symptoms may be a false positive; true acute infection usually has very high viral loads. Repeat testing settles it.

Baseline evaluation

  • CD4 count and percentage; plasma HIV RNA; genotypic resistance testing (reverse transcriptase and protease; add integrase if INSTI resistance is suspected)
  • Hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc) and hepatitis C antibody; syphilis, gonorrhea and chlamydia at exposed sites; latent TB testing; Toxoplasma IgG
  • Complete blood count, metabolic panel with creatinine, liver tests, lipids, glucose or HbA1c, urinalysis, pregnancy test where relevant; HLA-B*57:01 if abacavir is considered
  • If CD4 is below 100/mm3: serum cryptococcal antigen

Starting ART

ART is recommended for everyone with HIV regardless of CD4 count, as soon as possible after diagnosis, ideally the same day or within days (rapid start). Draw baseline labs, but do not wait for the genotype, CD4 or hepatitis B results. Early ART reduces AIDS and non-AIDS events, and a durably undetectable viral load means no sexual transmission (undetectable = untransmittable).

SituationTypical regimen
Rapid start, results pendingBictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine, or dolutegravir plus tenofovir (TAF or TDF) plus emtricitabine or lamivudine; boosted darunavir plus tenofovir/emtricitabine is an alternative
HIV acquired despite long-acting cabotegravir PrEPBoosted darunavir plus tenofovir/emtricitabine while an integrase genotype is pending (INSTI resistance risk)
Hepatitis B coinfectionMust include tenofovir (TAF or TDF) plus emtricitabine or lamivudine; stopping them can cause a hepatitis flare
Dolutegravir/lamivudine two-drug regimenOnly once HBV is excluded, genotype is known, and RNA is below 500,000 copies/mL
Abacavir-containing regimenOnly after a negative HLA-B*57:01 result and without HBV

NNRTI-based starts are avoided before genotype results because transmitted NNRTI resistance is the most common kind.

Monitoring and failure

Check HIV RNA a few weeks after starting, then every few months until suppressed, then every 3–6 months. Most adherent patients are suppressed within about 3 to 6 months. Virologic failure is a confirmed RNA above 200 copies/mL; first address adherence, drug interactions (cation-containing supplements with INSTIs, acid suppressants with rilpivirine or atazanavir) and food requirements, and send a resistance genotype while the patient is still taking the failing regimen.

When to delay ART

Two opportunistic infections are exceptions to immediate ART because early immune recovery inflames a closed space: cryptococcal meningitis (start ART several weeks after antifungal induction, commonly 4–6 weeks) and, with specialist input, tuberculous meningitis. For other tuberculosis, start ART within 2 weeks of TB treatment when CD4 is below 50/mm3 and within 8 weeks otherwise.

Rising serum creatinine of about 0.1–0.2 mg/dL in the first weeks of dolutegravir, bictegravir or cobicistat is from blocked tubular creatinine secretion and does not reflect a fall in true GFR.

sections.heading: HIV: prevention, opportunistic-infection prophylaxis, IRIS and pregnancy
sections.html:
Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)

Offer PrEP to sexually active adults and adolescents with a substantial chance of acquiring HIV (a partner with HIV who is not suppressed, inconsistent condom use with partners of unknown status, a bacterial STI in the past 6 months) and to people who inject drugs and share equipment. Options:

  • Daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine: for all populations; needs creatinine clearance of at least 60 mL/min.
  • Daily oral tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine: approved for people at risk through sex, except those exposed through receptive vaginal sex, in whom it has not been studied.
  • Long-acting injectable cabotegravir every 2 months after two loading injections a month apart; twice-yearly injectable lenacapavir is a newer option.

Before starting, confirm HIV-negative status with a laboratory Ag/Ab test (plus HIV RNA if there was recent exposure or before injectable PrEP), check kidney function and hepatitis B status, and screen for STIs. Repeat HIV testing every 3 months on oral PrEP and every 2 months on cabotegravir. If acute HIV symptoms are present, do not start PrEP until HIV RNA is negative, because two drugs are not a treatment regimen and resistance follows.

Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)

After a substantial exposure (mucosal or percutaneous contact with blood, semen, vaginal or rectal fluids from a person with HIV or unknown status) within 72 hours, start a 28-day three-drug regimen, preferably INSTI-based (for example bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide, or dolutegravir plus tenofovir/emtricitabine). Start as soon as possible; do not wait for the source's or the patient's test results. PEP is not recommended beyond 72 hours. Test for HIV at baseline and repeat testing during follow-up through about 3 months after the exposure. People with ongoing risk should move directly from PEP to PrEP once HIV infection is excluded.

Opportunistic-infection prophylaxis

InfectionStart whenPreferred agentStop when
Pneumocystis pneumoniaCD4 below 200/mm3, CD4 below 14%, or oropharyngeal candidiasisTMP-SMX; alternatives dapsone (check G6PD), atovaquone, inhaled pentamidineCD4 above 200 for at least 3 months on ART
Toxoplasma encephalitisCD4 below 100/mm3 and Toxoplasma IgG positiveTMP-SMX double strengthCD4 above 200 for at least 3 months on ART
Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complexNot needed if ART is started immediately; consider only for CD4 below 50 when not on fully suppressive ARTAzithromycin weeklyOnce on suppressive ART
Cryptococcal diseaseScreen serum cryptococcal antigen if CD4 below 100Positive antigen: lumbar puncture; if CSF negative, pre-emptive fluconazolePer treatment course
Latent TBPositive IGRA or tuberculin test (5 mm or more), after excluding active TBIsoniazid- or rifamycin-based regimen (watch ART interactions)Course completion

Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)

As ART restores pathogen-specific immunity, typically within the first 3 months, the patient may develop inflammation against a known infection (paradoxical IRIS: fever, enlarging lymph nodes, new pulmonary infiltrates or worsening meningitis in someone improving on TB or cryptococcal treatment) or against a previously undiagnosed one (unmasking IRIS, for example MAC lymphadenitis). Risk is highest with a very low CD4 count, a high viral load and a short gap between OI treatment and ART. The viral load falls and CD4 rises as expected. Diagnosis requires excluding treatment failure, drug resistance, a new infection and drug reactions. Management: continue ART and the OI treatment; give NSAIDs for mild disease and prednisone for moderate to severe paradoxical TB-IRIS. Stop ART only for life-threatening IRIS, such as rising intracranial pressure.

Pregnancy and perinatal transmission

  • Test every pregnant person at the first visit; retest in the third trimester if at risk; use rapid testing in labor if status is unknown.
  • Start ART as soon as possible regardless of CD4 count; dolutegravir-based regimens are preferred. Continue an effective pre-pregnancy regimen.
  • Viral load above 1,000 copies/mL near delivery (or unknown): scheduled cesarean delivery at 38 weeks plus intravenous zidovudine during delivery. With a sustained viral load below 50 copies/mL, vaginal delivery is appropriate and IV zidovudine is not needed.
  • All exposed newborns receive antiretroviral prophylaxis started within hours of birth: zidovudine alone for low risk, and a multidrug regimen for higher risk (no maternal ART, detectable maternal viral load, acute maternal HIV).
  • Diagnose infant infection with HIV nucleic acid tests (RNA or DNA), at birth for high risk and at about 14–21 days, 1–2 months and 4–6 months; maternal antibody makes antibody tests uninformative until about 18 months.
  • In the US, replacement feeding avoids postnatal transmission; people with sustained viral suppression who wish to breastfeed should receive counselling and support through shared decision-making.

Event-driven ("2-1-1") oral PrEP has been studied only for anal sex among men who have sex with men; it is not used for vaginal exposure, injection drug use, or with injectable PrEP.

sections.heading: Anaphylaxis and food allergy: recognition and management
sections.html:
Recognizing anaphylaxis

Anaphylaxis is a serious, rapid-onset systemic allergic reaction. Diagnose it clinically, without waiting for laboratory confirmation, when there is acute skin or mucosal involvement (hives, flushing, swollen lips or tongue) with respiratory compromise, hypotension or end-organ dysfunction, or severe gastrointestinal symptoms; or when two or more organ systems are involved after a likely allergen; or when hypotension, bronchospasm or laryngeal involvement follows a known allergen, even without skin findings. About 10–20% of cases have no skin signs.

Common triggers: foods (peanut, tree nuts, shellfish, fish, milk, egg, sesame), insect stings, drugs (beta-lactams, NSAIDs, perioperative neuromuscular blockers, chlorhexidine), latex and allergen immunotherapy. Risk of a fatal reaction is higher with asthma, delay in epinephrine, adolescence and peanut or tree-nut allergy.

Management

  1. Intramuscular epinephrine first, into the anterolateral thigh: 0.01 mg/kg of the 1 mg/mL solution, maximum 0.5 mg in adults and 0.3 mg in children; repeat every 5–15 minutes if needed. There is no absolute contraindication in anaphylaxis, including in older adults with heart disease.
  2. Call for help, remove the trigger, lay the patient supine with legs raised (sitting up if breathing is difficult; left lateral in pregnancy).
  3. Oxygen, large-bore IV access, and rapid crystalloid boluses for hypotension.
  4. Adjuncts after epinephrine: inhaled albuterol for persisting bronchospasm, H1 antihistamines for itch and hives. Antihistamines and glucocorticoids do not treat airway obstruction or shock and must never delay epinephrine.
  5. If shock persists after two or more IM doses and fluids: IV epinephrine infusion in a monitored setting. Patients taking beta-blockers may need glucagon.

Epinephrine works through α1 vasoconstriction (raises blood pressure, reduces mucosal edema), β1 inotropy and chronotropy, and β2 bronchodilation, and β2-mediated cAMP rises in mast cells reduce further mediator release.

Observe after resolution (longer after severe reactions or repeated epinephrine) because a biphasic reaction can recur hours later without re-exposure. At discharge: an epinephrine auto-injector prescription with hands-on teaching, a written action plan, trigger avoidance and allergist referral.

Tryptase

Serum tryptase peaks about 1 hour after onset and is best drawn within about 1–2 hours (up to 4 hours), with a baseline sample at least 24 hours after recovery. A rise of more than 20% plus 2 ng/mL over baseline supports mast-cell activation. A normal tryptase does not exclude anaphylaxis, especially food-induced reactions in children. A persistently elevated baseline suggests systemic mastocytosis or hereditary α-tryptasemia.

Food allergy

IgE-mediated food allergy causes hives, angioedema, vomiting, wheeze or anaphylaxis within minutes to 2 hours of ingestion. Diagnosis rests on a convincing history plus targeted testing (skin prick test or food-specific IgE to the suspected food). Positive tests without a history are common, so broad screening panels cause false labels and needless avoidance. The oral food challenge is the reference standard. Treatment is avoidance, epinephrine auto-injector and an action plan; peanut oral immunotherapy and omalizumab can reduce reactions to accidental exposure in selected patients.

SyndromeMechanism and clues
Pollen-food (oral allergy) syndromeCross-reacting pollen proteins in raw fruits and vegetables; itching of lips and mouth only; cooked forms tolerated
Alpha-gal syndromeIgE to galactose-α-1,3-galactose after lone star tick bites; hives or anaphylaxis 3–6 hours after red meat
Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndromeNon-IgE; repetitive vomiting 1–4 hours after cow's milk, soy, rice or oat in an infant, pallor and lethargy; treat with fluids and ondansetron, not epinephrine
Eosinophilic esophagitisFood-antigen-driven Th2 inflammation; dysphagia and food impaction, rings and furrows

Early introduction of peanut

Early, regular exposure prevents peanut allergy, whereas delayed introduction increases it. Current US guidance:

  • Severe eczema, egg allergy or both (highest risk): introduce peanut-containing foods as early as 4–6 months; an allergist evaluation or testing may be considered first so that the first feeding can be supervised if needed.
  • Mild to moderate eczema: introduce peanut-containing foods at home around 6 months of age.
  • No eczema or food allergy: introduce peanut-containing foods with other solids, according to family preference.

Give peanut in an age-safe form (thinned smooth peanut butter or peanut puffs, never whole nuts) and keep it in the diet a few times a week. Other allergenic foods, including egg, can also be introduced around 6 months. Exclusive breastfeeding, maternal avoidance diets in pregnancy and delayed solids do not prevent food allergy.

Delaying peanut until age 2–3 years in a child with eczema is outdated advice; it raises, not lowers, the chance of peanut allergy.

sections.heading: Drug hypersensitivity, contact dermatitis and tuberculin testing
sections.html:
Drug reactions are classified by timing: immediate (within about 1 hour of a dose; urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis; IgE or direct mast-cell activation) and delayed (hours to weeks; mostly T-cell mediated). The timing, the skin morphology and the organs involved decide both acute management and whether the drug can ever be given again.

ReactionOnset after starting drugFeaturesUsual culprits
Benign morbilliform eruption4–14 daysSymmetric pink macules and papules, no mucosal or organ involvementAminopenicillins, cephalosporins, sulfonamides
Serum sickness / serum sickness-like reaction1–3 weeksFever, urticarial rash, arthralgia; true serum sickness has low complement and possible nephritisAntithymocyte globulin, antivenom, chimeric antibodies; in children, cefaclor and amoxicillin (serum sickness-like)
DRESS2–8 weeksFever, facial edema, widespread rash, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytes, hepatitis, nephritis or pneumonitis; HHV-6 reactivationAromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, minocycline, vancomycin
SJS/TEN4–28 daysProdrome of fever and sore eyes, then painful dusky macules and atypical targets, blisters, positive Nikolsky sign, erosions at two or more mucosal sites; SJS under 10% of body surface detached, TEN over 30%Allopurinol, carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, sulfonamide antibiotics, nevirapine, oxicam NSAIDs
Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosisWithin daysMany small sterile pustules on erythema in skin folds, fever, neutrophiliaBeta-lactams, macrolides, diltiazem

Severe cutaneous adverse reactions: management

The single most important step is to stop every possible culprit drug immediately. Patients with SJS/TEN need admission to a burn or intensive care unit: fluid and electrolyte replacement, warming, nonadherent wound dressings without aggressive debridement, pain control, nutrition, infection surveillance (without prophylactic antibiotics), and early ophthalmology review to prevent scarring. Immunomodulators (cyclosporine, etanercept, IVIG) are used in some centers, but evidence is limited. Prognosis worsens with age, extent of detachment, tachycardia, malignancy, high blood urea nitrogen, high glucose and low bicarbonate. DRESS is treated by stopping the drug and, when organs other than skin are involved, systemic glucocorticoids tapered slowly over weeks to months; relapses and later autoimmune thyroiditis or diabetes can follow. The culprit and structurally similar drugs are avoided for life, and rechallenge or skin testing is not done.

Penicillin allergy evaluation

About 10% of patients carry a penicillin-allergy label, but more than 90% tolerate penicillin when tested, and the label leads to broader, costlier and more toxic antibiotics and more C. difficile and resistant infections. IgE sensitivity also wanes over time.

  • Low-risk history (isolated GI upset, headache, family history only, or a remote benign rash without mucosal involvement, blistering or organ injury): a direct oral amoxicillin challenge under observation, without prior skin testing.
  • Higher-risk immediate history (anaphylaxis, hives or angioedema soon after a dose, especially recent): penicillin skin testing with major and minor determinants, and an oral challenge if negative.
  • Severe delayed reaction (SJS/TEN, DRESS, drug-induced hemolysis or nephritis): avoid the drug; no testing or challenge.
  • Confirmed IgE allergy when penicillin is essential (syphilis in pregnancy, neurosyphilis): desensitization, which gives temporary tolerance only while the drug continues.

Cross-reactivity with cephalosporins depends mostly on similar R1 side chains and is low; patients with a non-severe penicillin reaction can usually receive a cephalosporin with a dissimilar side chain, and carbapenem cross-reactivity is very low.

Contact dermatitis

Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV reaction appearing 1–3 days after contact, with itchy, eczematous, often vesicular plaques that match the contact pattern: earlobes and umbilicus (nickel), linear streaks on the legs and arms (poison ivy, poison oak), eyelids (nail cosmetics), or around a wound (topical neomycin or bacitracin). Patch testing, read at about 48 hours and again at 72–96 hours, identifies the allergen when the cause is unclear. Irritant contact dermatitis is more common, is not immune-mediated, burns more than itches and affects anyone with enough exposure (frequent hand washing, wet work). Treatment is avoidance, barrier protection and topical glucocorticoids. Extensive or facial disease (for example poison ivy over more than about 20% of the body surface) warrants oral prednisone tapered over 2–3 weeks; shorter courses risk rebound.

Tuberculin skin test

Five tuberculin units of purified protein derivative are injected intradermally, and induration (not redness) is measured 48–72 hours later. A positive test reflects T-cell memory, not active disease.

IndurationPositive in
5 mm or moreHIV infection; recent close contact of active TB; fibrotic changes of old TB on chest radiograph; organ transplant recipients; other immunosuppression (for example prednisone 15 mg/day or more for a month or longer, TNF inhibitors)
10 mm or moreRecent arrivals (within 5 years) from high-prevalence countries; people who inject drugs; residents and employees of high-risk congregate settings; mycobacteriology laboratory staff; people with conditions such as diabetes or chronic kidney disease; children younger than 4 years, or any child exposed to high-risk adults
15 mm or moreEveryone, including people with no risk factors

False negatives occur with advanced HIV, high-dose immunosuppression, severe illness, malnutrition, very recent infection and live-virus vaccination within the preceding weeks; false positives with BCG vaccination and nontuberculous mycobacteria. An interferon-γ release assay is preferred in BCG-vaccinated people. Two-step testing at baseline for health care workers detects a boosted response from remote sensitization.

A widespread rash with mucosal erosions and skin pain is SJS/TEN until proven otherwise. Do not give a "test dose" or attempt desensitization; the culprit is permanently avoided.

sections.heading: Transplant medicine: crossmatch, rejection work-up and post-transplant infection
sections.html:
Before the transplant: compatibility testing

  • ABO compatibility is required for most solid organs (ABO-incompatible living-donor kidney transplantation is possible after desensitization at specialist centers).
  • HLA typing of donor and recipient.
  • Anti-HLA antibody screening with single-antigen bead assays identifies antibodies against specific HLA types. The calculated panel-reactive antibody (cPRA) estimates the percentage of donors to whom the candidate is sensitized; highly sensitized candidates (after pregnancy, transfusion or prior transplant) wait longer.
  • Crossmatch mixes recipient serum with donor lymphocytes. A positive complement-dependent cytotoxicity T-cell crossmatch generally precludes kidney transplantation from that donor because of the risk of hyperacute or early antibody-mediated rejection. Flow cytometry crossmatch is more sensitive. A "virtual crossmatch" compares the recipient's known antibodies with the donor's HLA type.
  • Options for an incompatible living donor: paired kidney exchange or desensitization with plasmapheresis and IVIG.

Pre-transplant work-up also includes serologies (CMV, EBV, HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis, varicella, Toxoplasma for heart recipients), latent TB testing, Strongyloides serology in people from endemic regions, age-appropriate cancer screening, dental review, and vaccination. Live vaccines must be given at least 4 weeks before transplantation, because they are contraindicated afterwards.

Rising creatinine after kidney transplantation

The differential is broad, and biopsy is usually needed: volume depletion, calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity (high trough level, often after a CYP3A4-inhibiting drug), urinary obstruction or urine leak (ultrasound), renal artery stenosis or thrombosis (Doppler), infection (urinary tract infection, BK polyomavirus nephropathy), recurrent disease (FSGS, IgA nephropathy) and rejection.

FindingPoints towardManagement
Tubulitis, interstitial lymphocytes, endarteritisAcute T-cell-mediated rejectionPulse IV methylprednisolone; antithymocyte globulin for steroid-resistant or vascular rejection; check adherence and drug levels
Glomerulitis, peritubular capillaritis, C4d, circulating donor-specific antibodyAntibody-mediated rejectionPlasmapheresis plus IVIG, with corticosteroids; sometimes rituximab
Tubular viral inclusions staining for SV40 large T antigen; plasma BK DNA rising; "decoy cells" in urineBK polyomavirus nephropathyReduce immunosuppression (usually the antimetabolite first); no proven antiviral
High tacrolimus trough, isometric tubular vacuolization, arteriolar hyalinosisCalcineurin-inhibitor toxicityReduce dose; look for an interacting drug

Infections after solid organ transplantation

[[figure:s23a-fig22]]
  • First month: infections of surgery and hospital care (wound, line, pneumonia, urinary tract, C. difficile), donor-derived infection, and reactivated herpes simplex.
  • 1–12 months: opportunists, when immunosuppression is most intense: CMV, Pneumocystis, BK virus, EBV-driven PTLD, Listeria, Nocardia, Toxoplasma, Aspergillus, reactivated hepatitis B or C and tuberculosis. Prophylaxis (TMP-SMX for Pneumocystis, antivirals for CMV) shifts or suppresses many of these.
  • After 12 months: mostly community-acquired infections; late CMV after prophylaxis stops, PTLD, zoster, cryptococcosis and skin cancers in those on heavier regimens.

Cytomegalovirus is the single most important post-transplant pathogen. Risk is highest in a seronegative recipient of a seropositive donor (D+/R−) and after lymphocyte-depleting induction. Prevention is either universal prophylaxis (valganciclovir, typically 3–6 months; letermovir is an alternative in some settings) or pre-emptive therapy guided by weekly CMV PCR. Disease ranges from CMV syndrome (fever, malaise, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) to tissue-invasive disease (colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, and injury to the graft itself), and it raises the risk of rejection and other opportunists. Treat with IV ganciclovir for severe or tissue-invasive disease, or oral valganciclovir for mild disease with reliable absorption, plus a reduction in immunosuppression; foscarnet or maribavir are used for ganciclovir-resistant virus (UL97 or UL54 mutations). Ganciclovir and valganciclovir cause neutropenia, which adds to mycophenolate myelosuppression.

Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) is usually an EBV-driven B-cell proliferation. Risk is highest in EBV-seronegative recipients of seropositive donors (so it is more common in children), with intensive T-cell-depleting therapy, and in the first year. It presents with fever, lymphadenopathy, a mononucleosis-like illness, or a mass in the graft, gut or CNS; biopsy with EBV-encoded RNA staining confirms it. First-line treatment is reducing immunosuppression, then rituximab for CD20-positive disease and chemoimmunotherapy if it does not respond.

BK nephropathy and acute rejection both raise creatinine months after transplant, but the treatments are opposite: more immunosuppression for rejection, less for BK. Check plasma BK PCR and biopsy before pulsing steroids.

Acute GVHD after allogeneic stem cell transplantation is graded by skin, liver and gut involvement; first-line therapy for significant disease is systemic glucocorticoids, and ruxolitinib is used for steroid-refractory disease.

sections.heading: Monitoring immunomodulating therapy: screening, immune-related adverse events and vaccine safety
sections.html:
Screening before immunosuppression or biologics

BeforeScreen forIf positive
TNF inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, long-term high-dose glucocorticoids, transplantLatent TB (IGRA or tuberculin test, plus chest radiograph if positive)Exclude active TB; start latent TB treatment, ideally at least a month before the biologic
Rituximab and other anti-CD20 agents, chemotherapy, TNF inhibitors, transplantHBsAg and anti-HBc (plus anti-HBs)HBsAg-positive, or HBsAg-negative/anti-HBc-positive before anti-CD20 therapy: antiviral prophylaxis with entecavir or tenofovir, continued for months after therapy ends
High-dose glucocorticoids in people from tropical or subtropical regionsStrongyloides serology (or empiric ivermectin)Ivermectin before or alongside steroids
Azathioprine, mercaptopurineTPMT (and NUDT15) activity or genotypeReduce dose or choose another drug
MethotrexateCBC, creatinine, liver tests, hepatitis B and C; pregnancy testAvoid with significant kidney or liver disease; reliable contraception

Before any of these, update vaccines: live vaccines at least 4 weeks before starting, inactivated vaccines ideally at least 2 weeks before. Avoid live vaccines during therapy. People on long-term glucocorticoids also need bone protection (calcium, vitamin D, and a bisphosphonate when fracture risk is high), glucose and blood-pressure monitoring, eye checks, and Pneumocystis prophylaxis when prednisone of about 20 mg/day or more is used for a month or longer together with another immunosuppressant or condition.

Glucocorticoid hazards that present acutely

  • Adrenal crisis after abrupt withdrawal or during illness in someone with HPA-axis suppression: taper, and give stress doses for surgery or acute illness.
  • Strongyloides hyperinfection: larvae disseminate through the gut wall, carrying gram-negative enteric bacteria into the blood; fever, abdominal pain, wheeze, larva currens and gram-negative sepsis or meningitis. Treat with ivermectin and reduce steroids.
  • Steroid psychosis, hyperglycemic crises and masked peritonitis.

Methotrexate toxicity

Low-dose methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis or psoriasis is taken once weekly. Accidental daily dosing, kidney impairment, dehydration and interacting drugs (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, high-dose NSAIDs, penicillins, proton-pump inhibitors) cause mucositis, pancytopenia and hepatotoxicity. Treatment is leucovorin (folinic acid), which bypasses dihydrofolate reductase, plus hydration; glucarpidase is reserved for toxic levels after high-dose intravenous methotrexate with kidney failure. Folic acid supplementation prevents some adverse effects of routine low-dose therapy but does not rescue an overdose.

Checkpoint-inhibitor immune-related adverse events

Grade the event (1 mild to 4 life-threatening), exclude infection and progression, then:

  • Grade 1: continue the checkpoint inhibitor with close monitoring (except some neurologic, hematologic and cardiac events).
  • Grade 2: hold the drug; oral prednisone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day if symptoms do not settle; resume when grade 1 or less and prednisone is 10 mg/day or less.
  • Grade 3–4: hold (often permanently for grade 4) and give high-dose glucocorticoids, such as methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day, tapered over at least 4–6 weeks.
  • Steroid-refractory colitis: infliximab or vedolizumab. Steroid-refractory hepatitis: mycophenolate (not infliximab).
  • Endocrinopathies are managed with hormone replacement (levothyroxine, hydrocortisone, insulin), and the checkpoint inhibitor can usually be continued once the patient is stable. The endocrine damage is usually permanent.
  • Myocarditis (troponin rise, arrhythmia, heart block, sometimes with myositis or myasthenia): stop permanently and give high-dose glucocorticoids urgently.

For colitis, a CTCAE grade 3 event is 7 or more stools a day above baseline, severe pain or interference with self-care; stool studies including C. difficile come first, and endoscopy helps define severity.

Vaccine contraindications and precautions

CategoryExamples
Contraindication to any vaccineSevere allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to a previous dose or a vaccine component
Contraindications to live vaccinesPregnancy; severe immunodeficiency (congenital T-cell defects, chemotherapy, HIV with CD4 below 200/mm3, biologics); prednisone 20 mg/day or more for 14 days or longer (wait at least 1 month after stopping)
Vaccine-specific contraindicationsPertussis-containing vaccines: encephalopathy within 7 days of a previous dose without another cause (give DT or Td instead). Rotavirus: severe combined immunodeficiency or prior intussusception
Precautions (weigh risk and benefit)Moderate or severe acute illness; Guillain-Barré syndrome within 6 weeks of a previous influenza or tetanus-toxoid vaccine; recent antibody-containing blood products before MMR or varicella; history of thrombocytopenia before MMR
Not contraindicationsMild illness with or without low-grade fever; current antibiotics; recovery from illness; breastfeeding; a pregnant or immunocompromised household member (for most vaccines); egg allergy for influenza or MMR vaccine; local reactions to previous doses; family history of adverse events

Adolescents and young adults may faint after injection, so they should be seated and observed for about 15 minutes.

Step 1 asks what a biologic targets; Step 2 CK asks what to check before the first dose and what to do when an immune-related adverse event appears.
