title: Blood & Lymphoreticular · Infections and neoplasms of blood and lymphoid tissue
meta: Blood-borne and lymphoid infections, hyperinflammatory and histiocytic disorders, and haematologic neoplasms: mechanisms and morphology.

sections.heading: Blood-borne infections: malaria, babesiosis and the intracellular pathogens
sections.html:
Several pathogens live inside blood cells or destroy them, so they present with fever plus cytopenias rather than with organ-specific signs. The pattern of which cell is infected, and of which blood line falls, is the most efficient way to reach the diagnosis.

Malaria

Four Plasmodium species commonly infect humans (P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae), with P. knowlesi as a zoonotic fifth. Female Anopheles mosquitoes inoculate sporozoites, which reach hepatocytes and undergo schizogony. Merozoites released into the blood invade erythrocytes, where the ring, trophozoite and schizont stages cycle; synchronous schizont rupture produces the paroxysms of chills, fever and sweats, with hemolysis and splenomegaly. P. vivax and P. ovale leave dormant hypnozoites in the liver that reactivate weeks to months later, which is why radical cure needs an 8-aminoquinoline after glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase testing.

[[figure:s23a-fig30]]

Species differ in the cells they can enter and so in the parasite burden they reach. P. vivax uses the Duffy antigen receptor for chemokines and prefers reticulocytes, so parasitemia stays low; Duffy-negative red cells are largely resistant. P. falciparum can invade red cells of any age through several redundant receptors and so reaches high parasitemia. Mature P. falciparum stages place the variant protein PfEMP1 on knobs at the red cell surface; PfEMP1 binds endothelial ICAM-1, EPCR and CD36, so infected cells stick in post-capillary venules of the brain, kidney, gut and placenta. This cytoadherence explains why only rings circulate, why the spleen cannot clear the parasite, and why severe disease takes the form of coma, acidosis, kidney injury and placental malaria.

Protective host polymorphisms illustrate the selection malaria exerts: sickle cell trait, thalassemia trait, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, hereditary ovalocytosis and Duffy negativity all reduce the risk of severe disease. Hemoglobin S heterozygotes are protected because infected cells sickle and are cleared, not because the parasite cannot enter.

Blood smears remain central. Thick films detect low parasite densities; thin films allow species identification and quantification. Clues include delicate double rings and banana-shaped gametocytes in falciparum disease, and enlarged red cells with amoeboid trophozoites and membrane stippling in vivax disease. Antigen-detection rapid tests are useful adjuncts. Thrombocytopenia with fever in a returning traveller is a strong pointer.

Antimalarial drugs are grouped by the stage they kill. Chloroquine is a weak base concentrated in the acidic food vacuole, where it prevents polymerization of free heme into inert hemozoin; resistance follows mutations in the PfCRT transporter. Artemisinins are activated by intraparasitic iron and generate free radicals, killing parasites faster than any other class. Atovaquone inhibits the parasite cytochrome bc1 complex and is paired with proguanil; pyrimethamine and proguanil inhibit parasite dihydrofolate reductase; doxycycline targets the apicoplast ribosome and acts slowly, so it is used for prophylaxis or as a partner drug.

Babesiosis

Babesia microti is transmitted by Ixodes ticks in the north-eastern and upper midwestern United States, and by transfused red cells. Trophozoites divide within erythrocytes and form rings and the characteristic cross-shaped tetrad, but, unlike Plasmodium, they produce no pigment and no gametocytes. Hemolysis with a raised lactate dehydrogenase, jaundice and thrombocytopenia follows. Splenectomy, older age, HIV infection and anti-B-cell therapy allow high parasitemia and severe disease, because splenic macrophages normally cull infected cells. Co-infection with Borrelia burgdorferi or Anaplasma phagocytophilum is common because the vector is shared.

Parvovirus B19 and marrow infection

Parvovirus B19 is a small single-stranded DNA virus that binds the P antigen (globoside) on erythroid progenitors and lyses them, pausing erythropoiesis for one to two weeks. With normal red cell survival this passes unnoticed; when survival is already short, as in sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis or thalassemia, hemoglobin falls steeply with a reticulocyte count near zero: transient aplastic crisis. In children the virus more often causes erythema infectiosum, in adults a symmetric arthropathy, in pregnancy fetal anemia with nonimmune hydrops, and in immunocompromised hosts chronic pure red cell aplasia.

Intraleukocytic bacteria and the effects of sepsis

Anaplasma phagocytophilum (Ixodes ticks, upper Midwest and north-east) multiplies in neutrophils, and Ehrlichia chaffeensis (Amblyomma americanum, south-central and south-east) in monocytes; both form morulae and cause fever with leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia and raised aminotransferases without a rash. Bartonella species cause intraerythrocytic bacteremia; B. quintana, spread by body lice, is a classic cause of culture-negative endocarditis. Sepsis itself alters every blood line: neutrophilia with left shift and toxic granulation (or neutropenia as a poor sign), anemia of inflammation through hepcidin, and consumption of platelets and clotting factors in disseminated intravascular coagulation, where endotoxin and cytokines induce tissue factor on monocytes and endothelium. Overwhelming infection can also trigger hemophagocytic syndrome.

Fever plus thrombocytopenia in a returning traveller means malaria until smears say otherwise; fever plus leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised aminotransferases after a tick bite means an intracellular tick-borne bacterium.

Chemoprophylaxis taken correctly does not exclude malaria, and a single negative smear does not either: repeat smears over 24 to 48 hours.

sections.heading: Infections of lymphoid tissue: mononucleosis syndromes and infectious lymphadenitis
sections.html:
A lymph node is organized into compartments, and each responds to a different kind of antigen. Knowing which compartment is expanded converts a biopsy report into a differential diagnosis.

[[figure:s23a-fig33]]

The cortex holds B-cell follicles with germinal centres; the paracortex is the T-cell zone, entered through high endothelial venules; macrophages line the sinuses; and plasma cells accumulate in medullary cords. Follicular hyperplasia with many germinal centres of varying size, brisk mitoses and tingible-body macrophages indicates sustained B-cell responses, as in rheumatoid arthritis, early HIV infection or toxoplasmosis. Paracortical hyperplasia with immunoblasts indicates viral infection, classically Epstein-Barr virus, and can mimic lymphoma. Sinus histiocytosis suggests drainage from a tumour or particulate material. Effacement of architecture by a monotonous population suggests lymphoma.

Epstein-Barr virus and infectious mononucleosis

Epstein-Barr virus, a gamma-herpesvirus, infects oropharyngeal epithelium and then B lymphocytes through CD21, and persists for life in memory B cells. Primary infection in adolescents and young adults produces mononucleosis: a week or more of fever, exudative pharyngitis with palatal petechiae, tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, fatigue and splenomegaly in about half of patients. The atypical lymphocytes on the smear are not infected B cells but reactive CD8+ cytotoxic T cells expanding to kill them; this vigorous T-cell response causes most of the symptoms. Mild transaminase elevation is usual.

Diagnosis uses the heterophile antibody test, which detects IgM antibodies produced by polyclonally activated B cells that agglutinate sheep or horse erythrocytes but do not bind Epstein-Barr virus antigens. The test may be negative in the first week and in young children; virus-specific serology then distinguishes acute infection (viral capsid antigen IgM, no nuclear antigen antibodies) from past infection (viral capsid antigen IgG with nuclear antigen antibodies). Important complications are splenic rupture in the first weeks, airway obstruction from tonsillar hypertrophy, autoimmune hemolytic anemia with cold agglutinins, thrombocytopenia, and a morbilliform rash after amoxicillin or ampicillin. Blood beneath the left hemidiaphragm after splenic rupture refers pain to the shoulder tip through the phrenic nerve. Epstein-Barr virus also drives Burkitt and other lymphomas, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease and hemophagocytic syndrome, and in X-linked lymphoproliferative disease (SH2D1A mutation) primary infection can be fatal.

Other causes of a mononucleosis-like illness

Cytomegalovirus causes heterophile-negative mononucleosis with less pharyngitis and adenopathy and more hepatitis; it stays latent in monocytes and myeloid progenitors, which is why it is transmitted by cellular blood products and transplanted organs. Acute HIV infection is a mandatory consideration, since it is treatable and transmissible. Acute toxoplasmosis, acquired from oocysts in cat feces or tissue cysts in undercooked meat, usually presents as painless posterior cervical lymphadenopathy with fatigue; the node shows follicular hyperplasia, small clusters of epithelioid histiocytes and monocytoid B cells in the sinuses.

Bacterial and mycobacterial lymphadenitis

Cat-scratch disease follows inoculation of Bartonella henselae by a kitten scratch: an inoculation papule appears within days, and tender regional adenopathy draining that site follows one to three weeks later. Nodes show necrotizing granulomas with stellate microabscesses, and silver staining reveals pleomorphic bacilli. Acute suppurative lymphadenitis in children is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes; the same organisms track along superficial lymphatics to cause lymphangitis, the tender red streak running from a wound toward the regional nodes.

Mycobacterial cervical lymphadenitis takes two forms. In adults and in people from high-prevalence regions, Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes scrofula: matted, often bilateral nodes with caseating granulomas and a positive interferon-gamma release assay. In otherwise healthy toddlers, nontuberculous mycobacteria such as Mycobacterium avium complex, acquired from soil and water through the oropharyngeal mucosa, cause a solitary painless node with violaceous thinning skin and negative tests for tuberculosis infection. Zoonoses are rarer but classic: Francisella tularensis after contact with rabbits or tick bites causes an ulcer with painful regional adenopathy, and Yersinia pestis after a flea bite causes an exquisitely tender bubo with rapid systemic illness; both are hazardous to laboratory staff, so the laboratory must be warned.

Tender nodes with an inoculation site point to a bacterial lymphadenitis; painless posterior cervical nodes with fatigue point to a viral or protozoal cause; hard fixed nodes point away from infection altogether.

Atypical lymphocytes and florid paracortical hyperplasia can look alarming on biopsy; preserved architecture and a polymorphous infiltrate argue for a reactive process rather than lymphoma.

sections.heading: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders of the lymphoreticular system
sections.html:
This group contains disorders in which the immune system itself, rather than an organism or a clone of malignant lymphocytes, produces the lymphoid enlargement and the cytopenias. Three mechanisms recur: failed shut-off of cytotoxic responses, cytokine excess, and clonal proliferation of histiocytes or dendritic cells.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and macrophage activation syndrome

Cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells kill their targets by releasing perforin and granzymes. Biallelic defects in this machinery (PRF1 encoding perforin, UNC13D, STX11, STXBP2, and the pigmentary syndromes Chediak-Higashi and Griscelli type 2) cause familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, usually within the first years of life. Because the target cell is engaged but never killed, antigen persists, the immune synapse is sustained, and activated T cells secrete interferon-gamma without restraint.

[[figure:s23a-fig31]]

Interferon-gamma converts macrophages into a hyperactivated state: they secrete IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-alpha, release ferritin, and phagocytose erythrocytes, leukocytes and platelets. The clinical syndrome follows directly from these mediators: unremitting fever, hepatosplenomegaly, two- or three-lineage cytopenias, hypertriglyceridemia (TNF-alpha inhibits lipoprotein lipase), hypofibrinogenemia with coagulopathy, hepatitis, and ferritin values in the thousands. Soluble CD25 (soluble interleukin-2 receptor) is raised as a marker of T-cell activation, and natural killer cell function is reduced.

Secondary (acquired) hemophagocytic syndrome shares this final pathway but is triggered in a person without an inherited cytotoxic defect. Triggers are infections (Epstein-Barr virus above all, also cytomegalovirus, other herpesviruses, leishmaniasis, and tick-borne intracellular bacteria), malignancy (especially T-cell and natural killer cell lymphomas), rheumatic disease, and immunotherapies. When it complicates a rheumatic disease, usually systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis or adult-onset Still disease, it is called macrophage activation syndrome. Its laboratory signature is a reversal of the expected inflammatory pattern: platelet count, leukocyte count, fibrinogen and consequently the erythrocyte sedimentation rate all fall, while ferritin, aminotransferases, triglycerides and D-dimer rise.

Castleman disease

Castleman disease is a lymphoproliferative disorder driven by interleukin-6. Unicentric disease is a solitary mass, often mediastinal, with hyaline-vascular histology (atrophic germinal centres penetrated by sclerotic vessels, giving a lollipop appearance, with expanded onion-skin mantle zones) and few systemic symptoms. Multicentric disease is systemic: fever, anemia, thrombocytopenia, hypoalbuminemia, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, a very high C-reactive protein and generalized adenopathy with splenomegaly, all explained by interleukin-6 action on the liver and on B cells. In people with uncontrolled HIV infection, multicentric disease is caused by human herpesvirus 8, whose infected plasmablasts make a viral interleukin-6 homolog; HHV-8 also causes Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma. Idiopathic multicentric disease is HHV-8 negative and is driven by host interleukin-6.

Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease and other reactive patterns

Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease (histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis) affects young adults with tender cervical adenopathy, fever, sometimes leukopenia and a raised sedimentation rate. Nodes show patchy paracortical necrosis full of karyorrhectic debris, crescentic histiocytes and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, with a conspicuous absence of neutrophils; this distinguishes it from suppurative lymphadenitis, while the absence of hematoxylin bodies and neutrophils helps separate it from lupus lymphadenitis, which it otherwise resembles. It is self-limited, and a minority of patients later develop systemic lupus erythematosus. Other reactive patterns include dermatopathic lymphadenopathy in chronic skin disease, drug-induced lymphadenopathy, and the florid follicular hyperplasia of early HIV infection, later replaced by follicular involution and lymphocyte depletion.

Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome

Heterozygous germline mutations in FAS impair extrinsic (death receptor) apoptosis, so activated lymphocytes are not deleted after an immune response. Children develop chronic, non-malignant lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, recurrent autoimmune cytopenias (immune thrombocytopenia, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, neutropenia), a raised vitamin B12 and soluble FAS ligand, and an expansion of alpha-beta double-negative (CD4-negative, CD8-negative) T cells. Lymphoma risk is increased, so persistent asymmetric nodal growth is biopsied.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis and sarcoidosis

Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a clonal neoplasm of myeloid dendritic cells with activating MAP kinase mutations, commonly BRAF V600E. The cells have grooved reniform nuclei, express CD1a, langerin (CD207) and S100, contain Birbeck granules on electron microscopy, and are accompanied by eosinophils. Presentations include punched-out lytic bone lesions, a seborrheic-like scalp and flexural rash, lymphadenopathy, pulmonary cysts in smokers, central diabetes insipidus from pituitary stalk infiltration, and marrow, liver and spleen involvement in multisystem disease. Sarcoidosis, by contrast, is a non-necrotizing granulomatous disease in which antigen-presenting cells activate CD4+ T-helper 1 cells; interferon-gamma and TNF-alpha turn macrophages into epithelioid and multinucleated giant cells. Hilar nodes, spleen and liver are often involved, and granuloma macrophages convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to its active form, which can raise calcium.

A falling erythrocyte sedimentation rate in a febrile child with systemic arthritis is not improvement: fibrinogen is being consumed, and macrophage activation syndrome should be excluded at once.

Ferritin is an acute-phase protein, but values in the thousands with cytopenias and splenomegaly belong to the hemophagocytic family and demand urgent action.

sections.heading: Haematologic neoplasms: lineage, genetics and morphology
sections.html:
Haematologic neoplasms are classified by lineage (myeloid or lymphoid), by maturity (precursor or mature), and by the genetic lesion. Each classification step has a morphologic or immunophenotypic handle that examinations reuse.

Acute leukemias

Acute leukemia is defined by at least 20% blasts in blood or marrow (or a defining genetic abnormality) and presents over weeks with the consequences of marrow failure: anemia, bleeding from thrombocytopenia, and infection from neutropenia. B-lymphoblastic leukemia is the commonest cancer of childhood, peaking at ages 2 to 5 years, and adds bone pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and meningeal or testicular involvement. Lymphoblasts express terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase, which adds untemplated nucleotides at antigen receptor junctions, with CD19 and CD10 and without surface immunoglobulin. Hyperdiploidy and ETV6::RUNX1 are favourable; infancy with KMT2A rearrangement, hypodiploidy and BCR::ABL1 are unfavourable. Because lymphoblasts seed the leptomeninges, where drug penetration is poor, every patient receives central nervous system-directed prophylaxis.

Acute myeloid leukemia is mainly a disease of older adults. Blasts express myeloperoxidase and CD33 and CD13, and Auer rods are fused myeloperoxidase-rich primary granules. Monocytic differentiation produces gum infiltration, and very high blast counts produce leukostasis with hypoxia and confusion. Prior alkylating agents cause therapy-related disease after five to seven years with loss of chromosome 5 or 7, whereas topoisomerase II inhibitors cause earlier disease with KMT2A rearrangement. Favourable genetics include core-binding factor abnormalities and mutated NPM1 without FLT3-ITD; complex karyotype and TP53 mutation are adverse.

Myelodysplastic syndromes and myelofibrosis

Myelodysplastic syndromes are clonal stem cell disorders of older adults in which the clone proliferates but its progeny die in the marrow. The result is ineffective hematopoiesis: a hypercellular marrow with peripheral cytopenias and a low reticulocyte count. Morphology shows oval macrocytes, hypolobated and hypogranular neutrophils, dysplastic megakaryocytes and sometimes ring sideroblasts (iron-laden perinuclear mitochondria, associated with SF3B1 mutation). Blasts stay below 20%; progression to acute myeloid leukemia is the feared outcome, and prognosis follows blast percentage, cytogenetics and depth of cytopenias. Isolated deletion of 5q is relatively favourable.

Primary myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by JAK2 V617F, CALR or MPL mutations. Clonal megakaryocytes release transforming growth factor-beta and platelet-derived growth factor, which stimulate reactive fibroblasts to lay down reticulin and collagen; the fibroblasts are not themselves neoplastic. Marrow aspiration yields a dry tap, hematopoiesis shifts to the spleen and liver, and the smear shows teardrop erythrocytes, nucleated red cells and immature granulocytes, with massive splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms.

Mature lymphoid neoplasms

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (identical to small lymphocytic lymphoma) is a neoplasm of small mature B cells coexpressing CD5 with CD19, CD23 and dim surface immunoglobulin; smudge cells on the smear reflect their fragility. Hypogammaglobulinemia, autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia complicate it, and transformation to aggressive large B-cell lymphoma can occur. Mantle cell lymphoma is the other CD5-positive neoplasm, but it is CD23 negative and carries t(11;14), placing CCND1 under the immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer so that cyclin D1 drives the G1 to S transition.

Follicular lymphoma is CD10 positive and CD5 negative with t(14;18), which overexpresses BCL2 and blocks apoptosis; it is indolent but can transform. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the commonest aggressive lymphoma and may arise de novo or by transformation. Extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma arises in tissue chronically stimulated by infection or autoimmunity: stomach with Helicobacter pylori, salivary gland in Sjogren disease, thyroid in Hashimoto thyroiditis. Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma follows HTLV-1 infection, whose Tax protein activates NF-kappa B and interleukin-2 signalling, producing clonal CD4+ CD25+ cells with lobulated nuclei, skin infiltration and hypercalcemia. Mycosis fungoides is a cutaneous CD4+ T-cell lymphoma with epidermotropism and cerebriform nuclei; Sezary syndrome is its erythrodermic leukemic variant.

Plasma cell disorders

Plasma cell neoplasms secrete a monoclonal immunoglobulin, detected as an M spike on serum protein electrophoresis and typed by immunofixation. Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance has a protein below 3 g/dL with under 10% clonal marrow plasma cells and no end-organ damage, and carries a small annual risk of progression. Smoldering myeloma has a larger burden without myeloma-defining events. Multiple myeloma produces hypercalcemia, kidney injury, anemia and lytic bone lesions, the last through RANK ligand-driven osteoclast activation with inhibition of osteoblasts. Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma secreting monoclonal IgM, nearly always with MYD88 L265P; because pentameric IgM is large and intravascular, high levels raise serum viscosity.

NeoplasmGenetic or phenotypic markerMorphologic clue

Acute myeloid leukemiaMyeloperoxidase+, CD33, CD13Auer rods

Two CD5-positive mature B-cell neoplasms exist: chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CD23 positive) and mantle cell lymphoma (cyclin D1 positive). CD23 separates them in one step.

sections.heading: Blood-borne infections: diagnosis and management
sections.html:
Fever in a returning traveller and fever after tick exposure are two of the commonest reasons a clinician must act before a diagnosis is confirmed. Both have treatable, rapidly fatal members, so the order of testing and the threshold for empiric therapy matter more than breadth of testing.

Suspected malaria

Any fever within a year of travel to an endemic area, and especially within three months, requires immediate thick and thin smears with a rapid antigen test; results should be available within hours, not the next morning. Report species and percentage parasitemia, because both drive management. If the first set is negative, repeat every 12 to 24 hours for three sets before abandoning the diagnosis.

Features that define severe falciparum malaria are impaired consciousness or seizures, respiratory distress or acidosis, a raised lactate, hypoglycemia, acute kidney injury, significant anemia, shock, bleeding, jaundice with organ dysfunction, and parasitemia above about 5 to 10%. Severe disease is treated with intravenous artesunate at any age and in pregnancy; it clears parasites faster than quinine and reduces mortality. Give glucose, treat seizures, use fluids cautiously because pulmonary edema is easily provoked, and avoid corticosteroids for cerebral malaria. Once oral therapy is tolerated, complete a full oral artemisinin-based combination course. Watch for delayed post-artesunate hemolysis in the following weeks.

Uncomplicated falciparum malaria is treated with an oral artemisinin-based combination such as artemether-lumefantrine, or with atovaquone-proguanil; chloroquine still works in the few chloroquine-sensitive regions. For P. vivax and P. ovale, blood-stage treatment is followed by primaquine or tafenoquine for radical cure, after testing glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity; these drugs are deferred in pregnancy, where weekly chloroquine suppression is used until after delivery. Travellers should be advised on chemoprophylaxis and bite avoidance for future trips.

Babesiosis

Suspect babesiosis in a patient from an endemic area with fever, sweats and hemolysis, and in anyone with hemolysis after a transfusion. Diagnosis is by smear with confirmatory polymerase chain reaction. Uncomplicated disease in an immunocompetent patient is treated with atovaquone plus azithromycin, which is as effective as and better tolerated than clindamycin plus quinine. Severe disease (parasitemia above about 10%, significant hemolysis, or organ dysfunction) is treated with intravenous clindamycin and quinine, with red cell exchange transfusion considered in the sickest patients. Asplenic and immunocompromised patients relapse and may need extended therapy with serial smears. Test for co-infection when the illness does not fit.

Tick-borne intracellular bacteria

In anaplasmosis and ehrlichiosis, confirmatory polymerase chain reaction and paired serology take days, and delay worsens outcome, so doxycycline is started on clinical suspicion and continued for about 10 days (or at least three days after fever resolves). Fever usually settles within 48 hours; failure to improve should prompt rethinking. Doxycycline is appropriate for children, since short courses do not meaningfully stain teeth. Severe complications include a syndrome resembling hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, acute respiratory distress and renal failure, particularly in older and immunosuppressed patients.

Parvovirus B19 and aplastic crisis

A sudden fall in hemoglobin with reticulocytopenia in a patient with chronic hemolysis points to transient aplastic crisis. Management is simple transfusion for symptomatic anemia and observation until reticulocytes recover, usually within one to two weeks; immunoglobulin is reserved for chronic infection in immunocompromised patients. Viremic patients are infectious: use droplet precautions and keep pregnant staff and other patients with hemolytic anemia away. In pregnancy, maternal infection is followed with serial ultrasonography and middle cerebral artery Doppler studies, and severe fetal anemia is treated by intrauterine transfusion.

Hematologic effects of bacteremia and sepsis

Treat the infection and achieve source control; blood products are given for bleeding or procedures rather than to normalize numbers. In sepsis-associated disseminated intravascular coagulation, transfuse platelets for bleeding or very low counts, plasma for prolonged clotting times with bleeding, and fibrinogen replacement when levels are very low; avoid antifibrinolytics. Prophylactic-dose anticoagulation for thromboprophylaxis is generally continued. Any patient with prolonged fever, cytopenias, splenomegaly and a very high ferritin should be evaluated for hemophagocytic syndrome, which is treated as a hyperinflammatory emergency alongside the trigger.

InfectionBest initial testFirst-line treatment
Uncomplicated falciparum malariaThick and thin smears plus rapid antigen testOral artemisinin-based combination
Severe falciparum malariaSmear with parasitemia quantificationIntravenous artesunate, then oral combination
P. vivax or P. ovaleSmear for speciesBlood-stage therapy plus primaquine or tafenoquine after G6PD testing
Babesiosis, mild to moderateSmear plus polymerase chain reactionAtovaquone and azithromycin
Anaplasmosis or ehrlichiosisPolymerase chain reaction (treat before results)Doxycycline

Step 1 asks why cytoadherence causes coma and why reticulocytopenia marks parvovirus; Step 2 CK asks who needs intravenous artesunate, who needs exchange transfusion, and who needs doxycycline before the test returns.

sections.heading: Lymphadenopathy and lymphadenitis: evaluation and management
sections.html:
Most lymphadenopathy in primary care is reactive and self-limited. The clinical task is to identify the minority who need imaging and tissue, and to do so without a long, expensive and anxious delay.

Assessing a lymph node

Localized adenopathy suggests a problem in its drainage field; generalized adenopathy suggests a systemic infection, a rheumatic disease, a drug reaction or a lymphoproliferative disorder. Features that raise concern are size above about 2 cm, hard or rubbery texture, fixation to surrounding tissue, supraclavicular location, age above 40 years, duration beyond four to six weeks or progressive growth, and B symptoms (fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss above 10%). A supraclavicular node is high risk at any age. Tenderness suggests rapid capsular stretch and is common in infection, but it does not exclude malignancy.

The first round of testing is directed by the history: complete blood count with differential and smear, and targeted serology or microbiology (Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, HIV, toxoplasmosis, Bartonella, interferon-gamma release assay). A chest radiograph is useful when mediastinal disease or tuberculosis is possible. Drug causes (notably phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, allopurinol and some antibiotics) should be reviewed. Where the picture suggests a self-limited reactive process and no red flags are present, observation for three to four weeks with a planned review is appropriate; where red flags are present, proceed directly to imaging and tissue.

Cross-sectional imaging of the involved region defines the extent of disease and can disclose a mucosal or pulmonary primary tumour; it is obtained before biopsy so that sampling targets the most informative site. Excisional biopsy is preferred when lymphoma is suspected, because classification depends on architecture as well as immunophenotype; an adequate core needle biopsy with tissue for flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry is acceptable in many centres. Fine-needle aspiration suits confirmation of metastatic carcinoma; a negative aspirate never closes the evaluation of a high-risk node.

Managing specific lymphadenitides

Infectious mononucleosis is treated supportively with fluids, analgesia and reassurance that fatigue may persist for weeks. Avoid amoxicillin and ampicillin, which commonly produce a rash. Corticosteroids are reserved for impending airway obstruction, not for symptom relief. Athletes should avoid contact and collision sports and heavy lifting for at least three weeks from symptom onset and while the spleen remains palpable, because splenic rupture may follow minimal trauma. Antivirals do not alter the course.

Acute suppurative lymphadenitis in a child is treated empirically with an antibiotic active against Staphylococcus aureus (including community-acquired methicillin-resistant strains where prevalent) and Streptococcus pyogenes; a fluctuant node is aspirated or drained. Cat-scratch disease usually resolves spontaneously over two to four months; azithromycin shortens bulky adenopathy and antibiotics are recommended for immunocompromised patients and systemic disease, while suppurative nodes are aspirated rather than incised. Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis in a young child is best treated by complete surgical excision, with a macrolide-based regimen when excision would endanger the facial nerve; incision and drainage risks a chronic sinus. Tuberculous lymphadenitis is treated with standard multidrug antituberculous therapy, and nodes may paradoxically enlarge early in treatment. Acute toxoplasmosis in an immunocompetent, non-pregnant adult needs no treatment; infection in pregnancy or in an immunocompromised host does.

Emphasis populations

In children, most cervical nodes are reactive and large tonsillar and jugulodigastric nodes are normal findings; persistent supraclavicular nodes, systemic symptoms or abnormal counts are the warning signs. In older adults, the prior probability of malignancy is far higher, so an unexplained persistent node earns early tissue diagnosis. In pregnancy, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus and toxoplasmosis testing all have implications for the fetus, and imaging choices account for radiation. In immunocompromised patients, consider mycobacterial, fungal and HHV-8-related causes and lower the threshold for biopsy.

PresentationMost likely causeNext step
Young adult, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegalyEpstein-Barr virusHeterophile test; EBV serology if negative
Tender axillary node weeks after a kitten scratchBartonella henselaeBartonella serology; azithromycin if bulky
Toddler, painless submandibular node, violaceous skin, negative IGRANontuberculous mycobacteriaComplete surgical excision
Older smoker, hard fixed supraclavicular nodeMalignancyCT of neck and chest, then biopsy

The compartment expanded on biopsy (Step 1) maps onto the clinical algorithm (Step 2 CK): T-zone hyperplasia follows viral illness and is observed, granulomas direct microbiology, and effaced architecture demands oncologic staging.

sections.heading: Hyperinflammatory and histiocytic disorders: diagnosis and management
sections.html:
These disorders are uncommon, but they appear repeatedly on examinations because recognizing them changes management abruptly: one group needs urgent immunosuppression, another needs nothing but follow-up, and a third needs an oncologic work-up.

When to suspect and how to confirm a hemophagocytic syndrome

Think of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis in any patient with prolonged fever that does not respond to antibiotics, especially with splenomegaly, falling blood counts and hepatitis. Send ferritin early: values in the thousands, and particularly above 10,000 ng/mL, are a strong pointer in adults, and extreme values are typical in children. Supporting findings are bicytopenia or pancytopenia, fasting triglycerides above about 265 mg/dL, fibrinogen below about 150 mg/dL, raised soluble CD25 and reduced natural killer cell activity, and hemophagocytosis in marrow, spleen, node or cerebrospinal fluid; hemophagocytosis is neither necessary nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

Evaluation runs in parallel with treatment because mortality is high. Bone marrow examination looks both for hemophagocytosis and for an occult trigger, particularly lymphoma; testing covers Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus viral loads, HIV, other regional infections, autoimmune serology, and imaging for malignancy. In children and in adults with recurrent or familial disease, genetic testing for cytotoxic pathway defects is indicated, because familial disease requires allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation after remission.

Treatment has two arms: control the immune activation, and treat the trigger. Corticosteroids are the backbone; etoposide-containing protocols are used in severe disease and in Epstein-Barr virus-driven disease, where rituximab is often added to reduce the infected B-cell burden. Intrathecal therapy is used for central nervous system disease. In macrophage activation syndrome complicating rheumatic disease, high-dose corticosteroids with anakinra or cyclosporine are standard, and etoposide is reserved for refractory cases; the interferon-gamma-neutralizing antibody emapalumab is approved for primary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Supportive care addresses coagulopathy, infection risk and organ failure.

Castleman disease

Unicentric Castleman disease is cured by complete surgical excision of the involved node or mass. Multicentric disease needs systemic therapy, chosen by HHV-8 status. HHV-8-associated disease in HIV infection is treated with rituximab together with antiretroviral therapy, which has transformed survival; concurrent Kaposi sarcoma may flare after rituximab and may require added chemotherapy, and the most severe presentations receive chemotherapy upfront. Idiopathic multicentric disease (HIV-negative, HHV-8-negative) is treated with the interleukin-6-directed antibody siltuximab, with corticosteroids; interleukin-6 receptor blockade and immunomodulators are alternatives. Patients need surveillance for progression and for associated conditions such as POEMS syndrome and paraneoplastic pemphigus.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis

Management depends on extent. A single bone lesion may be curetted, injected with corticosteroid or simply observed; isolated skin disease may respond to topical therapy. Multisystem disease, and any disease involving the marrow, liver or spleen, is treated with systemic chemotherapy, conventionally vinblastine with prednisone, and MAPK pathway inhibitors are used in refractory disease with BRAF V600E. Central diabetes insipidus is the commonest endocrine complication, is usually permanent, and is treated with desmopressin; growth hormone deficiency and other anterior pituitary deficits may follow. Pulmonary disease in adults demands smoking cessation. Long-term follow-up covers endocrine function, hearing, skeletal sequelae and a neurodegenerative syndrome that may appear years later.

Disorders that need recognition rather than treatment

Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease resolves over one to four months; management is analgesia or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with follow-up, and corticosteroids are reserved for severe or extranodal disease. Because the histology overlaps with lupus lymphadenitis, repeat autoimmune serology and watch for rash, arthritis, cytopenias or nephritis. Asymptomatic stage I sarcoidosis (bilateral hilar adenopathy with clear lungs) is observed, with monitoring of symptoms, spirometry and diffusing capacity, serum calcium and creatinine, liver tests, an electrocardiogram to screen for cardiac disease, and ophthalmologic examination for asymptomatic uveitis; corticosteroids are reserved for symptomatic or progressive pulmonary disease, hypercalcemia, and cardiac, neurologic, ocular or renal involvement. In autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome, the cytopenias are treated (corticosteroids and immune globulin acutely, then sirolimus or mycophenolate for maintenance), rituximab is avoided where possible because of prolonged hypogammaglobulinemia, and splenectomy is avoided because of overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis; chronic lymphadenopathy itself needs no treatment but is watched for lymphoma.

DisorderDecisive findingManagement

Macrophage activation syndromeFalling platelets and fibrinogen in systemic arthritis with soaring ferritinHigh-dose corticosteroids with anakinra or cyclosporine
Unicentric Castleman diseaseSolitary mass, hyaline-vascular histologySurgical excision
HHV-8 multicentric Castleman diseaseHHV-8-positive plasmablasts, high HHV-8 load in HIVRituximab plus antiretroviral therapy
Multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosisCD1a-positive histiocytes, lytic bone lesions, diabetes insipidusVinblastine with prednisone; desmopressin
Kikuchi-Fujimoto diseaseNeutrophil-poor necrotizing lymphadenitisSupportive care, follow-up for lupus

Step 1 explains why interferon-gamma and interleukin-6 produce these syndromes; Step 2 CK asks which patient needs urgent etoposide, which needs rituximab, and which needs only a review appointment.

sections.heading: Haematologic neoplasms: diagnosis, treatment and complications
sections.html:
Three clinical questions recur: does this cytopenia or lymphocytosis need marrow examination, does this patient need treatment now or surveillance, and which complication must be anticipated before the first dose.

Deciding who needs treatment

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia found incidentally in an asymptomatic patient is observed, since earlier treatment does not prolong life. Indications to treat are progressive marrow failure with anemia or thrombocytopenia, bulky or symptomatic lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly, rapid lymphocyte doubling, significant constitutional symptoms, and autoimmune cytopenias refractory to corticosteroids. First-line therapy is targeted: a covalent Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor, or time-limited venetoclax with an anti-CD20 antibody. Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors cause atrial fibrillation, hypertension and bleeding; venetoclax requires careful ramp-up because of tumor lysis risk. Infection prevention matters because of hypogammaglobulinemia: give recommended inactivated vaccines, avoid live vaccines, and consider immune globulin replacement for recurrent serious infections.

Monoclonal gammopathies are stratified by criteria. Myeloma requires 10% or more clonal marrow plasma cells (or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) plus a myeloma-defining event: hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency from the clone, anemia, lytic bone lesions on skeletal survey or low-dose whole-body CT, 60% or more clonal plasma cells, an involved to uninvolved free light chain ratio of 100 or more with an involved chain of at least 100 mg/L, or more than one focal lesion on MRI. Without a defining event, the patient has monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance or smoldering myeloma and is monitored, with risk-stratified intervals and counselling about symptoms that warrant earlier review.

Myelodysplastic syndrome and myelofibrosis

An older adult with unexplained macrocytic anemia and a low reticulocyte count, after vitamin B12, folate, thyroid and alcohol causes are excluded, needs marrow examination with cytogenetics and molecular testing. Lower-risk myelodysplastic syndrome is managed supportively with transfusions and iron chelation where appropriate, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents when the erythropoietin level is low, luspatercept for anemia with ring sideroblasts, and lenalidomide for isolated del(5q). Higher-risk disease is treated with hypomethylating agents, and allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation is the only curative option in fit patients. In primary myelofibrosis, ruxolitinib reduces spleen size and constitutional symptoms (anemia and thrombocytopenia are the main adverse effects), and transplantation is considered in higher-risk, fit patients.

Lymphomas

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is curable and treated with chemoimmunotherapy, conventionally rituximab with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone; cardiac function is assessed before anthracycline, hepatitis B serology is checked before anti-CD20 therapy because of reactivation risk, and central nervous system prophylaxis is considered in high-risk disease. Follicular lymphoma is indolent: asymptomatic low-burden disease is observed, while symptomatic or bulky disease receives anti-CD20-based therapy, and localized disease may be irradiated. Mantle cell lymphoma is treated with intensive regimens in fit younger patients and Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor-based approaches in others. Localized gastric MALT lymphoma with Helicobacter pylori regresses after eradication therapy in most patients, with endoscopic follow-up; persistent disease is irradiated. Early-stage mycosis fungoides is treated with skin-directed therapy (topical corticosteroids, topical chemotherapy or retinoids, phototherapy); Sezary syndrome needs systemic therapy such as extracorporeal photopheresis or targeted antibodies. Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma carries a poor prognosis, and patients from endemic areas should be screened and treated for strongyloidiasis before immunosuppression.

Complications to anticipate

Tumor lysis syndrome follows rapid cell death in bulky, highly proliferative disease: hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, hypocalcemia and acute kidney injury. High-risk patients receive vigorous hydration plus rasburicase, which converts existing urate to allantoin within hours but is contraindicated in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; allopurinol suits lower-risk patients, and urinary alkalinization is no longer recommended. Symptomatic hyperviscosity in Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (headache, blurred vision, mucosal bleeding, confusion, dilated sausage-shaped retinal veins) is treated first with plasmapheresis, before systemic therapy; rituximab is delayed because of the IgM flare, and red cell transfusion is deferred until viscosity falls. Hyperleukocytosis with leukostasis requires urgent cytoreduction. Febrile neutropenia requires blood cultures and immediate broad-spectrum antipseudomonal antibiotics within an hour. Long-term survivorship care covers second cancers, anthracycline cardiomyopathy, fertility counselling before treatment, bone health, vaccination and, in older adults, review of drug interactions and renal dosing.

Clinical situationMost appropriate action
Asymptomatic early-stage chronic lymphocytic leukemiaObservation with periodic assessment
Monoclonal protein with no myeloma-defining eventPeriodic monitoring
Symptomatic splenomegaly in primary myelofibrosisRuxolitinib
Localized gastric MALT lymphoma with H. pyloriEradication therapy, then endoscopic follow-up
IgM paraprotein with retinal vein changes and confusionPlasmapheresis
Bulky lymphoma with high lactate dehydrogenase and raised urateHydration plus rasburicase

The marker that defines the disease on Step 1 usually names the drug on Step 2 CK: JAK2 and ruxolitinib, CD20 and rituximab, cyclin D1 and Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibition, H. pylori and eradication therapy.

title: Blood · Anemias: production, hemolysis and hemoglobin disorders
meta: Mechanisms of underproduction anemias, hemolysis, hemoglobinopathies, membrane defects and porphyrias.

sections.heading: Approach to anemia; iron deficiency, inflammation, lead and sideroblastic anemia

furtherReading.label: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf): Iron Deficiency and Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia

sections.html:
Two questions that sort every anemia

Anemia is a hemoglobin below the sex-specific lower limit (13.5 g/dL in men, 12.0 g/dL in women on Naadi's lab table). Two measurements organise the differential. The first is whether the marrow is responding. The second is red cell size.

  • Reticulocyte response. The raw reticulocyte percentage overstates output when the hematocrit is low, so correct it: corrected reticulocyte count = reticulocyte % × (patient hematocrit ÷ 45). The reticulocyte production index (RPI) also divides by a maturation factor, because stress reticulocytes are released early and circulate longer. An RPI below about 2 means the marrow is not keeping up (decreased production). A clearly higher RPI means the marrow is working and red cells are being lost (bleeding) or destroyed (hemolysis).
  • MCV. Within the underproduction group, microcytosis (MCV below 80 fL) points to a defect in hemoglobin synthesis: too little iron, iron that cannot be used, too little globin, or a block in heme synthesis. Macrocytosis (above 100 fL) points to impaired DNA synthesis (megaloblastic) or to non-megaloblastic causes such as alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism and drugs. Normocytic underproduction is usually early iron deficiency, inflammation, kidney disease, or marrow failure or infiltration.
[[figure:s23a-fig40]]

Iron handling in one paragraph

Dietary non-heme iron is reduced to Fe2+ at the duodenal brush border (duodenal cytochrome b) and enters enterocytes through divalent metal transporter 1. Heme iron has its own, more efficient uptake. Iron leaves the enterocyte (and macrophages that recycle senescent red cells) through ferroportin, is oxidised by hephaestin or ceruloplasmin, and travels on transferrin. Hepcidin, made by hepatocytes, binds ferroportin and causes its internalisation and degradation. High hepcidin therefore traps iron in enterocytes and macrophages. Iron deficiency and active erythropoiesis (through erythroferrone) suppress hepcidin. Inflammation (IL-6) and iron loading raise it. The body has no regulated route of iron excretion, so absorption is the only control point.

Iron deficiency anemia

Stores fall first (low ferritin), then transport iron (transferrin saturation falls, TIBC rises because the liver makes more transferrin), and only then hemoglobin. The cells become microcytic and hypochromic with a raised RDW. Free erythrocyte protoporphyrin rises because ferrochelatase lacks iron. Mechanisms to remember:

  • Increased need: infancy and adolescent growth, pregnancy (fetal transfer and expanded red cell mass).
  • Loss: menstruation, and gastrointestinal bleeding in men and postmenopausal women, where occult colorectal or gastric cancer must be excluded.
  • Reduced intake or absorption: diets without heme iron, excess cow's milk in toddlers (low iron and occult intestinal loss), celiac disease (proximal small bowel villous atrophy), atrophic gastritis and acid suppression (less reduction of ferric iron), Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (food bypasses the duodenum).

Severe deficiency can cause pica (ice, clay), koilonychia, angular cheilitis, atrophic glossitis and, rarely, esophageal webs. Restless legs syndrome is associated with low iron stores.

Anemia of inflammation

Chronic infection, autoimmune disease, cancer and kidney disease raise IL-6, which drives hepcidin. Ferroportin is degraded, so iron sits in macrophages while serum iron falls. TIBC is normal or low and ferritin (an acute-phase protein) is normal or high. Inflammatory cytokines also blunt erythropoietin production and the marrow's response to it, and shorten red cell survival. The anemia is mild and normocytic, becoming microcytic when long-standing.

FindingIron deficiencyInflammationThalassemia traitSideroblastic
Serum ironLowLowNormalHigh
TIBC (transferrin)HighLow or normalNormalNormal or low
FerritinLowNormal or highNormalHigh
RDWHighNormalNormalHigh (dimorphic)
Marrow ironAbsentPresent in macrophagesPresentRinged sideroblasts

Lead poisoning

Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, so aminolevulinic acid and zinc protoporphyrin accumulate. It also inhibits pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase, so ribosomal RNA is not broken down and aggregates as coarse basophilic stippling. Children with exposure to old paint dust or contaminated soil develop irritability, abdominal pain, constipation, learning problems and, at high levels, encephalopathy. Adults with occupational exposure (battery recycling, smelting, renovation, firing ranges) develop abdominal colic, a motor neuropathy (wrist drop), hypertension, nephropathy and gout. Lead lines appear at the gingival margin and the metaphyses of long bones.

Sideroblastic anemia

Here iron reaches the erythroblast mitochondrion but cannot be inserted into protoporphyrin. Iron accumulates in mitochondria around the nucleus: ringed sideroblasts on Prussian blue stain of the marrow. The inherited form is X-linked, from mutations in ALAS2, the erythroid ALA synthase that needs pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6). Acquired causes are more common: alcohol, isoniazid (which depletes B6), copper deficiency (including from excess zinc intake), lead, and myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts. Serum iron, ferritin and transferrin saturation are high, and some patients respond to pyridoxine.

Myelophthisic anemia

When marrow is replaced by metastatic carcinoma (breast, prostate, lung), fibrosis or granulomas, the blood shows a leukoerythroblastic picture (nucleated red cells and immature myeloid cells) with teardrop cells. Aspiration is often dry, so the diagnosis comes from a core biopsy.

Iron deficiency can coexist with inflammation. Because ferritin rises with inflammation, a ferritin that is "normal" but under about 100 ng/mL, with a low transferrin saturation, can still mean depleted stores in a patient with active inflammatory disease.

The ratio of MCV to red cell count (in millions/mm3) is a quick screen: well below 13 favours thalassemia trait and above 13 favours iron deficiency. It is only a clue; ferritin and hemoglobin analysis decide

sections.html:
Why B12 and folate deficiency enlarge cells

DNA synthesis needs thymidine, made by thymidylate synthase using N5,N10-methylene tetrahydrofolate. When folate is short, or when it is "trapped" as 5-methyl-THF because B12 is missing, nuclear maturation lags behind cytoplasmic maturation. Precursors become large with open chromatin (megaloblasts), many die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis, so LDH and indirect bilirubin rise), and the blood shows oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils (six or more lobes). All rapidly dividing cells are affected, so pancytopenia and glossitis are common.

The two B12 enzymes

EnzymeCofactor formReactionLab marker when deficient
Methionine synthaseMethylcobalamin (plus 5-methyl-THF)Homocysteine → methionine; regenerates THFHomocysteine rises (also in folate deficiency)
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutaseAdenosylcobalaminMethylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoAMethylmalonic acid rises (B12 only)

Neurologic damage in B12 deficiency is thought to reflect impaired methylation (low S-adenosylmethionine) and abnormal fatty acids in myelin. It produces subacute combined degeneration: dorsal columns (loss of vibration and position sense, positive Romberg sign) and lateral corticospinal tracts (spasticity, extensor plantar responses), plus peripheral neuropathy and cognitive change. Neurologic disease can appear without anemia, and giving folate alone can correct the blood count while the neurologic damage progresses.

B12 absorption and its failures

Acid and pepsin free B12 from food protein; it binds haptocorrin, is released by pancreatic proteases in the duodenum, binds intrinsic factor from parietal cells and is taken up in the terminal ileum. Liver stores last years, so dietary deficiency (strict vegans, infants breastfed by B12-deficient mothers) develops slowly.

  • Pernicious anemia: autoimmune gastritis of the body and fundus with antibodies to parietal cells (H+/K+-ATPase) and to intrinsic factor. Achlorhydria removes acid feedback, so gastrin rises and enterochromaffin-like cells proliferate, raising the risk of gastric neuroendocrine tumours and adenocarcinoma. It clusters with Hashimoto thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes and vitiligo.
  • Ileal disease or resection: Crohn disease, resection of more than a short ileal segment. Pancreatic insufficiency and bacterial overgrowth or Diphyllobothrium latum compete for or fail to release the vitamin.
  • Drugs: long-term metformin and acid suppression (proton pump inhibitors, H2 blockers) reduce absorption. Nitrous oxide oxidises the cobalt of cobalamin and inactivates methionine synthase; recreational use can precipitate myelopathy even with a normal serum B12.

Folate deficiency

Folate is absorbed in the jejunum and stores last only months, so deficiency follows poor intake quickly (alcohol use disorder, older adults with poor diets), increased demand (pregnancy, chronic hemolysis, exfoliative skin disease) and drugs. Methotrexate, trimethoprim and pyrimethamine inhibit dihydrofolate reductase; phenytoin and other anticonvulsants reduce absorption. Homocysteine rises but methylmalonic acid is normal, and there is no myelopathy. Maternal folate deficiency raises the risk of neural tube defects.

Aplastic anemia

Aplastic anemia is pancytopenia with a hypocellular, fat-replaced marrow and no infiltrating cells or fibrosis. Most acquired cases are immune: cytotoxic T cells destroy hematopoietic stem cells, which is why immunosuppression works. Recognised triggers include drugs (chloramphenicol, carbamazepine, felbamate, some sulfonamides), benzene, radiation and cytotoxic chemotherapy (dose-dependent), and seronegative hepatitis. Small PNH clones are common because GPI-anchor–deficient stem cells escape the immune attack. Inherited marrow failure includes Fanconi anemia (DNA crosslink repair defect: short stature, thumb and radial anomalies, café-au-lait spots, later leukemia and squamous cancers) and telomere disorders. Patients have fatigue, bleeding and infection, but no splenomegaly and a low reticulocyte count.

Pure red cell aplasia

Only the erythroid line fails: severe normocytic anemia, reticulocytes near zero, normal leukocytes and platelets, and a marrow without erythroid precursors. Causes include thymoma (an autoimmune T-cell or antibody attack on erythroid progenitors), large granular lymphocytic leukemia, antibodies against erythropoietin after ESA therapy, and parvovirus B19, which enters erythroid progenitors through the P antigen (globoside) and kills them. In healthy people B19 halts erythropoiesis for days with no anemia. In chronic hemolysis it causes a transient aplastic crisis. In immunocompromised hosts who cannot make antibody it persists as chronic red cell aplasia. Diamond-Blackfan anemia is the congenital form (ribosomal protein genes, macrocytosis, thumb anomalies).

Anemia of chronic kidney disease

Erythropoietin is made by peritubular interstitial fibroblasts in the renal cortex under the control of hypoxia-inducible factor. As these cells are lost, erythropoietin is inappropriately low for the degree of anemia. Hepcidin rises (inflammation, reduced clearance), uremic toxins shorten red cell survival and dialysis causes blood loss. The anemia is normocytic and hypoproliferative. Recombinant erythropoietin and darbepoetin replace the hormone; hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors raise endogenous production.

Macrocytosis with a high reticulocyte count may simply reflect reticulocytes, which are larger than mature cells; this is a hemolysis or bleeding picture, not megaloblastic anemia.

Step 2 CK asks what to measure next: in suspected B12 deficiency with a borderline serum level, a raised methylmalonic acid confirms tissue deficiency.

sections.heading: Hemolysis: mechanisms, markers and the main hemolytic anemias

furtherReading.label: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf): Laboratory Evaluation of Immune Hemolytic Anemias

sections.html:
Where red cells are destroyed

Hemolysis shortens red cell survival below the normal 120 days. The marrow can raise output several-fold, so anemia appears only when destruction outpaces that response, or when the marrow is suppressed (for example by parvovirus B19 or folate deficiency).

  • Extravascular hemolysis is removal of altered cells by macrophages, mostly in the splenic red pulp and liver. Antibody-coated cells are recognised by Fc receptors, C3b-coated cells by complement receptors, and rigid or spherical cells are trapped in the splenic cords. Hemoglobin is broken down inside macrophages, so bilirubin rises but free hemoglobin does not appear in plasma in large amounts. Splenomegaly and pigment gallstones are typical.
  • Intravascular hemolysis releases hemoglobin into plasma. It binds haptoglobin, and the complex is cleared by macrophages (CD163), so haptoglobin becomes undetectable. When haptoglobin is saturated, free hemoglobin dimers pass the glomerulus (hemoglobinuria: dipstick positive for blood without red cells). Proximal tubular cells reabsorb hemoglobin, store its iron as hemosiderin and shed it, so urine hemosiderin appears days later and persists with chronic intravascular hemolysis. Free hemoglobin also scavenges nitric oxide, causing smooth muscle spasm (dysphagia, abdominal pain, erectile dysfunction) and contributing to thrombosis.
MarkerExtravascularIntravascular
Reticulocytes, indirect bilirubin, LDHRaisedRaised (LDH often very high)
HaptoglobinLowUndetectable
Plasma free hemoglobin, hemoglobinuriaAbsentPresent
Urine hemosiderinAbsentPresent (after several days)
Typical smearSpherocytesSchistocytes (mechanical), ghost cells, or few changes

Immune hemolysis

The direct antiglobulin test (DAT, direct Coombs) detects IgG or complement already on the patient's cells and separates immune from non-immune causes.

FeatureWarm autoimmuneCold agglutinin
AntibodyIgG, binds best at 37 °CIgM, binds below body temperature; targets I (or i) antigen
DATIgG with or without C3C3 (C3d) only; IgM dissociates on warming
Main siteSpleen, Fc receptor–mediated; partial phagocytosis leaves spherocytesLiver (C3b-coated cells); some complement lysis in vessels
AssociationsSLE, CLL and other lymphomas, immune deficiency, drugs; idiopathic in about halfMycoplasma pneumoniae (anti-I), EBV (anti-i), clonal B-cell disorder in primary disease
CluesSpherocytes, splenomegalyAgglutinates on smear, acrocyanosis in cold, falsely high MCV on automated counts

Drugs cause immune hemolysis by three main routes. Some bind firmly to the membrane and act as haptens: high-dose intravenous penicillin coats cells, and IgG against the drug–membrane complex causes extravascular hemolysis. Some induce antibodies that react only when the drug is present, often activating complement and causing brisk intravascular hemolysis (ceftriaxone and piperacillin are classic). A few, such as methyldopa and fludarabine, induce true autoantibodies that persist without the drug. Stopping the drug is central to treatment.

Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

A hematopoietic stem cell acquires a somatic mutation in PIGA, an X-linked gene needed to build the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor. Its progeny lack all GPI-anchored proteins, including CD55 (decay-accelerating factor, which limits C3 convertase) and CD59 (which blocks assembly of the membrane attack complex). Spontaneous alternative-pathway activity then lyses red cells in the vessels. The triad is intravascular hemolysis (dark urine, classically worse in the morning), thrombosis at unusual sites (hepatic veins, portal and mesenteric veins, cerebral sinuses) and marrow failure. Chronic urinary loss can add iron deficiency. Diagnosis is by flow cytometry showing absent CD55 and CD59 on red cells and loss of GPI-anchored proteins (FLAER binding) on granulocytes. A monoclonal antibody to C5 blocks the terminal pathway but also removes defence against encapsulated Neisseria.

Enzyme defects

G6PD deficiency is X-linked. G6PD makes NADPH in the pentose phosphate pathway; NADPH keeps glutathione reduced so it can detoxify hydrogen peroxide. Red cells cannot make new enzyme, so old cells are most vulnerable. Oxidant stress (infection, fava beans, primaquine and tafenoquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase, methylene blue) denatures hemoglobin into Heinz bodies, which splenic macrophages pluck out, leaving bite cells. Hemolysis is mixed intravascular and extravascular and begins one to three days after exposure. Rasburicase is a special case: converting urate to allantoin generates hydrogen peroxide directly in the blood. Heterozygous women vary in severity because of X inactivation.

Pyruvate kinase deficiency is autosomal recessive and the most common glycolytic enzyme defect. Mature red cells rely on glycolysis for ATP. Without it, the Na+/K+-ATPase fails, cells lose potassium and water, become rigid (echinocytes) and are removed in the spleen. Upstream intermediates accumulate, including 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, which shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, so patients tolerate their anemia better than expected. The DAT is negative and osmotic fragility is normal. Mitapivat is an oral allosteric activator of pyruvate kinase.

A G6PD activity measured during or just after a hemolytic episode can be falsely normal, because the surviving cells are young and enzyme-rich.

sections.heading: Sickle cell disease, sickle trait and hemoglobin C
sections.html:
Molecular basis

Hemoglobin S results from a single nucleotide change in codon 6 of the β-globin gene on chromosome 11, replacing glutamate with valine. The hydrophobic valine fits a pocket on a neighbouring β chain only when hemoglobin is deoxygenated, so deoxy-HbS polymerises into long fibres that distort and stiffen the cell. Polymerisation depends steeply on HbS concentration and is promoted by low oxygen tension, acidosis, raised temperature, raised 2,3-BPG and dehydration (which raises intracellular hemoglobin concentration). Fetal hemoglobin does not join the polymer, which is why newborns are protected for the first months and why drugs that raise HbF help.

Repeated sickling damages the membrane, so cells are destroyed (chronic extravascular and some intravascular hemolysis). Rigid cells, and sickled cells that adhere to activated endothelium, leukocytes and platelets, obstruct small vessels. Hemolysis also releases free hemoglobin that scavenges nitric oxide, contributing to pulmonary hypertension, priapism and leg ulcers.

Clinical picture by mechanism

MechanismManifestations
Vaso-occlusion in bone and marrowPainful crises; dactylitis (hand-foot swelling) in infants; avascular necrosis of the femoral and humeral heads
LungAcute chest syndrome: chest pain, fever, hypoxemia and a new infiltrate, from infection, fat embolism from infarcted marrow and in situ sickling
SpleenAcute splenic sequestration in young children; repeated infarction leads to functional asplenia and later a small fibrotic spleen
AspleniaSepsis and meningitis from encapsulated organisms, above all Streptococcus pneumoniae; Howell-Jolly bodies; increased Salmonella osteomyelitis
BrainIschemic stroke in children from large-vessel vasculopathy; silent infarcts; hemorrhagic stroke in adults
KidneyHyposthenuria (cannot concentrate urine, so dehydration comes easily), papillary necrosis with hematuria, albuminuria and chronic kidney disease
HemolysisJaundice, pigment gallstones, aplastic crisis with parvovirus B19
OtherPriapism, retinopathy, leg ulcers, pulmonary hypertension, delayed growth and puberty

Sickle cell trait

Heterozygotes (HbAS) have about 35-40% HbS, normal blood counts and a normal life expectancy, and the trait gives partial protection against severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria. The renal medulla is the one place where conditions (low oxygen, high osmolality, low pH) are harsh enough to sickle trait cells, so trait carriers can have hyposthenuria, painless hematuria from papillary necrosis, and a strong association with renal medullary carcinoma in young adults. Extreme exertion, heat and dehydration raise the risk of exertional rhabdomyolysis, and splenic infarction can occur at high altitude.

Hemoglobin C and compound states

HbC carries lysine instead of glutamate at β6. It does not polymerise, but it crystallises in dehydrated cells: HbCC gives mild hemolytic anemia, splenomegaly, target cells and rod-like intracellular crystals. HbSC disease is milder than HbSS in its anemia, but proliferative retinopathy, avascular necrosis and splenic sequestration (because the spleen stays enlarged into adulthood) are relatively prominent. HbS with β0-thalassemia behaves like HbSS; HbS with β+-thalassemia is milder.

Reading hemoglobin electrophoresis

At alkaline pH, the loss of a negative glutamate makes HbS migrate more slowly toward the anode than HbA, and the gain of a positive lysine makes HbC slower still (it runs with HbA2). Newborn screens report the hemoglobins present in order of amount: FA is normal, FAS is trait, FS is sickle cell disease (or HbS-β0-thalassemia), FSC is HbSC disease.

[[figure:s23a-fig41]]

Disease-modifying drugs by mechanism

  • Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase. Stress erythropoiesis raises HbF, and it also lowers neutrophil count and adhesion. It causes macrocytosis and dose-related myelosuppression and is teratogenic.
  • L-glutamine is thought to reduce oxidant stress by raising NAD redox potential in sickle cells.
  • Gene-based therapies either add an anti-sickling β-globin gene to autologous stem cells or edit the BCL11A erythroid enhancer so that γ-globin (HbF) is re-expressed. Allogeneic stem cell transplantation from a matched sibling is curative.

A positive sickle solubility test does not distinguish trait from disease; electrophoresis or HPLC does.

In a child with sickle cell disease, a sudden fall in hemoglobin with a reticulocyte count near zero means parvovirus aplastic crisis; the same fall with a high reticulocyte count and an enlarging spleen means sequestration.

sections.heading: Thalassemias, red cell membrane defects and porphyrias
sections.html:
Thalassemias: imbalance of globin chains

Thalassemias reduce production of normal α or β chains. Less hemoglobin is made (microcytosis, hypochromia) and, more importantly, the unpaired partner chain accumulates and damages the cell.

α-Thalassemia is usually caused by gene deletions. There are four α genes, two on each chromosome 16, so severity tracks the number lost.

GenotypeNamePicture
−α/ααSilent carrierNormal blood count
−α/−α (trans) or −−/αα (cis)α-Thalassemia traitMild microcytic anemia; adult electrophoresis normal. Cis deletion is common in Southeast Asian ancestry, trans in African ancestry.
−−/−αHbH diseaseExcess β chains form β4 tetramers (HbH) that precipitate; moderate hemolytic anemia, splenomegaly
−−/−−Hb Bart's hydrops fetalisγ4 tetramers bind oxygen too tightly to release it; fetal hydrops, usually fatal without in-utero transfusion

Because only a cis (−−/αα) parent can pass a chromosome with no α genes, Bart's hydrops arises mainly when both parents carry the cis deletion.

β-Thalassemia is usually caused by point mutations on chromosome 11 (splice-site, promoter, nonsense), giving no β chain (β0) or a reduced amount (β+). Trait (one abnormal gene) gives marked microcytosis with a normal or high red cell count, target cells and an HbA2 above about 3.5%. In β-thalassemia major (two severe alleles), the infant is well until γ-chain production falls after birth, then develops severe anemia in the first year. Free α chains precipitate in erythroblasts, which die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis). The marrow expands enormously: frontal bossing, maxillary overgrowth, "hair-on-end" skull films, osteoporosis, and extramedullary hematopoiesis with hepatosplenomegaly. Electrophoresis shows mostly HbF with raised HbA2 and little or no HbA.

Iron overload follows transfusion and also increased absorption, because erythroferrone from the expanded marrow suppresses hepcidin. Iron damages the heart (cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia, historically the main cause of death), liver, pancreas, pituitary, gonads and parathyroids. Chelators bind iron for excretion: deferoxamine (parenteral), deferasirox and deferiprone (oral).

Membrane disorders

The red cell membrane is tethered to a spectrin skeleton by vertical links (ankyrin, band 3, protein 4.2) and the skeleton itself is held together by horizontal spectrin-spectrin and spectrin-actin-protein 4.1 contacts.

  • Hereditary spherocytosis (mostly autosomal dominant) results from defects in vertical links, most often ankyrin, then spectrin and band 3. Unsupported lipid bilayer is lost as microvesicles, surface area falls relative to volume, and the cell becomes a dense sphere: raised MCHC, spherocytes without central pallor, raised RDW. Spheres cannot squeeze through the slits between splenic cords and sinuses, so they are trapped and eaten in the red pulp. Patients have anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly and pigment gallstones, sometimes from the neonatal period; parvovirus causes aplastic crises. The DAT is negative. Reduced eosin-5′-maleimide (EMA) binding on flow cytometry, reflecting less band 3, supports the diagnosis.
  • Hereditary elliptocytosis results from defects in horizontal links (mainly spectrin). Most carriers have elliptocytes but little or no hemolysis; homozygous or compound forms (hereditary pyropoikilocytosis) are severe.

Heme synthesis and the porphyrias

[[figure:s23a-fig42]]

Heme synthesis begins and ends in the mitochondrion. The rate-limiting step is ALA synthase, which needs pyridoxal phosphate. The hepatic isoform (ALAS1) is induced by drugs that induce cytochrome P450 and by fasting, and is repressed by heme and by glucose. Each porphyria is a partial deficiency of a later enzyme. Precursors that accumulate before the block determine the picture: early, water-soluble precursors (ALA, porphobilinogen) are neurotoxic; later porphyrins are photoactive and damage skin.

Acute intermittent porphyria is autosomal dominant deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (hydroxymethylbilane synthase), with low penetrance. Attacks are triggered by inducers of ALAS1: P450-inducing drugs (barbiturates, phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampin), alcohol, fasting and low-carbohydrate diets, and the progesterone of the luteal phase. Attacks bring severe diffuse abdominal pain with a benign examination, vomiting, constipation, tachycardia, hypertension, hyponatremia, dark urine that deepens on standing, anxiety or psychosis, seizures and a predominantly motor neuropathy that can paralyse respiratory muscles. There is no photosensitivity. Intravenous hemin works by negative feedback: it restores the hepatic heme pool and represses ALAS1 synthesis, cutting precursor production. Glucose loading does the same more weakly. Givosiran, a small interfering RNA against ALAS1 mRNA, prevents recurrent attacks.

Porphyria cutanea tarda is the most common porphyria: reduced hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity, usually acquired and driven by iron in hepatocytes, with susceptibility from alcohol, hepatitis C, HIV, estrogens, smoking and HFE mutations. Uroporphyrin accumulates in skin and causes blisters and erosions on sun-exposed hands, skin fragility, milia, hypertrichosis and hyperpigmentation, with tea-coloured urine that fluoresces pink. There are no neurovisceral attacks.

Erythropoietic protoporphyria (ferrochelatase) gives immediate burning pain on sun exposure without blisters, with high erythrocyte protoporphyrin.

Lead also inhibits two heme enzymes (ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase), so it can mimic acute porphyria with abdominal pain and neuropathy; a blood lead level and the smear (basophilic stippling) separate them.

On Step 2 CK, microcytosis with a normal ferritin and a high red cell count sends you to electrophoresis, and a normal electrophoresis in that setting sends you to α-globin gene testing.
