sections.heading: Iron deficiency, anemia of inflammation and anemia of CKD: evaluation and treatment

furtherReading.label: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf): Iron Deficiency and Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia
StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf): Anemia of Chronic Kidney Disease

sections.html:
Confirming iron deficiency

Start with a complete blood count with indices, a reticulocyte count and a smear. When microcytosis or a high RDW suggests iron deficiency, serum ferritin is the best single test: a ferritin below about 30 ng/mL confirms depleted stores in most adults. Ferritin rises with inflammation, liver disease and malignancy, so in those settings add transferrin saturation; a saturation below 20% with a ferritin up to about 100 ng/mL is consistent with iron deficiency alongside inflammation. Bone marrow iron staining is the historical gold standard but is almost never needed. Thrombocytosis is common in iron deficiency and resolves with treatment.

Finding the cause, by population

GroupUsual causeNext step
Infants and toddlersLow-iron diet, large volumes of cow's milkDietary history, limit cow's milk, oral iron; screen hemoglobin around 12 months
Adolescents and premenopausal womenMenstrual loss, pregnancy, low intakeMenstrual history, treat; evaluate GI tract if symptoms, family history of colorectal cancer, or no response
PregnancyIncreased demandOral iron; IV iron in the second or third trimester if oral fails or rapid repletion is needed
Men and postmenopausal womenGI blood loss until proven otherwiseBidirectional endoscopy (colonoscopy and upper endoscopy), celiac serology
After bariatric surgery, celiac disease, atrophic gastritisMalabsorptionIV iron if oral iron fails

If both endoscopies are normal and anemia recurs, capsule endoscopy looks for small-bowel lesions such as angiodysplasia. Test for Helicobacter pylori and celiac disease in unexplained iron deficiency. Blood donors, people taking NSAIDs or anticoagulants and endurance athletes have extra losses.

Treatment

  • Oral iron is first-line for most patients. A single dose of a ferrous salt (for example ferrous sulfate 325 mg, about 65 mg elemental iron) once daily or on alternate days is absorbed as well as split doses, with fewer GI effects, because each dose raises hepcidin for about a day. Take it on an empty stomach or with vitamin C, apart from tea, coffee, calcium and antacids. The reticulocyte count rises within about a week, hemoglobin should climb by about 1 g/dL in 2-4 weeks, and treatment continues for about 3 months after the hemoglobin normalises to refill stores.
  • Intravenous iron (ferric carboxymaltose, ferric derisomaltose, iron sucrose, ferumoxytol, low-molecular-weight iron dextran) is preferred for malabsorption, active inflammatory bowel disease, CKD (especially on dialysis or ESA therapy), intolerance or failure of oral iron, ongoing losses exceeding oral absorption, and late pregnancy when time is short. Serious hypersensitivity is uncommon with current products; infuse where reactions can be managed. Ferric carboxymaltose can cause symptomatic hypophosphatemia.
  • Transfusion is for hemodynamic instability, active bleeding or ischemic symptoms. In stable hospitalised adults a restrictive threshold of about 7 g/dL (about 8 g/dL with cardiovascular disease or for some surgical patients) is standard.

Anemia of inflammation

Treat the underlying disease. Coexisting absolute iron deficiency is treated, usually intravenously because hepcidin blocks oral absorption. ESAs have a narrow role (for example in CKD or selected patients receiving myelosuppressive chemotherapy), weighed against their risks.

Anemia of chronic kidney disease

Check hemoglobin at least yearly in CKD and more often as kidney function declines. Exclude other causes (iron, B12, folate, bleeding, hemolysis) before attributing anemia to the kidneys.

  1. Iron first. Many patients are iron deficient, and ESAs work poorly without iron. In CKD, a trial of iron is reasonable when transferrin saturation is 30% or lower and ferritin is 500 ng/mL or lower. Oral iron is acceptable before dialysis; IV iron is preferred on hemodialysis.
  2. ESA (epoetin alfa, darbepoetin) is considered when hemoglobin remains below 10 g/dL despite iron, aiming to reduce transfusions and symptoms. Avoid targeting a normal hemoglobin: trials that aimed for 13 g/dL or more showed more strokes, venous thrombosis, access thrombosis and hypertension, and in patients with cancer ESAs carry a risk of tumour progression. Most patients are kept below about 11.5 g/dL.
  3. Poor response to an ESA: look for iron deficiency, infection or inflammation, hyperparathyroidism, inadequate dialysis, aluminium toxicity and, rarely, anti-erythropoietin antibody–mediated pure red cell aplasia.

Oral hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors (daprodustat, vadadustat) are approved in the United States for anemia of CKD in adults on dialysis.

Lead and sideroblastic anemia in practice

Children at risk (including all children enrolled in Medicaid, at about 12 and 24 months) are screened with a blood lead level. A capillary level at or above the CDC blood lead reference value (3.5 µg/dL) is confirmed with a venous sample, because skin contamination causes false positives. Management depends on the confirmed level: source identification and removal, nutrition (adequate iron and calcium), and developmental follow-up for all; oral succimer for levels of 45 µg/dL or more; hospital admission with dimercaprol plus calcium disodium EDTA for 70 µg/dL or more or for encephalopathy. For sideroblastic anemia, stop alcohol, isoniazid and other offending drugs, check copper and zinc, try pyridoxine, and send a marrow examination when myelodysplasia is possible (older adult, cytopenias, macrocytosis).

A ferritin of 60 ng/mL in a patient with active Crohn disease does not exclude iron deficiency; transferrin saturation and the clinical setting decide.

Iron deficiency in an older adult is a GI evaluation, not just a prescription: start iron, but schedule both endoscopies.

sections.heading: Macrocytic anemia, aplastic anemia and red cell aplasia: diagnosis and management

furtherReading.label: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf): Pure Red Cell Aplasia

sections.html:
Working up macrocytosis

An MCV above 100 fL with a low reticulocyte count prompts a smear, serum vitamin B12 and folate, TSH, liver tests and a medication and alcohol history. Hypersegmented neutrophils and oval macrocytes point to megaloblastic anemia. Reticulocytosis suggests hemolysis or bleeding instead. Common non-megaloblastic causes are alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplastic syndrome, and drugs such as hydroxyurea, methotrexate, zidovudine and some anticonvulsants.

Vitamin B12 deficiency

  • Who to test: unexplained macrocytosis or neuropathy, cognitive decline in older adults, long-term metformin or acid-suppressing therapy, strict vegan diets, after gastrectomy or bariatric surgery, ileal Crohn disease or resection, autoimmune thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes with anemia, and recreational nitrous oxide use.
  • Tests: serum B12 first. When it is low-normal or symptoms are suggestive, methylmalonic acid (raised in B12 but not folate deficiency) and homocysteine (raised in both) confirm tissue deficiency. Nitrous oxide toxicity can present with a normal B12 but raised methylmalonic acid and homocysteine.
  • Cause: anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are highly specific for pernicious anemia but miss many cases; anti-parietal cell antibodies are sensitive but nonspecific. A high gastrin supports autoimmune gastritis. Upper endoscopy is reasonable at diagnosis of pernicious anemia because of the gastric neoplasm risk.

Treatment. Intramuscular cyanocobalamin (for example 1,000 µg) given frequently at first, then monthly for life in pernicious anemia, is the standard, and it is preferred when there are neurologic deficits. High-dose oral B12 (1,000-2,000 µg daily) is effective for many patients, including those with pernicious anemia, because about 1% is absorbed by passive diffusion, provided adherence and follow-up are reliable. Reticulocytes rise within a week. In severe megaloblastic anemia, watch potassium early in treatment because new cell production consumes it. Neurologic recovery is slower and may be incomplete, which is why early diagnosis matters. Stop nitrous oxide exposure.

Folate deficiency

Oral folic acid 1 mg daily for about 4 months, plus treatment of the cause (alcohol, diet, hemolysis). Never treat macrocytic anemia with folate alone until B12 deficiency is excluded. All people who could become pregnant should take 0.4-0.8 mg daily; those with a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect take a higher dose (4 mg) from before conception. Patients on methotrexate receive folic acid to reduce adverse effects, and leucovorin (folinic acid) rescues high-dose methotrexate because it bypasses dihydrofolate reductase.

Aplastic anemia

Pancytopenia with a low reticulocyte count needs a bone marrow aspirate and biopsy, which shows a hypocellular fatty marrow without fibrosis or abnormal cells. Also send PNH flow cytometry, B12 and folate, viral studies (hepatitis, HIV, parvovirus), and, in younger patients, chromosome breakage testing for Fanconi anemia and telomere studies, because inherited marrow failure does not respond to immunosuppression and changes transplant planning. Severe disease is defined by marrow cellularity below 25% plus at least two of: absolute neutrophil count below 500/mm3, platelets below 20,000/mm3, absolute reticulocyte count below 60,000/mm3.

  • Definitive therapy. For younger patients with severe disease and an HLA-matched sibling, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is first-line and can cure. Others receive immunosuppressive therapy: horse antithymocyte globulin plus cyclosporine, with eltrombopag (a thrombopoietin receptor agonist) added to improve response. Relapse and later clonal evolution (PNH, myelodysplasia) are risks after immunosuppression.
  • Supportive care. Leukoreduced, irradiated blood products; avoid transfusions from family members of possible transplant candidates (sensitisation); prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics for neutropenic fever; stop any suspected drug.

Pure red cell aplasia

Isolated severe anemia with reticulocytes near zero: examine the marrow (absent erythroid precursors; giant pronormoblasts suggest parvovirus), send parvovirus B19 PCR (serology is unreliable in immunosuppressed patients), and image the chest for thymoma. Treatment follows the cause:

  • Parvovirus B19 in an immunocompromised host (HIV, transplant, chemotherapy): intravenous immunoglobulin, which supplies neutralising antibody, plus reduction of immunosuppression or antiretroviral therapy where possible.
  • Thymoma: thymectomy; anemia often persists and needs immunosuppression (cyclosporine, with or without glucocorticoids).
  • Anti-erythropoietin antibodies after ESA therapy: stop all ESAs and give immunosuppression.
  • Transient aplastic crisis in chronic hemolysis: supportive red cell transfusion until reticulocytes return in 1-2 weeks.

Myelophthisis

A leukoerythroblastic smear with teardrop cells calls for bone marrow biopsy (aspiration is often dry) and a search for the infiltrating disease, most often metastatic carcinoma or primary myelofibrosis.

Pancytopenia with a high MCV in an older adult may be B12 deficiency, not marrow failure. Measure B12 and folate before (or alongside) the marrow biopsy.

Pregnant people on long-term hydroxyurea, methotrexate or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole need specific counselling; the drugs that impair folate metabolism also raise neural tube defect risk.

sections.heading: Hemolytic anemia: workup and management

furtherReading.label: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf): Laboratory Evaluation of Immune Hemolytic Anemias

sections.html:
A stepwise workup

  1. Confirm hemolysis: reticulocytosis, raised LDH and indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin. A normal haptoglobin with a low LDH makes hemolysis unlikely.
  2. Look at the smear. Spherocytes (immune hemolysis or hereditary spherocytosis), schistocytes (microangiopathy or valves; a different emergency), bite and blister cells (oxidant injury), agglutination (cold agglutinins), sickle cells, target cells.
  3. Direct antiglobulin test. Positive: immune hemolysis; characterise with anti-IgG and anti-C3. Negative: think membrane, enzyme, hemoglobin, PNH or mechanical causes.
  4. Targeted tests: PNH flow cytometry for Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis, thrombosis or cytopenias; G6PD assay; EMA binding; hemoglobin analysis; a search for lymphoma (CLL) or autoimmune disease in warm AIHA, and for a clonal B-cell disorder (serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation, sometimes marrow) in cold agglutinin disease.

Give folic acid to anyone with chronic hemolysis. Hemolytic anemias, especially AIHA and PNH, raise venous thrombosis risk, so hospitalised patients need thromboprophylaxis unless contraindicated.

Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia

  • First-line: prednisone about 1 mg/kg/day, tapered slowly over months once hemoglobin is stable. Most patients respond, but many relapse.
  • Second-line or relapse: rituximab (anti-CD20) is preferred; it is increasingly added early in severe disease. Splenectomy removes the main site of destruction and remains an option. Other immunosuppressants (azathioprine, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide) are used for refractory disease. IVIG works less reliably than in ITP.
  • Transfusion: do not withhold it in life-threatening anemia because crossmatching is difficult; the blood bank provides the least incompatible units.
  • Secondary disease: treat the driver (CLL, lymphoma, SLE) and stop suspected drugs. Evans syndrome (AIHA plus ITP) suggests an underlying immune disorder.

Cold agglutinin disease

Keep the patient warm: warm the room and extremities, and give blood and IV fluids through an in-line warmer. Glucocorticoids and splenectomy are generally ineffective because destruction is complement-mediated and mainly hepatic. For symptomatic or transfusion-dependent primary disease, rituximab, alone or with bendamustine, targets the clonal B cells. Sutimlimab, a monoclonal antibody to C1s, blocks the classical complement pathway and reduces hemolysis. Infection-associated cold agglutinins (Mycoplasma, EBV) are transient and need only supportive care.

Drug-induced immune hemolysis

Suspect it when a DAT turns positive days to weeks after starting a drug, typically a cephalosporin (especially ceftriaxone), piperacillin, or high-dose penicillin. Stopping the drug is the key intervention; avoid re-exposure and record the reaction. Severe drug-dependent hemolysis can cause acute kidney injury and death, so transfuse as needed. Glucocorticoids have no proven benefit when the drug has been stopped.

Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

Test peripheral blood flow cytometry (CD55 and CD59 on red cells, FLAER and CD24 or CD14 on granulocytes) in Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis, thrombosis at unusual sites (Budd-Chiari syndrome, mesenteric, portal or cerebral veins), aplastic anemia, or unexplained iron deficiency with hemoglobinuria.

  • Complement inhibition for symptomatic hemolysis or thrombosis: the C5 inhibitors eculizumab and ravulizumab stop intravascular hemolysis and greatly reduce thrombosis. Because terminal complement is needed to kill Neisseria, give meningococcal vaccines (MenACWY and MenB) at least 2 weeks before the first dose, or antibiotic prophylaxis if treatment cannot wait. Some patients have persistent anemia from C3-mediated extravascular hemolysis (DAT positive for C3); proximal inhibitors such as pegcetacoplan (C3) and oral iptacopan (factor B) address this.
  • Thrombosis is treated with anticoagulation plus complement inhibition.
  • Marrow failure with PNH is managed like aplastic anemia; allogeneic transplant is the only cure.

G6PD deficiency

Most episodes follow infection or an oxidant drug and resolve once the trigger is removed. Management is stopping the trigger, hydration (to protect the kidneys from hemoglobinuria) and transfusion for severe anemia. Confirm the diagnosis with a quantitative G6PD assay about 3 months after the episode, because reticulocytes falsely raise activity. Test G6PD before prescribing primaquine or tafenoquine (radical cure of Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale), rasburicase, or dapsone where possible. Methylene blue, the usual antidote for methemoglobinemia, can worsen hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Neonates with G6PD deficiency need close bilirubin monitoring.

Pyruvate kinase deficiency

Suspect PK deficiency in a child or adult with lifelong Coombs-negative hemolysis, normal EMA binding and normal G6PD; confirm with an enzyme assay and gene testing. Management includes folic acid, transfusions as needed, monitoring and chelation for iron overload (which can occur without transfusion), splenectomy for severe disease, and mitapivat for adults.

In a patient on a C5 inhibitor, a positive DAT with C3 coating and a persistently high reticulocyte count does not mean new AIHA; it reflects extravascular hemolysis of C3-coated PNH cells.

Step 1 asks which mechanism; Step 2 CK asks which test now (DAT, flow cytometry) and what to do first (stop the drug, keep warm, vaccinate before eculizumab).

sections.heading: Sickle cell disease: health maintenance and acute complications
sections.html:
Diagnosis and prevention in children

Every US newborn is screened. A pattern of FS (HbF and HbS with no HbA) is confirmed with repeat testing and family studies and referred to a comprehensive sickle cell program. Prevention then rests on four pillars:

  • Penicillin prophylaxis (oral penicillin V twice daily) from about 2 months until at least 5 years of age in HbSS and HbS-β0-thalassemia; it sharply reduces invasive pneumococcal disease.
  • Vaccines: the full childhood series plus extra pneumococcal coverage (conjugate vaccine and, depending on the conjugate used, the polysaccharide vaccine), meningococcal ACWY and B vaccines, and yearly influenza vaccine.
  • Stroke screening: annual transcranial Doppler ultrasonography from age 2 to 16 years in HbSS and HbS-β0-thalassemia. A time-averaged mean maximum velocity of 200 cm/s or more (confirmed) is abnormal and calls for a chronic transfusion program aiming to keep HbS below about 30%, which reduces first stroke dramatically. Some children with no severe vasculopathy can later switch to hydroxyurea after at least a year of transfusion.
  • Hydroxyurea offered from 9 months of age to all children with HbSS or HbS-β0-thalassemia regardless of symptoms, and to adults with recurrent pain, acute chest syndrome, severe symptomatic anemia or a history of complications. It reduces pain crises, acute chest syndrome, transfusions and mortality. Monitor the blood count for myelosuppression. It is teratogenic, so effective contraception is advised; discuss stopping it in pregnancy and lactation.

Families learn to palpate the spleen and to seek care at once for fever. Other screening includes yearly urine albumin, retinal examination from about age 10, and echocardiography when pulmonary hypertension is suspected.

Fever

A temperature of 38.5 °C (101.3 °F) or higher in a child with sickle cell disease is an emergency because of the risk of pneumococcal sepsis. Do a history and examination, CBC with reticulocyte count and blood culture, then give a parenteral third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone) promptly, without waiting for results. Add vancomycin for suspected meningitis or toxic appearance; obtain chest radiography for respiratory signs. Well-appearing children may go home after ceftriaxone if follow-up is assured.

Acute complications

ComplicationRecogniseManage
Vaso-occlusive painBone, chest, back or abdominal pain; labs may be unchangedRapid analgesia (parenteral opioids within about an hour of arrival for severe pain, with NSAIDs if renal function allows), reassessment every 15-30 minutes, oral or IV fluids for hypovolemia without overhydration, incentive spirometry. Transfusion is not indicated for uncomplicated pain.
Acute chest syndromeNew pulmonary infiltrate plus fever, chest pain, cough, tachypnea or hypoxemiaEmpiric parenteral cephalosporin plus a macrolide, oxygen to keep saturation at or above about 95%, incentive spirometry, bronchodilator if wheeze, analgesia. Simple transfusion when hemoglobin falls more than 1 g/dL below baseline; urgent exchange transfusion for rapid progression, saturation below 90% despite oxygen, multilobar disease or worsening respiratory distress.
Acute strokeFocal deficit, seizure, altered consciousnessEmergent imaging and exchange transfusion (simple transfusion if exchange will be delayed and hemoglobin is low), then a chronic transfusion program
Splenic sequestrationPallor, enlarging spleen, falling hemoglobin with high reticulocytes, possible shockFluid resuscitation and cautious transfusion (sequestered cells re-enter the circulation); splenectomy after recurrent episodes
Aplastic crisisFatigue and pallor, reticulocytes near zero, recent viral illnessTransfusion; isolate from pregnant contacts (parvovirus B19)
PriapismPainful erection more than 4 hoursUrology: corporal aspiration and irrigation with a sympathomimetic (phenylephrine)

Transfusion principles

Use leukoreduced red cells matched for at least the C, E and Kell antigens to limit alloimmunisation, and HbS-negative units. After a simple transfusion, keep hemoglobin no higher than about 10 g/dL, because higher values raise viscosity and can provoke vaso-occlusion. Before surgery under general anesthesia, simple transfusion to about 10 g/dL reduces perioperative complications in HbSS. Watch for delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions, which can cause hemoglobin to fall below the pretransfusion level days later. Chronically transfused patients need iron monitoring and chelation.

Curative and newer therapies

Matched sibling stem cell transplantation cures most children who receive it. Autologous gene-based therapies (gene addition or editing of the BCL11A erythroid enhancer to restore HbF) are approved for patients 12 years and older with recurrent vaso-occlusive events. Voxelotor, an HbS polymerisation inhibitor, was withdrawn from the market in 2024. L-glutamine is an oral option to reduce pain crises.

Pregnancy and sickle trait

Pregnancy in sickle cell disease carries higher risks of pain crises, preeclampsia, fetal growth restriction and venous thromboembolism; care is shared with maternal-fetal medicine, and partners should be offered hemoglobinopathy testing. People with sickle trait need no treatment. Offer partner testing and genetic counselling, investigate hematuria (including imaging for renal medullary carcinoma), and advise hydration and graded conditioning during intense exertion.

Do not give a large-volume transfusion to "normalise" hemoglobin in sickle cell disease; aim no higher than about 10 g/dL after simple transfusion.

Incentive spirometry during a pain crisis is cheap prevention of acute chest syndrome, especially with chest or back pain.

sections.heading: Thalassemia, hereditary spherocytosis and porphyrias: management

furtherReading.label: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf): Laboratory Evaluation of Alpha Thalassemia

sections.html:
Microcytosis without iron deficiency

Thalassemia trait is common and needs no treatment, but it is often misread as iron deficiency, leading to months of useless iron. Clues are microcytosis out of proportion to anemia, a normal or high red cell count, normal RDW, target cells, and a family history or relevant ancestry. Check ferritin first, because iron deficiency lowers HbA2 and can mask β-thalassemia trait. Then send hemoglobin analysis (HPLC or electrophoresis):

  • HbA2 above about 3.5% (often with slightly raised HbF): β-thalassemia trait.
  • Normal HbA2 and HbF with normal iron: probable α-thalassemia trait, confirmed by α-globin gene deletion analysis. HbH inclusions on supravital staining suggest HbH disease.

Carrier testing matters most in pregnancy planning. If both partners carry β-thalassemia, or both may carry the cis α deletion, offer genetic counselling and prenatal diagnosis (chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis). Bart's hydrops carries serious maternal risks, including preeclampsia.

Transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia

  • Regular transfusion every 2-5 weeks keeps pretransfusion hemoglobin around 9.5-10.5 g/dL, which suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis and allows normal growth and bone development.
  • Iron monitoring: serum ferritin every few months; MRI for liver iron concentration and cardiac T2* (a low T2* means myocardial iron and predicts heart failure).
  • Chelation usually starts after about 10-20 transfusions or a ferritin above about 1,000 ng/mL.
ChelatorRouteKey adverse effects and monitoring
DeferoxamineSubcutaneous or IV infusionHearing and visual toxicity (yearly audiology and eye exams), local reactions, Yersinia infection
DeferasiroxOral, dailyRenal injury (creatinine, urine protein), hepatic injury, GI bleeding
DeferiproneOralAgranulocytosis: check the absolute neutrophil count weekly; arthropathy; particularly effective at removing cardiac iron

Other options include luspatercept (promotes late-stage erythroid maturation and reduces transfusion burden), allogeneic stem cell transplantation (curative, best in young children with a matched sibling) and autologous gene therapy. Splenectomy is reserved for hypersplenism with rising transfusion needs. Endocrine follow-up covers growth, puberty, diabetes, thyroid, parathyroid and bone density. HbH disease usually needs only folic acid and transfusion during infections or pregnancy, plus avoidance of oxidant drugs.

Hereditary spherocytosis

Diagnose with a family history, spherocytes, a raised MCHC, a negative DAT and a reduced EMA binding test. Management depends on severity:

  • Folic acid supplementation for moderate and severe disease.
  • Phototherapy or exchange transfusion for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.
  • Transfusion for aplastic (parvovirus) or hemolytic crises.
  • Splenectomy (total or partial) for severe disease or moderate disease with poor growth, symptomatic anemia or frequent transfusion, ideally delayed until after about age 6 to lower the risk of overwhelming sepsis. Give pneumococcal, meningococcal (ACWY and B) and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccines at least 2 weeks before surgery, and plan cholecystectomy at the same operation if there are symptomatic gallstones. Afterwards: Howell-Jolly bodies and thrombocytosis are expected, patients need urgent evaluation for fever, and many clinicians give penicillin prophylaxis to children.

Acute intermittent porphyria

Suspect an acute porphyria in a young woman with recurrent severe abdominal pain, a soft abdomen, hyponatremia, hypertension, tachycardia, weakness or psychiatric change, especially after a new drug, dieting, alcohol or in the luteal phase. The best initial test is a spot urine porphobilinogen (normalised to creatinine) during the attack; a marked rise confirms an acute hepatic porphyria. Gene testing then identifies the type and allows family testing.

  1. Admit (hospitalise severe attacks; monitor sodium, magnesium and respiratory function).
  2. Stop all porphyrinogenic drugs; check each new drug against a porphyria drug-safety database.
  3. Give intravenous hemin as early as possible for any attack severe enough to need admission, opioids or with neurologic signs or hyponatremia.
  4. Carbohydrate loading (IV 10% dextrose) for mild attacks or while hemin is obtained; avoid hypotonic fluid with hyponatremia.
  5. Symptom control: opioids for pain, ondansetron for nausea, β-blockers for tachycardia and hypertension.

For recurrent attacks, givosiran (monthly subcutaneous siRNA to ALAS1) reduces attacks; monitor liver and kidney function. Long-term, patients have higher risks of hepatocellular carcinoma, hypertension and chronic kidney disease.

Porphyria cutanea tarda

Confirm with raised plasma or urine porphyrins (mainly uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl porphyrin), then look for susceptibility factors: test for hepatitis C and HIV, measure ferritin and check HFE genotype, and review alcohol, estrogen and smoking. Treatment is therapeutic phlebotomy to lower hepatic iron (target ferritin near the low end of normal) or low-dose hydroxychloroquine (standard doses can cause hepatotoxicity in PCT), plus sun protection and removal of triggers. Direct-acting antiviral treatment of hepatitis C often brings remission.

Barbiturates, phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampin and sulfonamides can precipitate acute porphyric attacks; avoid them in known carriers.

AIP has no rash; blistering on the backs of the hands with skin fragility suggests PCT instead.

title: Blood · Other anemias, cytopenias and cythemias
meta: Acute blood loss and systemic anemias, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, and the myeloproliferative and reactive cythemias.

sections.heading: Acute blood loss and anemia of systemic disease
sections.html:
Acute blood loss: what the numbers do over time

When whole blood is lost, red cells and plasma leave together. The hemoglobin concentration and hematocrit are therefore close to normal in the first minutes to hours, even after a large bleed, because concentration is a ratio, not a mass. The first signs of hemorrhage are hemodynamic: tachycardia, narrowing pulse pressure, orthostasis, then hypotension and falling urine output as losses pass roughly 15, 30 and 40% of blood volume.

Two processes then dilute the remaining red cells. Lower capillary hydrostatic pressure draws interstitial fluid into the vessels (transcapillary refill), and the kidney retains salt and water through the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and vasopressin. Intravenous crystalloid speeds the same change. The hemoglobin falls over the next hours and reaches its true new level only after about 24 to 72 hours of equilibration. A single early hemoglobin therefore underestimates the bleed.

[[figure:s23a-fig50]]

The marrow response is slower still. Renal peritubular interstitial cells sense lower oxygen delivery, hypoxia-inducible factor is stabilised, and erythropoietin rises within hours. Reticulocytes start to climb after a few days and peak around one week. In the meantime a neutrophilic leukocytosis and reactive thrombocytosis are common. A single acute bleed leaves the anemia normocytic; repeated or chronic loss drains iron stores and produces microcytic iron deficiency. Blood lost into a body cavity or tissue (for example a retroperitoneal or thigh hematoma) can raise unconjugated bilirubin as the pooled cells break down, which can mimic hemolysis.

Time after a large bleedHemoglobin / hematocritOther findings
Minutes to a few hoursNear baselineTachycardia, orthostasis; low central venous pressure
Hours to 3 daysFalls as plasma volume is restoredLeukocytosis, thrombocytosis; erythropoietin rising
About 3 to 10 daysLowest point, then begins to recoverReticulocytosis, polychromasia; slight rise in MCV
Weeks (if loss continues)Persistently lowFalling ferritin, microcytosis, rising RDW

A normal hemoglobin in a hypotensive trauma patient does not exclude major hemorrhage. Judge early blood loss by vital signs and perfusion, not by the first hemoglobin.

Liver disease and alcohol

Anemia in chronic liver disease is usually multifactorial: gastrointestinal bleeding from varices or portal hypertensive gastropathy, hypersplenism, folate deficiency, direct alcohol toxicity and the anemia of inflammation. Two membrane changes are characteristic.

  • Target cells (codocytes). Cholestasis raises plasma cholesterol and lecithin, which load passively into the red cell membrane. Surface area grows relative to volume, so the cell bulges in the centre on a dried smear. Target cells are harmless markers.
  • Spur cells (acanthocytes) and spur cell anemia. In advanced cirrhosis, abnormal lipoproteins transfer free cholesterol, out of proportion to phospholipid, into the membrane. The membrane stiffens, develops a few irregular thorny projections, and the cells are trapped and destroyed in an enlarged spleen. The result is brisk hemolysis that signals very advanced disease and a poor prognosis.

The red cells in liver disease are often mildly macrocytic without megaloblastic change (round macrocytes from excess membrane lipid), so the neutrophils are not hypersegmented unless folate deficiency is also present. Alcohol itself suppresses the marrow and can produce macrocytosis, thrombocytopenia and, with heavy binge drinking, ring sideroblasts from impaired heme synthesis. Many of these changes reverse within weeks of abstinence.

Endocrine causes

Thyroid hormone, androgens, cortisol and growth hormone all support erythropoiesis, mainly by raising tissue oxygen demand and so the erythropoietin drive.

  • Hypothyroidism: mild normocytic or macrocytic anemia with low erythropoietin and a low reticulocyte count. Look for associated autoimmune pernicious anemia (macrocytic, megaloblastic) and for iron deficiency from heavy menstrual bleeding.
  • Male hypogonadism or androgen deprivation therapy: hemoglobin drifts into the female range; testosterone stimulates erythropoietin and suppresses hepcidin.
  • Adrenal insufficiency and hypopituitarism: mild normocytic anemia that is often unmasked once glucocorticoid replacement corrects volume contraction.

An anemia of systemic disease is normocytic, hypoproliferative (low reticulocyte index) and mild. A hemoglobin far below 10 g/dL in a patient with hypothyroidism alone should prompt a search for a second cause.

Step 2 CK asks the next step: when to transfuse after a bleed, how to work up an older adult with new anemia, and how to manage iron deficiency in toddlers and pregnancy.

sections.heading: Physiologic, dilutional and life-stage anemias
sections.html:
Physiologic anemia of pregnancy

During pregnancy the plasma volume expands by about 40 to 50%, driven by estrogen and progesterone effects on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and vasodilation. Red cell mass also rises, but only by about 20 to 30%, so the hemoglobin concentration falls. The dilution is greatest in the second trimester. The benefit is lower blood viscosity for placental flow and a reserve against the blood lost at delivery. The red cell indices stay normal and the anemia is mild.

Iron needs rise sharply because of the larger red cell mass, the fetus and placenta, and delivery losses, which together total roughly 1 g of iron. True iron deficiency is therefore the most common pathologic anemia of pregnancy. Folate demand rises too.

Pregnancy lowers the hemoglobin threshold for anemia (about 11 g/dL in the first and third trimesters and 10.5 g/dL in the second). A pregnant patient below these values, or with microcytosis, has a real anemia, not dilution.

Infancy: the physiologic nadir and anemia of prematurity

The fetus lives at a low arterial oxygen tension and makes abundant red cells containing hemoglobin F. At birth, breathing air raises tissue oxygenation, erythropoietin falls sharply and red cell production almost stops for several weeks. Fetal red cells also have a shorter lifespan, and the infant's blood volume expands rapidly with growth. Together these produce the physiologic nadir: in term infants hemoglobin falls to roughly 9 to 11 g/dL at about 2 to 3 months, after which erythropoietin rises and production resumes. The infant is well, the indices are normal and no treatment is needed.

In preterm infants the fall comes earlier and goes deeper. They start with smaller iron stores (most iron transfers in the third trimester), have a blunted erythropoietin response to anemia, grow faster, and lose blood to frequent laboratory sampling. Anemia of prematurity is hyporegenerative: a low reticulocyte count with a low erythropoietin level for the degree of anemia. Iron supplementation, limiting phlebotomy losses and, when needed, transfusion are the main tools.

Cow's milk and toddler iron deficiency (nutrition)

Toddlers who drink large volumes of cow's milk develop iron deficiency through several linked mechanisms:

  • Cow's milk is poor in iron, and the iron it contains is poorly absorbed.
  • Its calcium and casein inhibit absorption of non-heme iron from other foods.
  • Its volume fills the child and displaces iron-rich foods.
  • In infants given whole cow's milk before 12 months, milk-protein enterocolitis causes occult intestinal blood loss.

The picture is a pale, often plump toddler with microcytic, hypochromic anemia, a high RDW and low ferritin. Iron deficiency in early childhood matters because it is linked to lasting effects on attention and cognitive development, which may occur even before anemia appears.

Athletes

Endurance training expands plasma volume more than red cell mass, so trained athletes can have a slightly low hemoglobin with normal MCV, normal ferritin and excellent oxygen delivery. This athletes' pseudoanemia is dilutional and needs no treatment. It must be separated from true problems seen in athletes: iron deficiency (menstrual loss, low intake, gastrointestinal loss, sweat losses, hepcidin rises after exercise) and mechanical intravascular hemolysis from repeated foot strikes in distance runners.

Mixed nutritional anemia

When microcytic and macrocytic processes coexist, for example iron deficiency plus folate or vitamin B12 deficiency after bariatric surgery, in alcohol use disorder or in celiac disease, the MCV can average out to normal. The clue is a high RDW and a dimorphic smear with both small hypochromic cells and large oval macrocytes, sometimes with hypersegmented neutrophils.

SettingMechanismMCVKey clue
Pregnancy (physiologic)Plasma volume rises more than red cell massNormalMild, greatest in second trimester
Term infant at 2 to 3 monthsErythropoietin falls after birthNormal for ageWell infant, self-limited
Preterm infantLow iron stores, blunted erythropoietin, phlebotomyNormalLow reticulocytes and low erythropoietin
Toddler with high milk intakeLow iron intake and absorptionLowLow ferritin, high RDW
Endurance athletePlasma volume expansionNormalNormal ferritin, no symptoms
Mixed deficiencyIron plus folate or B12Often normalHigh RDW, dimorphic smear

Older adults

Anemia is common in older adults but is not a normal consequence of ageing. Roughly a third of cases are nutritional (iron, folate, B12), a third are due to chronic kidney disease or inflammation, and the remainder are unexplained after standard testing; some of the unexplained group have early myelodysplastic syndrome or clonal hematopoiesis. Even mild anemia in older adults is associated with falls, frailty, cognitive decline and mortality.

Dilutional anemias (pregnancy, athletes) have a normal red cell mass and normal indices; any microcytosis or low ferritin means a true deficiency is also present.

sections.heading: Neutropenia, agranulocytosis and lymphopenia
sections.html:
Definitions and the neutrophil compartments

The absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is the total leukocyte count multiplied by the fraction of segmented neutrophils plus bands. In adults, neutropenia is an ANC below 1,500/mm3: mild 1,000 to 1,500, moderate 500 to 1,000, and severe below 500. Infection risk rises steeply below 500, and the risk of serious bacterial and fungal infection is highest below 100 or when the count stays low for more than a week. Agranulocytosis means a near-absence of neutrophils, usually an ANC below 500 and often below 100.

The ANC measures only the circulating pool. Neutrophils also sit in the marrow storage pool and in a marginated pool adhering to vessel walls. Shifts between these pools change the count without any change in production: glucocorticoids, epinephrine and exercise release marginated cells and raise the count, whereas sequestration in an enlarged spleen lowers it.

Benign and inherited neutropenias

  • Duffy-null associated neutrophil count. People who lack the Duffy antigen (ACKR1) on red cells, a genotype frequent in people with ancestry from sub-Saharan Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, have a lower circulating ANC (often 1,000 to 1,500) with normal marrow reserves and no excess infections. The Duffy-null red cell also resists Plasmodium vivax invasion. Recognising it prevents unnecessary marrow biopsies and the needless withholding of drugs such as chemotherapy or clozapine.
  • Cyclic neutropenia. Autosomal dominant variants in ELANE (neutrophil elastase) cause regular cycles, usually about every 21 days, of severe neutropenia lasting several days with fever, mouth ulcers and gingivitis. Serial counts two to three times a week for six weeks show the cycle. G-CSF shortens the nadirs.
  • Severe congenital neutropenia. Also often ELANE related (and HAX1 in the autosomal recessive form described by Kostmann); maturation arrests at the promyelocyte stage, infections start in infancy, and there is a lasting risk of myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia.

Acquired neutropenia

The most common acquired causes are viral infection (transient), drugs, nutritional deficiency (B12, folate, copper), autoimmune disease (systemic lupus erythematosus, Felty syndrome with rheumatoid arthritis and splenomegaly), hypersplenism, large granular lymphocyte leukemia and primary marrow disease.

Drug-induced agranulocytosis works by two mechanisms. In the immune type, the drug or a metabolite binds the neutrophil surface (hapten) or forms immune complexes, and antibodies destroy neutrophils abruptly, sometimes within days of re-exposure. In the toxic type, the drug or a reactive metabolite injures myeloid precursors in a dose-related way, and the count falls over weeks. Clozapine (a reactive nitrenium ion formed by neutrophil oxidation), the thionamides (methimazole and propylthiouracil), sulfasalazine and other sulfonamides, dapsone, procainamide and deferiprone are classic causes. Risk is highest in the first months of therapy, which is why clozapine and deferiprone have scheduled ANC monitoring and why patients on thionamides are told to stop the drug and get a count if they develop fever or sore throat.

DrugUsePractical point
ClozapineTreatment-resistant schizophreniaBaseline and scheduled ANC; risk concentrated in the first 6 months
Methimazole, propylthiouracilHyperthyroidismCounsel to stop and check a count with fever or sore throat
Sulfasalazine, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazoleInflammatory arthritis, IBD; infectionSulfonamide moiety; idiosyncratic
DeferiproneIron overloadWeekly ANC monitoring
DapsoneLeprosy, Pneumocystis prophylaxis, dermatitis herpetiformisAlso causes oxidant hemolysis and methemoglobinemia

Febrile neutropenia in brief

A fever in a patient with an ANC below 500 (or expected to fall below 500) is a medical emergency because the usual signs of inflammation, such as pus and infiltrates, may be absent. Gram-negative rods including Pseudomonas aeruginosa are the classic early killers, so empiric therapy is an intravenous anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam started promptly after cultures. Persistent fever after several days of antibacterial therapy raises concern for invasive fungal infection, especially Aspergillus and Candida.

Lymphopenia

Lymphopenia is an absolute lymphocyte count below about 1,000/mm3 in adults (higher thresholds apply in infants). Causes include:

  • Redistribution: glucocorticoids and physiologic stress shift lymphocytes into lymphoid tissue and marrow within hours (eosinophils fall at the same time).
  • Destruction: HIV (CD4 T cells), acute viral infections, radiation, cytotoxic chemotherapy and lymphocyte-depleting antibodies such as alemtuzumab and antithymocyte globulin.
  • Underproduction: inborn errors such as severe combined immunodeficiency (found by newborn screening for T-cell receptor excision circles), protein-calorie malnutrition and zinc deficiency.
  • Loss: intestinal lymphangiectasia and thoracic duct leaks, which lose lymph rich in lymphocytes.
  • Autoimmune and granulomatous disease: systemic lupus erythematosus and sarcoidosis.

A low total leukocyte count is not the same as neutropenia. Always calculate the ANC; a patient with a leukocyte count of 3,000/mm3 and 70% neutrophils has an ANC of 2,100 and is not neutropenic.

Step 2 CK applies this to management: when to observe a mildly low ANC, how to handle clozapine or thionamide-related agranulocytosis, and how to work up pancytopenia.

sections.heading: Thrombocytopenia: mechanisms, ITP and the differential
sections.html:
Four ways to lose platelets

Thrombocytopenia is a platelet count below 150,000/mm3. Normally about a third of the platelet mass is held in the spleen, and platelets survive 7 to 10 days. A low count reflects one or more of four mechanisms:

  1. Decreased production: marrow failure or infiltration, B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, chemotherapy, viral suppression, and reduced hepatic thrombopoietin in cirrhosis.
  2. Increased destruction or consumption: immune (ITP, drug-dependent antibodies, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, post-transfusion purpura, neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia) or non-immune (disseminated intravascular coagulation, thrombotic microangiopathies).
  3. Sequestration: an enlarged spleen can hold most of the circulating platelets.
  4. Dilution: massive transfusion of red cells and crystalloid, and the mild gestational fall of pregnancy.

A fifth possibility must always be excluded first: pseudothrombocytopenia, a laboratory artefact.

Pseudothrombocytopenia

EDTA, the anticoagulant in the usual blood-count tube, chelates calcium and changes the conformation of the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa complex, exposing hidden epitopes. Some healthy people have naturally occurring antibodies against these epitopes, which clump platelets in the tube, or which stick platelets to neutrophils (platelet satellitism). The analyser counts clumps as single large cells or as leukocytes, so the reported count is falsely low. The patient has no bleeding, the smear shows clumps, and a count in a citrate (or heparin) tube is normal. The antibodies cause no disease.

Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)

ITP is an acquired, isolated thrombocytopenia (below 100,000/mm3) caused by immune destruction and impaired production of platelets, with no other cause found. IgG autoantibodies, most often against glycoprotein IIb/IIIa or Ib/IX, coat platelets, which are then removed by splenic macrophages through Fc-gamma receptors. The same antibodies, and cytotoxic T cells, damage megakaryocytes, so production is inappropriately low for the degree of destruction. Thrombopoietin levels are normal or only mildly raised, which is the rationale for thrombopoietin-receptor agonists.

FeatureChildhood ITPAdult ITP
Typical onsetAbrupt, often a few weeks after a viral illness or vaccinationInsidious, often found on a routine count
SexBoys and girls equallyWomen more often in young and middle adulthood
CourseMost resolve within months, with or without treatmentChronic disease in most
Secondary causes to seekFewHIV, hepatitis C, lupus, antiphospholipid syndrome, CLL, H. pylori, drugs

Typical findings are petechiae, purpura and mucosal bleeding in a well patient with a normal examination. A palpable spleen argues against ITP. The smear shows fewer platelets, some of them large, with normal red and white cells. Bleeding correlates loosely with the count; serious bleeding is uncommon above 20,000 to 30,000/mm3.

Pharmacology by mechanism

AgentMechanismNotable adverse effects
Glucocorticoids (prednisone, dexamethasone)Reduce macrophage Fc-receptor clearance and autoantibody productionHyperglycemia, mood change, insomnia, infection
Intravenous immunoglobulinSaturates macrophage Fc receptors (blockade) and the neonatal Fc receptor, speeding autoantibody catabolismHeadache, aseptic meningitis, renal injury, thrombosis, hemolysis
Anti-D immunoglobulinCoats Rh(D)-positive red cells, which then occupy splenic Fc receptorsIntravascular hemolysis; useless after splenectomy or in Rh-negative patients
RomiplostimPeptide-antibody fusion that binds the extracellular domain of the thrombopoietin receptor (MPL)Weekly subcutaneous; marrow reticulin, thrombosis
Eltrombopag, avatrombopagSmall molecules that bind the transmembrane domain of MPL and activate JAK2-STAT signallingEltrombopag: hepatotoxicity, cataract; binds polyvalent cations, so separate from calcium, antacids and iron
RituximabAnti-CD20, depletes B cells that make autoantibodyInfusion reactions, hepatitis B reactivation
FostamatinibSYK inhibitor; blocks Fc-receptor signalling in macrophagesDiarrhea, hypertension, raised aminotransferases

Other causes in the differential

  • Gestational thrombocytopenia: mild (usually above 70,000/mm3), late in pregnancy, from dilution and faster clearance; no bleeding, no fetal effect, resolves after delivery.
  • Liver disease: splenic sequestration from portal hypertension plus less hepatic thrombopoietin; alcohol adds direct marrow toxicity.
  • Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: IgG against platelet factor 4-heparin complexes activates platelets through Fc-gamma RIIa; the count falls 5 to 10 days after heparin starts and the risk is thrombosis, not bleeding.
  • Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia: maternal IgG against a paternally inherited platelet antigen, most often HPA-1a, crosses the placenta; the mother's count is normal, and the first pregnancy can be affected.

An isolated low platelet count with no bleeding should first be checked on a smear. Clumps mean a citrate-tube recount, not steroids or a marrow biopsy.

sections.heading: Polycythemia vera and secondary erythrocytosis
sections.html:
Absolute versus relative erythrocytosis

A high hemoglobin or hematocrit has three explanations. In relative (apparent) polycythemia the red cell mass is normal and the plasma volume is reduced: dehydration, diuretics, burns, or the chronic low plasma volume seen in some people with obesity, hypertension and smoking. In absolute erythrocytosis red cell mass is truly increased, either from a clonal marrow disorder (polycythemia vera) or from an erythropoietin-driven process (secondary erythrocytosis). Serum erythropoietin is the key separating test: suppressed in polycythemia vera, normal or high in secondary causes.

Polycythemia vera (PV)

PV is a myeloproliferative neoplasm of a hematopoietic stem cell. About 95% of patients carry the JAK2 V617F mutation, and most of the rest have a JAK2 exon 12 mutation. JAK2 is the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase that signals for the erythropoietin, thrombopoietin and G-CSF receptors. The mutation removes autoinhibition by the pseudokinase domain, so precursors proliferate without, or with very little, erythropoietin. Because all three lineages share the signal, leukocytes and platelets are often high as well (panmyelosis), and the spleen enlarges from extramedullary hematopoiesis.

Clinical features and their mechanisms

  • Hyperviscosity and plethora: headache, dizziness, visual blurring, ruddy face, engorged retinal veins.
  • Thrombosis (arterial and venous, including unusual sites such as the hepatic veins in Budd-Chiari syndrome and the portal or mesenteric veins): from high hematocrit, activated platelets and leukocytes. A splanchnic vein thrombosis in a young adult should prompt JAK2 testing.
  • Aquagenic pruritus: intense itching after a warm bath or shower, attributed to clonal basophils and mast cells releasing histamine and other mediators.
  • Erythromelalgia: burning red painful hands and feet from platelet-mediated microvascular occlusion; relieved by aspirin.
  • Hyperuricemia and gout: from high cell turnover.
  • Bleeding: at very high platelet counts, from acquired von Willebrand syndrome.

Diagnosis in outline

Current criteria combine three main elements and one supporting test. The main elements are a hemoglobin or hematocrit clearly above the sex-specific upper limit (or a measured increase in red cell mass), a marrow biopsy showing hypercellularity of all three lineages with mature, pleomorphic megakaryocytes, and a JAK2 V617F or exon 12 mutation. A subnormal serum erythropoietin supports the diagnosis. A marrow biopsy can be skipped when the hemoglobin is markedly high and both the mutation and low erythropoietin are present.

Treatment by mechanism

  • Phlebotomy removes red cells and, by design, induces iron deficiency, which limits further red cell production. The target hematocrit is below 45%, a level shown to lower cardiovascular death and thrombosis compared with a looser target.
  • Low-dose aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1, reducing thromboxane A2; it lowers thrombotic events and relieves erythromelalgia.
  • Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, slowing DNA synthesis in all lineages; it is used for high-risk patients (age 60 or older, or prior thrombosis). Adverse effects: macrocytosis, cytopenias, mouth and leg ulcers, skin cancers.
  • Interferon alfa (ropeginterferon alfa-2b) is an alternative, especially in younger patients and pregnancy, because it is not teratogenic.
  • Ruxolitinib, a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor, treats hydroxyurea resistance or intolerance and refractory pruritus.

Long-term, PV can progress to post-polycythemia myelofibrosis (falling counts, teardrop cells, massive splenomegaly) or transform into acute myeloid leukemia.

Secondary erythrocytosis

GroupExamplesClue
Hypoxia-driven (appropriate)Chronic lung disease, obstructive sleep apnea, obesity hypoventilation, high altitude, right-to-left cardiac shuntLow arterial oxygen saturation, at least at night
Impaired oxygen releaseSmoking (carboxyhemoglobin), high-oxygen-affinity hemoglobin variants, 2,3-BPG deficiencyNormal pulse oximetry; low P50 in hemoglobin variants
Autonomous erythropoietin (inappropriate)Renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, cerebellar hemangioblastoma, uterine leiomyoma, pheochromocytoma, renal cysts, post-transplant erythrocytosisHigh erythropoietin with normal oxygenation
DrugsTestosterone, anabolic steroids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, SGLT2 inhibitorsTemporal link to drug start

Testosterone raises the hematocrit by stimulating erythropoietin and lowering hepcidin, which frees iron for erythropoiesis. SGLT2 inhibitors raise the hematocrit by a few percentage points through mild hemoconcentration and, it is thought, through less hypoxic stress in the proximal tubule, which lets the cortical interstitial cells resume erythropoietin production. In hereditary von Hippel-Lindau-related (Chuvash) erythrocytosis, hypoxia-inducible factor escapes degradation even in normoxia.

A normal pulse oximeter reading does not exclude hypoxic erythrocytosis in a smoker: carboxyhemoglobin reads as oxyhemoglobin on standard two-wavelength oximetry. Co-oximetry measures it.

Low erythropoietin with erythrocytosis points to PV. Normal or high erythropoietin points to a secondary cause: look at oxygenation, sleep, smoking, drugs, and the kidneys and liver.

sections.heading: Thrombocytosis, leukocytosis and eosinophilia
sections.html:
Thrombocytosis: reactive or clonal

A platelet count above 450,000/mm3 is thrombocytosis. In most patients it is reactive (secondary). Inflammation raises interleukin-6, which stimulates hepatic thrombopoietin production. Iron deficiency raises the count by mechanisms that probably include erythropoietin cross-talk and shared megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitors. After splenectomy the splenic pool is lost, and after acute bleeding or recovery from marrow suppression there is a rebound.

Essential thrombocythemia (ET) is the clonal alternative: a myeloproliferative neoplasm with a sustained high platelet count and large, mature, hyperlobulated megakaryocytes in clusters in the marrow. It is driven by one of three mutually exclusive mutations, all of which activate JAK2-STAT signalling through the thrombopoietin receptor:

  • JAK2 V617F in about half (highest thrombotic risk),
  • CALR (calreticulin) frameshift in about a quarter; the mutant protein binds and activates MPL,
  • MPL in a few percent; the rest are triple-negative.

ET is a diagnosis of exclusion: reactive causes and other myeloid neoplasms must be ruled out, especially CML (test for BCR-ABL1), which can present with a high platelet count alone.

FeatureReactive thrombocytosisEssential thrombocythemia
ContextInfection, inflammation, iron deficiency, malignancy, surgery, aspleniaOften an incidental finding in an otherwise well adult
Inflammatory markersCRP or ferritin often raised (ferritin low in iron deficiency)Normal
SpleenNormal, or absent after splenectomyMildly enlarged in some
Driver mutationAbsentJAK2, CALR or MPL in most
Thrombosis and bleedingLittle added riskArterial and venous thrombosis; bleeding at very high counts
CourseResolves with the causeChronic; small risk of myelofibrosis or leukemia

At platelet counts above about 1,000,000/mm3, large von Willebrand multimers adsorb to the platelet surface and are cleared, producing an acquired von Willebrand syndrome and a bleeding tendency. Anagrelide, an alternative cytoreductive drug, inhibits megakaryocyte maturation; it is also a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor, which explains palpitations, headache, fluid retention and heart failure.

Neutrophilia and the leukemoid reaction

Neutrophilia follows infection, inflammation, tissue necrosis, smoking, pregnancy, asplenia and drugs. Glucocorticoids raise the neutrophil count largely by demargination: they reduce adhesion molecule expression (L-selectin and integrins) so marginated cells enter the circulating pool, and they speed release from the marrow and slow migration into tissue. Epinephrine and vigorous exercise cause rapid demargination as well. Lithium and G-CSF raise production.

A leukemoid reaction is an extreme reactive leukocytosis, typically above 50,000/mm3, with a left shift to bands, metamyelocytes and a few myelocytes. Typical causes are severe infection (for example Clostridioides difficile colitis), severe hemorrhage or hemolysis, and tumours that secrete G-CSF. Distinguishing features from CML:

  • Toxic granulation, Döhle bodies and cytoplasmic vacuoles in neutrophils (signs of activation);
  • Mature neutrophils dominate, with no basophilia;
  • Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase is high in a leukemoid reaction and low in CML (now largely replaced by BCR-ABL1 testing, the definitive test);
  • An obvious cause, and resolution once it is treated.

Eosinophilia

Eosinophilia is an absolute eosinophil count above 500/mm3; above 1,500/mm3 is hypereosinophilia. Eosinophil production depends on IL-5 from type 2 helper T cells and innate lymphoid cells, which also drive allergy and the response to tissue-invasive helminths.

CategoryExamples
Allergic and atopicAsthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
Parasitic (tissue-invasive helminths)Strongyloides, hookworm, Toxocara, filariae, schistosomes, Trichinella
DrugsDRESS (for example with allopurinol, anticonvulsants, sulfonamides), interstitial nephritis
EndocrineAdrenal insufficiency (loss of the cortisol effect that normally keeps eosinophils low)
Vasculitis and immuneEosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, IgG4-related disease
NeoplasticHodgkin lymphoma and T-cell lymphomas (IL-5 secretion), systemic mastocytosis, myeloid neoplasms with PDGFRA, PDGFRB or FGFR1 rearrangement

Eosinophils damage tissue by releasing granule proteins such as major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein. In hypereosinophilic syndrome (sustained hypereosinophilia with organ damage), the heart is the most feared target: endomyocardial necrosis, mural thrombus and then fibrosis cause a restrictive cardiomyopathy. Lungs, skin, gut and nerves are also involved. The FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion, created by a small deletion on chromosome 4, makes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that responds well to imatinib.

Glucocorticoids suppress eosinophils within hours, so eosinophilia in a severely stressed patient (for example in septic shock) is unexpected and should raise concern for adrenal insufficiency.

Neonatal polycythemia

A newborn's venous hematocrit above 65% is polycythemia. Causes include fetal hypoxia that drives erythropoietin (placental insufficiency with growth restriction, maternal diabetes, maternal smoking, high altitude), extra placental transfusion (delayed cord clamping, the recipient twin in twin-twin transfusion) and conditions such as trisomy 21 and congenital hypothyroidism. Blood viscosity rises steeply above a hematocrit of about 65%, causing plethora, lethargy, poor feeding, respiratory distress, hypoglycemia (more red cells consuming glucose and less plasma glucose per volume), jaundice from the larger red cell mass, and, rarely, necrotizing enterocolitis or renal vein thrombosis.

sections.heading: Acute blood loss, transfusion thresholds and anemia in liver disease
sections.html:
Assessing the bleeding patient

In acute hemorrhage the decision to transfuse is driven by hemodynamics and ongoing loss, not by the first hemoglobin, which lags behind the true deficit until plasma volume is restored over the next one to three days. Estimate the loss from vital signs, mental status, capillary refill, urine output and lactate. Tachycardia and a narrow pulse pressure come before hypotension; hypotension in a young adult usually means a large loss. Beta-blockers, pacemakers, older age and athletic conditioning can blunt the tachycardia.

Initial steps are the same across causes: two large-bore intravenous lines, type and crossmatch, CBC, coagulation tests, fibrinogen, chemistry and lactate, then source control (endoscopy, angiographic embolisation, surgery). Limit crystalloid in hemorrhagic shock, because large volumes dilute clotting factors, worsen acidosis and cause hypothermia. Patients in hemorrhagic shock receive blood products early, in a balanced ratio of plasma, platelets and red cells (approximately 1:1:1) through a massive transfusion protocol, with tranexamic acid in trauma when it can be given within 3 hours of injury. Uncrossmatched group O red cells are used until type-specific blood is available (O-negative for females of childbearing potential when possible).

Restrictive transfusion thresholds for stable patients

For hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults without active brisk bleeding, large randomized trials show that a restrictive strategy is as safe as a liberal one and exposes patients to fewer units. Current guidance can be summarised as follows:

Patient groupUsual hemoglobin trigger
Most stable hospitalized adults, including the critically ill and those with upper gastrointestinal bleedingBelow 7 g/dL
Pre-existing cardiovascular disease, orthopedic surgery, cardiac surgeryBelow about 8 g/dL (some guidance uses 7.5 g/dL in cardiac surgery)
Symptoms of inadequate oxygen delivery at any hemoglobin (chest pain, heart failure, hypotension unresponsive to fluid)Transfuse on clinical grounds

Give one unit at a time to a stable patient and reassess; in an adult without ongoing loss, one unit of packed red cells raises hemoglobin by about 1 g/dL (hematocrit about 3%). Each unit also brings risk: transfusion-associated circulatory overload in older adults and those with heart or kidney failure, transfusion-related acute lung injury, febrile and allergic reactions, alloimmunisation and iron overload with chronic transfusion.

A stable patient with a hemoglobin of 7.4 g/dL and no cardiovascular disease does not need transfusion. Conversely, a hypotensive patient who is still bleeding needs blood even if the first hemoglobin is 12 g/dL.

Recovery after the bleed

After the source is controlled, replace iron. Each millilitre of whole blood carries about 0.5 mg of iron, so a 2-litre bleed removes roughly 1 g, which can exhaust stores. Oral iron is first-line when the patient can absorb it; intravenous iron is used for intolerance, malabsorption, ongoing loss, or when faster repletion is needed (for example before surgery). Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents have no role in acute bleeding in patients without chronic kidney disease.

Anemia in chronic liver disease and alcohol use

Work up anemia in cirrhosis systematically: look for gastrointestinal blood loss (varices, portal hypertensive gastropathy, peptic ulcer), iron deficiency, folate deficiency (poor diet in alcohol use disorder), hypersplenism, hemolysis, and medication effects (for example ribavirin in older hepatitis C regimens). Mild macrocytosis with target cells is typical and benign. A new, rapid fall in hemoglobin with jaundice, high LDH, low haptoglobin, a negative direct antiglobulin test and many spur cells on the smear indicates spur cell anemia, a marker of end-stage disease; liver transplantation is the definitive treatment and transfusion gives only short-lived benefit.

In alcohol use disorder, mild macrocytosis often appears before any anemia and settles over a few months of abstinence. Give thiamine before glucose in malnourished patients, and give folic acid when deficiency is likely.

Finding in a patient with cirrhosisMost likely explanationNext step
Microcytosis, low ferritinChronic gastrointestinal blood lossEndoscopy; iron repletion
Macrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophilsFolate deficiencyFolate level; replace
Mild macrocytosis, target cells, normal folateMembrane lipid change of liver diseaseNo specific treatment
Hemolysis with many spur cellsSpur cell anemia of advanced cirrhosisTransplant evaluation
Mild thrombocytopenia and leukopenia with splenomegalyHypersplenism from portal hypertensionUsually none; manage portal hypertension

Endocrine anemias

Hypothyroidism, hypogonadism and adrenal insufficiency cause mild hypoproliferative anemia that improves with hormone replacement over two to three months. Before attributing an anemia to hypothyroidism, check iron studies and B12: menorrhagia and coexisting autoimmune gastritis are common in these patients.

Step 1 explains why hemoglobin lags behind blood loss (transcapillary refill and renal retention); Step 2 CK turns that into the rule to treat the patient's hemodynamics, not the first number.

sections.heading: Anemia in pregnancy, infancy, toddlers, athletes and older adults
sections.html:
Pregnancy

Hemoglobin falls in normal pregnancy because plasma volume expands more than red cell mass. Anemia in pregnancy is defined by trimester-specific thresholds: hemoglobin below 11 g/dL in the first and third trimesters and below 10.5 g/dL in the second. Pregnant patients are screened with a CBC at the first prenatal visit and again at about 24 to 28 weeks, and are usually advised to take low-dose iron, typically in a prenatal vitamin.

When anemia is found, iron deficiency is by far the most likely cause. Check ferritin; a ferritin below about 30 ng/mL confirms deficiency in pregnancy. Treat with oral iron (alternate-day dosing improves absorption and tolerance), and use intravenous iron in the second or third trimester when oral iron fails, is not tolerated, or the deficit is large close to delivery. Microcytosis with a normal ferritin raises the possibility of a thalassemia trait, which matters for partner testing. Folate deficiency (macrocytosis) is less common now that folic acid is routinely supplemented.

A hemoglobin of 10.8 g/dL with normal indices at 24 weeks is within the expected range for the second trimester. The same value with an MCV of 74 fL is iron deficiency until proven otherwise.

Infants and toddlers

  • Physiologic nadir. A well term infant of 2 to 3 months with a hemoglobin around 9.5 to 11 g/dL and normal indices needs reassurance only.
  • Preterm infants need iron supplementation from about the first month of life until about 12 months if they are breastfed, because stores are small; anemia of prematurity is managed by minimising phlebotomy and transfusing by gestational-age-specific thresholds.
  • Exclusively breastfed term infants receive iron supplementation from about 4 months until iron-rich complementary foods are established.
  • Universal screening with a hemoglobin level is done at about 12 months, with assessment of risk factors (prematurity, low birth weight, high milk intake, low-iron diet, lead exposure).

Cow's milk anemia (nutrition)

A typical patient is an 18-month-old who drinks more than about 24 oz (700 mL) of whole milk a day, often from a bottle, and eats little meat or iron-fortified cereal. The CBC shows a microcytic, hypochromic anemia with a high RDW, and the ferritin is low. Management:

  1. Limit cow's milk to about 16 to 24 oz (500 to 700 mL) a day, wean from the bottle, and increase iron-rich foods.
  2. Give oral elemental iron (about 3 mg/kg/day, between meals and not with milk).
  3. Recheck the hemoglobin in about 4 weeks. A rise of at least 1 g/dL confirms iron deficiency; continue iron for about 3 months after the count normalises to replete stores.
  4. If there is no response, check adherence, then consider ongoing blood loss, malabsorption (celiac disease), thalassemia trait or lead poisoning.

Cow's milk is not introduced as the main drink before 12 months. Screen for lead in at-risk children, because lead exposure and iron deficiency share risk factors and iron deficiency increases lead absorption.

Athletes

An endurance athlete with a slightly low hemoglobin, normal MCV, normal ferritin and no symptoms most likely has dilutional pseudoanemia from plasma volume expansion; no treatment is needed. Low ferritin in an athlete, especially a menstruating athlete or one with restricted energy intake, is true iron deficiency and deserves oral iron, dietary assessment, and evaluation for relative energy deficiency in sport. Hemoglobinuria after long runs reflects foot-strike hemolysis.

Older adults

Treat anemia in an older adult as a finding that needs an explanation. A practical work-up:

  1. CBC with indices, reticulocyte count and peripheral smear.
  2. Ferritin and transferrin saturation, vitamin B12 (with methylmalonic acid if borderline) and folate.
  3. Creatinine and estimated GFR, TSH, and markers of inflammation as indicated.
  4. Iron deficiency in an older adult or a postmenopausal woman means gastrointestinal evaluation (colonoscopy and upper endoscopy) for occult malignancy or other lesions, even if stool testing is negative.
  5. Unexplained cytopenias, macrocytosis without deficiency, or more than one low lineage prompt hematology referral and consideration of a marrow examination for myelodysplastic syndrome.

Polypharmacy is a frequent contributor: proton pump inhibitors and metformin lower B12 absorption, antiplatelet drugs and anticoagulants increase gastrointestinal loss, and methotrexate and some antiepileptic drugs interfere with folate.

PatientMost likely explanationBest next step
24 weeks pregnant, Hb 10.7 g/dL, MCV 88 fLPhysiologic dilutionContinue routine prenatal iron
10-week-old term infant, Hb 10 g/dL, thrivingPhysiologic nadirReassurance
Toddler drinking 1.2 L of milk daily, MCV 62 fLIron deficiencyLimit milk, oral iron, recheck in 4 weeks
Marathon runner, Hb 12.6 g/dL, normal ferritinPseudoanemiaNo treatment
74-year-old man, ferritin 8 ng/mLGastrointestinal blood lossColonoscopy and upper endoscopy

Do not attribute anemia in an older adult to "old age". And do not treat iron deficiency in an older man with iron alone without looking for the source.
