sections.heading: Neutropenia, pancytopenia and lymphopenia: evaluation and management
sections.html:
The incidentally low neutrophil count

Start by confirming the finding and calculating the ANC. Then ask four questions: Is the patient ill or infected? Are other lineages low? Is there a drug that could be responsible? Is this a long-standing, stable pattern?

  • Well patient, isolated mild neutropenia (ANC 1,000 to 1,500), normal examination: review old counts and medications, and repeat the CBC with a smear in a few weeks. Transient post-viral neutropenia is the most common explanation.
  • Stable lifelong mild neutropenia in a person of African or Middle Eastern ancestry with no infections: consider Duffy-null associated neutrophil count; Duffy red cell phenotyping confirms it. No marrow biopsy, no G-CSF, and no need to withhold indicated drugs.
  • Recurrent fevers and mouth ulcers every few weeks: serial CBCs two to three times a week for 6 weeks to look for cyclic neutropenia.
  • Neutropenia with anemia or thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, blasts, or severe neutropenia without a cause: refer to hematology; smear review and usually marrow biopsy.

Laboratory work-up for persistent unexplained neutropenia includes B12, folate and copper levels, HIV and hepatitis B and C testing, antinuclear antibodies and rheumatoid factor when autoimmune features exist, and peripheral flow cytometry for large granular lymphocytes in patients with rheumatoid arthritis or splenomegaly.

Drug-induced agranulocytosis

Suspect it in a patient who develops fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers within the first months of a new high-risk drug. Management:

  1. Stop the suspected drug immediately and do not rechallenge (clozapine rechallenge is a specialist decision after careful risk assessment).
  2. If febrile, treat as febrile neutropenia: blood cultures and empiric intravenous broad-spectrum anti-pseudomonal antibiotics.
  3. G-CSF can shorten recovery in severe cases.
  4. Recovery usually occurs within 1 to 3 weeks of stopping the drug.

For thionamides, patients are told before starting to stop the drug and obtain a CBC if they develop fever or sore throat; routine monitoring catches few cases because onset is abrupt. Agranulocytosis with one thionamide is a contraindication to the other because of cross-reactivity; definitive therapy (radioactive iodine or surgery) is then chosen. For clozapine, ANC monitoring is most frequent early in therapy; mild drops in a patient with a known Duffy-null associated neutrophil count are interpreted against that patient's own baseline.

Febrile neutropenia (in brief)

A single oral temperature of 38.3 °C (101 °F) or higher, or 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) sustained for an hour, with an ANC below 500 or expected to fall below 500, is febrile neutropenia. Obtain blood cultures (from each lumen of a central catheter and a peripheral site) and give the first dose of an anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam, such as cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem, within about an hour. Add vancomycin only for specific indications (hemodynamic instability, suspected catheter or skin infection, pneumonia, known MRSA colonisation). Carefully selected low-risk outpatients may receive oral therapy. Fever persisting for 4 to 7 days despite antibiotics prompts a search and empiric therapy for invasive fungal infection.

Pancytopenia

Pancytopenia means anemia, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia together. The causes fall into two groups.

MechanismExamplesUseful clue
Marrow failureAplastic anemia, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria overlap, inherited marrow failureHypocellular marrow; low reticulocytes
Ineffective hematopoiesisB12 or folate deficiency, myelodysplastic syndrome, copper deficiencyMacrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils or dysplasia
Marrow infiltrationAcute leukemia, lymphoma, myeloma, metastatic cancer, myelofibrosis, granulomatous infectionLeukoerythroblastic smear (nucleated red cells, immature myeloid cells, teardrop cells), blasts
Peripheral destruction or sequestrationHypersplenism from cirrhosis, lupus, overwhelming sepsis, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosisSplenomegaly; normal or busy marrow
Drugs and toxinsChemotherapy, methotrexate, azathioprine with low TPMT activity, linezolid, alcohol, radiationTemporal link
InfectionHIV, hepatitis, parvovirus B19 in immunosuppressed patients, tuberculosis, visceral leishmaniasisExposure and travel history

Initial evaluation: peripheral smear, reticulocyte count, B12 and folate, LDH, liver tests, HIV and hepatitis serologies, and abdominal ultrasound for spleen size. The bone marrow aspirate and biopsy is the most informative test when the cause is not apparent, and it is urgent if blasts are seen. Supportive care includes transfusion by thresholds, prompt treatment of fever, and avoidance of transfusion from family members when transplant is a possibility.

Lymphopenia

Lymphopenia on a routine count is most often transient (recent viral infection, glucocorticoids, acute illness). Persistent unexplained lymphopenia warrants HIV testing and lymphocyte subset analysis. In infants, an abnormal newborn screen for T-cell receptor excision circles needs urgent flow cytometry to look for severe combined immunodeficiency; until immune status is known, avoid live vaccines (including rotavirus) and give only irradiated, leukoreduced, CMV-safe blood products.

Pancytopenia with macrocytosis in an older adult may be B12 deficiency rather than a marrow malignancy. Check B12 and folate before, or alongside, the marrow biopsy.

sections.heading: Thrombocytopenia: approach, ITP management and special populations
sections.html:
A stepwise approach

[[figure:s23a-fig51]]
  1. Confirm it is real. Review the smear for clumps; if present, repeat the count in a citrate tube.
  2. Judge urgency. Bleeding, neurologic signs, fever, or a count below about 20,000/mm3 needs same-day evaluation. Look at the whole CBC, the smear and the clinical context.
  3. Isolated or not? Other cytopenias suggest marrow disease, B12 deficiency or hypersplenism. Schistocytes suggest a thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP, HUS, DIC), which is an emergency.
  4. Context clues: heparin exposure in the last 5 to 10 days (HIT), new drugs, pregnancy, cirrhosis, recent transfusion, sepsis, travel.

ITP management

ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion. In adults, testing for HIV and hepatitis C is recommended because treating them can improve the count, and many clinicians test for H. pylori and check thyroid function, immunoglobulins and a direct antiglobulin test. A bone marrow biopsy is not needed for typical ITP; it is reserved for atypical features (other cytopenias, abnormal smear, splenomegaly, lack of response), and older age alone no longer mandates it.

SituationManagement
Child with new ITP and skin bleeding only (petechiae, bruising), whatever the countObservation with education; most recover within months
Child with mucosal bleeding or reduced quality of lifeShort course of glucocorticoids, or IVIG when a fast rise is needed
Adult with new ITP and platelets below 30,000/mm3, or with bleedingGlucocorticoids: prednisone for no more than about 6 weeks including taper, or a short course of high-dose dexamethasone
Adult with platelets at or above 30,000 and no bleedingObservation, unless surgery, anticoagulation or high bleeding risk
Need for a rapid rise (significant bleeding, urgent surgery)Add IVIG to glucocorticoids
Life-threatening bleeding (intracranial, massive gastrointestinal)Platelet transfusion plus IVIG plus high-dose intravenous glucocorticoids at once
Steroid-dependent or relapsing ITPThrombopoietin-receptor agonist (eltrombopag, romiplostim, avatrombopag), rituximab, or splenectomy (usually delayed at least 12 months); fostamatinib later

Before splenectomy, vaccinate against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Haemophilus influenzae type b, ideally at least 2 weeks ahead. Avoid long-term steroids, which add toxicity without durable benefit. Platelet transfusion alone gives only a brief rise in ITP and is used for life-threatening bleeding or emergencies.

Pregnancy

CauseCluesManagement
Gestational thrombocytopeniaLate second or third trimester, usually above 70,000/mm3, no prior history, no bleedingReassurance and monitoring; resolves after delivery; no fetal risk
ITPOnset any trimester, often first; prior low counts; may fall below 50,000/mm3Treat for bleeding or low counts, and to reach a safe count for delivery and neuraxial anesthesia; glucocorticoids or IVIG first-line; neonatal count after birth
Preeclampsia with severe features or HELLPHypertension, raised aminotransferases, hemolysis after 20 weeksDelivery planning, magnesium sulfate
Thrombotic microangiopathySchistocytes, neurologic or renal signsTTP: plasma exchange

Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (NAIT)

NAIT presents as petechiae, bruising or, most seriously, intracranial hemorrhage (sometimes in utero) in an otherwise well newborn whose mother has a normal platelet count. Maternal antibodies target a paternal platelet antigen, most often HPA-1a, and the first pregnancy can be affected. A severely low count in the newborn (often below 30,000/mm3) is treated with platelet transfusion (antigen-negative platelets if available, otherwise random-donor platelets without delay) and often IVIG; head ultrasound screens for hemorrhage. Confirm with maternal antibody and parental platelet antigen typing. In later pregnancies the risk is high, and antenatal maternal IVIG, with or without prednisone, is given under specialist care. By contrast, a newborn of a mother with ITP is thrombocytopenic because maternal autoantibody crosses the placenta, and the mother herself has (or has had) a low count.

Liver disease and HIT

Thrombocytopenia from cirrhosis is mild to moderate, stable and accompanied by splenomegaly. Before procedures, oral thrombopoietin-receptor agonists approved for this setting (avatrombopag, lusutrombopag) can raise the count. HIT is suspected when the count falls by more than half 5 to 10 days after heparin exposure; stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant without waiting for confirmatory testing.

A child with abrupt petechiae after a viral illness, a normal examination and a platelet count of 12,000/mm3 but no mucosal bleeding can be observed. The count alone is not the indication to treat.

sections.heading: Erythrocytosis and polycythemia vera: work-up and management
sections.html:
Working up a high hematocrit

[[figure:s23a-fig52]]
  1. Confirm and exclude relative polycythemia. Repeat the CBC when the patient is well hydrated; review diuretics.
  2. History and examination: smoking, snoring and daytime sleepiness, lung or heart disease, altitude, testosterone or anabolic steroid use, SGLT2 inhibitor use, kidney transplant; splenomegaly, aquagenic pruritus, erythromelalgia, prior thrombosis.
  3. First tests together: JAK2 V617F mutation and serum erythropoietin. A JAK2 mutation with a low erythropoietin strongly suggests PV. If JAK2 V617F is negative but erythropoietin is low, test for a JAK2 exon 12 mutation.
  4. Normal or high erythropoietin and no JAK2 mutation: look for a secondary cause with pulse oximetry at rest and with exertion, overnight oximetry or polysomnography, carboxyhemoglobin by co-oximetry in smokers, and abdominal imaging (kidney and liver) for an erythropoietin-secreting lesion.

Polycythemia vera management

All patients receive two treatments:

  • Phlebotomy to keep the hematocrit below 45%. Typical removal is about 450 to 500 mL at a time, with smaller volumes in older or frail patients. The resulting iron deficiency is intended; do not give iron unless symptomatic iron deficiency demands it, because it will drive red cell production.
  • Low-dose aspirin (81 to 100 mg daily), unless contraindicated (for example a history of major bleeding or acquired von Willebrand syndrome at very high platelet counts).

Cytoreduction is added for high-risk patients, defined by age 60 or older or a previous thrombosis, and for others with poor tolerance of phlebotomy, progressive splenomegaly, symptomatic thrombocytosis or leukocytosis, or severe symptoms.

AgentWhen chosenMonitoring and cautions
HydroxyureaUsual first-line cytoreduction in older high-risk patientsCBC for cytopenias; mouth and leg ulcers; skin cancer surveillance; teratogenic
Ropeginterferon alfa-2b (or pegylated interferon)Younger patients, pregnancy or planned pregnancy; hydroxyurea intoleranceDepression, thyroid dysfunction, autoimmunity, flu-like symptoms
RuxolitinibHydroxyurea resistance or intolerance; severe pruritus or splenomegalyAnemia, thrombocytopenia, infections including herpes zoster, skin cancers

Address cardiovascular risk factors aggressively (smoking cessation, blood pressure, lipids), because thrombosis is the major cause of morbidity. Pruritus may respond to antihistamines, phototherapy, interferon or ruxolitinib. Treat hyperuricemia when symptomatic. Before surgery, control the hematocrit and platelet count where possible because perioperative thrombosis and bleeding are both increased. Monitor for progression: new anemia, rising LDH, teardrop cells and enlarging spleen suggest post-PV myelofibrosis; circulating blasts suggest leukemic transformation.

Microcytosis in a patient with PV on phlebotomy is expected iron deficiency. Iron replacement raises the hematocrit again and defeats the treatment.

Secondary erythrocytosis management

  • Hypoxic lung disease or sleep apnea: treat the cause (CPAP for obstructive sleep apnea, supplemental oxygen when hypoxemia criteria are met, smoking cessation). Phlebotomy is not routine and is reserved for symptomatic hyperviscosity, because the extra red cells are compensatory.
  • Cyanotic congenital heart disease: avoid routine phlebotomy, which causes iron deficiency and worsens oxygen delivery; phlebotomy only for hyperviscosity symptoms, with fluid replacement.
  • Testosterone therapy: check hematocrit at baseline, at 3 to 6 months and then yearly. If the hematocrit rises above about 54%, stop testosterone, evaluate for hypoxia or sleep apnea, and restart at a lower dose once it falls. Do not start testosterone in a patient whose hematocrit is already high.
  • SGLT2 inhibitors: a rise of a few percentage points in hematocrit is expected and benign; it does not require stopping the drug. A larger rise needs evaluation for another cause.
  • Post-renal transplant erythrocytosis: ACE inhibitors or ARBs lower the hematocrit.
  • Erythropoietin-secreting tumours: resect; erythrocytosis resolves, and its return can signal recurrence.

Relative polycythemia

In a patient with dehydration or diuretic use, rehydrate and repeat the count. Chronic relative polycythemia associated with obesity, hypertension and smoking improves with weight loss, blood pressure control and smoking cessation; it does not need phlebotomy.

The best initial tests for unexplained erythrocytosis are serum erythropoietin and JAK2 V617F; a marrow biopsy comes later, if needed, to confirm PV or assess fibrosis.

sections.heading: Thrombocytosis, leukocytosis, eosinophilia and neonatal polycythemia: management
sections.html:
A high platelet count

Most thrombocytosis is reactive. The first steps are to repeat the count, review the smear and look for a cause: ferritin and iron studies, CRP, recent surgery or trauma, infection, inflammatory disease, malignancy and splenectomy. If the count stays above 450,000/mm3 without a cause, test for JAK2 V617F, CALR and MPL mutations and BCR-ABL1, and refer for marrow examination.

Management of essential thrombocythemia is guided by thrombotic risk:

Risk groupFeaturesUsual approach
Very low or lowAge 60 or younger, no thrombosis (JAK2 status refines risk)Observation or low-dose aspirin (aspirin especially with JAK2 mutation or cardiovascular risk factors)
IntermediateAge over 60, no JAK2 mutation, no thrombosisAspirin; cytoreduction decided case by case
HighPrior thrombosis, or age over 60 with a JAK2 mutationAspirin plus hydroxyurea; interferon or anagrelide as alternatives

Before starting aspirin when the platelet count is above about 1,000,000/mm3, check von Willebrand factor activity (ristocetin cofactor); if it is low, aspirin raises the bleeding risk. Platelet counts in reactive thrombocytosis need no antiplatelet therapy; treat the cause, for example iron replacement in iron deficiency.

A very high leukocyte count

For neutrophilia, look first for infection, inflammation, glucocorticoid use, smoking and recent stress. A count above 50,000/mm3 with a left shift in an ill patient is often a leukemoid reaction, for example from C. difficile colitis, and resolves with treatment of the cause. Features that point to a myeloid neoplasm instead are splenomegaly, basophilia, eosinophilia, a spectrum of immature myeloid cells with a myelocyte peak, blasts, or no plausible reactive trigger; these call for peripheral blood BCR-ABL1 testing by FISH or PCR. Blasts, especially with a leukocyte count above 100,000/mm3 and dyspnea or confusion (leukostasis), are a hematologic emergency.

Eosinophilia

History is the most useful tool: atopy, travel or residence in areas endemic for helminths, walking barefoot, raw or undercooked food, new medications, asthma with sinus disease or neuropathy, and constitutional symptoms.

  1. Confirm the absolute eosinophil count and look for organ involvement: skin, lungs (chest radiograph), heart (troponin, ECG, echocardiography), gut, nerves and kidneys (urinalysis).
  2. Exclude parasites: Strongyloides serology and stool examinations for ova and parasites, plus targeted tests by exposure.
  3. Stop any suspect drug; look for DRESS (fever, rash, facial edema, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis weeks after a new drug).
  4. Persistent hypereosinophilia without a cause: peripheral smear, serum tryptase, vitamin B12, flow cytometry for an aberrant T-cell population, and testing for the FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion; marrow biopsy.

Before giving glucocorticoids to a patient with eosinophilia who has lived in or travelled to an endemic area, test or empirically treat for Strongyloides (ivermectin). Steroids can trigger hyperinfection with gram-negative sepsis.

Treatment follows the cause. Myeloid neoplasms with PDGFRA or PDGFRB rearrangement respond to low-dose imatinib. Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with organ involvement is treated with glucocorticoids; mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) allows steroid sparing, and hydroxyurea or interferon are options. Cardiac involvement may need anticoagulation for mural thrombus and, later, valve surgery. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is treated with glucocorticoids and, depending on severity, mepolizumab, rituximab or cyclophosphamide.

Neonatal polycythemia

Screen infants at risk (infant of a diabetic mother, growth restriction, recipient twin, delayed cord clamping with symptoms). A capillary (heel-stick) hematocrit runs higher than venous blood, so confirm with a venous sample before acting.

  • Check glucose and bilirubin, because hypoglycemia and jaundice are the most frequent problems.
  • Asymptomatic infants: ensure adequate feeding and hydration and monitor glucose and bilirubin.
  • Symptomatic hyperviscosity (lethargy, poor feeding, respiratory distress, seizures), especially at higher hematocrits: partial exchange transfusion, replacing blood with normal saline to lower the hematocrit; evidence of long-term benefit is limited, so it is reserved for symptomatic infants.
FindingMost likely causeNext step
Platelets 720,000/mm3, ferritin 6 ng/mLReactive thrombocytosis from iron deficiencyIron replacement; find the blood loss
Platelets 900,000/mm3 for a year, CALR mutation, age 45, no thrombosisLow-risk essential thrombocythemiaObservation or aspirin
Leukocytes 62,000/mm3 with bands and toxic granulation in severe colitisLeukemoid reactionTreat the infection
Eosinophils 3,000/mm3, dyspnea and new heart failureHypereosinophilic syndrome with cardiac involvementEchocardiography, troponin; urgent treatment
Newborn, venous hematocrit 71%, jittery, glucose 30 mg/dLNeonatal polycythemia with hyperviscosityTreat hypoglycemia; consider partial exchange

title: Blood · Coagulation disorders and transfusion reactions
meta: Hemostasis tests, bleeding and thrombotic disorders, anticoagulant mechanisms and transfusion reaction mechanisms.

sections.heading: Hemostasis and the screening coagulation tests
sections.html:
Two linked steps

Primary hemostasis builds a platelet plug. At a site of injury, von Willebrand factor (vWF) unfolds on exposed subendothelial collagen and binds platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V (adhesion). Adherent platelets are activated by collagen, thrombin, ADP and thromboxane A2, release granule contents and change shape. Activation switches GpIIb/IIIa (integrin αIIbβ3) into a high-affinity state, so fibrinogen can bridge neighbouring platelets (aggregation). Secondary hemostasis is the coagulation cascade, which generates thrombin and turns the loose plug into a cross-linked fibrin clot.

The clinical pattern tracks the step that fails. Defects of primary hemostasis (thrombocytopenia, platelet function disorders, von Willebrand disease) cause mucocutaneous bleeding: petechiae, epistaxis, gum bleeding, heavy menses and immediate oozing after cuts. Defects of secondary hemostasis (hemophilia, other factor deficiencies) cause deep bleeding into joints and muscles and bleeding that starts hours after a procedure, because the initial platelet plug forms but is not stabilized.

The cell-based model and the test model

In vivo, coagulation starts when tissue factor (TF) on cells outside the vessel meets factor VIIa. TF-VIIa makes small amounts of Xa and thrombin (initiation). That thrombin activates platelets and factors V, VIII and XI (amplification). On the activated platelet surface the tenase complex (IXa + VIIIa) and prothrombinase complex (Xa + Va) then make a burst of thrombin (propagation). This explains why hemophilia A or B bleeds severely even though factor VII is normal: the TF-VIIa pathway alone cannot sustain thrombin generation.

The in vitro tests still use the older split into pathways, which is useful for interpreting results.

TestWhat starts itFactors measuredClassic causes of prolongation
Prothrombin time (PT) / INRTissue factor (thromboplastin) + calciumVII, X, V, II, fibrinogenWarfarin, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, factor VII deficiency
Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)Contact activator + phospholipid + calciumXII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, fibrinogenUnfractionated heparin, hemophilia A/B, factor XI or XII deficiency, lupus anticoagulant
Thrombin timeAdded thrombinFibrinogen conversion to fibrinHeparin, direct thrombin inhibitors, low or abnormal fibrinogen
Fibrinogen (Clauss)High-dose thrombinFunctional fibrinogenDIC, liver failure, massive transfusion, inherited afibrinogenemia
Platelet count and smear—Number, size, morphologyThrombocytopenia, giant platelets, schistocytes

The INR standardizes the PT for warfarin monitoring by correcting for the sensitivity of each thromboplastin reagent. Factor VII has the shortest half-life of the vitamin K-dependent factors (a few hours), so warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency and early liver failure prolong the PT before the aPTT.

Normal PT and aPTT do not exclude a serious bleeding disorder. Platelet function defects, most von Willebrand disease, factor XIII deficiency, fibrinolytic defects (α2-antiplasmin or PAI-1 deficiency) and vascular fragility (scurvy, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) all have normal screening times.

Interpreting an abnormal result

[[figure:s23a-fig60]]

An isolated prolonged aPTT is first repeated to exclude heparin contamination (samples drawn from a heparinized line), then tested with a 1:1 mixing study. Normal plasma supplies about 50% of every factor, enough to normalize the aPTT. If the time corrects, a factor deficiency is present (VIII, IX, XI or XII; assay them individually). If it does not, an inhibitor is present. A lupus anticoagulant acts immediately and is confirmed with phospholipid-dependent tests such as the dilute Russell viper venom time; it causes thrombosis rather than bleeding. A factor VIII autoantibody is classically time- and temperature-dependent: the mix may correct at first and then prolong again after 1–2 hours of incubation at 37 °C. The Bethesda assay measures the inhibitor's strength.

Deficiency of factor XII, prekallikrein or high-molecular-weight kininogen prolongs the aPTT, sometimes markedly, but causes no bleeding, because the contact pathway is not needed for hemostasis in vivo. These patients come to attention through preoperative screening.

Platelet function testing

The bleeding time is no longer recommended. Platelet aggregometry exposes platelet-rich plasma to agonists (ADP, collagen, epinephrine, arachidonic acid, ristocetin). Ristocetin makes vWF bind GpIb, so it tests the vWF-GpIb axis rather than true aggregation. Absent ristocetin response with normal response to the other agonists suggests von Willebrand disease or Bernard-Soulier syndrome; the reverse pattern suggests Glanzmann thrombasthenia. Aspirin abolishes the arachidonic acid response.

On Step 2 CK the same tests appear as decisions: whether a prolonged aPTT before surgery needs a mixing study, whether an INR needs correcting before a procedure, and which product to give for which abnormal test.

Fibrinolysis

Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) converts plasminogen to plasmin on the fibrin surface. Plasmin cleaves cross-linked fibrin into fragments that include D-dimer; a raised D-dimer therefore means clot has formed and been broken down. Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) and α2-antiplasmin restrain the system. Tranexamic acid blocks lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, preventing it from binding fibrin, and is useful for mucosal bleeding (dental extraction, heavy menses) and trauma.

sections.heading: Inherited and acquired factor disorders
sections.html:
Hemophilia A and B

Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency, F8) and hemophilia B (factor IX deficiency, F9) are X-linked recessive. Hemophilia A is several times more common. About a third of cases arise from new mutations, so a negative family history does not exclude it; an inversion within intron 22 of F8 causes almost half of severe hemophilia A. Heterozygous females can have low factor levels (skewed X inactivation) and bleed after surgery or delivery.

SeverityFactor activityTypical bleeding
Severebelow 1%Spontaneous hemarthroses and muscle bleeds from infancy or crawling age
Moderate1–5%Bleeding after minor trauma; occasional spontaneous bleeds
Mildabove 5% to below 40%Bleeding after surgery, dental extraction or major trauma; may be diagnosed in adulthood

Signature bleeds are hemarthroses (knees, elbows, ankles) and deep muscle hematomas (iliopsoas bleeding can compress the femoral nerve). Recurrent joint bleeding causes synovitis and a destructive arthropathy. Intracranial hemorrhage is the main cause of death. Neonates may bleed after circumcision or heel sticks. Labs: prolonged aPTT that corrects with mixing, normal PT and platelet count, low factor VIII or IX activity. von Willebrand factor is normal in hemophilia A.

Treatment replaces the missing factor (recombinant or plasma-derived concentrates, including extended half-life products). Mild hemophilia A can respond to desmopressin, which releases stored factor VIII and vWF from endothelial cells; desmopressin does not raise factor IX. Antifibrinolytics help mucosal bleeding. Nonfactor prophylaxis (a bispecific antibody that mimics factor VIIIa) is used in hemophilia A, with or without inhibitors.

Inhibitors are neutralizing IgG alloantibodies against infused factor. They develop in roughly a quarter to a third of patients with severe hemophilia A, usually within the first 50 exposure days, and less often in hemophilia B (where they can come with anaphylaxis to factor IX). An inhibitor shows up as bleeding that no longer responds to usual doses and an aPTT that no longer corrects on mixing. High-titer inhibitors are bypassed with recombinant factor VIIa or activated prothrombin complex concentrate; immune tolerance induction can eradicate them.

Acquired hemophilia A

An autoantibody against factor VIII in a person without a prior bleeding history. It is most common in older adults and in the year after childbirth, and is associated with autoimmune disease and cancer; about half the cases have no cause. Bleeding is mostly into skin, soft tissue and muscle (large ecchymoses, hematomas) rather than joints, and it can be life-threatening. The isolated long aPTT does not correct on mixing (often prolongs further after incubation), factor VIII is low, and the Bethesda titer is positive.

von Willebrand disease

vWF carries factor VIII in plasma (protecting it from clearance) and anchors platelets via GpIb. von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder and presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, especially heavy menstrual bleeding and bleeding after dental work.

TypeDefectInheritance / key features
1Partial quantitative deficiencyAutosomal dominant; most common; usually responds to desmopressin
2ALoss of large multimersActivity much lower than antigen
2BGain of function: excess binding to GpIbLarge multimers lost, mild thrombocytopenia; desmopressin can worsen the platelet count
2MReduced platelet binding, multimers normalActivity low relative to antigen
2NCannot bind factor VIIILow factor VIII with normal vWF antigen; mimics mild hemophilia A but autosomal
3Near-absent vWFAutosomal recessive; low factor VIII causes joint bleeds too

Testing includes vWF antigen, vWF activity (platelet-binding assay), factor VIII activity and multimer analysis. The aPTT may be normal or prolonged (if factor VIII is low). vWF levels rise with stress, inflammation, estrogen and pregnancy and are lower in blood group O, so a single normal value does not exclude mild disease.

Factor XIII deficiency

Factor XIIIa is a transglutaminase that cross-links fibrin. Severe deficiency is autosomal recessive and presents with umbilical stump bleeding in the first days of life, delayed bleeding after trauma, poor wound healing, intracranial hemorrhage and recurrent miscarriage. PT, aPTT, fibrinogen and platelets are all normal; the clot dissolves in 5 M urea, and a factor XIII activity assay confirms. Factor XIII concentrate (or cryoprecipitate) is given as prophylaxis.

Vitamin K deficiency

Vitamin K is the cofactor for γ-glutamyl carboxylase, which adds a carboxyl group to glutamate residues of factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S. The γ-carboxyglutamate residues bind calcium, which lets these proteins attach to phospholipid membranes. Without carboxylation the liver secretes inactive proteins (PIVKAs). Vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), the warfarin target, regenerates the active reduced form.

  • Newborns: little placental transfer, a sterile gut and low vitamin K in breast milk. Vitamin K deficiency bleeding is early (first 24 h, maternal anticonvulsants, rifampin or warfarin), classic (days 2–7) or late (2–12 weeks, exclusively breastfed infants or infants with cholestasis; often intracranial). A single intramuscular dose at birth prevents it.
  • Adults: poor intake (alcohol use disorder, prolonged NPO), fat malabsorption (cholestasis, celiac disease, cystic fibrosis, short bowel, bariatric surgery) and broad-spectrum antibiotics that remove menaquinone-producing gut flora.

PT prolongs first (factor VII), then the aPTT. Parenteral vitamin K corrects the PT within about 12–24 hours; failure to correct points to liver disease.

Liver disease

The liver makes most clotting factors, fibrinogen, plasminogen and the natural anticoagulants (protein C, protein S, antithrombin). Factor VIII is the exception: it comes mainly from sinusoidal and other endothelial cells and is normal or high in cirrhosis, whereas it is low in DIC. Portal hypertension sequesters platelets in the spleen and thrombopoietin production falls. Because procoagulants and anticoagulants fall together, hemostasis is rebalanced; the INR does not predict procedural bleeding, and patients with cirrhosis still develop portal vein thrombosis and DVT.

Scurvy causes gum bleeding, perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs and hemarthroses with entirely normal coagulation tests: the defect is weak vessel collagen (ascorbate is needed for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation), not a clotting factor.

furtherReading.label: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf): Vitamin K Deficiency in Neonates and Adults

sections.heading: Platelet function disorders and consumptive coagulopathy
sections.html:
Inherited platelet function disorders

Platelet function disorders give mucocutaneous bleeding with a normal or near-normal platelet count. The two classic inherited forms are autosomal recessive defects in the two main platelet glycoproteins.

FeatureBernard-Soulier syndromeGlanzmann thrombasthenia
Missing receptorGpIb-IX-V (vWF receptor)GpIIb/IIIa (αIIbβ3, fibrinogen receptor)
Step that failsAdhesionAggregation (platelet-to-platelet bridging)
Platelet count and sizeMild thrombocytopenia, giant plateletsNormal count and size
Aggregation studiesAbsent ristocetin response, not corrected by adding normal plasma; other agonists normalNo aggregation with ADP, collagen, epinephrine or arachidonic acid; ristocetin response normal
OtherCan be misdiagnosed as immune thrombocytopeniaAbsent clot retraction; flow cytometry shows missing CD41/CD61

The ristocetin test separates von Willebrand disease from Bernard-Soulier syndrome: both lack a ristocetin response, but adding normal plasma (a source of vWF) corrects it only in von Willebrand disease. Treatment of both disorders is local measures, antifibrinolytics and platelet transfusion for serious bleeding or surgery. Repeated transfusion can induce antibodies against the missing glycoprotein, making later transfusions ineffective; recombinant factor VIIa is an alternative in Glanzmann thrombasthenia. Storage pool disorders (dense or α-granule deficiency, such as gray platelet syndrome) are milder.

Acquired platelet dysfunction

  • Drugs: aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1, blocking thromboxane A2 for the platelet's lifespan (about 7–10 days); P2Y12 inhibitors (clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor) block ADP signalling; GpIIb/IIIa antagonists block aggregation; NSAIDs inhibit COX reversibly. SSRIs reduce platelet serotonin uptake.
  • Uremia: retained uremic toxins, excess nitric oxide and anemia impair platelet adhesion and GpIIb/IIIa activation. Platelet count and coagulation times are normal. Dialysis, correcting anemia (red cells push platelets toward the vessel wall), desmopressin for rapid effect and conjugated estrogens for longer effect all help. Transfused platelets become dysfunctional in the uremic milieu.
  • Myeloproliferative neoplasms, paraproteins (myeloma, Waldenström macroglobulinemia), cardiopulmonary bypass and severe liver disease.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation

DIC is not a disease but a syndrome secondary to a strong trigger that exposes blood to tissue factor or other procoagulants. Systemic thrombin generation overwhelms antithrombin and protein C, so microthrombi form in small vessels (organ ischemia) while platelets and factors are consumed and plasmin is activated (bleeding).

Trigger groupExamples and mechanism
SepsisEndotoxin and cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α) induce tissue factor on monocytes and endothelium and suppress thrombomodulin and protein C activation
ObstetricPlacental abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, retained dead fetus, severe preeclampsia/HELLP: placental tissue factor enters the circulation
MalignancyAcute promyelocytic leukemia (granule procoagulants and strong fibrinolysis); mucin-secreting adenocarcinomas (chronic, compensated DIC)
Tissue injuryMajor trauma, burns, brain injury (brain is rich in tissue factor), pancreatitis, crush injury
OtherSnake envenomation, severe transfusion reactions, heat stroke, large vascular malformations (Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon)

Acute DIC shows thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, very high D-dimer and schistocytes. Fibrinogen is an acute phase protein, so a "normal" level in a septic patient may already be falling; serial values matter more than a single one. Chronic DIC in cancer may have a near-normal PT and fibrinogen with mainly thrombosis (migratory thrombophlebitis, nonbacterial endocarditis).

DICLiver diseaseVitamin K deficiencyTTP
PlateletsLowLow (spleen)NormalVery low
PT / aPTTLong / longLong / normal or longLong first / later longNormal
FibrinogenLowLow (late)NormalNormal
Factor VIIILowNormal or highNormalNormal
Corrects with vitamin KNoNoYes—

In a sick patient with a long PT, factor VIII separates the causes: low in DIC (consumed), normal or raised in liver disease (made outside hepatocytes). Factor V is low in both, but normal in vitamin K deficiency because it is not vitamin K-dependent.

Step 2 CK asks what to give: treat the trigger, then platelets, plasma or cryoprecipitate only for bleeding or before procedures, guided by the platelet count, PT and fibrinogen.

sections.heading: Thrombophilia and the mechanisms of anticoagulant drugs
sections.html:
Virchow triad

Thrombosis needs one or more of: stasis (immobility, long travel, heart failure, venous compression by a gravid uterus), endothelial injury (surgery, trauma, catheters, vasculitis, smoking for arterial disease) and hypercoagulability (inherited or acquired). Venous clots are red, fibrin- and red cell-rich and form in low-flow valve pockets; arterial clots are platelet-rich and form on ruptured plaques. That is why anticoagulants are the mainstay for venous thromboembolism (VTE) and antiplatelet drugs for most arterial disease.

Natural anticoagulants

[[figure:s23a-fig61]]

Antithrombin is a serpin that inactivates thrombin and factor Xa (and IXa, XIa). Heparan sulfate on endothelium and heparin drugs accelerate it about a thousandfold. Protein C is activated when thrombin binds thrombomodulin on intact endothelium (enhanced by the endothelial protein C receptor). Activated protein C, with its cofactor protein S, cleaves and inactivates factors Va and VIIIa. Tissue factor pathway inhibitor blocks TF-VIIa-Xa. Proteins C and S are vitamin K-dependent; about 60% of protein S circulates bound to C4b-binding protein and only free protein S is active.

Inherited thrombophilias

ConditionMechanismDistinctive points
Factor V LeidenArg506Gln makes factor Va resistant to cleavage by activated protein CMost common inherited thrombophilia in people of European ancestry; heterozygotes have a modest increase in VTE risk
Prothrombin G20210AVariant in the 3′ untranslated region raises mRNA stability and plasma prothrombin levelsSecond most common; also detected only by genetic testing
Protein C deficiencyLess inactivation of Va and VIIIaWarfarin-induced skin necrosis; homozygous neonates develop purpura fulminans
Protein S deficiencyLoss of the cofactor for activated protein CFree protein S also falls in pregnancy, with estrogen, in liver disease and in inflammation
Antithrombin deficiencyLess inactivation of thrombin and XaHighest-risk single inherited defect; heparin resistance (heparin works through antithrombin)
Elevated factor VIII, hyperhomocysteinemia, dysfibrinogenemiaMore thrombin generation; endothelial toxicity; abnormal fibrinHomocysteine raises arterial and venous risk; folate, B6 and B12 status affect it

Inherited defects are mostly autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance: they raise the baseline risk, and a second factor (surgery, pregnancy, estrogen) usually precipitates the clot. Unusual sites (cerebral venous sinus, mesenteric veins) and clots at a young age raise suspicion.

Acquired hypercoagulable states

  • Antiphospholipid syndrome: antibodies directed at phospholipid-binding proteins, mainly β2-glycoprotein I. They cause venous and arterial thrombosis and pregnancy loss by activating endothelium, platelets, monocytes and complement. In vitro the same antibodies interfere with the phospholipid in clotting assays, so the aPTT is prolonged (lupus anticoagulant) and does not correct with mixing. Anticardiolipin antibodies can give a false-positive nontreponemal syphilis test. Diagnosis needs a clinical event plus persistent antibodies on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart.
  • Malignancy: tumor cells express tissue factor and other procoagulants (mucins activate selectins and platelets); add chemotherapy, catheters and immobility. Trousseau syndrome (migratory superficial thrombophlebitis) is linked to pancreatic, gastric and lung adenocarcinoma.
  • Estrogen (combined oral contraceptives, oral hormone therapy) and pregnancy: more hepatic synthesis of fibrinogen and factors II, VII, VIII and X, lower free protein S and acquired resistance to activated protein C. Pregnancy adds venous compression; risk peaks in the weeks after delivery. Transdermal estrogen carries less risk than oral.
  • Nephrotic syndrome: urinary loss of antithrombin plus higher hepatic synthesis of procoagulants; renal vein thrombosis, especially with membranous nephropathy.
  • Others: myeloproliferative neoplasms (JAK2: Budd-Chiari and splanchnic thrombosis), paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, inflammatory bowel disease, obesity, L-asparaginase (lowers antithrombin).

Anticoagulant pharmacology by mechanism

DrugMechanismNotes
Unfractionated heparinBinds antithrombin via a pentasaccharide; long chains bridge antithrombin to thrombin, so IIa and Xa are inhibitedIV; aPTT or anti-Xa monitoring; full reversal by protamine; HIT risk highest
Low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin)Antithrombin-mediated, mainly anti-Xa (chains too short to bridge thrombin)SC; renal clearance; anti-Xa level in pregnancy, obesity, renal impairment; protamine reverses only partly
FondaparinuxSynthetic pentasaccharide: antithrombin-mediated Xa inhibition onlyRenally cleared; no protamine reversal
Apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxabanDirect, antithrombin-independent factor Xa inhibitorsOral, fixed dose, no routine monitoring
DabigatranDirect thrombin inhibitor (oral)Mostly renal; idarucizumab is the specific reversal antibody
Argatroban, bivalirudinDirect thrombin inhibitors (IV)Used in HIT; argatroban is hepatically cleared
WarfarinInhibits VKORC1, so new II, VII, IX, X, C and S are not carboxylatedINR monitoring; many interactions (CYP2C9); teratogenic

A patient whose aPTT barely moves despite escalating heparin doses may have antithrombin deficiency (inherited, nephrotic syndrome, L-asparaginase, consumption) or very high factor VIII and fibrinogen from inflammation. An anti-Xa level separates true resistance from an aPTT artefact.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of transfusion reactions
sections.html:
Why reactions happen

A unit of blood carries foreign red cell antigens, plasma proteins and antibodies, leukocytes and their cytokines, and sometimes bacteria; it also adds volume, citrate and potassium. Each reaction is one of these components meeting the recipient's immune system or physiology. The timing of onset is the most useful first clue.

[[figure:s23a-fig63]]

Hemolytic reactions

Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction is almost always ABO incompatibility caused by a clerical or identification error. Group O, A and B people have naturally occurring IgM anti-A and/or anti-B (isohemagglutinins), formed in infancy against gut-flora carbohydrates that resemble A and B antigens. IgM fixes complement efficiently, so the membrane attack complex lyses donor red cells inside vessels within minutes. Free hemoglobin causes hemoglobinemia and hemoglobinuria and scavenges nitric oxide; anaphylatoxins and cytokines cause fever, chills, flank or back pain, pain at the infusion site, hypotension and DIC; acute kidney injury follows. Labs show a positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT), pink plasma, low haptoglobin, high LDH and indirect bilirubin. Severity scales with the volume transfused.

Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction occurs 3–14 days later in someone sensitized by an earlier pregnancy or transfusion whose antibody had fallen below detection at crossmatch. Re-exposure triggers an anamnestic IgG response, typically against Kidd (Jk), Rh (E, c), Kell or Duffy antigens. IgG-coated cells are removed by splenic macrophages (extravascular hemolysis): falling hemoglobin, mild jaundice, spherocytes, a positive DAT with IgG and a newly identified alloantibody. Kidd antibodies are known for fading quickly and then returning strongly. A delayed serologic reaction is the same new antibody without hemolysis.

Nonhemolytic reactions

ReactionMechanismKey featuresPrevention
Febrile non-hemolyticCytokines from donor leukocytes accumulated during storage; recipient antibodies to donor leukocytesFever and chills during or within hours; diagnosis of exclusionPrestorage leukoreduction
Urticarial (allergic)Recipient IgE against donor plasma proteins; mast cell degranulationHives and itching only, stable vital signsPremedication is not routinely effective
AnaphylacticRecipient anti-IgA (in IgA deficiency) or other plasma-protein antibodies react with donor proteinWithin minutes: hypotension, bronchospasm, angioedema, no feverWashed cellular products; plasma from IgA-deficient donors
TRALIDonor anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies activate recipient neutrophils primed in the lung (two-hit model)Hypoxemia and bilateral infiltrates within 6 h; fever, hypotension, transient leukopenia; normal filling pressuresPlasma from male or antibody-screened donors
TACOHydrostatic overload exceeding cardiac reserveDyspnea, hypertension, raised jugular venous pressure, high BNP within 12 h; responds to diureticsSlow rates, single units, assess fluid balance
SepticBacterial contamination, mostly skin floraHigh fever, rigors, hypotension during or soon after; platelets carry the highest riskDonor skin preparation, diversion pouch, bacterial testing, pathogen reduction
TA-GVHDViable donor T cells engraft in a host that cannot reject themFever, rash, diarrhea, liver injury and marrow aplasia 1–6 weeks later; mostly fatalIrradiation (or pathogen reduction) of cellular products
Post-transfusion purpuraAlloantibody, usually anti-HPA-1a, in a previously sensitized recipient destroys donor and own plateletsSevere thrombocytopenia about a week later, mostly in multiparous womenAntigen-negative products; treat with IVIG

Platelets are stored at room temperature (20–24 °C) with agitation, which keeps them functional but lets bacteria multiply; gram-positive skin flora (coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus) are the most frequent contaminants, while gram-negative organisms cause the most severe endotoxic shock. Refrigerated red cells favour cold-growing, iron-loving organisms such as Yersinia enterocolitica.

TA-GVHD needs a recipient who cannot recognize donor lymphocytes as foreign: profound cellular immunodeficiency (congenital T-cell defects, stem cell transplantation, Hodgkin lymphoma, purine analogues such as fludarabine), fetuses and some neonates, or a donor who is homozygous for an HLA haplotype the recipient shares (directed donation from a relative, HLA-matched platelets). Leukoreduction does not reliably prevent it.

Metabolic effects of large-volume transfusion

  • Hypocalcemia: citrate in stored products chelates ionized calcium. The liver normally clears citrate quickly; massive transfusion, hypothermia, shock and liver failure overwhelm this. Effects: perioral tingling, hypotension, reduced contractility, QT prolongation and impaired coagulation (calcium is factor IV). Hypomagnesemia also occurs.
  • Hyperkalemia: potassium leaks from stored red cells, increasing with storage age and after irradiation; dangerous with rapid infusion, in neonates and in renal failure. Later, hypokalemia may follow as transfused cells take potassium back.
  • Metabolic alkalosis after resuscitation, as citrate is metabolized to bicarbonate; acidosis during shock.
  • Hypothermia from cold products, which slows enzymatic coagulation and platelet function.
  • Dilutional coagulopathy: red cells contain almost no platelets or clotting factors.
  • Iron overload with chronic transfusion (each unit carries about 200–250 mg of iron).

Fever with a transfusion reaction points away from anaphylaxis and toward hemolysis, sepsis, TRALI or a febrile non-hemolytic reaction; hypertension points to TACO, hypotension to TRALI, sepsis, hemolysis or anaphylaxis.

sections.heading: Evaluating bleeding and managing inherited bleeding disorders
sections.html:
History first

The bleeding history predicts risk better than screening tests. Ask about bleeding after previous surgery, dental extraction, childbirth and circumcision; heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche (flooding, changing products every 1–2 hours, iron deficiency); spontaneous bruises larger than a coin on the trunk; joint swelling; family history; and drugs (aspirin, NSAIDs, P2Y12 inhibitors, anticoagulants, SSRIs, fish oil and other supplements). A structured bleeding assessment tool scores this. A patient who has had a tonsillectomy and several dental extractions without bleeding is unlikely to have a significant inherited disorder, whatever the aPTT.

Initial tests: complete blood count with smear, PT/INR, aPTT and fibrinogen. A suggestive history with normal results warrants von Willebrand testing (vWF antigen, activity, factor VIII), then platelet function testing and, if those are normal, factor XIII and fibrinolytic studies.

An isolated long aPTT in a person with no bleeding history, found before elective surgery, is most often factor XII deficiency or a lupus anticoagulant; neither causes surgical bleeding, and neither should be treated with plasma. Mixing study and factor assays sort it out without delaying surgery for long.

Hemophilia: principles of care

  • Treat first, image later. For any suspected significant bleed (joint, muscle, head injury, neck or throat swelling), give factor concentrate immediately, before imaging or other testing. Head trauma in severe hemophilia warrants factor replacement even when the child looks well.
  • Targets: life-threatening bleeds (intracranial, airway, iliopsoas) need correction to near-normal activity and maintenance for days; joint bleeds need lower peaks for a shorter time. Hemarthrosis also gets rest, ice, compression, elevation and physiotherapy after the bleed. Arthrocentesis is rarely needed.
  • Prophylaxis is standard for severe hemophilia, started in early childhood to prevent arthropathy: regular factor concentrate (standard or extended half-life) or, in hemophilia A, a subcutaneous nonfactor agent.
  • Avoid intramuscular injections (give vaccines subcutaneously or intramuscularly with a fine needle and pressure, per local protocol), aspirin and NSAIDs. Hepatitis B vaccination is recommended.
  • Mild hemophilia A: desmopressin (IV or intranasal) raises factor VIII two- to fourfold for minor procedures if a test dose shows a response. Watch for hyponatremia (fluid restriction) and tachyphylaxis after several doses; avoid in young children at seizure risk. Desmopressin is not useful in hemophilia B or severe A.
  • Tranexamic acid for oral, nasal and menstrual bleeding (not for hematuria, where it can cause obstructing clots).

Inhibitors: suspect when bleeding responds poorly to the usual factor dose or recovery of factor activity after infusion is low. Measure with the Bethesda assay. Low-titer inhibitors (under 5 Bethesda units) can sometimes be overwhelmed with higher factor doses; high-titer inhibitors need bypassing agents (recombinant factor VIIa or activated prothrombin complex concentrate). Long-term options include immune tolerance induction and nonfactor prophylaxis. Patients on nonfactor prophylaxis need specialist guidance before receiving activated PCC for breakthrough bleeds.

Acquired hemophilia A: management

Suspect acquired hemophilia in an older adult or postpartum woman with new extensive bruising or muscle bleeding and an isolated long aPTT. Do not wait for confirmation to involve hematology. Hemostasis uses bypassing agents (recombinant VIIa or activated PCC) or recombinant porcine factor VIII; human factor VIII and desmopressin are usually ineffective against a strong inhibitor. Eradicate the antibody with glucocorticoids, alone or with cyclophosphamide or rituximab, and look for an underlying cause (autoimmune disease, cancer, drugs). Avoid invasive procedures and intramuscular injections. Relapse can occur after remission, so factor VIII is monitored.

von Willebrand disease: management

  • Type 1: desmopressin after a documented test response; antifibrinolytics for mucosal bleeding; vWF-containing concentrate for major surgery or if desmopressin fails.
  • Type 2B: desmopressin may cause thrombocytopenia; use vWF concentrate. Type 3 and most other type 2: vWF concentrate.
  • Heavy menstrual bleeding: hormonal therapy (combined hormonal contraceptives or levonorgestrel intrauterine system) or tranexamic acid; treat iron deficiency.
  • Pregnancy: vWF and factor VIII rise in the third trimester in type 1 disease, but they fall quickly after delivery, so delayed postpartum hemorrhage is a risk. Check levels in the third trimester and plan neuraxial anesthesia and delivery with hematology.

Platelet function disorders and factor XIII deficiency

Bernard-Soulier syndrome and Glanzmann thrombasthenia: local pressure, antifibrinolytics and hormonal control of menses for minor bleeding; platelet transfusion for major bleeding or surgery (leukoreduced, HLA-matched where possible to limit alloimmunization). Recombinant factor VIIa is used in Glanzmann thrombasthenia when platelets are ineffective or antibodies have formed. Factor XIII deficiency: regular factor XIII concentrate prophylaxis prevents intracranial hemorrhage and pregnancy loss; cryoprecipitate if concentrate is unavailable.

Before surgery in a patient with a known bleeding disorder, the plan names the product, the target level, the timing and the duration, and is arranged with hematology and the blood bank in advance.

sections.heading: Acquired coagulopathies: vitamin K, liver disease, DIC and uremia
sections.html:
Vitamin K deficiency

Newborn prophylaxis. Every newborn should receive a single intramuscular dose of vitamin K (phytonadione) soon after birth. Oral regimens protect less well against late vitamin K deficiency bleeding, which typically affects exclusively breastfed infants at 2–12 weeks and often presents as intracranial hemorrhage. When parents decline the injection, explore the reason (fear of pain, misinformation linking it to childhood cancer, which has not been supported), explain the risk of late bleeding, and document the informed refusal; oral regimens are a less effective fallback. Teach warning signs (bleeding, bruising, poor feeding, lethargy, vomiting, a bulging fontanelle).

An infant with vitamin K deficiency bleeding has a markedly prolonged PT (and often aPTT) with a normal platelet count. Give vitamin K parenterally without waiting for the factor assays; add fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate for serious bleeding. Infants with unexplained late bleeding need evaluation for cholestasis (biliary atresia, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, cystic fibrosis).

Adults: think of vitamin K deficiency in malnourished, ICU or postoperative patients on broad-spectrum antibiotics with poor oral intake, and in fat malabsorption (cholestatic liver disease, celiac disease, cystic fibrosis, short bowel, bariatric surgery). The PT is prolonged out of proportion to the aPTT, platelets and fibrinogen are normal, and vitamin K corrects the PT within about a day. Give it IV (slow infusion) when the PT must correct quickly, or orally otherwise; subcutaneous absorption is unreliable. For active serious bleeding add four-factor PCC or plasma.

Coagulopathy of liver disease

  • INR and platelet count are poor guides to bleeding risk. Most bleeding in cirrhosis is from portal hypertension, not from the INR.
  • Do not give prophylactic plasma or platelets to "correct" an INR or platelet count before low-risk procedures such as paracentesis, thoracentesis or endoscopy. Plasma adds volume, can raise portal pressure, carries TACO and TRALI risk and rarely normalizes the INR.
  • For high-risk procedures or active non-variceal bleeding, decisions are individualized; viscoelastic testing (TEG or ROTEM) helps target products. Low fibrinogen is replaced with cryoprecipitate.
  • A trial of vitamin K is reasonable when malnutrition or cholestasis may contribute.
  • Cirrhosis does not protect against VTE; pharmacologic prophylaxis is indicated for hospitalized patients without active bleeding, even with a raised INR.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation: management

The only definitive treatment is removing the trigger: antibiotics and source control in sepsis, delivery of the fetus and placenta in obstetric DIC, all-trans retinoic acid in acute promyelocytic leukemia. Blood products treat bleeding, not numbers.

AbnormalityGiveWhen
Platelets lowPlatelet transfusionActive bleeding or procedure with platelets below about 50,000/mm3; nonbleeding patients only at very low counts (about 10,000–20,000/mm3)
PT and aPTT prolongedFresh frozen plasmaActive bleeding or invasive procedure
Fibrinogen lowCryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrateBleeding with fibrinogen below about 150 mg/dL (1.5 g/L) despite plasma
Thrombosis predominatesHeparin (therapeutic or prophylactic)Purpura fulminans, large-vessel thrombosis, chronic DIC of cancer, retained dead fetus

Antifibrinolytic drugs are generally avoided in DIC because they can worsen microvascular thrombosis; exceptions are specialist decisions in hyperfibrinolytic states. Hospitalized patients with DIC who are not bleeding generally receive standard VTE prophylaxis.

Postpartum hemorrhage with DIC consumes fibrinogen early. A fibrinogen below about 200 mg/dL during obstetric bleeding predicts progression to severe hemorrhage; replacement (cryoprecipitate or concentrate) is started early rather than after many units of red cells.

Uremic bleeding

Patients with advanced kidney disease bleed from mucosa, puncture sites and the gastrointestinal tract despite normal platelet counts and coagulation times. For active bleeding or before an urgent procedure (kidney biopsy, line placement), give desmopressin, which acts within about an hour and lasts several hours; repeated doses lose effect. Conjugated estrogens act over days and last about 2 weeks, which suits recurrent bleeding (for example from angiodysplasia). Dialysis and correcting anemia (erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, transfusion toward a hematocrit around 30%) improve platelet function. Cryoprecipitate is a second-line option. Platelet transfusion has a limited role because transfused platelets acquire the same defect.

Scurvy and other vascular bleeding

Older adults living alone, people with alcohol use disorder, severe psychiatric illness, restrictive diets or malabsorption can develop vitamin C deficiency. Look for perifollicular hemorrhages on the legs, corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums, poor wound healing, hemarthrosis or muscle hematomas, fatigue and iron deficiency anemia. Coagulation tests and platelets are normal. A low plasma ascorbate level supports the diagnosis, but treatment with oral vitamin C should start on clinical suspicion; bleeding stops within days. Nutritional counselling and screening for coexisting deficiencies (folate, iron, vitamin D) complete care.

Step 1 asks why a test is abnormal (factor VII half-life, factor VIII from endothelium); Step 2 CK asks whether to act on it (do not correct an INR in cirrhosis before paracentesis; give vitamin K to the newborn whose parents declined it).
