sections.heading: Diagnosing deep vein thrombosis
sections.html:
Clinical picture

Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the leg causes unilateral swelling, pain, warmth and dilated superficial veins, but the examination alone is unreliable: many swollen legs are cellulitis, ruptured Baker cyst, muscle injury, lymphedema or venous insufficiency, and many DVTs are clinically silent. Proximal DVT (popliteal vein and above) carries most of the risk of pulmonary embolism (PE). Phlegmasia cerulea dolens (massive iliofemoral thrombosis with a cyanotic, painful leg and threatened arterial supply) is an emergency that needs anticoagulation and urgent vascular consultation for thrombus removal.

Pretest probability

Diagnosis starts by estimating pretest probability, most often with the Wells score for DVT. One point each for: active cancer; paralysis, paresis or recent plaster cast of the leg; bedridden 3 days or more or major surgery within 12 weeks; localized tenderness along the deep veins; entire leg swollen; calf swelling more than 3 cm compared with the other side; pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg; collateral superficial (non-varicose) veins; previously documented DVT. Two points are subtracted if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely. A score of 2 or more is "DVT likely"; 1 or less is "DVT unlikely".

[[figure:s23a-fig62]]

The testing pathway

  • DVT unlikely: a high-sensitivity D-dimer. A negative result excludes DVT without imaging. A positive result leads to compression ultrasonography.
  • DVT likely: go straight to compression ultrasonography. A D-dimer cannot exclude DVT when pretest probability is high, and a positive one adds nothing. If the first scan is limited to the proximal veins and is negative, a D-dimer or repeat ultrasound in about a week is needed; a single negative whole-leg scan is enough.
  • If ultrasound will be delayed and probability is high, start anticoagulation while waiting, unless bleeding risk is high.

Compression ultrasonography is the first-line imaging test: a vein that does not collapse under probe pressure contains thrombus. Contrast venography, once the reference standard, is now rarely used. CT or MR venography is reserved for suspected pelvic or IVC thrombosis.

D-dimer: strengths and limits

D-dimer is sensitive but not specific. It is raised after surgery or trauma, in cancer, infection, pregnancy, older age, hospitalization, DIC and liver disease. In those settings a positive result is expected and testing often adds little; a negative result remains useful when probability is low. For suspected PE, an age-adjusted cutoff (age × 10 µg/L FEU in patients over 50) increases specificity in older adults without losing safety. A D-dimer should not be ordered for patients in whom it will not change management, or for screening asymptomatic people.

Never order a D-dimer to "rule out" DVT in a high-probability patient (for example, active cancer, a whole leg swollen and calf asymmetry). Go to ultrasound. Conversely, imaging a low-probability patient without a D-dimer exposes them to false-positive findings.

Special situations

  • Pregnancy: DVT is more often left-sided and iliofemoral. Use compression ultrasonography (including the iliac veins with Doppler if suspected); D-dimer rises through normal pregnancy. Treat with low-molecular-weight heparin.
  • Isolated distal (calf) DVT: if symptoms are mild and risk factors for extension are absent, serial ultrasound over 2 weeks is an alternative to anticoagulation; severe symptoms or risk factors (cancer, positive D-dimer, extensive clot near the popliteal vein, inpatient) favour anticoagulation.
  • Upper-extremity DVT: usually from central venous catheters, pacemaker leads or cancer; effort thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter syndrome) occurs with thoracic outlet compression in young athletes. Diagnosed by ultrasound and treated with anticoagulation.
  • Superficial thrombophlebitis: a tender cord in a superficial vein. Long segments (5 cm or more) or clots close to the saphenofemoral junction need ultrasound and usually anticoagulation (prophylactic-dose fondaparinux for long segments, therapeutic dosing when close to the junction) because of extension into the deep system. Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis warrants evaluation for cancer.
  • Suspected PE: the same logic applies with PE-specific tools (Wells for PE, PERC rule in low-risk patients, CT pulmonary angiography; ventilation-perfusion scan when contrast is contraindicated). Leg ultrasound showing a DVT in a patient with suspected PE confirms the need for anticoagulation.

Prevention in hospitalized patients

Assess VTE risk on admission and after surgery. Pharmacologic prophylaxis (LMWH, unfractionated heparin, fondaparinux or a DOAC after hip or knee arthroplasty) is given to at-risk patients without high bleeding risk; mechanical prophylaxis (intermittent pneumatic compression) is used when bleeding risk is high. Early mobilization helps everyone.

sections.heading: Treating VTE: drug choice, duration and thrombophilia testing
sections.html:
Three phases

VTE treatment has an initial phase (first days), a primary phase (usually 3 months) and an optional extended phase with no planned stop date. The decision at 3 months, whether to stop or continue, depends on why the clot happened and on bleeding risk.

Choosing the anticoagulant

SituationPreferred approachWhy
Most patients with DVT or PEDirect oral anticoagulant (apixaban or rivaroxaban started directly; dabigatran or edoxaban after 5 days of parenteral heparin)As effective as warfarin with less major bleeding, no INR monitoring
PregnancyLow-molecular-weight heparinDoes not cross the placenta; warfarin is teratogenic; DOACs lack safety data and cross the placenta
Cancer-associated VTEApixaban, rivaroxaban or edoxaban, or LMWHDOACs at least as effective as LMWH; caution in luminal GI or genitourinary cancers (more bleeding with some DOACs), drug interactions, thrombocytopenia
Antiphospholipid syndrome (especially triple-positive or arterial events)Warfarin (INR 2–3), after initial heparinDOACs had more arterial events in APS trials
Mechanical heart valveWarfarin (DOACs contraindicated)Dabigatran caused more valve thrombosis and bleeding than warfarin
Severe renal impairmentUnfractionated heparin initially, then warfarin (apixaban has some use in dialysis)Renal clearance of LMWH, fondaparinux, dabigatran
Heparin-induced thrombocytopeniaNon-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, DOAC)Heparin exposure perpetuates platelet activation
Hemodynamically unstable PE or need for possible thrombolysis/procedureUnfractionated heparin infusionShort half-life, fully reversible

When warfarin is chosen, overlap it with heparin for at least 5 days and until the INR is 2 or higher for 24 hours, because warfarin first lowers protein C (short half-life) and the antithrombotic effect lags. Breastfeeding mothers can take warfarin or heparins.

How long to treat

Type of VTEDuration
Provoked by a major transient risk factor (surgery, major trauma, immobilization with hospitalization)3 months, then stop
Provoked by a minor transient factor (estrogen, pregnancy, long travel, minor injury)Usually 3 months; individualize (risk of recurrence is intermediate)
Unprovoked proximal DVT or PE, or persistent risk factorExtended anticoagulation with no planned stop date if bleeding risk is not high; reassess at least yearly. Reduced-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban can be used in the extended phase
Active cancerExtended, as long as the cancer or its treatment is active
Second unprovoked VTEExtended
Isolated distal DVT, provoked3 months (or serial imaging instead, see above)

Aspirin reduces recurrence after unprovoked VTE but much less than an anticoagulant; it is a fallback only for patients who decline or cannot take anticoagulation. An IVC filter is indicated only for acute proximal DVT or PE when anticoagulation is contraindicated (for example, active bleeding); retrieve it and start anticoagulation once safe.

Thrombophilia testing: when it helps

Testing for inherited thrombophilia rarely changes management and is not indicated after VTE provoked by a major transient risk factor, in patients who will be treated indefinitely anyway, or in unselected relatives. Reasons to consider testing include:

  • Suspected antiphospholipid syndrome (unprovoked VTE in a young patient, arterial thrombosis at a young age, thrombosis at an unusual site, recurrent pregnancy loss, unexplained prolonged aPTT, thrombocytopenia with thrombosis): a positive result changes drug choice (warfarin rather than a DOAC).
  • A woman with a first-degree relative with VTE and a known familial thrombophilia who is considering estrogen therapy or pregnancy, where a result would change advice or prophylaxis.
  • Thrombosis at unusual sites (cerebral venous sinus, splanchnic veins), which also calls for tests for myeloproliferative neoplasm (JAK2) and paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.

Timing matters. Protein C, protein S and antithrombin levels fall during acute thrombosis, warfarin lowers protein C and S, heparin lowers antithrombin and DOACs and heparin interfere with lupus anticoagulant assays. Genetic tests (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A) are unaffected. Testing functional levels on the day of diagnosis produces false positives.

Prevention in high-risk groups

  • Pregnancy: prophylactic LMWH antepartum and for 6 weeks postpartum for women with a prior unprovoked or estrogen-associated VTE; postpartum prophylaxis for selected thrombophilias with family history. Women with obstetric APS receive low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic heparin.
  • Estrogen: combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated after VTE and in known high-risk thrombophilia and APS; progestin-only methods (levonorgestrel IUD, implant) or copper IUD are alternatives. Transdermal is preferred to oral estrogen for menopausal therapy when appropriate.
  • Cancer: outpatients starting chemotherapy who are at high risk on a validated score may be offered primary prophylaxis.

Factor V Leiden explains a clot (Step 1 mechanism) but rarely changes the anticoagulation plan (Step 2 CK decision): duration depends on whether the event was provoked, not on the variant.

furtherReading.label: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf): Anticoagulant Therapy In Pregnancy

sections.heading: Blood products: indications and managing transfusion reactions
sections.html:
Red blood cells

A restrictive strategy is standard for hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults: transfuse at a hemoglobin below 7 g/dL (including most ICU patients and those with GI bleeding). Higher thresholds (about 7.5–8 g/dL) are used in cardiac or orthopedic surgery and preexisting cardiovascular disease. Thresholds do not apply to active hemorrhage, where volume of blood lost and hemodynamics drive transfusion, or to symptomatic anemia (angina, dyspnea at rest). Give one unit at a time in stable patients and reassess; one unit raises hemoglobin by about 1 g/dL in an average adult. Iron deficiency and vitamin deficiencies are treated with replacement, not transfusion, unless symptoms are severe.

Platelets

SituationUsual threshold to transfuse
Prophylaxis in hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia (chemotherapy, leukemia, marrow failure) without bleedingBelow 10,000/mm3
Central venous catheter placementBelow 20,000/mm3
Lumbar puncture, major non-neuraxial surgery, active bleedingBelow 50,000/mm3
Neurosurgery, intracranial or ocular bleedingBelow about 100,000/mm3

One apheresis unit raises the count by roughly 30,000/mm3 in an adult. A poor increment at 1 hour after repeated transfusions suggests alloimmunization (anti-HLA antibodies; use HLA-matched or crossmatched platelets), while a good 1-hour increment that disappears by 24 hours suggests consumption (fever, sepsis, splenomegaly, DIC). Platelets are generally avoided in TTP and HIT unless bleeding is life-threatening, and are not effective in immune thrombocytopenia except as a temporizing measure with IVIG and glucocorticoids for critical bleeding.

Plasma and cryoprecipitate

  • Fresh frozen plasma contains all coagulation factors. Indications: bleeding (or urgent procedure) with multiple factor deficiencies, as in massive transfusion, DIC or liver disease; therapeutic plasma exchange for TTP; replacement of single factors with no concentrate available. Warfarin reversal for major bleeding uses four-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K in preference to plasma. Plasma is not a volume expander and does not normalize a mildly raised INR.
  • Cryoprecipitate is the cold-insoluble fraction of plasma and is rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII and fibronectin. Main use: replacing fibrinogen in bleeding with fibrinogen below about 150 mg/dL (obstetric hemorrhage targets higher), and as a fallback for factor XIII deficiency, vWD and uremic bleeding when specific products are unavailable.

Modified products

ModificationWhat it preventsWho needs it
LeukoreductionFebrile non-hemolytic reactions, HLA alloimmunization, CMV transmissionNow routine for most products
IrradiationTA-GVHDStem cell transplant recipients, congenital T-cell immunodeficiency, Hodgkin lymphoma, purine analogue or anti-T-cell therapy, intrauterine and neonatal exchange transfusion, products from blood relatives, HLA-matched platelets
WashingReactions to plasma proteins; excess potassiumRecurrent severe allergic reactions, anaphylaxis with anti-IgA when IgA-deficient products are unavailable
CMV-safe (seronegative or leukoreduced)CMV infectionCMV-seronegative transplant recipients, pregnant women, premature infants

What to do when a reaction starts

For any reaction other than isolated mild hives: stop the transfusion, keep the IV line open with normal saline, check vital signs, recheck the patient's identity against the unit label, and notify the blood bank. Return the bag and tubing and send a new patient sample for repeat ABO/Rh typing, DAT and hemolysis tests (plasma free hemoglobin, haptoglobin, LDH, bilirubin, urinalysis).

ReactionManagement
Acute hemolyticStop; aggressive IV fluids to maintain urine output; treat hypotension and DIC; report as a sentinel safety event
Febrile non-hemolyticStop; exclude hemolysis and sepsis; antipyretic; usually do not restart the same unit
Mild urticarialPause; antihistamine; resume the same unit slowly once hives resolve if there are no other symptoms
AnaphylaxisStop; IM epinephrine, airway, fluids; measure IgA and anti-IgA; future washed or IgA-deficient products
TRALIStop; oxygen and ventilatory support; avoid diuretics; notify blood bank so the donor can be investigated
TACOStop or slow; sit upright, oxygen, IV loop diuretic
SepticStop; blood cultures from the patient and the unit; broad-spectrum antibiotics; resuscitation; quarantine co-components from the same donation
Delayed hemolyticUsually supportive; identify the antibody and give antigen-negative units in the future; give the patient an antibody card

Fever during a transfusion is never assumed to be febrile non-hemolytic at the bedside. Stop the transfusion first; the diagnosis is made only after hemolysis and bacterial contamination are excluded.

Consent and alternatives

Discuss benefits, risks (including rare infections and reactions) and alternatives before nonemergency transfusion. Patients who decline blood products (for example, many Jehovah's Witnesses) can accept individualized alternatives: iron, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, cell salvage, antifibrinolytics and, for some, fractions such as albumin or factor concentrates. Patient blood management (treating preoperative anemia, minimizing phlebotomy, restrictive thresholds) reduces transfusion need.

furtherReading.label: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf): Noninfectious Complications of Blood Transfusion

sections.heading: Massive transfusion and hemostatic resuscitation
sections.html:
Definitions and activation

Massive transfusion is commonly defined as replacement of a patient's blood volume within 24 hours (about 10 units of red cells in an adult) or rapid transfusion such as 3–4 units within an hour. Because these definitions are retrospective, hospitals use a massive transfusion protocol activated on clinical grounds. In trauma, a simple score (penetrating mechanism, systolic pressure 90 mm Hg or less, heart rate 120/min or more, positive FAST) with 2 or more criteria predicts the need. Similar protocols serve obstetric hemorrhage, ruptured aneurysm and major GI bleeding.

Damage control resuscitation

  • Stop the bleeding: direct pressure, tourniquets, pelvic binder, then surgery, angiographic embolization or endoscopy. Products buy time; they do not replace hemorrhage control.
  • Limit crystalloid. Large volumes dilute clotting factors, worsen acidosis and hypothermia and cause edema. Start blood products early.
  • Balanced ratio: give plasma, platelets and red cells in a ratio close to 1:1:1 (whole blood, where available, provides the same). A randomized trial of 1:1:1 versus 1:1:2 showed no difference in overall mortality but better hemostasis and fewer early deaths from exsanguination with 1:1:1.
  • Uncrossmatched group O red cells (Rh-negative for girls and women of childbearing potential) and group AB (or low-titer group A) plasma until type-specific products are available.
  • Permissive hypotension: a systolic pressure around 80–90 mm Hg until bleeding is controlled in penetrating torso trauma; not in traumatic brain injury, where cerebral perfusion matters.
  • Tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury (a loading dose then an infusion) reduces death from bleeding; given late it gives no benefit and may harm. It is also used in postpartum hemorrhage.
  • Goal-directed therapy once results return: viscoelastic testing (TEG or ROTEM) or laboratory values guide extra cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen), platelets and plasma.

The lethal triad and its fourth corner

Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy reinforce each other: cold slows coagulation enzymes and platelets, acidosis reduces factor activity, and bleeding from coagulopathy deepens shock and acidosis. Hypocalcemia is now considered a fourth corner, because ionized calcium is a cofactor for several coagulation steps and supports vascular tone and contractility.

ComplicationCausePrevention and treatment
HypocalcemiaCitrate anticoagulant chelates ionized calcium faster than the liver can metabolize it, worse with shock, hypothermia or liver diseaseMeasure ionized calcium often; give IV calcium chloride (central line) or calcium gluconate
HyperkalemiaPotassium leak from stored or irradiated red cellsFresher units for neonates; monitor; standard hyperkalemia treatment (calcium, insulin with glucose)
HypothermiaRefrigerated products, exposure, cold fluidsFluid and blood warmers, warm room, forced-air blankets
Dilutional coagulopathy and thrombocytopeniaRed cells and crystalloid without factors or plateletsBalanced ratios, fibrinogen replacement, platelets
Acidosis, later alkalosisShock and lactate; later citrate converted to bicarbonateRestore perfusion; routine bicarbonate is not recommended
TACO, TRALIVolume and donor antibodiesReassess need as bleeding slows; stop the protocol promptly

Special populations

  • Postpartum hemorrhage: fibrinogen falls early and predicts severity; give uterotonics, tranexamic acid, early cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate, and definitive procedures.
  • Anticoagulated patients: reverse warfarin with four-factor PCC and IV vitamin K, dabigatran with idarucizumab, heparin with protamine; factor Xa inhibitors are commonly managed with PCC or a specific reversal agent where available.
  • Older adults: may not mount tachycardia (beta-blockers, pacemakers) and tolerate both hypotension and volume overload poorly; lactate and base deficit help.
  • Children: products are given in mL/kg; hypothermia and hyperkalemia develop faster.

Stopping the protocol

Deactivate the protocol once surgical or radiologic control is achieved and the patient is stabilizing; continuing ratio-based products after bleeding stops causes overload and waste. Notify the blood bank, then switch to targeted, laboratory-guided transfusion. Document products given, and watch for delayed complications: TRALI, TACO, abdominal compartment syndrome, VTE (start prophylaxis once bleeding is controlled, usually within 24–48 hours) and delayed hemolytic reactions from emergency-release units.

In a bleeding trauma patient who becomes hypotensive and develops a prolonged QT or poor response to vasopressors after many units, check the ionized calcium before reaching for more products or pressors.

sections.heading: Mechanical and microangiopathic red-cell destruction
sections.html:
Fragmentation hemolysis is red-cell destruction caused by physical force rather than by antibody, complement or an intrinsic membrane or enzyme defect. Cells are cut, torn or heat-damaged inside the circulation, so the hemolysis is predominantly intravascular and the direct antiglobulin test (DAT) is negative. Two broad settings produce it: macrovascular shear (abnormal heart valves, ventricular assist devices, repetitive external impact) and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA), in which cells are sliced by fibrin or platelet thrombi in small vessels.

How a fragment forms

A normal red cell survives about 120 days because its spectrin-actin skeleton lets it deform and recover. When a cell is forced across a fibrin strand or through a high-velocity jet, part of the membrane is pinched off. The two edges reseal, leaving a smaller cell with a straight edge or sharp angles. Each fragment has lost surface area relative to volume, so it is less deformable and is soon removed by the spleen, while some cells rupture outright and release hemoglobin into plasma.

[[figure:s23a-fig70]]

On the smear, schistocytes include helmet cells, triangular fragments and keratocytes (horn cells), often with microspherocytes. A few fragments are seen in healthy people; laboratories generally regard more than about 1% of red cells as meaningful when the clinical picture fits. Severe thrombocytopenia alongside schistocytes points to a thrombotic microangiopathy; a normal platelet count with fragments points to a valve, device or external source.

Laboratory signature of intravascular hemolysis

  • Raised LDH and unconjugated bilirubin; reticulocytosis if the marrow is healthy.
  • Haptoglobin falls because it binds free hemoglobin dimers and the complex is cleared by macrophages (CD163). Hemopexin, which binds free heme, falls as well.
  • Hemoglobinemia (pink plasma) and hemoglobinuria: the dipstick is positive for blood but microscopy shows few or no red cells.
  • Hemosiderinuria appears days later as tubular cells that absorbed filtered hemoglobin are shed. Chronic urinary iron loss can produce iron deficiency, a classic late finding with leaking prosthetic valves.

Macrovascular causes

Prosthetic heart valves. Mild subclinical hemolysis is common with mechanical valves; clinically important hemolysis is most often caused by a paravalvular leak, where a narrow regurgitant jet produces very high shear. Bioprosthetic valves cause it less often, mainly when degenerated. Severe aortic stenosis can cause similar fragmentation. Left ventricular assist devices cause low-grade hemolysis; a sudden rise in LDH, plasma free hemoglobin and dark urine suggests pump thrombosis. High shear also unfolds von Willebrand factor so that ADAMTS13 cleaves its largest multimers, giving an acquired von Willebrand syndrome that contributes to mucosal bleeding with these devices and with severe aortic stenosis.

Exertional (march) hemoglobinuria follows repeated impact on the soles or palms, as in long-distance running on hard surfaces, marching or hand drumming. Cells are crushed in superficial capillaries; hemoglobinuria appears soon after exertion and clears within hours. Schistocytes are scant, CK is normal (distinguishing it from rhabdomyolysis), and cushioned footwear or softer surfaces prevent it.

Thermal injury. In extensive burns, red cells heated above roughly 49 °C have denatured spectrin; they bud off fragments and become microspherocytes, producing acute hemolysis in the first day or two.

Microangiopathic causes

DisorderCore mechanismDistinguishing features
Immune TTPAutoantibody inhibits ADAMTS13, so ultra-large vWF multimers persist and capture platelets via GPIbPlatelets often below 30,000/mm3; ADAMTS13 activity below 10%; PT, aPTT and fibrinogen normal; kidney injury usually mild
Congenital TTPBiallelic ADAMTS13 mutationsNeonatal or childhood onset, or first episode in pregnancy; no inhibitor
STEC-HUSShiga toxin binds Gb3 on glomerular endothelium and removes an adenine from 28S rRNA, halting protein synthesisChildren; bloody diarrhea days before; prominent acute kidney injury
Complement-mediated (atypical) HUSLoss of regulation of the alternative pathway (factor H, factor I, MCP/CD46 variants, factor H antibodies, C3 or factor B gain of function)No STEC; ADAMTS13 not severely low; may follow infection or pregnancy; C3 may be low
DICTissue factor-driven thrombin generation consumes factors and platelets; secondary fibrinolysisProlonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer
HELLP, malignant hypertensionEndothelial injury (placental factors; fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles)Pregnancy over 20 weeks or postpartum with raised aminotransferases; markedly raised BP with retinopathy and kidney injury

Normal coagulation times with schistocytes and thrombocytopenia argue for a platelet-driven microangiopathy (TTP, HUS); prolonged times and low fibrinogen argue for DIC.

Pharmacology by mechanism

Caplacizumab is a humanized single-domain antibody fragment against the A1 domain of von Willebrand factor; it blocks vWF binding to platelet GPIb and so stops new microthrombi, at the cost of bleeding risk. Rituximab (anti-CD20) depletes the B cells that make anti-ADAMTS13 antibody and lowers relapse. Plasma exchange both removes the inhibitor and supplies ADAMTS13. Eculizumab and ravulizumab bind C5 and prevent formation of C5a and the membrane attack complex; because terminal complement is needed to kill Neisseria, meningococcal vaccination is required before use.

Antibiotics in STEC enteritis can increase Shiga toxin release and are avoided; this is a mechanism question (phage-encoded toxin induction and bacterial lysis) as well as a management one.

Step 2 CK asks you to act on these mechanisms: treat suspected TTP before ADAMTS13 returns, keep platelets for life-threatening bleeding, and vaccinate before complement blockade.

sections.heading: Splenic structure, filtering and immune function
sections.html:
The spleen is the body's largest secondary lymphoid organ and its main blood filter. It lies in the left upper quadrant under ribs 9 to 11, receives about 5% of cardiac output, and holds a reserve of platelets and monocytes. Understanding its two compartments explains every consequence of losing it.

Development and anatomy

  • The spleen develops from mesenchyme in the dorsal mesogastrium (mesoderm), yet it is supplied by the splenic artery, a branch of the celiac trunk (the foregut artery). Failure of mesenchymal buds to fuse leaves accessory spleens, most often near the hilum or in the gastrosplenic ligament or near the pancreatic tail.
  • The gastrosplenic ligament carries the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels. The splenorenal ligament carries the splenic artery and vein and the tail of the pancreas, which can be injured during splenectomy and present as a pancreatic leak.
  • The splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein, so portal hypertension congests the spleen.
  • Diaphragmatic irritation by blood from a splenic injury can refer pain to the left shoulder through the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5).
[[figure:s23a-fig71]]

White pulp: immune surveillance

Arterial branches are wrapped by the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS), rich in T cells. Next to it sit follicles of B cells, which form germinal centers after antigen exposure. Surrounding both is the marginal zone, where blood slows and is sampled by specialized macrophages and marginal-zone B cells. These B cells mount rapid, largely T-cell-independent IgM responses to polysaccharide capsules, and marginal-zone macrophages clear antibody- and complement-coated bacteria. This is why the spleen is the key defense against bloodstream encapsulated organisms.

Red pulp: filtration

Most arterial blood empties into the splenic cords (an open circulation) and must re-enter the venous sinuses through narrow slits between elongated endothelial cells. A healthy discocyte folds and passes; a rigid, old or antibody-coated cell is trapped and eaten.

FunctionWhat happensWhat you see after splenectomy or hyposplenism
CullingMacrophages engulf whole senescent or damaged red cellsMore target cells and irregular forms survive
PittingInclusions are removed and the cell returns to circulationHowell-Jolly bodies (DNA remnants), Pappenheimer bodies (iron granules), Heinz bodies
Immune clearanceOpsonized and encapsulated bacteria removed; IgM to polysaccharidesRisk of overwhelming sepsis with Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae type b
ReservoirAbout one third of platelets pooledReactive thrombocytosis and leukocytosis after splenectomy

Howell-Jolly bodies on a smear are the bedside marker of absent splenic function. Their absence after splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenia suggests a functioning accessory spleen.

Causes of asplenia and hyposplenism

  • Surgical: trauma, immune thrombocytopenia or hereditary spherocytosis, hematologic cancer.
  • Functional: sickle cell anemia, where repeated sickling and infarction cause functional asplenia in infancy and a small fibrotic spleen (autosplenectomy) by later childhood; celiac disease; alcohol-related liver disease; systemic lupus erythematosus; amyloidosis; graft-versus-host disease; splenic irradiation.
  • Congenital: isolated congenital asplenia and heterotaxy syndromes (asplenia with right isomerism and complex heart disease).

Organisms that exploit asplenia

Encapsulated bacteria head the list, with S pneumoniae the most common cause of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection. Capnocytophaga canimorsus after dog bites, and intraerythrocytic parasites (Babesia, Plasmodium), cause unusually severe disease because the spleen normally pits infected cells. In sickle cell disease, Salmonella osteomyelitis also reflects impaired splenic and bone defenses.

Polysaccharide-only vaccines rely on T-cell-independent B-cell responses and are weak in young children; conjugate vaccines link the polysaccharide to a protein carrier, recruit T-cell help and give memory, which is why conjugate pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccines are central for asplenic patients.

On Step 2 CK the same physiology becomes vaccine timing around splenectomy, standby antibiotics and immediate empiric therapy for fever.

sections.heading: Splenomegaly, hypersplenism, rupture and infarction: mechanisms
sections.html:
Disease reaches the spleen in three ways: it enlarges (splenomegaly), it overworks (hypersplenism), or it is damaged by tearing or loss of blood supply. Each has a mechanism worth knowing for Step 1 and a management that Step 2 CK will test.

Splenomegaly by mechanism

MechanismExamples
Work hypertrophy from red-cell removalHereditary spherocytosis, thalassemia, autoimmune hemolysis, early sickle cell disease
Immune hyperplasiaInfectious mononucleosis (EBV), CMV, endocarditis, HIV, malaria, SLE
CongestionCirrhosis with portal hypertension, portal or splenic vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, right heart failure
Infiltration by neoplasmCML, primary myelofibrosis, hairy cell leukemia, lymphomas including splenic marginal zone lymphoma
Infiltration by storage or depositGaucher disease, Niemann-Pick disease, amyloidosis
Extramedullary hematopoiesisMyelofibrosis, thalassemia major

Massive splenomegaly (crossing the midline or reaching the pelvis) narrows the list to myeloproliferative neoplasms (CML, myelofibrosis), hairy cell leukemia, some lymphomas, Gaucher disease, thalassemia major, chronic malaria and visceral leishmaniasis. Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), transmitted by phlebotomine sand flies, presents with fever, weight loss, massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia; amastigotes fill macrophages of spleen, liver and marrow.

Hypersplenism

Hypersplenism is the combination of splenomegaly, one or more cytopenias, a normal or hypercellular marrow, and correction after splenectomy. An enlarged spleen pools a larger fraction of the platelets and neutrophils, and increased macrophage mass shortens red-cell survival. In cirrhosis, portal congestion is the usual cause; reduced hepatic thrombopoietin production adds to the thrombocytopenia. The cytopenias are usually moderate, and patients rarely bleed from them alone.

Rupture

The spleen's thin capsule and rich blood supply make it the most commonly injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma, especially with left lower rib fractures. Atraumatic rupture occurs in an abnormal spleen: EBV infectious mononucleosis (usually in the first 3 weeks), malaria, leukemia and lymphoma infiltration. Blood irritating the left hemidiaphragm refers pain to the left shoulder (Kehr sign). In mononucleosis, splenic enlargement results from proliferation of lymphocytes, chiefly cytotoxic T cells responding to infected B cells; the reactive cells appear on the smear as atypical lymphocytes.

Infarction

The spleen has an end-arterial supply, so occlusion of a segmental branch produces a wedge-shaped, pale (anemic) infarct with coagulative necrosis, its base at the capsule. Causes are embolic (atrial fibrillation, infective endocarditis, left ventricular thrombus), local thrombosis in a massively enlarged spleen (myelofibrosis, CML), hypercoagulable states, and sickling. People with sickle cell trait can infarct the spleen at high altitude or with intense exertion. Presentation is left upper quadrant pain, sometimes pleuritic, with fever and raised LDH; contrast CT shows a peripheral wedge-shaped hypodensity.

Sickle cell disease and the spleen over time

In infants with HbSS the spleen enlarges with trapped sickled cells and then progressively infarcts. Before autosplenectomy, a sudden pooling of blood in the spleen causes acute splenic sequestration: rapid enlargement of the spleen, an acute fall in hemoglobin with a maintained or raised reticulocyte count, often thrombocytopenia, and risk of hypovolemic shock. It is typical between about 6 months and 5 years in HbSS. In HbSC disease and sickle beta+-thalassemia the spleen often persists, so sequestration and infarction can occur in older children and adults.

A low reticulocyte count with a sudden fall in hemoglobin in sickle cell disease is aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19), not sequestration; the spleen size and reticulocyte count separate the two.

After splenectomy

Expect Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells and a transient rise in platelets and white cells. Long-term risks are overwhelming infection and a modestly increased risk of venous thrombosis, including portal vein thrombosis after splenectomy for a large spleen. When ITP relapses after splenectomy, retained accessory splenic tissue should be sought; it can be localized with scintigraphy using heat-damaged, radiolabelled red cells, which the spleen avidly removes.

A splenic infarct in a patient with fever and a new murmur is endocarditis until proven otherwise; obtain blood cultures and echocardiography.

Step 2 CK turns these into decisions: CT or laparotomy by hemodynamic status after trauma, sports restriction in mononucleosis, transfusion for sequestration, and when splenectomy is offered.

sections.heading: Antithrombotic drugs: mechanisms, toxicity and reversal
sections.html:
Antithrombotic drugs work at two levels: antiplatelet agents prevent platelet activation and aggregation (arterial, platelet-rich clots), and anticoagulants reduce thrombin generation or activity (venous, fibrin-rich clots, and cardioembolism). Their shared adverse effect is bleeding, and each class has its own specific toxicities, laboratory monitoring and reversal.

[[figure:s23a-fig72]]

Antiplatelet agents

DrugMechanismKey adverse effects and pitfalls
AspirinIrreversibly acetylates COX-1, blocking thromboxane A2 for the platelet's lifetime (about 7 to 10 days)GI ulceration and bleeding; aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease; Reye syndrome in children with viral illness; tinnitus and mixed acid-base disorder in overdose
ClopidogrelProdrug; CYP2C19 forms an active metabolite that irreversibly blocks P2Y12Reduced effect in CYP2C19 poor metabolizers (loss-of-function alleles such as *2, *3); rare TTP
PrasugrelProdrug, irreversible P2Y12 block, more reliable activationMore bleeding; avoided after prior stroke or TIA
TicagrelorActive drug, reversible (allosteric) P2Y12 antagonistDyspnea; bradyarrhythmia; effect blunted by high-dose aspirin
Eptifibatide, tirofiban (abciximab historically)Block GP IIb/IIIa, the final common pathway of fibrinogen cross-linkingBleeding; acute severe thrombocytopenia within hours, from antibodies that recognize the drug-occupied receptor

Heparins and fondaparinux

Unfractionated heparin (UFH) binds antithrombin and accelerates its inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa; to inhibit thrombin, heparin must be long enough to bridge antithrombin and thrombin. Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) chains are shorter, so they act mainly on Xa. Fondaparinux is a synthetic pentasaccharide with pure antithrombin-mediated anti-Xa activity. UFH is monitored by aPTT or anti-Xa, has a short half-life and is fully neutralized by protamine, a basic protein that binds the acidic heparin; protamine reverses LMWH only partially and fondaparinux not at all. LMWH and fondaparinux are renally cleared. Adverse effects include bleeding, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (IgG to platelet factor 4-heparin complexes that activate platelets through FcγRIIa), osteoporosis with long use, and hyperkalemia from aldosterone suppression.

Warfarin

Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), so reduced vitamin K is not regenerated and the hepatic gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S fails. The PT/INR rises first because factor VII has the shortest half-life, but full antithrombotic effect needs depletion of prothrombin over several days. Protein C also falls early, creating a transient procoagulant state; therefore acute thrombosis is treated with a parenteral anticoagulant overlapping warfarin for at least 5 days and until the INR is therapeutic. Warfarin is metabolized mainly by CYP2C9; variants in CYP2C9 and VKORC1 lower the dose needed. It crosses the placenta and causes an embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses) in the first trimester. Reversal uses vitamin K (slow, needs new factor synthesis) and, for serious bleeding, 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC), which supplies II, VII, IX and X immediately.

Direct oral anticoagulants

  • Dabigatran directly and reversibly inhibits thrombin (free and clot-bound) without antithrombin. It is mostly renally excreted, can be removed by hemodialysis, and causes dyspepsia. Idarucizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody fragment (Fab) that binds dabigatran with very high affinity.
  • Apixaban, rivaroxaban and edoxaban directly inhibit free and prothrombinase-bound factor Xa, again without antithrombin. Reversal options are andexanet alfa, a recombinant, catalytically inactive factor Xa decoy that binds the drug, or 4-factor PCC.
  • Parenteral direct thrombin inhibitors (argatroban, hepatically cleared; bivalirudin) are used in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and during PCI.

Vitamin K and protamine do nothing for a direct oral anticoagulant; matching the reversal agent to the mechanism is the tested skill.

DOACs need dose adjustment for renal function and have fewer interactions than warfarin, but strong combined CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin) lower their levels and strong inhibitors raise them.

Step 2 CK asks which reversal to give for a specific bleed, how to start warfarin safely and how to recognise drug-induced thrombocytopenia.

sections.heading: Drug-induced cytopenias, hemolysis, methemoglobinemia and tumor lysis
sections.html:
Drugs injure blood cells by four main mechanisms: dose-dependent marrow toxicity (cytotoxic chemotherapy), immune destruction (drug-dependent antibodies against neutrophils, platelets or red cells), oxidant injury (methemoglobin and Heinz bodies, worst in G6PD deficiency), and metabolic consequences of rapid cell kill (tumor lysis syndrome).

Chemotherapy myelosuppression

Most cytotoxic drugs kill dividing marrow progenitors. Because neutrophils survive only hours to days in blood, the neutrophil count falls first, usually reaching its nadir 7 to 14 days after a dose and recovering by 3 to 4 weeks; platelets follow; anemia develops slowly because red cells live about 120 days. Nitrosoureas and mitomycin cause delayed, prolonged nadirs. Vincristine and bleomycin are relatively marrow-sparing. Filgrastim and pegfilgrastim (recombinant G-CSF) stimulate neutrophil precursor proliferation and release; bone pain is the typical adverse effect.

Drug-induced neutropenia and agranulocytosis

Agranulocytosis means an absolute neutrophil count below 500/mm3. Non-chemotherapy causes include methimazole and propylthiouracil, clozapine, sulfasalazine, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, dapsone, deferiprone and procainamide. With thionamides it is usually immune-mediated, appears most often within the first 3 months, and presents abruptly as fever and sore throat. The drug is stopped and a CBC with differential obtained; because cross-reactivity between methimazole and propylthiouracil is possible, the other thionamide is not substituted.

Drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia

Drug-dependent antibodies bind platelet glycoproteins (GP IIb/IIIa or GP Ib/IX) only when the drug is present. Typical culprits are quinine (including tonic water), vancomycin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, beta-lactams such as piperacillin, carbamazepine and GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors. Platelets fall abruptly about 5 to 10 days after a first exposure (within hours on re-exposure or with GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors), often to below 20,000/mm3 with petechiae and mucosal bleeding. Unlike heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, the antibodies do not activate platelets, so thrombosis is not a feature. Stopping the drug leads to recovery, usually within about a week.

Drug-induced hemolysis

MechanismExample drugsPattern
Hapten (drug adsorbed to membrane)High-dose IV penicillinIgG-coated cells, extravascular, DAT IgG positive
Drug-dependent antibody, complement activationCeftriaxone, quinineAbrupt intravascular hemolysis, DAT C3 positive, can be severe
True autoantibody inducedMethyldopa, fludarabineWarm autoimmune hemolysis that persists without the drug present
Oxidant stressPrimaquine, dapsone, rasburicase, nitrofurantoin, sulfonamidesHeinz bodies and bite cells; severe with G6PD deficiency

Acquired methemoglobinemia

Oxidant drugs convert heme iron from ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric (Fe3+). Methemoglobin cannot carry oxygen, and the remaining ferrous hemes in the same tetramer hold oxygen more tightly (left shift), so tissue delivery falls more than the percentage suggests. Causes include topical benzocaine and other local anesthetics (prilocaine, high-dose lidocaine), dapsone, nitrites and nitrates (amyl nitrite, nitrate-contaminated well water in infants), primaquine and rasburicase. Patients have cyanosis unrelieved by oxygen and chocolate-brown blood; arterial PO2 is normal, pulse oximetry reads around 85% regardless of severity, and co-oximetry confirms the diagnosis. Methylene blue is reduced by NADPH-dependent methemoglobin reductase to leukomethylene blue, which reduces Fe3+ back to Fe2+. Because the NADPH comes from G6PD, methylene blue is ineffective and can trigger hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Methylene blue also inhibits monoamine oxidase and can precipitate serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs.

Tumor lysis syndrome

Rapid lysis of a large, chemosensitive tumor burden (Burkitt lymphoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia with high counts, bulky high-grade lymphoma) releases potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids. Purines are degraded to uric acid, which crystallizes in acidic renal tubules; calcium phosphate precipitates as well, and secondary hypocalcemia follows. The result is hyperkalemia (arrhythmia), hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia (tetany, seizures) and acute kidney injury.

  • Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, preventing new uric acid formation but not removing uric acid already present; it raises xanthine and hypoxanthine. Doses of azathioprine and mercaptopurine must be cut when it is co-prescribed.
  • Rasburicase is recombinant urate oxidase, converting uric acid to soluble allantoin and lowering levels within hours. The reaction produces hydrogen peroxide, which in G6PD deficiency causes severe hemolysis and methemoglobinemia.

Rasburicase falsely lowers uric acid in blood samples left at room temperature, because the enzyme keeps working in the tube; samples go on ice.

On Step 2 CK, these mechanisms become actions: stop the culprit drug, screen for G6PD deficiency in at-risk patients before rasburicase, and give methylene blue for symptomatic methemoglobinemia.

title: Blood · Hemolysis from mechanical injury, spleen disorders and drug toxicity: diagnosis and management
meta: Managing thrombotic microangiopathy and mechanical hemolysis, caring for asplenic patients and splenic emergencies, and reversing or treating drug effects on blood.

sections.heading: Thrombotic microangiopathy and mechanical hemolysis: diagnosis and management
sections.html:
When a patient has anemia with schistocytes, the first job is to decide whether the problem is a thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), which can kill within days, or mechanical damage from a valve, device or external trauma, which is rarely urgent. Thrombocytopenia is the hinge: fragments with severe thrombocytopenia mean TMA until proven otherwise.

Initial evaluation

  • Confirm hemolysis: hemoglobin, reticulocytes, LDH, indirect bilirubin, haptoglobin, peripheral smear reviewed by a person, and a negative DAT.
  • Separate TMA from DIC: PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen and D-dimer.
  • Look for the cause: creatinine and urinalysis, aminotransferases, blood pressure and fundi, pregnancy test, stool testing for Shiga toxin or STEC in anyone with diarrhea, HIV, and a drug history (quinine, gemcitabine, mitomycin, calcineurin inhibitors, VEGF inhibitors, cocaine).
  • Draw ADAMTS13 activity (and inhibitor) before plasma is given, but never wait for the result to treat.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

Clinical probability of TTP is high when a patient has MAHA with a platelet count below about 30,000/mm3, a normal INR, creatinine that is normal or only mildly raised, no cancer, no transplant, and no other explanation. Fever, neurologic signs and renal injury together are present in only a minority, so do not wait for the full picture. ADAMTS13 activity below 10% confirms the diagnosis.

Management of immune TTP is an emergency:

  1. Therapeutic plasma exchange daily, started as soon as possible. If exchange is delayed, infuse plasma as a bridge.
  2. Glucocorticoids (for example methylprednisolone or prednisone).
  3. Caplacizumab, which shortens time to platelet recovery and reduces exacerbations; it is continued after exchange until ADAMTS13 activity recovers, and its main risk is mucocutaneous bleeding.
  4. Rituximab to suppress the anti-ADAMTS13 antibody and reduce relapse.

Platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening bleeding, because it can fuel microthrombi. Response is followed by platelet count and LDH. After remission, ADAMTS13 activity is checked periodically; a fall to low levels prompts pre-emptive rituximab. Congenital TTP is treated with plasma infusion or recombinant ADAMTS13 rather than immunosuppression.

Pregnancy

Pregnancy can unmask congenital TTP or trigger immune TTP, usually in the second or third trimester. HELLP syndrome, by contrast, occurs after 20 weeks or postpartum, is usually accompanied by hypertension and clearly raised aminotransferases, has milder thrombocytopenia, and resolves with delivery. TTP is treated with plasma exchange whatever the gestational age; delivery does not cure it. Postpartum TMA with progressive kidney injury suggests complement-mediated HUS.

Shiga toxin-associated HUS

Typically a child under 5 has bloody diarrhea, often after undercooked beef, unpasteurized products or animal contact, and 5 to 10 days later develops pallor, petechiae and reduced urine output. Management is supportive:

  • Isotonic IV fluids early, with careful monitoring of weight, urine output and electrolytes.
  • No antibiotics and no antimotility agents for suspected STEC enteritis.
  • Red-cell transfusion for symptomatic or severe anemia; platelets only for bleeding or procedures.
  • Dialysis for refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, fluid overload, uremic symptoms or prolonged anuria.

Most children recover kidney function, but a meaningful minority are left with hypertension, proteinuria or chronic kidney disease, so long-term follow-up of blood pressure, urinalysis and creatinine is needed. STEC infection is reportable to public health.

Complement-mediated (atypical) HUS

Suspect it when TMA with prominent kidney injury occurs without STEC and with ADAMTS13 activity that is not severely reduced, especially with a family history, recurrence, or onset after infection or pregnancy. Plasma exchange may be started while ADAMTS13 is pending; once TTP and STEC are excluded, a C5 inhibitor (eculizumab or ravulizumab) is first-line. Before starting, give meningococcal vaccines (MenACWY and MenB); if treatment cannot wait, cover with antibiotic prophylaxis until vaccine protection is expected.

Other TMA settings

SettingCluesManagement priority
DICSepsis, trauma, abruption, acute promyelocytic leukemia; long PT/aPTT, low fibrinogenTreat the cause; replace platelets, cryoprecipitate and plasma for bleeding or procedures
HELLP syndromeAfter 20 weeks, hypertension, RUQ pain, raised aminotransferasesStabilize, magnesium sulfate, control BP, deliver
Malignant hypertensionSevere BP elevation, retinal hemorrhages or papilledema, kidney injuryControlled IV blood pressure reduction
Drug-induced TMAQuinine, chemotherapy, calcineurin or VEGF inhibitorsStop the drug

Mechanical hemolysis without TMA

Prosthetic valves. New or worsening hemolysis with a mechanical valve, often with a new regurgitant murmur, suggests a paravalvular leak. Transthoracic echocardiography comes first, but acoustic shadowing from the prosthesis often hides mitral paravalvular jets, so transesophageal echocardiography is the most accurate test. Mild cases get iron and folate replacement and transfusion as needed; severe hemolysis or heart failure leads to surgical repair or percutaneous leak closure. Chronic urinary iron loss means these patients often need iron. LVAD hemolysis with rising LDH, dark urine or abnormal pump power suggests pump thrombosis and needs urgent evaluation by the device team, intensified anticoagulation and sometimes pump exchange.

Exertional hemoglobinuria in a runner or marcher with transient red-brown urine, normal CK, normal kidney function and a normal smear needs reassurance and cushioned footwear or softer surfaces. Persistent hemoglobinuria at rest, cytopenias or thrombosis would instead prompt flow cytometry for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.

A normal platelet count makes TTP very unlikely; with fragments and a normal platelet count, look at the heart, the device or the patient's feet.

In suspected TTP the order is: send ADAMTS13, start plasma exchange and steroids, then add caplacizumab and rituximab. Waiting for the assay costs lives.
