sections.heading: Caring for the asplenic patient: vaccines, prophylaxis and fever
sections.html:
Every patient without a functioning spleen carries a lifelong risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI): fulminant bacteremia, usually pneumococcal, that can progress from a flu-like illness to septic shock, DIC and purpura fulminans within hours. The risk is highest in the first years after surgery and in children but never disappears. Prevention rests on vaccination, education and a low threshold for antibiotics.

Who is functionally asplenic

Treat as asplenic: anyone after splenectomy; children and adults with sickle cell anemia (HbSS) or sickle beta0-thalassemia; congenital asplenia; and people with marked hyposplenism (for example Howell-Jolly bodies in celiac disease or after splenic irradiation).

Vaccination

Recommendations follow the current CDC/ACIP schedules for adults and children with asplenia. In outline:

VaccineAsplenic adult who has not been vaccinated
PneumococcalA conjugate vaccine: PCV20 or PCV21 alone, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23
Meningococcal ACWY (conjugate)2-dose primary series at least 8 weeks apart, then boosters every 5 years while the risk persists
Meningococcal BPrimary series, then periodic boosters while the risk persists
Haemophilus influenzae type b1 dose if not previously vaccinated
InfluenzaAnnual inactivated vaccine (secondary bacterial infection risk)

Timing around splenectomy. For an elective splenectomy, give vaccines at least 2 weeks before surgery, so that antibody responses form while the spleen is present. After an emergency splenectomy, vaccinate 2 weeks or more after the operation, when responses are better; if the patient may not return, vaccinate before discharge rather than miss the opportunity. If rituximab or other B-cell-depleting therapy is planned, vaccinate beforehand where possible.

Asplenia alone is not a contraindication to live vaccines such as MMR or varicella. Routine childhood vaccines continue on schedule.

Antibiotic prophylaxis and education

  • Children with sickle cell anemia take daily oral penicillin from diagnosis (by about 2 months of age) until at least age 5, together with their conjugate vaccines.
  • After splenectomy, daily prophylaxis is often given to young children and is considered for adults in the first years after surgery or after a prior episode of OPSI.
  • Every asplenic patient should carry a standby antibiotic (for example amoxicillin-clavulanate, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone or cefuroxime with penicillin allergy), start it at the first sign of fever if care is not immediately available, and then seek urgent assessment.
  • Advise a medical alert card or bracelet; malaria and Babesia precautions in endemic areas; and prompt amoxicillin-clavulanate after any dog or cat bite, because of Capnocytophaga canimorsus.

Fever in an asplenic patient

Fever is a medical emergency. Obtain blood cultures and give empiric IV ceftriaxone immediately, without waiting for laboratory results or imaging. Add vancomycin when the patient is hypotensive or looks septic, when meningitis is suspected (with meningitic doses and dexamethasone as usual), or where pneumococcal resistance to cephalosporins is a concern. Treat shock aggressively, and look for DIC and adrenal hemorrhage. In children with sickle cell disease and fever, the same rule applies: urgent assessment, cultures and parenteral ceftriaxone.

Waiting for a white-cell count, a chest radiograph or culture results before the first antibiotic dose is the classic error; OPSI can kill within 24 hours.

Preserving the spleen

Because of these risks, nonoperative management or partial splenectomy is preferred in hemodynamically stable trauma, particularly in children, and splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenia is now usually reserved for disease that fails other second-line therapies.

A previously vaccinated asplenic patient still needs fever education and standby antibiotics: vaccines do not cover all serotypes, and OPSI occurs in vaccinated patients.

The Step 1 reason for all of this is the marginal-zone defense against encapsulated bacteria; conjugate vaccines work because they recruit T-cell help.

sections.heading: Splenomegaly, splenic trauma, infarction and sequestration: management
sections.html:
The spleen problems that come up most in clinical practice and on Step 2 CK are an enlarged spleen found on examination, a ruptured spleen after trauma or in mononucleosis, left upper quadrant pain from infarction or abscess, and acute splenic sequestration in a young child with sickle cell disease.

Approach to splenomegaly

Confirm enlargement with ultrasound when examination is uncertain. Then use the setting: fever and adenopathy in a young adult suggest EBV; stigmata of liver disease suggest portal hypertension; weight loss, night sweats and massive splenomegaly suggest a myeloproliferative neoplasm or lymphoma; travel history raises malaria or visceral leishmaniasis. Start with a CBC with differential and a smear reviewed by a person, liver tests, LDH, reticulocyte count, and directed tests (heterophile antibody, HIV, BCR::ABL1 and JAK2 testing, flow cytometry). Biopsy of the marrow or a lymph node is preferred to splenic biopsy.

Hypersplenism

Mild pancytopenia in cirrhosis is usually from splenic pooling plus reduced thrombopoietin and needs no specific therapy. Treat the cause; splenectomy or partial splenic embolization is rarely needed.

Traumatic splenic injury

  • Follow ATLS: airway, breathing, circulation with hemorrhage control, and a FAST examination.
  • Hemodynamically unstable despite resuscitation with intraperitoneal fluid on FAST: exploratory laparotomy (splenectomy or splenorrhaphy).
  • Hemodynamically stable: CT of the abdomen with IV contrast to grade the injury and look for active extravasation. Most stable patients are managed nonoperatively with monitoring, serial examinations and hemoglobin checks; a contrast blush or pseudoaneurysm is treated with angioembolization. Failure of nonoperative management (falling hemoglobin, instability) leads to surgery.
  • Children are managed nonoperatively even more often, because their thicker capsules and the infection risk after splenectomy both favor preservation.

Delayed rupture can occur days after injury, so patients managed nonoperatively are counseled to avoid contact activity for several weeks and to return with abdominal or left shoulder pain or dizziness.

Infectious mononucleosis

Most patients with EBV have an enlarged spleen, even when it cannot be felt. Rupture is uncommon but occurs mostly within the first 3 weeks and can follow trivial trauma. Advise avoiding contact or collision sports and heavy lifting for at least 3 to 4 weeks from symptom onset, and until the patient is well and the spleen is no longer palpable; ultrasound is not routinely required. Sudden left upper quadrant or left shoulder pain with lightheadedness needs urgent assessment and imaging or surgery depending on stability.

Splenic infarction and abscess

Infarction presents with left upper quadrant pain and sometimes fever, nausea or left pleuritic pain; contrast CT shows a peripheral wedge-shaped defect. Management is analgesia and treatment of the source: anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation or a cardiac thrombus, blood cultures and echocardiography for possible endocarditis, and evaluation for a myeloproliferative neoplasm or hypercoagulable state when no source is clear. A splenic abscess (endocarditis, injection drug use, immunosuppression) causes fever, left upper quadrant pain and sometimes a left pleural effusion; treatment is antibiotics plus percutaneous drainage, with splenectomy for multiloculated or refractory cases.

Acute splenic sequestration in sickle cell disease

A child, typically between 6 months and 5 years with HbSS, becomes pale and lethargic with a rapidly enlarging, often tender spleen. Hemoglobin falls by 2 g/dL or more below baseline, the reticulocyte count stays high, and platelets often drop. Hypovolemic shock can develop quickly.

  • Restore circulating volume and give red-cell transfusion promptly, in modest volumes, because the spleen releases trapped cells as it shrinks and over-transfusion can cause hyperviscosity.
  • Teach caregivers to palpate the spleen and to come in immediately if it enlarges.
  • Recurrence is common; after recurrent or life-threatening episodes, splenectomy (often after age 2) or a chronic transfusion program is considered.

Distinguish aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19): falling hemoglobin with a reticulocyte count near zero and no new splenic enlargement.

Splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenia and the accessory spleen

Splenectomy produces durable remission in many adults with chronic ITP, but thrombopoietin receptor agonists and rituximab are now usually tried first. If ITP relapses after splenectomy and the smear shows no Howell-Jolly bodies, suspect an accessory spleen; scintigraphy with heat-damaged radiolabelled red cells localizes it, and laparoscopic removal can restore remission.

A positive FAST does not mean laparotomy in a stable patient; stability, not the amount of blood, decides between CT and the operating room.

Splenic sequestration and aplastic crisis both cause sudden severe anemia in sickle cell disease; the spleen size and reticulocyte count separate them in seconds.

sections.heading: Antithrombotic bleeding: reversal and safe prescribing
sections.html:
Bleeding on an antithrombotic drug is managed in the same order every time: stop the drug, assess the site and severity of bleeding, resuscitate and apply local measures, and give a specific reversal agent when bleeding is life-threatening, in a critical site (intracranial, pericardial, spinal, intraocular) or when emergency surgery cannot wait. Know when the last dose was taken and the kidney function, because these set how long the drug will persist.

Warfarin

Starting it safely

  • For acute venous thromboembolism, overlap a parenteral anticoagulant with warfarin for at least 5 days and until the INR has been in range (usually 2 to 3) for 24 hours.
  • Start lower in older adults, people with liver disease or heart failure, poor nutrition, or interacting drugs; check the INR frequently in the first weeks.
  • Warfarin, not a DOAC, is the oral anticoagulant for mechanical heart valves and for high-risk (triple-positive) antiphospholipid syndrome.
  • Warfarin is avoided in pregnancy (embryopathy, fetal bleeding); LMWH is the anticoagulant of choice.

Interactions

INR rises with CYP2C9 inhibitors and other potentiators (metronidazole, fluconazole and other azoles, amiodarone, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), with acute illness, and with reduced vitamin K intake; INR falls with inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin) and with a sudden increase in leafy green vegetables. Check the INR within a few days of starting or stopping an interacting drug.

Reversal

SituationManagement
INR above range, no bleedingHold or reduce doses, recheck; vitamin K not needed for modest elevations
INR above 10, no bleedingHold warfarin and give oral vitamin K
Major or life-threatening bleedingHold warfarin; IV vitamin K plus 4-factor PCC; plasma only if PCC is unavailable

Vitamin K alone takes 12 to 24 hours because the liver must make new factors; PCC corrects the INR within minutes and needs far less volume than plasma, which matters in older adults with heart failure.

Direct oral anticoagulants

  • Dabigatran: idarucizumab for life-threatening bleeding or urgent surgery. Dabigatran is renally cleared, so bleeding risk rises in kidney injury; hemodialysis can remove it if idarucizumab is unavailable. A normal thrombin time essentially excludes a meaningful dabigatran effect.
  • Apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban: andexanet alfa or 4-factor PCC, according to local availability and protocols. Andexanet carries a thrombotic risk.
  • Activated charcoal can be given if the last dose was within a few hours.
  • Standard PT and aPTT do not reliably measure DOAC effect; drug-specific anti-Xa levels or dilute thrombin time are used where available.

Heparins

Unfractionated heparin has a short half-life; for serious bleeding give protamine sulfate, dosed on the heparin given in the previous few hours. Protamine only partly neutralizes LMWH and does not reverse fondaparinux. Protamine can cause hypotension and anaphylaxis, with higher risk after protamine-containing (NPH) insulin, previous protamine exposure, or fish allergy.

Antiplatelet therapy

Aspirin and P2Y12 inhibitors cannot be reversed by a drug. For elective surgery, clopidogrel and ticagrelor are usually stopped 5 days and prasugrel 7 days beforehand, unless a recent coronary stent makes interruption dangerous; in that case surgery is ideally deferred, after discussion with cardiology. After spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage on antiplatelet drugs, routine platelet transfusion is not beneficial for patients not undergoing neurosurgery. Eptifibatide and tirofiban wear off within hours once stopped.

Drug-induced thrombocytopenia on antithrombotics

  • A platelet drop within hours of a GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor, with clumping excluded by a citrate tube count, is drug-induced; stop the infusion and transfuse platelets for bleeding.
  • A fall of more than 50% 5 to 10 days after heparin starts suggests heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant.

Older adults

Older patients have the highest bleeding risk and the greatest benefit. Review indication, kidney function, interacting drugs (NSAIDs, SSRIs, antiplatelet agents) and the dose at each visit. Dose-reduction criteria for DOACs must be applied exactly, because inappropriate under-dosing increases stroke risk.

Plasma and vitamin K are not reversal agents for a DOAC; and for warfarin-associated intracranial hemorrhage, vitamin K alone is too slow.

Match reversal to mechanism: missing vitamin K-dependent factors (PCC + vitamin K), a drug to bind (idarucizumab, andexanet), or a polyanion to neutralize (protamine).

sections.heading: Chemotherapy and drug toxicity to blood: recognition and management
sections.html:
Hematologic toxicity is one of the commonest serious adverse drug effects. On Step 2 CK, the tested skills are recognizing which drug is responsible, stopping it, ordering the right test, and treating the complication: febrile neutropenia, agranulocytosis, methemoglobinemia, tumor lysis syndrome, immune thrombocytopenia and hemolysis.

Chemotherapy and neutropenia

The absolute neutrophil count (ANC) equals the white-cell count multiplied by the fraction of segmented neutrophils plus bands. Neutropenia is graded as mild (1,000 to 1,500/mm3), moderate (500 to 1,000/mm3) and severe (below 500/mm3). Febrile neutropenia is an oral temperature of 38.3 °C (101 °F) or higher once, or 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) or higher sustained over an hour, with an ANC below 500/mm3 or expected to fall below 500/mm3.

  • Afebrile neutropenia in a well patient does not need antibiotics. Teach temperature checks and fever precautions, and arrange urgent return for fever.
  • Febrile neutropenia: blood cultures (peripheral and from any line) and an empiric antipseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem) within an hour. Add vancomycin for suspected catheter infection, skin or soft-tissue infection, pneumonia, hemodynamic instability or known MRSA colonization. Selected low-risk patients can be treated as outpatients with oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate. Persistent fever after 4 to 7 days in high-risk patients prompts evaluation for invasive fungal infection.
  • Prevention: G-CSF (filgrastim or pegfilgrastim) as primary prophylaxis when a regimen carries a high risk of febrile neutropenia (about 20% or more) or the patient has strong risk factors, and as secondary prophylaxis after a previous episode. Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis is reserved for expected profound, prolonged neutropenia, as in acute leukemia induction.
  • Avoid rectal examinations and rectal temperatures in neutropenic patients.

Antithyroid drug agranulocytosis

Methimazole and propylthiouracil can cause agranulocytosis, most often in the first 3 months. Every patient is told to stop the drug and get a CBC with differential immediately if fever or sore throat develops. If the ANC is below 500/mm3, the drug is stopped permanently; febrile patients are admitted for broad-spectrum antibiotics, and G-CSF may be used. The other thionamide is not substituted because of cross-reactivity; definitive therapy is radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy after control with beta-blockers and other measures. PTU additionally causes severe hepatotoxicity, so methimazole is preferred except in the first trimester of pregnancy and in thyroid storm.

Acquired methemoglobinemia

Suspect it in a patient with cyanosis and pulse oximetry around 85% that does not improve with oxygen, a normal PaO2 on blood gas, and recent exposure to benzocaine spray (endoscopy, echocardiography), dapsone, nitrites or nitrates, or rasburicase. Co-oximetry confirms the level.

  • Stop the agent and give high-flow oxygen.
  • Give IV methylene blue for symptomatic patients or high levels (commonly above about 20 to 30%).
  • In G6PD deficiency, methylene blue is avoided; options are ascorbic acid, exchange transfusion and hyperbaric oxygen.
  • Dapsone has a long half-life and can cause rebound methemoglobinemia, so repeated doses may be needed.
  • Infants fed formula made with nitrate-rich well water are at particular risk because their methemoglobin reductase activity is low.

Tumor lysis syndrome

Risk is high with Burkitt lymphoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia with a high white count, and bulky, rapidly growing lymphomas, especially with kidney impairment or a raised uric acid before treatment. Prevention and treatment:

  • Aggressive IV hydration to maintain high urine output.
  • Allopurinol (or febuxostat) for intermediate risk; it prevents new uric acid but does not lower existing levels.
  • Rasburicase for high risk or established hyperuricemia; screen patients at risk for G6PD deficiency first, and use allopurinol instead if deficient.
  • Monitor potassium, phosphate, calcium, uric acid and creatinine every several hours early in treatment.
  • Treat hyperkalemia urgently. Give calcium only for symptomatic hypocalcemia, because added calcium can precipitate with phosphate.
  • Dialysis for refractory hyperkalemia, severe hyperphosphatemia, fluid overload or oliguric kidney injury.
  • Urine alkalinization is no longer recommended.

Drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia and hemolysis

A sudden, severe platelet fall 5 to 10 days after starting a drug such as vancomycin, piperacillin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or quinine, with no heparin exposure, suggests drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia. Stop the suspected drug and substitute an unrelated agent; give platelets for bleeding and consider IVIG for severe bleeding. Counts recover over about a week, and the drug is listed as an allergy. Drug-induced hemolysis is handled the same way: stop the drug (ceftriaxone, piperacillin and others), check the DAT, transfuse for severe anemia, and avoid re-exposure.

Switching from methimazole to propylthiouracil after agranulocytosis is wrong: cross-reactivity is possible, and definitive therapy is the safer route.

Before rasburicase, ask about G6PD status; before methylene blue, ask the same question. One enzyme deficiency spoils both drugs.

title: Human development · Normal infancy, childhood and adolescence
meta: Newborn physiology, growth, nutrition, milestones, primitive reflexes, normal variants and the physiology of puberty.

sections.heading: Newborn physiology, growth and infant nutrition
sections.html:
The first weeks of life compress three big physiological shifts into a short window: the circulation re-plumbs itself for air breathing, the liver takes over bilirubin clearance from the placenta, and the infant begins to rely on its own immune system while still borrowing antibody from its mother. Each shift explains a "normal" finding that students are asked to tell apart from disease.

Transitional circulation

With the first breaths, alveolar expansion and the rise in alveolar oxygen dilate pulmonary arterioles, so pulmonary vascular resistance falls steeply. Clamping the cord removes the low-resistance placenta, so systemic resistance rises. Pulmonary venous return now fills the left atrium, left atrial pressure exceeds right, and the flap of septum primum is pushed against septum secundum: the foramen ovale closes functionally within minutes to hours.

The ductus arteriosus constricts because two signals change together: arterial PO2 rises, and circulating prostaglandin E2 falls (the placenta that made it is gone and the now-perfused lungs metabolise it). Functional closure in a term infant usually occurs in the first 1–3 days; fibrosis later leaves the ligamentum arteriosum. The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum, the umbilical vein the ligamentum teres, and the distal umbilical arteries the medial umbilical ligaments.

The same physiology is used as therapy. An infusion of a prostaglandin E1 analogue (alprostadil) keeps the ductus open in duct-dependent heart lesions; a cyclo-oxygenase inhibitor (indomethacin or ibuprofen) or acetaminophen is used to close a persistent ductus in a preterm infant.

Growth in the first years

MeasureTypical term pattern
WeightFalls in the first days (normally by less than about 10%); back to birth weight by about 10–14 days; then roughly 20–30 g/day for the first 3 months. About double birth weight by 4–6 months, triple by 12 months.
LengthAbout 50 cm at birth; rises by about half in the first year; about doubles by 4 years. Measured lying down before age 2.
Head circumferenceAbout 34–35 cm at birth; grows fastest in the first 3 months (about 2 cm/month), adding roughly 12 cm in the first year as the brain grows.
FontanellesPosterior closes by about 2 months; anterior usually by 12–18 months (wide normal range).

WHO growth standards are used from birth to 2 years and CDC references from 2 to 20 years. A single measurement matters less than the trajectory: crossing two major percentile lines downward, or a weight-for-length below the 2nd percentile, needs evaluation. Preterm infants are plotted by corrected age until about 2 years.

Physiologic jaundice

Almost every newborn has a rise in unconjugated bilirubin. The causes stack up:

  • more bilirubin made: a high red cell mass and a shorter fetal red cell lifespan (roughly 70–90 days rather than 120);
  • less bilirubin conjugated: hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) activity is low at birth and matures over the first weeks;
  • more bilirubin reabsorbed: intestinal beta-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin in a gut with few bacteria to convert it to urobilinogen, so enterohepatic recirculation is high.

In a term infant, physiologic jaundice becomes visible after the first 24 hours, peaks around days 3–5 and fades over 1–2 weeks. Features that point away from "physiologic" include jaundice in the first 24 hours (think hemolysis, such as ABO or Rh isoimmunization or G6PD deficiency), a rapid rise toward treatment thresholds, an ill infant, jaundice persisting beyond about 2 weeks, and any rise in direct (conjugated) bilirubin above about 1.0 mg/dL, which is pathologic at any age and raises concern for cholestasis such as biliary atresia.

Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble; at high levels, unbound bilirubin crosses the blood–brain barrier and stains the basal ganglia (especially the globus pallidus), brainstem auditory nuclei and oculomotor nuclei. Phototherapy works by converting bilirubin to water-soluble photoisomers that are excreted in bile and urine without conjugation.

Passive immunity and the IgG nadir

Maternal IgG is the only antibody class actively carried across the placenta, by the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) on syncytiotrophoblast. Most transfer happens in the third trimester, so preterm infants start with less. Maternal IgG has a half-life of about 3–4 weeks; the infant's own IgG synthesis rises slowly, so total IgG reaches its lowest point at about 3–6 months. This explains why boys with X-linked agammaglobulinemia usually stay well until after about 6 months. IgM does not cross the placenta, so a raised cord-blood IgM points to an intrauterine infection. Breast milk adds secretory IgA, made by mammary plasma cells primed in the maternal gut, which coats the infant's intestinal mucosa without being absorbed.

Infant nutrition

Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for about the first 6 months. Colostrum (the first days) is rich in protein, secretory IgA and lactoferrin. Mature milk provides about 20 kcal/oz, is whey-predominant, carries lactose as its main sugar and contains oligosaccharides that feed bifidobacteria. Milk at the end of a feed (hindmilk) is richer in fat than the first milk.

Gap in breast milkWhat prevents it
Vitamin K (and a sterile gut, poor placental transfer)One intramuscular dose of vitamin K at birth prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding.
Vitamin D400 IU of vitamin D daily, starting in the first days, for breastfed and partially breastfed infants. Formula-fed infants need it until they take about 1 L (32 oz) of formula a day.
IronFetal iron stores last about 4–6 months in a term infant. Breastfed infants need iron from about 4 months (supplement, then iron-rich foods such as meat and fortified cereal); formula should be iron-fortified.
Vitamin B12Supplement the infant (and mother) when the mother follows a strict vegan diet.

Complementary foods start at about 6 months (not before about 4 months). Honey is avoided before 12 months because of infant botulism. Whole cow's milk is delayed until 12 months: it is low in iron, its calcium and casein reduce iron absorption, and in infants it can cause occult intestinal blood loss. After 12 months, intake above about 24 oz a day displaces iron-rich foods and is a classic cause of iron deficiency anemia in toddlers.

Teeth and sleep

The first primary teeth, usually the lower central incisors, erupt at about 6 months; all 20 primary teeth are present by about 2½–3 years. The first permanent teeth (first molars and lower incisors) appear at about 6 years. Newborns sleep about 14–17 hours a day in short bouts, with a large share of active (REM) sleep; sleep consolidates into longer night stretches over the first 4–6 months.

A jaundiced 1-week-old with pale stools and dark urine does not have "breast milk jaundice". Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is never part of normal newborn physiology; measure the direct bilirubin.

sections.heading: Developmental milestones, primitive reflexes and normal variants
sections.html:
Development is assessed in four streams: gross motor, fine motor/visual-motor, language and social-emotional. Progress is cephalocaudal (head control before sitting before walking) and proximal-to-distal (whole-hand raking before a pincer grasp). For infants born preterm, use corrected age until about 2 years. The CDC milestone checklists (revised 2022) list what most children (about 3 in 4) can do at each age, so a missing item is a prompt to screen, not a diagnosis.

Milestones by age

AgeGross motorFine motorLanguageSocial
2 moLifts head when proneOpens hands brieflyCoosSocial smile
4 moHolds head steady; pushes up on forearmsBrings hands together and to mouthLaughs; starts babblingSmiles to get attention
6 moRolls both ways; sits with supportRaking grasp; passes toy hand to handConsonant babbleKnows familiar faces
9 moSits alone; pulls to standEarly pincer"Mama/dada" without meaningStranger wariness
12 moCruises; first stepsNeat pincer; releases on requestOne or two words with meaningWaves; simple games
18 moRuns stiffly; climbs stairs with helpScribbles; small towerSeveral to about 20 words; points to body partsPoints to show; early pretend play
2 yKicks a ball; jumps with both feetTower of about 6; copies a lineTwo-word phrases; about half understood by strangersParallel play
3 yPedals a tricycle; alternates feet going upstairsCopies a circleThree-word sentences; about three quarters understoodTakes turns; imaginative play
4 yHops on one footCopies a cross; scissorsTells a story; fully understood by strangersCooperative play
5 ySkipsCopies a triangle; prints some lettersCounts to 10; uses future tenseFollows game rules

Red flags

  • Loss of any skill at any age (regression) needs prompt evaluation.
  • No babbling, pointing or other gestures by 12 months; no single words by 16 months; no spontaneous two-word phrases by 24 months: screen for autism spectrum disorder and refer for a formal hearing test.
  • Not walking by 18 months, or persistent toe-walking with tight heel cords.
  • A clear hand preference before about 12–18 months suggests weakness of the other arm (for example hemiplegic cerebral palsy or brachial plexus injury).
  • Primitive reflexes that persist past their expected window, or asymmetric reflexes.

Primitive reflexes

Primitive reflexes are brainstem and spinal patterns present at birth. As the cortex and corticospinal tracts myelinate, descending inhibition suppresses them and voluntary movement takes over. A reflex that is absent at birth suggests CNS depression or a neuromuscular disorder; one that is asymmetric suggests a focal problem (a clavicle fracture or brachial plexus palsy blunts the Moro on that side); one that persists beyond its window, especially with hypertonia and brisk reflexes, suggests an upper motor neuron lesion such as cerebral palsy.

[[figure:s23a-fig80]]
ReflexHow it is elicitedUsually gone by
MoroSudden head drop: arms extend and abduct, then flex4–6 months
RootingStroking the cheek turns the head and opens the mouthabout 4 months
Palmar graspPressure in the palm closes the fingers4–6 months
Asymmetric tonic neckTurning the head extends the arm on the face side and flexes the other4–6 months
Plantar graspPressure on the sole curls the toes9–12 months
Extensor plantar responseStroking the lateral sole extends the great toe12–24 months
Parachute (postural reaction)Tipping the infant forward brings the arms outAppears at 8–9 months and persists

Normal musculoskeletal variants

Lower-limb alignment follows a predictable arc. Infants and young toddlers are bow-legged (physiologic genu varum) until about 18–24 months; the legs straighten around 2 years, swing to knock-knees (physiologic genu valgum) that peak at about 3–4 years, and approach adult alignment by about 7–8 years. Physiologic varus and valgus are symmetric, painless and found in children of normal height.

Cause of in-toeingTypical ageKey findingCourse
Metatarsus adductusInfancyForefoot curves inward ("bean-shaped" sole), heel normalMost flexible cases resolve; casting if rigid
Internal tibial torsion1–3 yearsThigh–foot angle turned inwardResolves by about 4–5 years
Increased femoral anteversion3–8 yearsKneecaps point inward; W-sitting; excess hip internal rotationUsually improves by about 8–10 years

Braces, wedges and special shoes do not change the natural history of these rotational variants. A flexible flatfoot, in which the arch reappears when the child stands on tiptoe, is also normal and needs no treatment.

Bowing that is asymmetric, progressive, painful, present after about 2–3 years, or seen with short stature is not physiologic. Consider tibia vara (Blount disease; risk rises with obesity and early walking), rickets (widened wrists, rachitic rosary, high alkaline phosphatase) or a skeletal dysplasia, and obtain standing radiographs.

The parachute reaction is a useful asymmetry test: a 10-month-old who extends only one arm when tipped forward has weakness on the other side.

sections.heading: Physiology of puberty and adolescent development
sections.html:
Puberty is the reawakening of a reproductive axis that was briefly active before and after birth and then held quiet through childhood. Two separate processes run in parallel: gonadarche, driven by hypothalamic GnRH and pituitary gonadotropins, and adrenarche, the maturation of the adrenal zona reticularis.

Reactivating the axis

After the "mini-puberty" of early infancy, GnRH neurons are restrained by central inhibitory input (GABA and inhibitory genes such as MKRN3, whose loss of function causes familial central precocious puberty). At puberty, kisspeptin neurons in the arcuate nucleus, signalling through the KISS1 receptor on GnRH neurons together with neurokinin B, release that brake. Leptin from adipose tissue is permissive: puberty needs adequate energy stores, which is why very low body fat (endurance athletes, anorexia nervosa) delays it.

The first hormonal sign is a sleep-associated rise in LH pulse amplitude; daytime pulses follow later. GnRH must be pulsatile (roughly every 1–2 hours) to sustain gonadotropin release. Continuous exposure to GnRH or a long-acting GnRH agonist first causes a brief flare and then downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors, which shuts the axis down: the basis of GnRH-agonist treatment for central precocious puberty.

HormoneTargetMain pubertal effect
LHLeydig cells; ovarian theca cellsTestosterone; ovarian androgen substrate for estradiol
FSHSertoli cells; granulosa cellsSeminiferous tubule growth and spermatogenesis, inhibin B; follicle growth and aromatase activity
Estradiol (both sexes)Breast, uterus, growth plateThelarche; GH pulse amplitude; epiphyseal fusion
Adrenal androgens (DHEA, DHEA-S)Pilosebaceous unitPubic and axillary hair, body odour, acne

Adrenarche versus gonadarche

Adrenarche begins at about 6–8 years, independent of gonadotropins, as the zona reticularis matures and secretes more DHEA and DHEA-S. It produces body odour, oily skin and, later, pubic and axillary hair (pubarche). Gonadarche produces breast development, testicular growth and the growth spurt. Because the two are separate, a child can have pubic hair with no breast or testicular change (premature adrenarche), or the reverse in disorders of adrenal androgen production.

Sexual maturity ratings

Sexual maturity rating (SMR, Tanner) stages run from 1 (prepubertal) to 5 (adult). Described simply:

  • Breast: stage 2 is a small bud under an enlarging areola; stage 3 is further growth with breast and areola in one contour; stage 4 has the areola and nipple forming a mound above the breast; stage 5 is the adult contour with only the nipple projecting.
  • Male genital: stage 2 is testicular enlargement (volume about 4 mL or length about 2.5 cm) with thinner, redder scrotal skin; stage 3 adds penile lengthening; stage 4 adds penile widening and a darker scrotum; stage 5 is adult size.
  • Pubic hair: stage 2 is a few long, fine hairs at the base of the penis or along the labia; stage 3 is darker, coarser, curlier hair spreading over the pubis; stage 4 is adult-type hair over a smaller area; stage 5 spreads to the inner thighs.

Order and timing

[[figure:s23a-fig81]]

Girls: breast budding (thelarche) is the first sign in most, at about 10–11 years (normal range roughly 8–13). Pubic hair follows. The growth spurt comes early, with peak height velocity at SMR 2–3. Menarche comes about 2–2½ years after thelarche, typically at SMR 4 and about 12–13 years, when growth is already slowing; most girls grow only a few more centimetres afterwards. Early cycles are often anovulatory and irregular.

Boys: testicular enlargement is the first sign, at about 11–12 years (range roughly 9–14); most of testicular volume is seminiferous tubules, so the growth reflects FSH-driven Sertoli and germ cell expansion. Pubic hair and penile growth follow. The growth spurt is later (SMR 3–4) and larger; the extra prepubertal years of growth plus the larger peak explain the average adult height difference between sexes. Voice change, facial hair and peak muscle gain come late.

In both sexes, estrogen (in boys made by aromatization of testosterone) drives growth-plate fusion. Men with aromatase deficiency or estrogen-receptor defects keep open epiphyses and keep growing into adulthood. Sex steroids also raise GH pulse amplitude, so IGF-1 peaks in mid-puberty. Adolescence lays down a large share of peak bone mass.

Normal findings that worry families

Pubertal gynecomastia is common in mid-puberty (about SMR 2–4): a firm, sometimes tender, disc of tissue under one or both areolae. It reflects a transient rise in the estradiol-to-testosterone ratio and usually regresses within about 6 months to 2 years. It is not normal if it appears before puberty, is very large, or comes with small firm testes (Klinefelter syndrome), a testicular mass, or exposure to drugs such as anabolic steroids, spironolactone or cannabis.

Sleep-phase delay: during puberty the circadian clock shifts later (evening melatonin onset moves later) and sleep pressure builds more slowly, so adolescents fall asleep later yet still need about 8–10 hours. Early school start times create chronic sleep restriction; catch-up sleep on weekends is the typical pattern.

Brain maturation and risk-taking: cortical grey matter thins through synaptic pruning while white matter (myelination) increases into the mid-20s. Reward and emotional circuits (ventral striatum, amygdala) become highly reactive early in puberty, whereas prefrontal control matures later. The gap favours sensation-seeking and peer-influenced risk, especially in emotionally charged settings; it is a developmental pattern, not a disorder.

Do not assume the growth spurt sits at the same pubertal stage in both sexes: it is early in girls and late in boys. A 12-year-old girl who has just had her first period is near the end of her growth; a 12-year-old boy with SMR 2 testes has most of his growth spurt still ahead.

sections.heading: Newborn screening and childhood surveillance
sections.html:
Well-child care for the first years follows the AAP Bright Futures periodicity schedule: a sequence of visits at which the clinician measures growth, screens for conditions that are silent but treatable, and gives age-matched guidance. Step 2 CK questions ask which screen is due, how to read a result, and what the next step is after an abnormal one.

Newborn screening

The dried blood-spot screen is collected at about 24–48 hours of age. A sample taken earlier than 24 hours (for example after an early discharge) can miss disorders whose markers rise only after feeding begins, so a repeat sample is needed. States follow the federal Recommended Uniform Screening Panel, which includes, among others, phenylketonuria and other amino-acid disorders, fatty-acid oxidation defects such as MCAD deficiency, galactosemia, biotinidase deficiency, congenital hypothyroidism, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, sickle cell disease and other hemoglobinopathies, cystic fibrosis (immunoreactive trypsinogen), severe combined immunodeficiency (T-cell receptor excision circles) and spinal muscular atrophy.

A positive screen is not a diagnosis: it triggers confirmatory testing, with urgency matched to the disorder. Some results require same-day action, for example stopping lactose-containing feeds when galactosemia is suspected, checking electrolytes in a possible salt-wasting adrenal hyperplasia, or confirming thyroid function and starting levothyroxine without delay in congenital hypothyroidism.

Hearing

Universal newborn hearing screening uses otoacoustic emissions or automated auditory brainstem response (ABR). The program goals are often summarised as screen by 1 month, diagnose by 3 months, intervene by 6 months. An infant who does not pass the screen and the rescreen needs a diagnostic audiologic evaluation (including diagnostic ABR) before 3 months; waiting for speech delay forfeits the critical period for language. Infants who spent more than about 5 days in the NICU are screened with automated ABR, because otoacoustic emissions miss auditory neuropathy. Risk factors for late-onset or progressive loss (congenital CMV, family history of childhood hearing loss, bacterial meningitis, exchange transfusion, ototoxic drugs, ECMO) call for audiology follow-up even after a passed screen. Objective hearing screening is repeated at intervals through childhood and adolescence.

Critical congenital heart disease

Pulse oximetry screening is performed after 24 hours of age on the right hand (pre-ductal) and either foot (post-ductal). It aims at duct-dependent and cyanotic lesions that can look well at birth (hypoplastic left heart, pulmonary atresia, tetralogy of Fallot, transposition, total anomalous pulmonary venous return, truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia).

ResultAction
95% or more in the right hand or foot, and a hand–foot difference of 3 percentage points or lessPass
Below 90% in either siteFail: evaluate now (echocardiogram and a search for other causes of hypoxemia)
90–94% in both, or a difference above 3 pointsRepeat; if the repeat does not pass, the screen is failed

A failed screen is followed by a full examination and echocardiography; sepsis and pulmonary causes of hypoxemia are considered at the same time. A passed screen does not exclude all heart disease (coarctation in particular can be missed).

Other newborn and infant checks

  • Red reflex at every infant visit: a white or absent reflex (leukocoria) needs urgent ophthalmology for cataract or retinoblastoma.
  • Hips: Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres in early infancy and hip abduction thereafter until walking; infants with risk factors such as breech position late in pregnancy are imaged (ultrasound in early infancy).
  • Bilirubin risk assessment before newborn discharge, using hour-specific treatment thresholds.
  • Maternal depression screening at infant visits in the first 6 months.

Development and autism

Developmental surveillance happens at every visit. Formal standardised developmental screening is done at 9, 18 and 30 months, and autism-specific screening at 18 and 24 months, or whenever a parent or clinician is concerned. A positive screen leads to three things at once: referral for diagnostic evaluation, referral to early-intervention services (which do not require a diagnosis) and a formal hearing evaluation.

Vision

Amblyopia is treatable when found early. The USPSTF recommends vision screening at least once between 3 and 5 years. Instrument-based screening (photoscreening or autorefraction) can be used in young children; optotype visual acuity charts are used once a child can cooperate. A constant eye turn at any age, or an intermittent one after about 4 months, needs ophthalmology referral.

Laboratory screens in childhood

ScreenWhenNotes
Hemoglobin (anemia)At 12 months; risk assessment at other agesIron deficiency peaks in toddlers with high cow's milk intake
Blood leadRisk assessment at visits; blood test at 12 and 24 months for Medicaid-enrolled or at-risk childrenAn elevated capillary result is confirmed with a venous sample
Blood pressureYearly from age 3Earlier if risk factors such as prematurity or kidney disease
LipidsUniversal screen once at 9–11 years and once at 17–21 yearsA nonfasting non-HDL cholesterol (or lipid panel) is acceptable; earlier risk-based screening from age 2 for family history of early cardiovascular disease or familial hypercholesterolemia
BMI percentileYearly from age 2Overweight 85th to below 95th percentile; obesity 95th percentile or above

Oral health

Dental caries is the most common chronic disease of childhood. The USPSTF recommends that primary care clinicians apply fluoride varnish to the primary teeth of all infants and children from the time the first tooth erupts through age 5, and prescribe oral fluoride supplements from 6 months for children whose water supply is low in fluoride. Children should have a dental home by about age 1; parents are counselled to avoid bedtime bottles and to brush with a smear of fluoride toothpaste once teeth appear.

A newborn who "failed" the hearing screen and looks well is not reassured by a normal startle to loud noise or by the parents' impression. Only a diagnostic audiologic evaluation answers the question.

USPSTF: Prevention of dental caries in children younger than 5 years

sections.heading: Immunization principles, anticipatory guidance and growth faltering
sections.html:
This section covers the counselling and immunization tasks of the routine visit, plus the approach to a child whose weight gain has slowed. Exam questions focus on principles: when a vaccine must be withheld, when it must not be withheld, how to catch up a child who has fallen behind, and how to turn a growth chart into a diagnosis.

Immunization principles

The core childhood series (diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis; inactivated polio; Haemophilus influenzae type b; pneumococcal conjugate) is given in infancy with boosters, and measles-mumps-rubella and varicella are given from 12–15 months with a second dose at 4–6 years. Recommendations for several other vaccines have changed recently and the CDC and AAP schedules no longer match on every point, so check the current-year schedule in practice rather than relying on memory.

True contraindication or precautionNot a reason to delay (a false contraindication)
Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to a previous dose or to a vaccine componentMild illness such as a cold, otitis media or diarrhea, with or without low-grade fever
Live vaccines: severe immunodeficiency (for example SCID, chemotherapy, or high-dose corticosteroids, meaning at least 2 mg/kg/day or 20 mg/day of prednisone for 14 days or more) and pregnancyCurrent antibiotic treatment, or recovering from an illness
Pertussis-containing vaccine: encephalopathy within 7 days of a previous dose with no other causePrematurity (vaccinate by chronological age)
Rotavirus vaccine: history of intussusception, or SCIDBreastfeeding; a pregnant or immunocompromised person in the household
Moderate or severe acute illness (a precaution: defer until improved)Family history of a vaccine reaction or of sudden infant death; local redness after a prior dose
Recent blood products or immune globulin (delays response to MMR and varicella)Egg allergy

Practical rules: inactivated vaccines can be given together or at any interval; two live parenteral vaccines (MMR, varicella) are given on the same day or at least 28 days apart. After stopping high-dose steroids, wait at least 1 month before a live vaccine. Tuberculin skin testing is done on the same day as MMR or at least 4 weeks later, because measles vaccine can blunt the skin test.

Catch-up principles

  • Never restart a series because of a long gap; give the next dose and continue at minimum intervals.
  • Respect minimum ages and minimum intervals (a dose given up to 4 days early is counted).
  • Some vaccines have maximum ages: rotavirus is not started after 14 weeks 6 days of age and no dose is given after 8 months 0 days; H. influenzae type b and pneumococcal conjugate are generally not needed in healthy children from age 5.
  • Give every vaccine the child is eligible for at the visit; missed opportunities are the main cause of under-immunization.

Anticipatory guidance

TopicCore advice
Safe sleepBack to sleep for every sleep; firm, flat, separate surface (crib or bassinet) with a fitted sheet only; room-sharing without bed-sharing; no pillows, bumpers, blankets or soft toys; no inclined sleepers; smoke-free home; breastfeeding and an offered pacifier are protective; avoid overheating
Car seatsRear-facing seat for as long as possible, until the child reaches the seat's height or weight limit; then a forward-facing seat with harness; then a belt-positioning booster until the adult belt fits (about 4 ft 9 in, often 8–12 years); back seat until 13 years
WaterWithin-arm's-reach supervision; four-sided fencing with a self-latching gate around pools; swim lessons can start from about 1 year; drowning happens silently and quickly, including in bathtubs and buckets
FirearmsThe safest home has no firearm; otherwise store firearms unloaded and locked, with ammunition locked separately
Injury at homeWater heater at or below 120 °F (49 °C); stair gates; window guards; medicines and button batteries out of reach; Poison Control number; no whole grapes, nuts or hard candy for young children
ScreensAvoid digital media other than video-chatting before about 18–24 months; for ages 2–5, limit to about 1 hour a day of high-quality content watched with a parent; no screens at meals or before bed; a family media plan for older children

Childhood obesity

BMI is plotted from age 2. Obesity is a BMI at or above the 95th percentile for age and sex; severe obesity is at or above 120% of the 95th percentile. The USPSTF recommends screening from age 6 and offering or referring to comprehensive, intensive behavioural interventions (26 or more contact hours). The 2023 AAP guideline advises treating promptly rather than "watchful waiting": intensive health behaviour and lifestyle treatment for all, with pharmacotherapy offered to adolescents 12 years and older with obesity, and referral for metabolic and bariatric surgery evaluation for adolescents 13 and older with severe obesity. Children with obesity are screened for comorbidities (from about age 10: lipids, ALT and glucose or HbA1c), plus blood pressure, sleep-disordered breathing and mood.

Growth faltering

Growth faltering (failure to thrive) describes inadequate weight gain: for example weight or weight-for-length below the 2nd percentile, or weight crossing two major percentile lines downward. The pattern of the curves narrows the cause.

[[figure:s23a-fig82]]
  • Weight falls first, with length and head circumference preserved: inadequate intake, absorption or excess losses. Most cases in high-income settings are from inadequate intake (feeding technique, formula preparation errors, family stress, food insecurity, neglect).
  • Length falls first or with weight preserved: an endocrine cause (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency) or a skeletal dysplasia.
  • Weight, length and head circumference all small from early on: a prenatal or genetic cause (congenital infection, teratogen, chromosomal disorder).

The most useful evaluation is a detailed feeding and dietary history (what, how much, how prepared, who feeds), a psychosocial history, a careful examination and, where possible, observation of a feed. Broad laboratory testing without clues in the history or examination rarely finds the cause; a limited set (blood count, metabolic panel, urinalysis, and tests suggested by symptoms) is reasonable. Treatment is nutritional: more calories than the usual age requirement to allow catch-up growth, with close weight checks. Admission is reserved for severe malnutrition, failure of outpatient management, or safety concerns; in severe malnutrition, start refeeding cautiously and monitor phosphate, potassium and magnesium.

A child with a mild cold and a temperature of 38.0 °C who is on amoxicillin for otitis media is not "too sick" to vaccinate. Deferring creates a missed opportunity; reserve deferral for moderate or severe illness.

furtherReading.label: USPSTF: High BMI in children and adolescents

sections.heading: The adolescent preventive visit
sections.html:
The adolescent preventive visit is mostly conversation. The leading threats to adolescent health are behavioural: injury (motor vehicle crashes and, in the US, firearm injuries, which are now the leading cause of death among children and adolescents), suicide, substance use, unintended pregnancy and sexually transmitted infection. The visit is built to find these risks confidentially.

The confidential interview

From early adolescence, spend part of every visit with the adolescent alone. At the start, tell the parent and the adolescent together that what the adolescent says will be kept confidential, with limits: information will be shared if there is a serious risk of harm to the adolescent or others, or if abuse is disclosed. Then ask open questions, moving from less to more sensitive topics:

  • home and relationships; school or work performance and plans;
  • activities, friends, social media and sleep; eating and body image;
  • tobacco, vaping, alcohol, cannabis and other drugs;
  • sexual orientation, gender identity, sexual activity and consent;
  • mood, self-harm and suicidal thoughts;
  • safety: seat belts, driving, weapons, bullying, dating violence.

Strengths are asked about too; they make the conversation two-sided and inform counselling.

Consent and confidentiality (general principles)

Minors generally need a parent's consent for care, with exceptions that vary by state. In general: emergency care proceeds without consent; emancipated minors (for example married, serving in the military, or living independently and self-supporting) consent for themselves; and minors can consent on their own to specific services, most consistently STI testing and treatment, and in most states contraception and prenatal care, with variable rules for substance use and mental health services. Confidentiality is broken when there is a serious risk of harm (suicidal or homicidal intent) or abuse, which must be reported. Insurance statements can disclose confidential services; clinicians should anticipate this.

Screening

TargetRecommendationNext step if positive
Major depressionScreen adolescents 12–18 years (USPSTF), for example with an adolescent PHQ formClinical interview to confirm the diagnosis and directly ask about suicidal thoughts, plans and means; safety plan; treatment and follow-up
AnxietyScreen children and adolescents 8–18 years (USPSTF)Diagnostic assessment
Substance useAsk every adolescent at preventive visits with a validated tool (for example CRAFFT)No use: praise; lower-risk use: brief advice; higher risk: brief intervention with motivational interviewing, follow-up, and referral when needed
Chlamydia and gonorrheaSexually active females under 25 years, yearly (USPSTF); for males, evidence for routine screening is insufficient except in higher-risk groups such as men who have sex with menTreat the patient and partners; test of reinfection about 3 months later
HIVAt least once from age 15 (USPSTF), and younger adolescents at increased riskConfirmatory testing; prompt treatment

For chlamydia and gonorrhea, a vaginal swab NAAT (self-collected is acceptable) is the preferred specimen in females; urine NAAT is acceptable. Cervical cancer screening does not start before age 21, whatever the age of sexual debut, and a pelvic examination is not required to screen for STIs or to start contraception.

Contraception

Long-acting reversible contraception (LARC), the etonogestrel implant and intrauterine devices, is recommended as first-line for adolescents who want contraception: it is the most effective reversible option because it does not depend on daily or monthly action, and it is safe in adolescents and in people who have never been pregnant. The implant is the most effective reversible method. Other methods (pills, patch, ring, injection) are offered according to preference. Every method is paired with counselling on condoms for STI prevention, and on emergency contraception. Depot medroxyprogesterone lowers bone mineral density while used, which is reversible and not a reason to deny it.

Immunizations at the adolescent visit

The 11–12-year visit is the platform for the adolescent vaccines: a tetanus-diphtheria-acellular pertussis booster (Tdap), human papillomavirus vaccine and meningococcal vaccines, plus seasonal influenza, given as the current CDC schedule specifies (dose numbers for some of these depend on age at the start of the series and on immune status). The same contraindication rules apply as in childhood: no live vaccine during pregnancy or significant immunosuppression.

Injury prevention

Counselling targets seat-belt use every trip; no phone use while driving; never driving after alcohol or drugs or riding with an impaired driver; graduated driver-licensing limits on night driving and teen passengers; helmets; safe firearm storage; and recognising dating violence and bullying, including online.

Eating-disorder red flags

Weight loss or failure to gain during growth, loss of periods, excessive exercise, bradycardia, orthostatic changes, hypothermia, and electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis suggests purging) are red flags. An adolescent with marked bradycardia, hypotension, syncope, significant electrolyte abnormality or arrhythmia needs inpatient medical stabilization.

Asking about suicide does not plant the idea. When a depression screen is positive, the next step is to ask directly about suicidal thoughts and plans, not to start a medication or simply schedule follow-up.

furtherReading.label: USPSTF: Depression and suicide risk in children and adolescents

sections.heading: Disorders of pubertal timing and the pre-participation evaluation
sections.html:
Pubertal timing questions ask whether a child is outside the normal window, whether the cause is likely benign, and which single test separates the possibilities. Pre-participation sports evaluations ask which history or examination finding should stop clearance until a cardiac evaluation is done.

Precocious puberty

Puberty is precocious when secondary sexual characteristics begin before 8 years in girls or 9 years in boys. Progressive precocious puberty comes with accelerated growth velocity and an advanced bone age, and it threatens adult height because early estrogen exposure closes the growth plates early.

TypeMechanismMain causesHormone pattern
Central (gonadotropin-dependent)Early activation of the hypothalamic GnRH pulse generatorIdiopathic in most girls; in boys a CNS lesion is more often found (hypothalamic hamartoma, tumors, hydrocephalus, prior cranial irradiation)LH in the pubertal range (or rising after GnRH-agonist stimulation); sex steroid raised
Peripheral (gonadotropin-independent)Sex steroid made without GnRH driveCongenital adrenal hyperplasia, adrenal or gonadal tumors, McCune–Albright syndrome, familial male-limited precocious puberty, hCG-secreting tumors in boys, exposure to topical testosterone or estrogenLH suppressed; sex steroid raised

The examination of a boy's testes is a shortcut: bilateral enlargement points to gonadotropin action (central precocious puberty, or an activating LH-receptor mutation); a unilateral enlarged testis suggests a Leydig cell tumor; small prepubertal testes with virilization point to an adrenal source or exogenous androgen.

Evaluation: growth chart and growth velocity, bone-age radiograph of the left hand, a morning ultrasensitive LH (with FSH and estradiol or testosterone), and a GnRH or GnRH-agonist stimulation test when the basal value is not conclusive. Add 17-hydroxyprogesterone, DHEA-S, TSH or hCG according to the pattern. Once central precocious puberty is confirmed, brain MRI is obtained in all boys, and in girls with neurological signs or very early onset (younger ages carry a higher chance of a lesion).

Treatment of central precocious puberty is a long-acting GnRH agonist (depot leuprolide or triptorelin, or a histrelin implant): continuous stimulation downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors. Goals are preserving adult height and easing psychosocial burden; therapy is stopped at an age-appropriate time to let puberty resume. Peripheral causes are treated at their source.

Benign variants do not progress and do not advance bone age: premature thelarche (isolated breast tissue, most often in girls under 2) and premature adrenarche (body odour and pubic hair from adrenal androgens). They need a growth check and follow-up, not suppression therapy.

Delayed puberty

Puberty is delayed when there is no breast development by 13 years in a girl, or no testicular enlargement (volume 4 mL or more) by 14 years in a boy. Puberty that starts but stalls (for example no menarche by 15 or more than about 3 years after thelarche) is also evaluated.

CategoryExamplesLH/FSH
Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (most common, especially in boys)Family history of late puberty; short for age with normal growth velocity; delayed bone age; eventually normal pubertyLow (prepubertal) for age
Functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadismChronic illness (inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease), undernutrition, eating disorders, intense training, hypothyroidism, hyperprolactinemiaLow
Permanent hypogonadotropic hypogonadismIsolated GnRH deficiency (with anosmia: Kallmann syndrome), pituitary or hypothalamic tumors such as craniopharyngiomaLow
Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (primary gonadal failure)Turner syndrome in girls; Klinefelter syndrome in boys (puberty starts but testes stay small and firm); gonadal damage from chemotherapy or radiationHigh

Evaluation: review the growth chart and parents' pubertal timing; obtain a bone age; measure LH, FSH and estradiol or testosterone; screen for chronic disease (blood count, inflammatory markers, metabolic panel, celiac serology, TSH and free T4, prolactin). A high FSH means gonadal failure and calls for a karyotype. Low gonadotropins mean either constitutional delay or hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, which can be hard to distinguish at first; anosmia, midline defects or neurological signs favour a permanent cause and prompt MRI.

Management of constitutional delay is reassurance and follow-up of growth. A short course of low-dose testosterone (boys) or estradiol (girls) can be offered when the delay causes distress; it starts secondary sexual development without compromising adult height. Permanent hypogonadism needs long-term sex steroid replacement.

Short, healthy childGrowth velocityBone agePubertyAdult height
Familial (genetic) short statureNormal, tracking a low percentileMatches chronological ageOn timeShort, consistent with parents
Constitutional delayNormal after an early downward shiftDelayedLateWithin target range
Endocrine cause (hypothyroidism, GH deficiency)Low; weight relatively preservedDelayedOften lateReduced unless treated

Pre-participation sports evaluation

Its main safety goal is to identify adolescents at risk of sudden cardiac death during exertion, most often from inherited cardiomyopathies (such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), anomalous coronary arteries, channelopathies (long QT syndrome) and aortic disease (Marfan syndrome). The history carries most of the yield:

  • chest pain, fainting or near-fainting, unexplained shortness of breath or palpitations during exercise;
  • a prior murmur or high blood pressure;
  • a relative who died suddenly or unexpectedly before about age 50, or a family history of cardiomyopathy, long QT syndrome or Marfan syndrome.

On examination: blood pressure; femoral pulses (coarctation); Marfan features; and auscultation lying, standing and with Valsalva. A systolic murmur that gets louder with standing or Valsalva and softer with squatting suggests the dynamic outflow obstruction of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. A positive history or examination means no clearance until cardiac evaluation (ECG and echocardiography, with cardiology referral). Routine ECG screening of every athlete is not part of general US recommendations.

Other pre-participation issues include concussion history (return only after symptoms resolve, through a graduated return-to-play plan, never on the same day), a single paired organ (counselling about contact sports), sickle cell trait (hydration and gradual conditioning), relative energy deficiency in sport (low energy availability with menstrual disturbance and low bone density), and recent infectious mononucleosis (avoid contact sports while the spleen may be enlarged, at least the first 3 weeks).

In delayed puberty, a girl's short stature with high FSH is not "constitutional delay". Turner syndrome may present only with short stature and absent breast development; the karyotype makes the diagnosis.

title: Human development · Adulthood and aging: normal physiology
meta: Normal physiology from early adulthood through older age: bone, fitness, menopause, male reproductive aging, organ aging, drug handling and cognition.

sections.heading: Physiology across adulthood: bone, fitness, sleep, sexual response and grief
sections.html:
Adult physiology: peaks and slow declines

Most organ systems reach their highest functional capacity in the third decade and then decline slowly and in parallel. Exam questions in this area ask you to separate an expected, age-appropriate change from disease, and to explain the mechanism of the change. The key word is reserve: a healthy 55-year-old has normal resting values but less capacity to respond to stress than a 25-year-old.

Bone mass

Peak bone mass is reached by the late twenties to about age 30. Genetics account for most of the variation between individuals; the modifiable contributors are sex steroids during puberty, adequate calcium, vitamin D and protein intake, body weight and weight-bearing exercise. Anything that removes estrogen or adds catabolic stress in adolescence and young adulthood (hypothalamic amenorrhea, restrictive eating, delayed puberty, glucocorticoids, hyperthyroidism) lowers the peak, and a low peak is never fully recovered later. A woman's fracture risk in old age therefore reflects two quantities: the peak she reached and how fast she lost bone afterwards.

After the peak, both sexes lose bone slowly. Women have an additional phase of rapid, high-turnover loss that starts in the late menopausal transition and continues for several years after the final menstrual period, falling hardest on trabecular bone (vertebrae, distal radius).

Cardiorespiratory fitness

By the Fick principle, maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) equals maximal cardiac output multiplied by the maximal arteriovenous oxygen difference. VO2max falls steadily from early adulthood, faster in sedentary people. The largest single contributor is the fall in maximal heart rate, which reflects reduced sinoatrial responsiveness to catecholamines rather than any change in resting heart rate. Maximal stroke volume and peripheral oxygen extraction (capillary density, mitochondrial content) decline less and respond strongly to training. Endurance training at any age raises VO2max, but even lifelong athletes show the age-related fall in maximal heart rate.

Body composition and energy needs

From midlife, lean (fat-free) mass declines and fat mass rises, with a shift toward visceral fat. Basal metabolic rate falls mostly because there is less metabolically active muscle, so energy needs fall while protein, calcium and micronutrient needs do not: diet quality per calorie matters more with age. Visceral adiposity drives insulin resistance, a rise in triglycerides and a fall in HDL cholesterol, which is the physiologic background to the adult cardiometabolic screening covered in the Step 2 CK chapter.

Sleep

Adults need at least 7 hours of sleep a night. Normal sleep cycles about every 90 minutes through N1, N2, N3 and REM. Stage N2 occupies the largest share of the night; slow-wave sleep (N3) is concentrated in the first third and REM in the last third, with REM periods lengthening toward morning. Chronic short sleep is associated with weight gain, insulin resistance, hypertension, mood disorders and accidents. Shift work misaligns the circadian clock, which is entrained mainly by light acting on the suprachiasmatic nucleus.

Normal sexual response

The sexual response is described in four phases: excitement, plateau, orgasm and resolution. Each phase has a distinct autonomic or somatic driver, and drug or surgical injuries map onto these drivers.

EventMain efferent pathwayMechanismClinical correlate
Erection; clitoral engorgement and vaginal lubricationParasympathetic, pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4)Nitric oxide from nerves and endothelium activates guanylyl cyclase; cGMP relaxes cavernosal smooth muscle, sinusoids fill and compress outflow veinsPelvic nerve injury (radical prostatectomy, pelvic fracture) causes erectile dysfunction; PDE5 inhibitors slow cGMP breakdown
EmissionSympathetic, thoracolumbar outflow via hypogastric nervesα1-mediated contraction of vas deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate; internal urethral sphincter closesα1 blockers and retroperitoneal lymph node dissection reduce emission or cause retrograde ejaculation
Ejaculation and orgasmSomatic, pudendal nerveRhythmic contraction of bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosusSerotonergic antidepressants delay orgasm
ResolutionSympathetic tone returnsPhosphodiesterase degrades cGMP; detumescenceThe male refractory period lengthens with age

With age, men need more direct stimulation and longer to achieve erection, and women have less lubrication after menopause; desire and capacity for satisfying sexual activity persist well into older age. Erectile dysfunction in a middle-aged man is often the first sign of endothelial disease and should prompt cardiovascular risk assessment.

Grief

Normal grief after a death comes in waves of sadness and longing, with preoccupation with the deceased, sleep and appetite change, and sometimes brief experiences of hearing or seeing the person. Self-worth is preserved, and function gradually returns. Prolonged grief disorder is diagnosed in adults when intense yearning or preoccupation persists, most days, at least 12 months after the loss and impairs function. A major depressive episode can occur during bereavement and is suggested by pervasive worthlessness, psychomotor slowing, suicidal thinking or impairment out of proportion to the loss.

Brief perceptions of the dead person's voice or presence during early bereavement are not psychosis. Treating normal grief with antidepressants is not indicated; supportive follow-up is.

Step 2 CK turns these mechanisms into prevention: bone peak and loss underlie osteoporosis screening, visceral fat underlies diabetes and statin decisions, and erectile dysfunction is a cardiovascular risk marker.

sections.heading: Perimenopause, menopause and the aging male axis
sections.html:
The menopausal transition

A woman is born with a finite pool of primordial follicles that is depleted by atresia and ovulation. As the pool shrinks, fewer antral follicles are recruited each cycle, and the ovary's hormonal output changes in a predictable order. Menopause is defined retrospectively as 12 months without menses after the final menstrual period; the median age in the United States is about 51. Cessation of ovarian function before age 40 is primary ovarian insufficiency, a disease rather than normal aging.

Hormonal sequence

  1. Falling inhibin B and anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH). Both come from granulosa cells of small growing follicles, so both fall as the follicle pool shrinks. AMH is the best single serum marker of ovarian reserve.
  2. Rising FSH. Inhibin B selectively suppresses FSH. Its loss lets FSH rise early, first in the early follicular phase, while LH is still near normal. The FSH rise accelerates recruitment of the remaining follicles.
  3. Erratic estradiol. In the transition, estradiol can be normal, low or even high (multiple follicles stimulated by high FSH). Cycles become shorter and then irregular; anovulatory cycles lack a corpus luteum, so progesterone is absent, which explains heavy or irregular bleeding in the perimenopause.
  4. Postmenopause. Estradiol is low, FSH and LH are both high (FSH more than LH, because FSH has also lost inhibin feedback), and the main circulating estrogen is estrone, made by aromatization of androstenedione in adipose stromal cells. The androstenedione comes from the adrenal cortex and the ovarian stroma, which keeps making androgens. Women with more adipose tissue have higher estrone levels.
[[figure:s23a-fig90]]

A serum FSH level is not needed to diagnose menopause in a woman over 45 with typical symptoms and amenorrhea, and a single FSH value in the transition is unreliable because levels swing from cycle to cycle.

Vasomotor symptoms

Hot flashes and night sweats affect most women in the transition and can persist for years. Estrogen withdrawal releases a group of arcuate nucleus neurons that co-express kisspeptin, neurokinin B and dynorphin. Their neurokinin B output, acting on neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptors in the preoptic thermoregulatory area, narrows the thermoneutral zone, so a small rise in core temperature triggers peripheral vasodilation, flushing and sweating. Pharmacology follows the mechanism:

  • Estrogen (with a progestogen if the uterus is present, to prevent endometrial hyperplasia) is the most effective treatment.
  • NK3 receptor antagonists (fezolinetant) act directly on the thermoregulatory pathway without hormonal effects; liver enzymes need monitoring.
  • Low-dose SSRIs or SNRIs and gabapentin are nonhormonal alternatives.

Bone

Estrogen restrains bone resorption. It reduces RANKL expression by osteoblast-lineage cells and T cells, increases osteoprotegerin (the decoy receptor that binds RANKL), and promotes osteoclast apoptosis. Estrogen deficiency therefore causes high-turnover bone loss: resorption outpaces formation, and trabecular bone is lost fastest. Serum calcium, phosphate, PTH and alkaline phosphatase stay normal, which separates postmenopausal osteoporosis from metabolic bone diseases.

Genitourinary syndrome of menopause

The vaginal epithelium is estrogen-dependent. Without estrogen it thins and stores less glycogen; lactobacilli, which ferment glycogen to lactic acid, decline, and vaginal pH rises above about 5. Findings are dryness, dyspareunia, pale thin mucosa with loss of rugae, urinary urgency and recurrent urinary infections, and parabasal cells on wet mount. Low-dose vaginal estrogen treats it with minimal systemic absorption.

Cardiometabolic and other changes

LDL cholesterol rises across the transition, fat redistributes toward the abdomen, and cardiovascular risk climbs toward that of men. Sleep disruption, mood symptoms and skin collagen loss are also common.

The aging male reproductive axis

Men have no equivalent of menopause. Total testosterone falls gradually from middle age, and sex hormone–binding globulin (SHBG) rises, so free testosterone falls more than total. Leydig and Sertoli cell function decline slowly; spermatogenesis continues into old age, although semen volume and motility fall and new mutations accumulate in sperm (advanced paternal age raises the risk of some autosomal dominant conditions such as achondroplasia). Obesity lowers SHBG and total testosterone. "Late-onset hypogonadism" is diagnosed only when consistent symptoms accompany unequivocally low morning testosterone on at least two occasions.

FeatureFemale menopauseMale aging
OnsetRelatively abrupt, median about 51Gradual, over decades
GametesOocyte pool exhaustedSpermatogenesis continues
Sex steroidEstradiol falls to low levelsTestosterone declines modestly; free fraction falls more
GonadotropinsFSH and LH markedly elevatedNormal or mildly elevated
FertilityEndsReduced but preserved

In the early transition, a woman with regular-but-shortening cycles can have a normal estradiol and a modestly raised early-follicular FSH. A "normal estrogen" does not exclude the perimenopause, and contraception is still needed until menopause is confirmed.

Postmenopausal women with obesity make more estrone, which helps protect bone but increases endometrial stimulation; unopposed estrogen from any source raises endometrial hyperplasia risk.
