sections.heading: Physiology of aging by organ system
sections.html:
Aging as loss of reserve

Normal aging rarely changes resting laboratory values or vital signs, but it narrows the margin between baseline and failure, a concept often called homeostenosis. A healthy 80-year-old has a normal serum sodium, creatinine and resting cardiac output, yet becomes hypernatremic in a heat wave, toxic on a usual drug dose, or hypotensive when standing after a meal. Exam items test whether you can name the age-related change behind such a presentation and resist labelling an expected change as disease.

Cardiovascular

  • Arterial stiffening from elastin fragmentation and collagen cross-linking raises systolic pressure and widens pulse pressure; isolated systolic hypertension is the typical pattern. Reflected pressure waves return earlier and add to late systolic load.
  • The left ventricle thickens and relaxes more slowly, so early diastolic filling falls and the atrial contribution becomes important; an S4 can be heard and loss of atrial kick in atrial fibrillation is poorly tolerated.
  • β-adrenergic responsiveness falls, so maximal heart rate and contractile reserve decline even though circulating norepinephrine is higher. Resting cardiac output is roughly preserved in healthy people.
  • Baroreflex sensitivity declines. Standing, diuretics, vasodilators or a large meal produce less reflex tachycardia, which underlies orthostatic and postprandial hypotension and many falls.

Respiratory

Lung elastic recoil falls and the chest wall stiffens. Airways close earlier in expiration, so residual volume and functional residual capacity rise while vital capacity falls; total lung capacity is about unchanged. FEV1 and FVC decline and the ratio drifts slightly downward. Ventilation–perfusion mismatch widens the alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient, so resting PaO2 is a little lower. Cough strength, mucociliary clearance and ventilatory responses to hypoxia and hypercapnia are blunted, which helps explain aspiration and pneumonia risk.

Renal, water and electrolytes

  • Nephron number and renal blood flow fall, and GFR declines on average from middle age. Because creatinine production falls with muscle mass, serum creatinine can stay "normal" while GFR is markedly reduced. Drug dosing needs an estimated GFR or creatinine clearance that accounts for age and weight.
  • Concentrating and diluting capacity both decline. Combined with a reduced thirst response to hyperosmolality and lower total body water, this predisposes to hypernatremia during illness or heat; impaired free-water excretion predisposes to hyponatremia with thiazides or SSRIs.
  • Renin and aldosterone are lower, raising hyperkalemia risk with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics and NSAIDs.

Body composition

Between young adulthood and old age, fat rises as a share of body weight while total body water and lean mass fall. These shifts change drug distribution (next section).

[[figure:s23a-fig91]]

Musculoskeletal

Sarcopenia is the age-related loss of muscle mass, strength and function. Motor units are lost, and type II (fast-twitch) fibers atrophy preferentially, so power and the ability to recover from a stumble decline faster than endurance. Inactivity, low protein intake, inflammation and falling anabolic hormones accelerate it; progressive resistance training reverses much of it at any age. Bone loss continues in both sexes.

Nervous system and special senses

  • Presbyopia: the lens loses elasticity, so accommodation fails and near vision blurs from the mid-40s; distance vision is unaffected. Cataract, reduced dark adaptation and glare sensitivity follow.
  • Presbycusis: bilateral, symmetric, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss from loss of hair cells at the base of the cochlea (and strial and neural changes). Consonant sounds are lost first, so speech in noisy rooms is hardest to follow.
  • Smell and taste decline; vibration sense and proprioception in the feet decline; reaction time slows.

Sleep

Older adults spend less time in slow-wave (N3) sleep, wake more often, have lower sleep efficiency, and shift their circadian phase earlier (sleepy in the early evening, awake before dawn). REM sleep is relatively preserved. These changes are normal unless daytime function suffers.

Immune system

Immunosenescence begins with thymic involution, which reduces output of naive T cells; the T-cell repertoire narrows toward expanded memory clones. Antibody responses to new antigens and vaccines are weaker, and varicella-zoster virus–specific cell-mediated immunity wanes, which is why zoster incidence rises with age. Low-grade chronic inflammation ("inflammaging") coexists. Fever and leukocytosis may be blunted, so infection can present as delirium, falls or functional decline.

Gastrointestinal, hepatic and endocrine

Liver mass and hepatic blood flow fall, reducing phase I (cytochrome P450 oxidative) metabolism. Atrophic gastritis reduces acid and intrinsic factor, predisposing to vitamin B12 deficiency. Colonic transit slows. Insulin sensitivity falls, skin makes less vitamin D, and thermoregulation is impaired in both directions.

SystemExpected changeClinical consequence
ArteriesStiffeningIsolated systolic hypertension, wide pulse pressure
BaroreflexBluntedOrthostatic and postprandial hypotension
LungLower elastic recoilHigher residual volume; slightly lower PaO2
KidneyLower GFR, normal creatinineDrug accumulation; dose by estimated clearance
ThirstReducedHypernatremia with illness or heat
MuscleSarcopenia, type II fiber lossWeakness, falls
CochleaBasal hair cell lossHigh-frequency hearing loss
ThymusInvolutionWeaker vaccine responses, zoster

A "normal" creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL in a frail 85-year-old woman weighing 45 kg corresponds to a markedly reduced creatinine clearance. Always estimate clearance before dosing renally excreted drugs.

sections.heading: Drug handling in older adults and normal cognitive aging
sections.html:
Pharmacokinetics in older adults

Drug-related harm is one of the most preventable problems in older adults. Each pharmacokinetic step changes with age, and the changes are predictable from physiology.

Absorption

Absorption is largely preserved. Reduced gastric acid lowers absorption of a few drugs and nutrients that need acid (vitamin B12 from food, calcium carbonate, some azole antifungals), and slower transit can delay the onset of effect.

Distribution

With more fat and less water and lean mass:

  • Water-soluble drugs (lithium, digoxin, ethanol, aminoglycosides) distribute into a smaller volume, so the same dose gives a higher plasma concentration.
  • Lipid-soluble drugs (diazepam and other long-acting benzodiazepines, many anesthetics) distribute into a larger volume. Because half-life is proportional to volume of distribution divided by clearance (t½ = 0.693 × Vd/CL), a larger Vd prolongs half-life and the drug accumulates with repeated doses.
  • Serum albumin is often modestly lower, especially with illness, raising the free fraction of highly bound acidic drugs (phenytoin, warfarin). Total drug levels can then underestimate the active concentration.

Metabolism

Smaller liver mass and reduced hepatic blood flow lower phase I (oxidation, reduction, hydroxylation by cytochrome P450 enzymes) capacity. Phase II conjugation, especially glucuronidation, is relatively preserved. This is why, when a benzodiazepine is truly needed in an older adult, agents cleared by direct glucuronidation without active metabolites (lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam) are preferred over agents with oxidative metabolism and long-lived active metabolites (diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, flurazepam).

Excretion

GFR and tubular secretion decline, so renally excreted drugs (gabapentin, pregabalin, many antibiotics, direct oral anticoagulants, digoxin, lithium, metformin, low-molecular-weight heparin) accumulate unless dosed to estimated clearance. Because muscle mass is low, serum creatinine overestimates kidney function; clearance estimates that include age and weight (such as the Cockcroft–Gault equation) are used for many dosing tables.

StepAge-related changeExample effect
Distribution, hydrophilicSmaller VdHigher lithium and digoxin levels per dose; ethanol more intoxicating
Distribution, lipophilicLarger VdDiazepam half-life prolonged, sedation lasts days
Protein bindingLower albuminHigher free phenytoin with "therapeutic" total level
Hepatic phase IReducedSlower oxidation of many drugs
Hepatic phase IIRelatively preservedLorazepam clearance little changed
RenalLower clearanceGabapentin sedation, DOAC bleeding, digoxin toxicity

Pharmacodynamics

Older adults are more sensitive to the central effects of benzodiazepines, opioids, sedative hypnotics and anticholinergic drugs because neuronal and especially cholinergic reserve is reduced. Muscarinic blockade causes confusion, dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention and blurred vision; cumulative "anticholinergic burden" from several modest agents adds up. Responses to β-agonists and β-blockers are blunted, and impaired baroreflexes turn α-blockers, nitrates, diuretics and antihypertensives into causes of orthostatic hypotension. The practical rule is to start with a low dose, increase slowly, and review every drug for an ongoing indication.

Normal cognitive aging

Some cognitive change is normal. Processing speed and reaction time slow; working memory, divided attention and the speed of learning new information decline; and word or name retrieval becomes effortful ("tip-of-the-tongue"), with the item recalled later or with a cue. Vocabulary, general knowledge and other crystallized abilities are maintained or improve. Crucially, normal aging does not impair independence in daily activities.

Structural correlates include modest loss of brain volume, ventricular enlargement and white matter changes, without the spreading neurofibrillary tangle and amyloid plaque burden that defines Alzheimer disease.

FeatureNormal agingMild neurocognitive disorderMajor neurocognitive disorder (dementia)Delirium
OnsetGradual, lifelongInsidiousInsidious (most types)Acute, hours to days
Objective testingWithin age normsBelow age normsClearly impairedInattention, fluctuating
Daily functionIndependentIndependent, may need more effortImpaired independenceAcutely impaired
Typical complaintSlow name recall, later rememberedRepeating questions, missed appointmentsGetting lost, unable to manage finances or medicinesConfusion, altered arousal

A patient worried about memory who still manages money, medicines and driving, and scores within norms on testing, most likely has normal aging. Reassure and follow; do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor.

On Step 2 CK, these principles become deprescribing decisions: stopping strongly anticholinergic drugs, tapering benzodiazepines, and dosing by estimated clearance.

sections.heading: Adult screening from 18 to 64
sections.html:
Principles of adult screening

A screening test is worth offering when the condition is common or serious, has a detectable preclinical phase, and earlier treatment improves outcomes enough to outweigh harms such as false positives, overdiagnosis and procedural complications. US exam questions follow the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) grades: A or B means offer the service, C means offer selectively after individual discussion, D means do not offer, and I means the evidence is insufficient. Where the CDC recommends more broadly (hepatitis B and C), the more inclusive approach is acceptable.

[[figure:s23a-fig92]]

Cardiometabolic

  • Blood pressure: screen all adults 18 and older, yearly from 40 or with risk factors (elevated-normal pressure, obesity), and every 3–5 years for low-risk adults 18–39. Confirm an elevated office reading with ambulatory or home measurement before diagnosing hypertension.
  • Prediabetes and type 2 diabetes: screen adults 35–70 with overweight or obesity using fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c or an oral glucose tolerance test. Consider earlier screening with a family history, prior gestational diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome, or membership of a higher-risk group. Prediabetes (HbA1c 5.7–6.4%, fasting glucose 100–125 mg/dL) leads to referral to an intensive lifestyle program.
  • Lipids and statins: in adults 40–75 with at least one risk factor (dyslipidemia, diabetes, hypertension or smoking), estimate 10-year cardiovascular risk. Offer a statin when risk is 10% or higher; at 7.5% to under 10%, offer selectively after discussion. Moderate-intensity statin therapy is the usual starting point in primary prevention. Adults with LDL cholesterol of 190 mg/dL or more need statin therapy regardless of calculated risk.
  • Aspirin is no longer routine primary prevention: do not start it for this purpose at 60 or older; at 40–59 with 10% or higher risk it is an individual decision weighed against bleeding.

Cancer

CancerWhoHow and how often
Cervical21–65 with a cervix21–29: cytology every 3 years. 30–65: high-risk HPV testing every 5 years, co-testing every 5 years, or cytology every 3 years
BreastWomen 40–74Mammography every 2 years
Colorectal45–75Annual FIT, stool DNA-FIT every 1–3 years, CT colonography or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, or colonoscopy every 10 years; any positive non-colonoscopy test needs colonoscopy
Lung50–80 with at least 20 pack-years who smoke or quit within 15 yearsAnnual low-dose CT
ProstateMen 55–69PSA only after shared decision-making; not recommended at 70 or older

Do not screen for cervical cancer before 21, and stop after total hysterectomy (cervix removed) for a benign indication when there is no history of high-grade precancer. Screening for ovarian, pancreatic, thyroid and testicular cancer in average-risk adults is not recommended.

BRCA-related risk: women with a personal or family history of breast, ovarian, tubal or peritoneal cancer, or an ancestry associated with BRCA1/2 founder variants, should have a brief familial risk assessment with a validated tool. A positive result leads to genetic counseling, then testing if indicated. Women without such a history should not be routinely assessed or tested.

Infections

  • HIV: screen everyone 15–65 at least once, plus younger or older people at increased risk and all pregnant patients.
  • Hepatitis C: one-time antibody screening for adults (USPSTF ages 18–79; CDC all adults 18 and older), repeated for ongoing risk such as injection drug use, and in each pregnancy. Positive antibody is followed by HCV RNA.
  • Hepatitis B: the CDC recommends that all adults 18 and older be screened at least once with a triple panel (HBsAg, anti-HBs and total anti-HBc), which identifies current infection, past infection and vaccine immunity in one draw. Risk-based screening (birth in a region of 2% or higher prevalence, injection drug use, men who have sex with men, HIV, household contacts) is the minimum.
  • Chlamydia and gonorrhea: sexually active women 24 and younger, and older women at increased risk. Syphilis and latent tuberculosis: adults at increased risk.

Mental health and substance use

  • Screen all adults for depression, and adults 64 and younger for anxiety, with systems in place for diagnosis and follow-up. A positive two-item screen is followed by a full diagnostic assessment (for example the nine-item questionnaire plus a clinical interview).
  • Screen adults for unhealthy alcohol use with a brief validated tool and give brief behavioral counseling to those who drink above low-risk limits.
  • Ask about drug use when accurate diagnosis and treatment can be offered, and ask every adult about tobacco.
  • Screen women of reproductive age for intimate partner violence and connect those who disclose it with ongoing support services.

"Annual physical" items often tempt you with tests that have no screening role in asymptomatic adults: resting ECG, chest radiograph, TSH, vitamin D, urinalysis, CA-125. Pick the test the patient's age, sex and risk profile actually call for.

Read the stem for the trigger that makes a screen indicated: overweight plus age 35 (glucose), age 40 plus a risk factor (statin decision), a cervix and age (cervical), smoking history with the dates (lung), relatives with breast or ovarian cancer (BRCA risk tool).

sections.heading: Counselling, chemoprevention and immunizations in adults
sections.html:
Counselling that changes outcomes

Tobacco

Ask every adult about tobacco use, advise users to quit, and offer both behavioral support and FDA-approved pharmacotherapy to nonpregnant adults; the combination works better than either alone.

DrugMechanismKey adverse effects and cautions
VareniclinePartial agonist at α4β2 nicotinic receptors: relieves craving and blunts reward from smokingNausea, vivid dreams; renal dose adjustment; the most effective single agent
Nicotine replacementReplaces nicotine without combustion productsCombine a long-acting patch with a short-acting form (gum, lozenge, inhaler); local irritation, insomnia with overnight patch
BupropionNorepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibitorLowers the seizure threshold: avoid with seizure disorder, bulimia or anorexia, or abrupt alcohol or sedative withdrawal; insomnia

Evidence is insufficient to recommend electronic cigarettes for cessation. In pregnancy, behavioral interventions are recommended; evidence on pharmacotherapy is insufficient.

Alcohol

A single question about heavy-drinking days or a three-item tool identifies unhealthy use. Low-risk limits commonly used in the United States are no more than 3 drinks on any day and 7 per week for women, and no more than 4 per day and 14 per week for men. Unhealthy use without features of alcohol use disorder calls for brief counselling (feedback, advice, goal setting, follow-up). Alcohol use disorder is treated with counselling plus medication such as naltrexone or acamprosate.

Physical activity, diet and weight

  • Adults should aim for 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity (or 75–150 minutes of vigorous) aerobic activity each week, plus muscle-strengthening activity on at least 2 days.
  • Adults with cardiovascular risk factors benefit from behavioral counselling on a healthy diet and activity.
  • Adults with a BMI of 30 or more should be offered or referred to an intensive, multicomponent behavioral intervention (many sessions over a year covering diet, activity, self-monitoring and problem solving). Anti-obesity medication is added for BMI 30 or more, or 27 or more with a weight-related condition, when lifestyle measures are insufficient. Metabolic and bariatric surgery is considered at higher BMI thresholds, particularly with obesity-related disease.

Folic acid

Everyone who could become pregnant should take 0.4–0.8 mg of folic acid daily, starting at least 1 month before conception and continuing through early pregnancy, because the neural tube closes by about 4 weeks after conception, often before pregnancy is recognized. After a pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect, a higher dose of 4 mg daily is recommended before and in early pregnancy.

Intimate partner violence

Ask privately, without the partner present. When a patient discloses abuse, assess immediate safety, document, offer a safety plan and referral to advocacy and support services, and respect the decisions of a competent adult; reporting to police without consent is generally not required for adult victims, apart from specific injuries some states mandate.

Adult immunizations (ages 19–64)

VaccineRoutine adult useNotes
Influenza (inactivated or recombinant)Every yearLive intranasal vaccine is an option only for healthy nonpregnant people up to 49
Tdap / TdOne Tdap if never received, then Td or Tdap every 10 yearsTdap in every pregnancy at 27–36 weeks
MMRAdults born in 1957 or later without evidence of immunity: at least 1 dose2 doses for health-care workers, students and international travellers; live vaccine
Varicella2 doses 4–8 weeks apart without evidence of immunityLive vaccine
HPVThrough age 26 (catch-up)27–45: shared clinical decision-making; 3 doses if started at 15 or older; no testing needed beforehand
Hepatitis BAll adults 19–5960 and older with risk factors, or on request
PneumococcalAll adults 50 and older; 19–49 with risk conditionsOne dose of PCV20 or PCV21, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23
Recombinant zosterAll adults 50 and older, 2 doses 2–6 months apartAlso adults 19 and older who are immunocompromised

Wound tetanus prophylaxis

For a patient with 3 or more documented prior tetanus doses, a clean minor wound needs a booster only if the last dose was 10 or more years ago; a contaminated or major wound needs a booster if the last dose was 5 or more years ago. Tetanus immune globulin is added only when the primary series is incomplete or unknown and the wound is not clean and minor.

Special situations

  • Pregnancy: Tdap each pregnancy, inactivated influenza in season, and seasonal RSV vaccine at 32–36 weeks (or infant nirsevimab instead). Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) are contraindicated; HPV is deferred until after delivery. A nonimmune woman planning pregnancy receives MMR and should avoid conceiving for 4 weeks.
  • Asplenia or sickle cell disease: pneumococcal vaccine, MenACWY (2-dose primary series, boosters every 5 years), MenB, and one dose of Hib. Give at least 2 weeks before elective splenectomy, or about 2 weeks after an emergency splenectomy.
  • HIV: inactivated vaccines as for other adults (HPV through 26, hepatitis B, pneumococcal, MenACWY); avoid MMR and varicella if the CD4 count is below 200/mm3.
  • Health-care personnel: hepatitis B with anti-HBs testing 1–2 months after the final dose, 2 doses of MMR and of varicella (or proof of immunity), annual influenza, and Tdap; baseline tuberculosis screening.
  • Travel: hepatitis A and typhoid for many destinations, yellow fever (live) for some, rabies pre-exposure for long stays in remote areas or animal work, and malaria chemoprophylaxis matched to region.

Prior sexual activity or a previous abnormal Pap test is not a reason to withhold HPV vaccine in someone 26 or younger, and HPV testing before vaccination is not recommended.

sections.heading: Comprehensive geriatric assessment, falls and medication safety
sections.html:
Comprehensive geriatric assessment

A comprehensive geriatric assessment is a structured, usually interprofessional evaluation of an older adult's medical, functional, cognitive, psychological and social status, leading to a coordinated plan. It reduces hospital readmission and institutional placement in frail patients. Its domains are:

  • Function: basic activities of daily living (bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, feeding) and instrumental activities (managing medicines, finances, telephone, shopping, meals, housework, transport). Instrumental activities are lost first in early cognitive decline.
  • Mobility and falls: falls history, gait speed, the Timed Up and Go test.
  • Cognition and mood: a brief cognitive tool when there is concern, and a depression screen.
  • Nutrition: weight trend, appetite, dentition, swallowing.
  • Sensory function: hearing and vision.
  • Continence.
  • Medications: a full list including over-the-counter and herbal products.
  • Social and environment: living situation, caregiver strain, finances, home safety, signs of neglect or abuse.
  • Goals of care and advance directives.

Falls

Falls are the leading cause of injury and injury-related death in adults 65 and older. Ask at least yearly whether the person has fallen, feels unsteady, or worries about falling. A positive answer, or a fall with injury, leads to a multifactorial assessment:

  1. History of the fall: activity, prodrome, loss of consciousness (syncope needs its own work-up), injury, ability to get up.
  2. Medication review for fall-risk drugs.
  3. Gait, strength and balance: a Timed Up and Go of 12 seconds or longer suggests increased risk; chair-stand and balance tests add detail.
  4. Orthostatic blood pressure and heart rate.
  5. Vision, feet and footwear, cognition, continence, and home hazards.

Interventions

  • Exercise that trains balance, gait and strength (supervised physical therapy, group programs, tai chi) has the strongest evidence for preventing falls in community-dwelling older adults at increased risk.
  • Reduce or stop fall-risk medications, treat orthostatic hypotension, and correct vision (first-eye cataract surgery reduces falls).
  • Home safety modification by an occupational therapist for those at high risk.
  • Assess bone health after any fall-related fracture.
  • Vitamin D is replaced when a deficiency is found; routine vitamin D supplementation to prevent falls in community-dwelling older adults who are not deficient is not recommended.

Polypharmacy and potentially inappropriate medicines

Polypharmacy (commonly defined as five or more regular medicines) raises the risk of adverse drug events, interactions, nonadherence, falls and hospitalization. A prescribing cascade occurs when an adverse effect is misread as a new condition and treated with another drug: calcium channel blocker edema treated with a diuretic, cholinesterase inhibitor urinary urgency treated with an antimuscarinic, or metoclopramide parkinsonism treated with levodopa.

Drug groupMain harm in older adultsSafer approach
Strongly anticholinergic drugs (first-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine, bladder antimuscarinics such as oxybutynin, tertiary-amine tricyclics)Confusion, delirium, constipation, urinary retention, fallsStop or substitute (for overactive bladder, behavioral therapy and a β3 agonist)
Benzodiazepines and "Z-drug" hypnoticsFalls, hip fracture, cognitive impairment, crashesGradual taper; cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia
Long-acting sulfonylureas (glyburide)Prolonged hypoglycemiaStop when glucose is overcontrolled; choose agents with low hypoglycemia risk
Antipsychotics for behavioral symptoms of dementiaStroke, death, fallsNondrug measures first; lowest dose for shortest time only for dangerous symptoms
Chronic NSAIDsGI bleeding, kidney injury, heart failureAcetaminophen, topical NSAIDs
Long-term PPIs without an indicationC. difficile infection, fractures, B12 deficiencyTaper and stop if no ongoing indication
Skeletal muscle relaxantsSedation, anticholinergic effectsAvoid

Deprescribing

Deprescribing is the planned, supervised reduction or withdrawal of medicines whose harms outweigh their benefits for that person. Steps: list every medicine and its indication; weigh benefit against harm in light of life expectancy, time to benefit, and the patient's goals; prioritize the most harmful or least useful drug; stop or taper one drug at a time; and monitor for withdrawal or return of symptoms. Drugs that need tapering include benzodiazepines (for example reducing the dose by a fraction every 2–4 weeks), β-blockers, antidepressants and PPIs.

In frail older adults with diabetes, glycemic targets are relaxed (often HbA1c below 8.0%, and in very poor health, avoiding hypoglycemia and symptomatic hyperglycemia matters more than any number). An HbA1c in the low-6% range on a sulfonylurea or insulin in such a patient signals overtreatment.

New confusion, constipation or urinary retention in an older adult on a recently started anticholinergic drug is an adverse drug effect until proven otherwise. The next step is to stop the drug, not to start a dementia medication.

sections.heading: Screening, immunization and stopping rules after 65
sections.html:
Screening after 65

Screening decisions in older adults hinge on two questions: does the patient meet the age and risk criteria, and is life expectancy long enough to gain from finding disease early? Most cancer screening benefits appear only after about 10 years, so screening is individualized or stopped when life expectancy is shorter or comorbidity would preclude treatment.

Osteoporosis

Screen all women 65 and older with bone mineral density testing by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) of the hip and lumbar spine. Postmenopausal women younger than 65 are screened when a clinical risk tool shows increased risk (low body weight, parental hip fracture, smoking, alcohol excess, glucocorticoid use, rheumatoid arthritis). Evidence is insufficient for routine screening of men. Treatment is indicated for a T-score of −2.5 or lower, a hip or vertebral fragility fracture, or osteopenia with a high calculated 10-year fracture probability.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm

Men 65–75 who have ever smoked (100 or more cigarettes in a lifetime) should have a one-time abdominal ultrasound. In men who have never smoked, screening is offered selectively (for example with a first-degree relative with an aneurysm). Women who have never smoked should not be screened; for women who have smoked, the evidence is insufficient. A normal aortic diameter (under 3.0 cm) on screening needs no repeat study. Aneurysms are followed with ultrasound at intervals that shorten with size, and repair is considered at 5.5 cm or larger in men, with rapid growth, or with symptoms.

When to stop cancer screening

CancerOlder-adult rule
ColorectalRoutine through 75; 76–85 individualized by health, prior screening and preference (most benefit for those never screened); not recommended over 85
CervicalStop after 65 if prior screening was adequate (3 consecutive negative cytology results, or 2 consecutive negative HPV or co-tests, within 10 years, the most recent within 5 years) and there is no history of high-grade precancer; women without adequate prior screening should still be screened
BreastBiennial mammography through 74; evidence insufficient at 75 and older, so decide individually
LungAnnual low-dose CT through 80 if criteria are met; stop once 15 years since quitting or if health would not allow curative treatment
ProstatePSA screening not recommended at 70 and older

Hearing, vision and cognition

Evidence is insufficient for routine screening of asymptomatic older adults for hearing loss, impaired visual acuity or cognitive impairment, but symptoms and family concerns must be evaluated. Hearing concerns go to audiometry; hearing aids improve communication and quality of life, and untreated loss is associated with isolation and cognitive decline. Vision concerns go to eye examination (cataract, macular degeneration, glaucoma; yearly retinal examination for people with diabetes).

When the patient or family reports cognitive decline, evaluate with: history from the patient and an informant, functional status (especially instrumental activities), a brief cognitive test, a depression screen, a medication review for sedating and anticholinergic drugs, laboratory tests for reversible contributors (vitamin B12 and TSH, with metabolic panel and blood count; syphilis or HIV testing by risk), and structural brain imaging (CT or MRI) in the diagnostic work-up. Amyloid PET, cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers and APOE genotyping are not first-line tests.

Immunizations at 65 and older

  • Influenza every year; for 65 and older, a high-dose inactivated, recombinant, or adjuvanted inactivated vaccine is preferred because immunosenescence blunts the response to standard-dose vaccine. If none is available, any age-appropriate inactivated vaccine is given rather than delaying. Live intranasal vaccine is not used at this age.
  • Pneumococcal: if no prior conjugate vaccine, one dose of PCV20 or PCV21 completes the series; alternatively PCV15 followed by PPSV23 at least 1 year later. Someone who received only PPSV23 gets a conjugate vaccine at least 1 year later.
  • RSV: a single dose for all adults 75 and older, and for adults 60–74 at increased risk (chronic heart or lung disease, diabetes with complications, chronic kidney disease, immunocompromise, nursing-home residence, frailty). It is not an annual vaccine.
  • Recombinant zoster vaccine: 2 doses 2–6 months apart, given regardless of a prior episode of shingles (once the rash has resolved) or prior receipt of the old live zoster vaccine.
  • Td or Tdap every 10 years; hepatitis B for those with risk factors.

"Too old to screen" is a trap in both directions: a healthy 66-year-old woman with no record of cervical screening still needs it, while an 87-year-old with a normal colonoscopy at 77 needs no more colorectal screening.

A single normal aortic ultrasound at 65 settles AAA screening for life; it is not repeated.

sections.heading: Continence, frailty, nutrition, driving and advance care planning
sections.html:
Urinary incontinence

Incontinence is common but not a normal part of aging. First look for transient, reversible contributors: delirium, urinary infection, atrophic vaginitis, drugs (diuretics, sedatives, anticholinergics causing retention), high urine output (hyperglycemia, heart failure), restricted mobility and fecal impaction. Then classify the established type with history, examination, urinalysis and a post-void residual volume.

TypeMechanismClueFirst-line management
StressUrethral hypermobility or sphincter deficiencyLeak with cough, sneeze, liftingPelvic floor muscle training; pessary; midurethral sling if refractory
UrgeDetrusor overactivitySudden urge, frequency, nocturiaBladder training with timed voiding and pelvic floor exercises; then a β3 agonist (preferred over antimuscarinics in older adults)
OverflowRetention from outlet obstruction (BPH) or detrusor underactivity (diabetic neuropathy, drugs)Dribbling, high post-void residualTreat the cause; stop offending drugs; catheterization
FunctionalCannot reach the toilet in time (mobility, cognition)Normal bladder functionPrompted voiding, mobility aids, environment

Frailty

Frailty is a state of reduced physiologic reserve that raises vulnerability to stressors. A widely used phenotype counts unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, weak grip strength, slow walking speed and low physical activity; three or more indicate frailty. Clinical frailty scales grade the person by function. Frailty predicts falls, delirium, hospitalization, surgical complications and death, and it should shape treatment intensity and goals. Interventions are progressive resistance and balance exercise, adequate protein and energy intake, deprescribing, and treatment of contributing illness.

Nutrition and unintentional weight loss

Unintentional loss of about 5% of body weight over 6–12 months is clinically significant and predicts mortality. Causes fall into a few groups:

  • Psychiatric and cognitive: depression (the most common reversible cause), dementia.
  • Medical: cancer, GI disease, hyperthyroidism, heart failure, COPD, uncontrolled diabetes.
  • Medications: drugs causing anorexia, nausea, dry mouth or altered taste (digoxin, cholinesterase inhibitors, metformin, many others).
  • Oral and swallowing: poor dentition, ill-fitting dentures, dysphagia.
  • Social: isolation, bereavement, poverty, inability to shop or cook.

Evaluation begins with history (diet, mood, cognition, social situation, medications), examination including the mouth, a validated nutrition screen, and basic tests (blood count, metabolic panel, TSH, and age-appropriate cancer screening), with further testing directed by findings. Management treats the cause, liberalizes restrictive diets (low-salt, diabetic or low-cholesterol diets add little in frail adults and reduce intake), adds oral nutritional supplements, assistance at meals and meal delivery. Older adults generally need at least as much protein per kilogram as younger adults, and more when ill. Appetite stimulants such as megestrol cause thrombosis and fluid retention and do not improve survival; mirtazapine is reasonable when depression coexists. Watch for vitamin B12 deficiency (atrophic gastritis, metformin, long-term acid suppression) and vitamin D deficiency (housebound, less skin synthesis).

Older drivers

No age by itself ends driving. Driving depends on vision, cognition (attention, executive and visuospatial function) and motor function (neck rotation, leg strength, reaction time), and on sedating drugs. Warning signs are new crashes or near-misses, getting lost on familiar routes, and family concern. Concern leads to a formal on-road assessment by a driving rehabilitation specialist. People with moderate or severe dementia should not drive. Reporting requirements differ by state.

Advance care planning

Advance care planning is an ongoing conversation about the person's values, goals and preferences for future care, started while the person has decision-making capacity and revisited when health changes. Its products are:

  • A designated health care proxy (durable power of attorney for health care), who speaks for the patient if the patient loses capacity, using substituted judgment.
  • A written advance directive (living will) describing treatments wanted or refused in defined situations.
  • For seriously ill or frail people, portable medical orders (such as a POLST form) that translate preferences into actionable orders across settings.

Without a proxy, state law sets a surrogate hierarchy, usually spouse, then adult children, then parents and siblings. Resuscitation status follows the patient's informed choice; it is not decided by age.

The best time to raise advance care planning is a stable outpatient visit, not the emergency department. Asking "Who would you want to make decisions for you if you could not?" is a practical first step.

An older adult with new urge incontinence and dementia should not be started on oxybutynin by reflex; behavioral therapy comes first, and antimuscarinics worsen cognition.
